text_en:
Ieji River. It is a small station located in Nakatosa-cho, Kochi Prefecture, where the Dosan Line trains run deep into the mountain gorge. Since its opening in 1933, it has seen off countless travelers surrounded by the clear waters of the Ieji River, a tributary of the Shimanto River, and deep greenery. There was a time when it was a key hub for lumber transportation and played an important role in supporting people's lives.

The station is now unmanned, and when you get off to the platform, all you can hear is the murmuring of the river and the voices of birds. However, it is this quietness that gives us a deep feeling of traveling away from the hustle and bustle of modern society. In autumn, the autumn leaves of the Iejigawa Valley weave a brocade pattern, highlighting the station's charm as an unexplored region. The sound of an express train passing in the distance gently tells us about the passage of time in this place. Unlike Nakatosa Town's rich seafood, such as pole-and-line caught bonito, the rustic atmosphere of the mountain village is certainly alive and well here.

Uchii River. It is a very quiet station located in Shimanto Town, Kochi Prefecture, on the banks of the Uchiigawa River, a tributary of the Shimanto River. The sight of Yodo Line trains threading their way through this deep green mountain range, making a thudding sound, truly gives you a sense of the original landscape of Japan. I hear that there was once a time when the station was a hub for lumber transportation due to its rich forest resources, but now it's hard to find any trace of that, and it's a quiet, unmanned station. However, in recent years, Kaiyodo Hobby Museum Shimanto, located a little further away, has become more and more crowded, and even if you are not a long-time railway fan, you may be surprised by the changes. Coupled with the unexplored station boom, there are many people visiting in search of a new travel experience. A journey where you surrender to the slow flow of time in this place is sure to touch your heart.
product_ja:
四万十地栗（じぐり）のモンブラン
「しまんと地栗」は、通常の栗よりも大きく、糖度が高いことで知られる四万十の宝。山あいの急斜面で太陽を浴びて育った栗を贅沢に使ったモンブランは、一口食べた瞬間に栗本来の力強い香りが広がります。余計なものを加えず、素材の良さを引き出した上品な甘みは、まさに「大地の宝石」。秘境・打井川の静かな山並みを思い浮かべながら楽しみたい逸品です。
product_en:
Mont Blanc from Shimanto Jiguri
Shimanto chestnuts are the treasure of Shimanto and are known for being larger than regular chestnuts and having a high sugar content. Mont Blanc is made with generous amounts of chestnuts grown in the sun on the steep slopes of the mountains, and the moment you take a bite, the powerful aroma of chestnuts spreads out. The elegant sweetness that brings out the goodness of the ingredients without adding anything unnecessary is truly a ``gem of the earth.'' This is a masterpiece that you will want to enjoy while imagining the quiet mountain range of the unexplored Uchiigawa River.
product_fr:
Mont Blanc depuis Shimanto Jiguri
Les châtaignes Shimanto sont le trésor de Shimanto et sont connues pour être plus grosses que les châtaignes ordinaires et pour avoir une teneur élevée en sucre. Le Mont Blanc est composé de généreuses quantités de châtaignes cultivées au soleil sur les pentes abruptes des montagnes, et dès que vous en prenez une bouchée, l'arôme puissant des châtaignes se répand. La douceur élégante qui fait ressortir la qualité des ingrédients sans rien ajouter d'inutile est un véritable « joyau de la terre ». C'est un chef-d'œuvre que vous voudrez apprécier en imaginant la paisible chaîne de montagnes de la rivière Uchiigawa inexplorée.
product_tw:
四萬十治栗的萬寶龍
四萬十栗子是四萬十的瑰寶，以比普通栗子大、含糖量高而聞名。萬寶龍採用大量生長在陡峭山坡上、在陽光下生長的栗子製成，咬下去的那一刻，濃鬱的栗子香氣就瀰漫開來。不添加任何不必要的東西，將食材的精華發揮出來的優雅甜味，確實是「大地的寶石」。這是您在想像未開發的內井川寧靜的山脈時想要享受的傑作。

text_en: Tosa Taisho. This station opened in October 1920 as a station on the Yodo Light Line (later Yodo Line), and is now part of the quiet town that bears its name. It once prospered as a key hub for transporting lumber, a source of the rich blessings of the Shimanto River, and enjoyed a vibrant era, but today the wooden station building, which still retains the vestiges of the past, continues to welcome travelers. This station, located in the middle reaches of the clear Shimanto River, has a somewhat nostalgic scent, and is a place where you can feel the slow flow of time. Once you get off the train, you'll be greeted by the idyllic landscape of magnificent nature and the scattered submerged bridges that will soothe your soul. The rich local ingredients, such as sweetfish fishing in the summer and chestnuts and wild boar meat in the fall, will enhance the enjoyment of your trip.

Tosa Showa era. When you get off at Tosa-Yamada Station, you can definitely see the vestiges of the city's former bustle still alive amidst the quiet mountain range and the murmuring of the Monobe River. This station, which opened in 1923, once flourished as a major hub for the forestry industry, where the Dosan Line and the Tosa Electric Railway Aki Line intersected, and where timber cut from the surrounding mountains was brought in by the forest railway. It can be said that the ``wood culture'' that supported Tosa's booming economy was condensed here.

Nowadays, it welcomes new travelers as a stop on the Anpanman train, where the cheers of children echo, and as a gateway to the beautiful countryside. Although its appearance has changed with the passage of time, the station building still has an atmosphere that quietly tells the story of the traveler's spirit and the history of this place. It gives us a sense of the Tosa Yamada landscape, where the prosperity of the past intersects with hope for the future.
product_ja:
四万十川産 天然青のり（原藻）
昭和の時代から変わらぬ清流の風景が残るこの地で、冬の訪れとともに収穫される天然の青のり。その香りは市販のものとは一線を画します。袋を開けた瞬間に立ち昇る、胸がすくような磯の香りと清流の香り。お味噌汁にひと摘み落とすだけで、食卓が四万十の川辺へと変わります。自然の恵みをそのまま乾燥させた、贅沢すぎる「香りの魔法」です。
product_en:
Natural green seaweed (raw algae) from Shimanto River
Natural green seaweed is harvested with the arrival of winter in this area, where the scenery of clear streams remains unchanged since the Showa era. Its scent is different from commercially available products. The heart-warming scent of the ocean and clear stream rises as soon as you open the bag. Just drop a pinch into your miso soup and your dining table will transform into a Shimanto riverside setting. It is a luxurious "magic of fragrance" made by drying the blessings of nature.
product_fr:
Algues vertes naturelles (algues brutes) de la rivière Shimanto
Les algues vertes naturelles sont récoltées avec l'arrivée de l'hiver dans cette région, où le paysage de ruisseaux clairs reste inchangé depuis l'ère Showa. Son parfum est différent des produits disponibles dans le commerce. Le parfum réconfortant de l’océan et du ruisseau clair monte dès que vous ouvrez le sac. Il suffit d'en verser une pincée dans votre soupe miso et votre table à manger se transformera en un décor au bord de la rivière Shimanto. Il s'agit d'une luxueuse « magie du parfum » réalisée en séchant les bénédictions de la nature.
product_tw:
四萬十川天然綠海藻（原海藻）
隨著冬季的到來，這裡收穫了天然的綠色海藻，清澈的溪流景色自昭和時代以來從未改變過。其氣味與市售產品不同。打開袋子，一股溫暖的海洋和清澈溪流的香味撲面而來。只要在味噌湯中滴一點，您的餐桌就會變成四萬十河邊的環境。這是透過乾燥大自然的恩惠而製成的奢華「芳香的魔法」。

text_en: Togawa Station. Located on the Yodo Line, which runs along the meandering Shimanto River, this station overlooks the river from atop a raised embankment. This area was once a busy area for transporting lumber, but now only one concrete platform remains. However, as the birthplace of the ``river crossing'' where carp streamers are flown to the opposite bank in the spring, you can feel the strong vitality of this area. When the sound of a diesel car's engine reverberates through the mountains and you are sucked into the silence, you feel that you have been embraced by the deep bosom of Shimanto. I can't help but think that the appearance of this station, which seems to have been left behind by the waves of modernization, is actually a sign of true affluence.

Half house.
The Yodo Line train rolled into this quiet station along the clear waters of the Shimanto River. The two characters ``Hage'' written on the station name sign have a special resonance in the hearts of travelers who visit the place, and when you learn that the origin of the place's name is related to the legend that far back in the Genpei era, a Heike clan refugee lived there in hiding, you can feel the atmosphere of a remote village even more profoundly. The simple appearance of the unmanned station, along with the sound of the wind blowing across the river, is enveloped in a quietness that seems to convey the lives of people in the past. While trolley trains carrying tourists come and go, this station quietly but surely functions as a means of transportation for local people, and it truly evokes the atmosphere of Showa era rail travel that is still alive today.

Ekawasaki. This station, located in the western part of Kochi Prefecture where the clear Shimanto River flows leisurely, is a perfect riverside base on the abyssal journey of the Yodo Line. This station, which has a history of more than a century since its opening in 1913 during the Tosa Line era, was once bustling with traffic such as transporting lumber, and is filled with tranquility that seems to be a reminder of the hustle and bustle of that time. The atmosphere of the station building is reminiscent of the Showa era, and is sure to evoke a sense of nostalgia in visitors. In recent years, its name has become well-known due to the country's hottest records, and many travelers have come to visit as a base for cycling and canoeing that takes advantage of the rich nature of the Shimanto River. However, here you can still feel the timeless spirit of local train travel and the slow flow of time.
product_ja:
四万十川産 落ち鮎の煮付け
「日本一暑い場所」としても知られる江川崎は、四万十川の中流域に位置する鮎の聖地。苔を食べて育った天然鮎は、スイカのような清々しい香りが特徴です。特に産卵を控えた「落ち鮎」をじっくりと煮上げた逸品は、卵のプチプチとした食感と、凝縮された白身の旨味が絶妙。頭から丸ごと食べられる柔らかさは、熟練の職人技の賜物です。
product_en:
Boiled fallen sweetfish from Shimanto River
Ekawasaki, also known as the ``hottest place in Japan,'' is a sacred place for sweetfish, located in the middle reaches of the Shimanto River. Natural ayu that has grown up eating moss has a refreshing scent similar to watermelon. In particular, the special dish is made by slowly boiling fallen sweetfish that are about to spawn, and the chewy texture of the egg and the concentrated flavor of the white meat are exquisite. The softness that allows you to eat the whole head is the result of skilled craftsmanship.
product_fr:
Poisson sucré bouilli tombé de la rivière Shimanto
Ekawasaki, également connu comme « l'endroit le plus chaud du Japon », est un lieu sacré pour les poissons doux, situé au milieu de la rivière Shimanto. L'ayu naturel qui a grandi en mangeant de la mousse a un parfum rafraîchissant semblable à celui de la pastèque. En particulier, ce plat spécial est préparé à partir de poissons doux tombés et sur le point de frayer, bouillis lentement, et la texture moelleuse de l'œuf et la saveur concentrée de la viande blanche sont exquises. Le moelleux qui permet de manger la tête entière est le fruit d'un savoir-faire artisanal.
product_tw:
四萬十川的煮落香魚
江川崎又被稱為“日本最熱的地方”，是香魚的聖地，位於四萬十川中游。吃苔蘚長大的天然香魚有著類似西瓜的清爽香味。尤其是這道特色菜，是用即將產卵的下落香魚慢火熬煮而成，雞蛋的嚼勁和白肉的濃縮風味堪稱絕妙。能讓你吃掉整個頭的柔軟，是熟練工藝的成果。

text_en: Nishikata. The main line once served as a major artery that ran through this area from north to south, supporting people's lives. Since the line was opened in the Meiji era, many towns have been born along the line, and the line has enjoyed a lively life. Even now, the wooden station building still retains its Showa era feel, giving us a sense of the same humanity that has remained unchanged since the olden days. In front of the station, there is a lively market selling fresh locally grown vegetables. The rice from this region is famous nationwide, and you can see posters posted inside train stations promoting its deliciousness. Additionally, the Harvest Autumn Festival, which is held around this time of year, is said to be a lively event centered around the station, attracting many tourists. Traveling by train is not only a means of transportation, but also a valuable experience that allows you to experience the history, culture, and people of the area.

Mado Station. This small station, located on the prefectural border between Ehime and Kochi, so to speak, is like a punctuation mark in a railway travelogue. The prefectural border marker at the edge of the platform conveys the former border between Iyo and Tosa to the present day. Surrounded by the silence of only a handful of passengers getting on and off each day, the regular sound of the rails' joints seems to be the only link between this mountainous village and the outside world. The old water tank in front of the station, filled with fresh water, is a reminder of the old days of steam locomotives, creating an indescribable atmosphere. This is exactly what it feels like to travel to the frontier.

Yoshino. Yoshino Station is a station on the Yodo Line that stands quietly in a rich mountain village surrounded by the clear Shimanto River. This land, which was once known as ``Yoshinobe,'' was renamed in 1966, giving us the feeling that the reason behind its name change to the current ``Yoshinobu'' may have been an attempt to express the literal richness of this place.

The good old wooden station building retains a nostalgic feel from the Showa era and gently welcomes travelers. As you stand on the platform, you can hear the murmuring of the Shimanto River in the distance and the clear mountain air, slowly relaxing your mind and body, which have become stiff due to city life, and make you feel deeply the feeling of traveling. This is a truly precious place where time flows more slowly and you can enjoy to your heart's content the ``luxury of nothing'' that is the best part of train travel.

Matsumaru. Oigawa Railway, located in the scenic area of ​​central Shizuoka Prefecture, still retains the romance of Showa era railways. Shin-Kanaya Station, the base for the SL service, is more than just a transfer station; it is a truly emotional place that excites visitors. Inside the premises, there is a powerful steam locomotive, and the smell of coal and the sound of the whistle make you feel like you are entering a timeless journey that takes you back to the good old golden age of Japanese railways.

The Oigawa Railway, which has a history of being built from the end of the Taisho period to the beginning of the Showa period for power development and transportation of forestry resources, is also known as a pioneer in preserving steam locomotives, and Shin-Kanaya Station is a key location that conveys that technology and passion to the present day. Even in the Reiwa era, it continues to create new attractions such as the operation of the Thomas the Tank Engine train, and it is a truly interesting station where the smiles of children and the nostalgia of old railway boys intertwine.
product_ja:
松野町産 森のジビエ（鹿肉・猪肉セット）
愛媛県に入り、最初の主要駅。山深い松野町は、古くから狩猟が盛んな「ジビエの町」です。ここで処理される鹿や猪の肉は、驚くほど臭みがなく、野生のエネルギーに満ち溢れています。赤身の濃い鹿肉はヘルシーで柔らかく、猪肉は脂の甘みが絶品。四国の山々の恵みをダイレクトに感じる、キャンプ飯や特別な日のディナーに最適な野生の御馳走です。
product_en:
Forest game from Matsuno Town (venison/boar meat set)
The first major station after entering Ehime Prefecture. Matsuno Town, deep in the mountains, has been known as a game town where hunting has been popular since ancient times. The deer and boar meat processed here is surprisingly odorless and full of wild energy. The lean venison is healthy and tender, and the wild boar meat has an exquisite sweetness from its fat. It is a wild treat that is perfect for camping meals or special occasion dinners, where you can directly feel the blessings of the mountains of Shikoku.
product_fr:
Gibier forestier de la ville de Matsuno (ensemble de viande de venaison/sanglier)
La première grande gare après être entrée dans la préfecture d'Ehime. La ville de Matsuno, située au cœur des montagnes, est connue comme une ville de gibier où la chasse est populaire depuis l'Antiquité. La viande de cerf et de sanglier transformée ici est étonnamment inodore et pleine d'énergie sauvage. Le chevreuil maigre est sain et tendre, et la viande de sanglier possède une douceur exquise grâce à sa graisse. C'est un délice sauvage parfait pour les repas de camping ou les dîners d'occasions spéciales, où vous pouvez directement ressentir les bénédictions des montagnes de Shikoku.
product_tw:
松野町的森林遊戲（鹿肉/野豬肉套餐）
進入愛媛郡後的第一個主要車站。深山中的松野町自古以來就以狩獵盛行聞名。這裡加工的鹿肉和野豬肉出奇地無味，而且充滿野性能量。瘦鹿肉健康嫩滑，野豬肉則帶著油脂的細膩甜味。這是一種野生美食，非常適合露營餐或特殊場合晚餐，您可以直接感受到四國山脈的祝福。

text_en:
Roll. I have now accepted the position of a new railway travel writer, transcending time and space and conveying the spirit of the Showa era to the Reiwa world. With the travel-filled writings of my predecessors such as Shunzo Miyawaki and Hiroyuki Agawa in mind, I dream of a journey that goes beyond simply following the railroad, to delving deeply into the history, folklore, and people's lives of the region.

The whistle of a steam locomotive disappearing beyond the tracks, the hustle and bustle of the period of high economic growth, and the quiet breathing of local lines. We will unravel all of this using accurate geographic information and academic knowledge, and reconstruct it from a modern perspective. We listen to the bustle of festivals and the stories of forgotten stations that we may encounter during our travels, and we sincerely hope to convey these scenes to everyone, sometimes with humor. Now, I pledge to embark on an unknown journey.

Chikinaga. It is a station on the Uwajima Railway, which has continued to watch over this area since its opening in 1912, and later on the Yodo Line. In the past, it served as the center of Kihokucho and was also responsible for freight transportation, with a lively shopping street in front of the station and a lively terminal where many people came and went.

Even though it is quiet now, some traces of the past remain, and the simple station building welcomes travelers. In Kihoku-cho, known as the town of demons, monuments with a rich local flavor delight the eyes of travelers, and this area, close to the source of the pure Shimanto River, makes you feel that it is full of rich nature and the warmth of the people. The scent of the local yuzu citrus fruit wafts in the wind, making it a place that evokes a sense of travel.
product_ja:
鬼北（きほく）の熟成きじ肉セット
日本で唯一「鬼」の字がつく自治体、鬼北町。ここで育てられる「きじ肉」は、かつての貴族も愛した高貴な味わいです。鶏肉よりもコクが深く、それでいて後味は非常に上品。お取り寄せの鍋セットなら、きじのガラから出る黄金色の出汁が野菜に染み込み、震えるほどの旨味を体験できます。心も体も温まる、鬼北の伝説を味わうようなひとときを。
product_en:
Kihoku aged pheasant meat set
Kihoku Town is the only municipality in Japan that has the character ``oni'' in its name. The pheasant meat grown here has a noble taste that was loved by the aristocrats of the past. It has a deeper flavor than chicken, and yet has a very refined aftertaste. If you order a hotpot set, you can experience the golden-brown soup from the pheasant bones that soaks into the vegetables, giving you a trembling flavor. Enjoy a moment that will warm your heart and body as you experience the legend of Onihoku.
product_fr:
Ensemble de viande de faisan vieilli Kihoku
La ville de Kihoku est la seule municipalité du Japon dont le nom contient le caractère « oni ». La viande de faisan cultivée ici a un goût noble qui était apprécié des aristocrates du passé. Il a une saveur plus profonde que celle du poulet, tout en ayant un arrière-goût très raffiné. Si vous commandez un ensemble de fondues, vous pourrez découvrir la soupe dorée provenant des os de faisan qui pénètre dans les légumes, vous donnant une saveur tremblante. Profitez d'un moment qui réchauffera votre cœur et votre corps en découvrant la légende d'Onihoku.
product_tw:
紀北熟成山雞肉套餐
紀北町是日本唯一一個名稱中含有「鬼」字的町。這裡出產的山雞肉味道高貴，深受歷代貴族的喜愛。它的味道比雞肉更深，但餘味非常精緻。如果你點了火鍋套餐，你可以體驗到山雞骨頭金黃的湯汁浸透在蔬菜中，讓人顫抖的味道。體驗鬼北的傳奇，享受溫暖身心的時刻。

text_en:
Fukada. When you hear Ueno Station, you can't help but think of the soot of steam locomotives and the sound of the departure bells of long-distance trains heading north. In the past, famous trains such as the ``Aoba'' and ``Hatsukari'' on the Tohoku Main Line and Joban Line carried the heavy responsibility of being the ``gateway to the north,'' carrying the hopes and dreams of people leaving their hometowns, as well as the sadness of parting ways.

Times have changed, and the Shinkansen has taken over some of that role, but this station still retains a strong sense of the travel atmosphere of those days. The sight of people passing through the station, the fragrant smell of ekiben, and just as you exit the station, you can see the lively Ameyoko Street and Ueno Park, a cultural temple, all of which keep visitors entertained. Ueno Station is not just a transit point, but a living museum where people's emotions intertwine.

Ouchi station. This station stands quietly in the area where the Yodo Line temporarily leaves the flow of the Shimanto River and changes its appearance to a slightly inland rural landscape. The surrounding calm mountains and the well-organized fields spread out at their base. The original scenery of Japan, unrelated to the hustle and bustle of the city, is alive and well here. Waiting for the next train in the waiting room, which is too simple to be called a station building, is strange because even the speed of the moving clouds seems to be slow. This area of ​​Ouchi once again teaches me that the real pleasure of traveling by train is the disconnect from everyday life that gives the illusion that the hands of the clock have stopped.

Two people. When you look out the window of a train heading north on the Soya Main Line, and you see a vast meadow and beyond that the deep blue Sea of ​​Japan, you will see a good old wooden station building at Bakkai Station. Since its opening in 1926, this station has withstood many harsh northern winters, and its appearance, which seems to be a reminder of the days of herring fishing and pioneering, evokes a sense of nostalgia among travelers.

As the northernmost unmanned station, it has often been chosen as a filming location for movies and TV dramas.It is a place filled with tranquility that makes it seem as if time has stopped, and is a place far removed from the hustle and bustle of the city, giving visitors a sense of deep peace and the romance of traveling to the far reaches of the north.

Iyo Miyanoshita. The atmosphere created by this station building on the Yodo Line journey is truly reminiscent of the dreams of the Taisho era and the breath of the Showa era. The wooden station building has gone through many changes since it opened as a station for the Uwajima Railway in 1922, and still continues to welcome and see off travelers.

This once bustling place is now a quiet, unmanned station, and when you step onto the platform, you are greeted by a rural landscape where you can hear frogs in the distance. However, it is in this quietness that you can feel that the history of the railway, which has been closely connected to the lives of the region, and the lives of the people are still alive.

Nowadays, the tourist train "Shiman Torokko" sometimes stops there, giving a breath of fresh air to this quiet station, but the unchanging rustic appearance still gives visitors a deep sense of nostalgic travel. The flow of time that you can feel at this station will give you a rare experience that will make you feel as if you have traveled back in time to the Showa era.

Muta. Bathed in the bright early spring sunlight, I am riding a slow train on a local private railway. The scenery of the Satoyama flowing outside the window has a nostalgic feel of the Showa era, and makes you feel that time passes slowly. The terminal station, Yuunagi, once flourished as a coal mining town and has a history of supporting the movement of many people. The decaying wooden station building is a silent witness to the hustle and bustle of those days, and the remains of the rusted freight siding can be seen on the platform. Nowadays, only a few trains a day pass by, but travelers are still reminded of the people who once existed here and the great role that railways played.

Kitauwajima. This station, where the Yodo Line and Yosan Line intersect, has played an important role as a railway hub in Nanyo since the days of the Uwajima Railway. It is the gateway to the castle town that leads to the Uwajima city area, and although limited express trains pass through it, the station building has a somewhat nostalgic appearance that attracts the hearts of travelers. The Yodo Line that runs from here to the Shimanto River is known as the Shimanto Green Line, and in recent years, sightseeing trains have added color to the line, providing exciting scenery even for non-railway fans. It's fun to immerse yourself in the atmosphere of traveling on a local train while thinking about Uwajima's rich seafood, such as sea bream and jakoten, and the bustle of the Ushioni Festival in summer.

Uwajima. This station is the terminal station of the Yosan Line and is located at the end of the railway that leads to the southwestern part of Shikoku.Beyond the rails covered with bollards, you can feel the bottomless depths of the country of Iyo. As a former castle town of the Uwajima domain's Date 100,000 koku clan, this station is home to bullfighting and the majesty of Uwajima Castle, and it has a profound travel atmosphere that is unique to a terminal station. From here on, the rails stop, but I can't help but think of this as a powerful starting point for the journey that continues further south to Sukumo and Nakamura. The open feel of the station plaza lined with palm trees is the perfect finale to your trip to Nanyo.

Gomen town. Standing at this stop, located at the eastern end of Tosa, near the former starting point of the Noneyama Kaido, you can feel the mixture of pride as Japan's longest existing tram network and a sense of a leisurely lifestyle. The sight of a tram that leaves a strong vestige of the Taisho and Showa eras running past the eaves of private houses evokes a sense of intimacy that has been lost in modern urban transportation, as well as a somewhat nostalgic memory of the Toden.

This railway, which extends from Gomen in the east to Ino in the west and Pier in the north and south, is the capillary blood vessel of the city of Kochi, and the diamond crossing at Harimaya Bridge is a sight that can be called a sacred place for tram fans. This railway, which was once called the Tosa Electric Railway and has survived many wars and disasters, has now been renamed ``Tosaden Kotsu,'' but the unchanging spirit of the Tosa people is still alive in the flowers blooming beside the tracks and the dignified demeanor of the train drivers. The diversity of foreign cars from all over the world and the latest ultra-low-floor cars coming together on the same track makes you feel as if you are traveling through a ``living tram museum.''

text_en:
Gomen town. This is the place where the tram from Kochi City with the destination ``Gomen'' on it quietly stops as its eastern terminus. Since the opening of the Tosa Electric Railway in 1902, this area has a history of supporting people's lives as the end point of the main artery connecting the center of Nankoku City and the prefectural capital. In the past, the Aki Line that continued to Aki branched off from here, and it was a thriving hub with direct trains passing by in a hurry.

If you look up right next to the tram stop, you'll see the huge elevated bridge of the modern Gomen-Nahari Line, standing there watching over the old trains crawling along the road. This sight of old and new railroads intersecting symbolizes the tenacity of Tosa, which overcame the tragic fate of abolishing the Aki Line in 1960 and regained the bonds of railroad ties in the Heisei era.

Nearby, characters drawn by Anpanman's creator, Takashi Yanase, blend into the street corners and soothe the hearts of visitors. At dusk, with the sound of the train ringing its bell as it makes its way back, and thinking back to the days when wooden cars ran in the background, one can feel that this mysterious-sounding town of ``Gomen'' is still overflowing with a warm, all-encompassing love.

product_ja:
土佐の生姜（高知県産 黄金しょうが）
路面電車の東の起点、南国市。ここは日本一の生姜の産地です。南国の太陽と豊かな水で育った「黄金しょうが」は、切り口が鮮やかな黄金色。一口かじれば、突き抜けるような爽快な香りと、力強い辛みが全身を駆け巡ります。お取り寄せでは、すりおろしやジンジャーエールベースも人気。土佐の情熱が詰まった、体温まる「大地の結晶」です。
product_en:
Tosa ginger (golden ginger from Kochi prefecture)
Nankoku City is the eastern starting point for the tram. This is Japan's number one producer of ginger. ``Gold ginger'' grown in the tropical sun and abundant water has a bright golden color when cut. When you take a bite, the refreshing aroma and powerful spiciness rush through your entire body. Grated and ginger ale bases are also popular for ordering. It is a ``crystal of the earth'' that warms your body and is filled with Tosa's passion.
product_fr:
Gingembre Tosa (gingembre doré de la préfecture de Kochi)
La ville de Nankoku est le point de départ oriental du tramway. C'est le premier producteur de gingembre au Japon. Le « gingembre doré » cultivé sous le soleil tropical et dans une eau abondante a une couleur dorée brillante une fois coupé. Lorsque vous prenez une bouchée, l’arôme rafraîchissant et le piquant puissant se répandent dans tout votre corps. Les bases de soda râpé et au gingembre sont également populaires pour la commande. C'est un « cristal de la terre » qui réchauffe votre corps et est rempli de la passion de Tosa.
product_tw:
土佐薑（高知縣的金薑）
南國市是有軌電車的東部起點。這是日本第一大生薑生產地。在熱帶陽光和充足的水源下生長的「金薑」切開後呈現明亮的金黃色。咬上一口，清爽的香氣和濃鬱的辣味就竄遍全身。磨碎的薑汁汽水也很受歡迎。它是溫暖你的身體並充滿土佐熱情的「大地的水晶」。

text_en:
Gomenhigashimachi. It is a charming tram stop that conveys the pride of the old town of Nankoku City, which was once called ``Gomen.'' Until 1960, the Aki Line trains running to Aki ran from here, and the remnants of the bustle of the days when direct trains from Kochi City were frequent can be seen in the narrow alleyways and the appearance of the townscape.

As soon as you stand at the bus stop, you'll see a shopping street with strong Showa-era charms right in front of you, and you'll be greeted by the smell of people preparing for dinner and the steady activities of the local people. This place is also connected to the manga artist Takashi Yanase, and you can feel that the history of his ancestors living here is being quietly passed down through the stone statues and signboards placed on the street corners.

The rattling sound of the train carving the rails on the road surface is not drowned out by the hustle and bustle of cars, and echoes like the heartbeat of this city. Although it is only a short section heading towards Gomen-cho, the final stop, the way the train passes the eaves of the wooden houses outside the window reminds travelers of the intimacy of the tram.

text_en:
Gomen Nakamachi (Gomen Nakamachi). Deep in the heart of the shopping district of Nankoku City, the tram rails are intertwined with the scent of daily life, making it a truly thin yet powerful stop. This tram stop, which was founded in the last years of the Meiji era, was once a kind of tea room in the area, where shoppers and students would huddle together and wait for trains when direct service to the Aki Line was popular.

Right next to the bus stop, characters related to Takashi Yanase watch over the alleyway, giving us the feeling that the memories of that day when children of the Showa era ran through are connected to the smiling faces of modern children. The benefit of tax exemption during the Edo period, from which this place's name derives, gives the town's people a somewhat calm, yet reasonable, ethos.

The silence after the train has rumbling away, mixed with the bustle of the shopping district and the hustle and bustle of the distance, offers a sense of peace of mind that cannot be experienced in modern travel, which pursues efficiency.

text_en:
Gomenishimachi (Gomenishimachi). The stop is modestly located near the city hall, which is the administrative center of Nankoku City, at the entrance of an alley that still retains the bustle of its former post town. During the Edo period, the name Gomen, which was exempted from taxes due to the suggestion of Kaneyama Nonaka, the ruler of the Tosa domain, is not just a symbol, but a symbol of the spirit of freedom and independence that took root in this area.

The sight of a train gently sliding along the tracks, and students in uniforms and housewives running errands getting on and off the train gives us a sense of the original scenery of local public transportation, which has remained unchanged no matter how many years have passed since its opening in the Meiji era. As you walk around the stop, you will find old warehouse-style buildings and historic temples dotted around the area, quietly testifying to the excitement of the days when the tram ran in competition with the Aki Line's diesel cars.

Although the scenery has changed little by little due to redevelopment in recent years, the sound of the chiming departure signal remains the same, connecting the memories of the Showa era to the skies of the Reiwa era.

text_en:
In front of Tokyo Kogyo. As the name suggests, it is a stop where young enthusiasm and aspirations for the future intersect, overlooking the school building of Kochi Prefectural Kochi East Technical High School right next to it. This railway, which has continued since the Meiji era, continued to transport many young people aspiring to become engineers even during the high economic growth period of the Showa era, and played a role in supporting Japan's industrial development from the bottom up.

When you stand at the bus stop, you can hear the lively voices after school and the hustle and bustle of cars on the national highway, creating a unique and lively atmosphere. The way the rails, carrying the dream of connecting to the old Aki Line, shine dullly as they reflect the setting sun, matches the straight-forward eyes of the students as they work hard to make things, giving us a sense of reliability.

The sight of an old train car lurching forward as the departure signal chimes with a chirp sounds, reminding us of the value of steady progress, which remains unchanged even as times change. This small station, where technology, tradition, and youthful energy resonate, is still alive with a simple passion that we have almost forgotten in modern times.

text_en:
Sumiyoshi street. The bus stop is located quietly, but with a certain presence, on the border of Gomen, Nankoku City, which passes through the city center to the west and reaches the verdant countryside. This place, which has seen off countless students and local residents since its opening in 1909, is truly a living relic that has carved out the history of life in Tosa.

As the name suggests, it is located near Sumiyoshi Shrine, which has been watching over the peace of this area since ancient times, and was once bustling with worshipers and people doing local business. During the heyday of the Showa era, the majestic train that ran directly from the Gomen Line to the Aki Line passed through here, and as part of the main artery connecting Kochi City and the eastern part of the country, you can feel the history of the area, which echoed the powerful sounds of the railway.

Although it has now blended into a quiet residential area, waiting for the rattling trams to come by brings us back to the intimacy of the trams that we have lost in exchange for efficiency.

text_en:
Shinohara. As you move a little further from the center of Nankoku City and the green color starts to grow on the train windows, this stop will appear along National Route 195. It gives us a sense of the tenacity of the railway, which has continued to carry people through Tosa's harsh summers and mild winters since its opening in 1909.

If you stand at the bus stop, you can see through the rows of plastic greenhouses that still remain the vestiges of a time when the area was once a vast rural area. During its heyday in the Showa era, the vibrant scene of people wearing farm clothes carrying baskets on their backs and heading to the market in Kochi was a daily sight here.

Nowadays, it is turning into a quiet residential area, but at dusk, the sound of trains running in the distance seems somehow reminiscent of the Showa era. If you forget about the rush of traveling and surrender to the leisurely rhythm of a single train car, you will once again feel the weight of the years that railways have remained close to the hearts of local people.

text_en:
Kogome-dori (Kogome-dori). It's a truly humble stop located on the railroad that runs along the national highway, on the banks of the Kogogawa River, which separates the border between Nankoku City and Kochi City. Since its opening in 1901, this area has seen off many people as a nodal point in the transition from rural to urban areas.

Particularly in the 1960s, after the Kochi National College of Technology opened nearby, it became a daily scene at this station to see aspiring young engineers, who would carry the future of Japan on their shoulders, waiting for trains while carrying heavy bags. In the past, direct trains from the Aki Line used to run through this area, but now a single streetcar makes a long, quiet sound as it crosses the border river. Its unpretentious appearance reminds us of the ``joy of swinging'' that is the origin of travel in today's world where efficiency is the only pursuit.

When you stand on the platform at dusk, after the hustle and bustle of students rushing home has passed, the nostalgic after-school smell wafts in the air, mixed with the breeze blowing across the river, making you keenly aware of the long history of railroads.

text_en:
Nagasaki. The bus stop is located at the eastern end of Kochi City, at the first place you cross the Kogogawa River, which separates it from Nankoku City, and finally enter the heart of the prefectural capital. Since its opening in 1902, this area has also played the role of a signal station controlling the crossing of single-track sections, and was once a strategic point on the railway where direct trains from the Aki Line bravely crossed.

The thin rails that are laid out next to the national highway allow you to ignore the hustle and bustle of passing cars and keep track of the eternal time that is unique to streetcars. A peaceful countryside spreads out just behind the bus stop, and as dusk falls, the train's headlights illuminate the road like fireflies, giving you a sense of the travel atmosphere of the Showa era.

Those quiet moments of waiting for an oncoming train at a signal station are what taught me the luxury of "waiting" when traveling. Watching a train leave with the echoing sound of its joints reminds us of the long history of railways that have remained close to the hearts of local people.

text_en:
Akemi Bridge. It is a quiet stop on the railway that runs parallel to the national highway in the peaceful streets of Otsu, Kochi City. Since its opening in 1902, many people have come to the town from this small platform as a key point connecting the eastern part of Tosa.

The name of the stop originates from the bridge that spans the Funairi River that flows nearby. When the Aki Line was still in operation, the wind pressure from the diesel cars that ran through this area still feels like it's still dormant in the rusty color of the rails. The surrounding Otsu area was once a prosperous farming village with vast wetlands, but now it is lined with houses, quietly testifying to the changing times.

If you surrender yourself to the rumbling sound of a train coming your way, the hustle and bustle of everyday life will fade away and you will feel the time in Tosa passing by more slowly. The moment you wait for the sound of the next train while being blown by the wind across the river provides an irreplaceable peace of mind in this day and age where efficiency is valued.

text_en:
Ichijo Bridge. In a place where the old townscape of Otsu, Kochi City still continues to breathe, this bus stop literally stands like a ``signpost.'' Since its opening in 1902, it has stood at the foot of Ichijo Bridge, which crosses the Funari River, and has continued to quietly watch over the coming and going of people.It is a testament to the history of hardship and glory that Tosa's streetcars have had.

It is too humble to call it a home, and the ``intimacy'' inherent in streetcars, where the only boundary is the safe zone on the road, remains strongly here. The heat of the Showa era, when the brave trains running directly to the Aki Line ran through this narrow space, still feels like it's melting into the dull glow of the rails.

The smell of evening snacks begins to waft from the nearby houses, and a train car rings a nostalgic bell before disappearing into the next town. In modern travel, where convenience is the only pursuit, this scene presents us with an irreplaceable ``original view of a stop.''

text_en:
In front of Seiwa Gakuen. Established in 1985, it is relatively new on the Gomen Line, but it is now the gateway to an indispensable school building. This section, which is just a stone's throw away from the neighboring Ichijobashi stop and just over 60 meters above the tracks, is one of the shortest connections in Japan, and is proof that the tram has carefully responded to the needs of the local community and students.

In the mornings and evenings, the area is filled with the fresh energy of the students of Seiwa Gakuen, and the sight of an old train chugging along, carrying their dreams and futures, gives you a sense of the simple atmosphere that existed in educational settings in the Showa era. This place was once a girls' school called ``Seiwa Joshi Gakuin-mae,'' but with the passage of time it became co-educational and the station name changed, but the sounds of daily life, interwoven with the sound of railroad crossing alarms and the sound of train bells, still exude the atmosphere of a student town that hasn't changed since then.

It's less than a minute's walk from Ichijo Bridge. The luxury of taking this ``too short journey'' by train is a pleasure that can only be found in Kochi, the land of tramways, and it also feels like a modest resistance to the modern era's emphasis on efficiency.

text_en:
Ryoseki Street. This place, on the western edge of Otsu, Kochi City, where the Ryoseki Road that continues to the north splits off, has long been famous as a key logistics hub connecting mountain villages and the prefectural capital. It is not hard to imagine that travelers who have crossed the steep mountain pass since the railway opened in 1909 must have breathed a sigh of relief when they finally saw the brilliance of the railway.

In the past, firewood and crops brought from the mountains were transported to the city's markets via this stop, and the tram was not just a substitute for passenger carriages, but fulfilled its mission as the backbone of the local economy. Although the surrounding area has now turned into a calm residential area, the busy flow of cars passing through the intersection in front of the stop gives us a strong sense that this is still a transportation hub.

As the departure signal chirps, and the train accelerates again as it runs parallel to the national highway, the vibrancy of the Showa era and the vestiges of the good old Tosa roads still remain strong.

text_en:
Kitaura. The train station is located east of Kochi City, on the way to the railroad that runs parallel to National Route 195 and cuts straight through the vast plains of Otsu. Since its opening in 1902, this area has served as an important node connecting rural areas and the prefectural capital, absorbing Tosa's harsh sunlight and sea breeze.

In the Showa era, the countryside used to stretch out as far as the eye could see, but now the scenery has transformed into a landscape that shows the economic development of the region, with rows of houses and factory roofs. The memory of the brave diesel trains that once ran directly through the Aki Line, making the ground rumble as they ran through here, still seems to be sleeping quietly in the dull glow of the rails.

At dusk, a train carrying people rushing home quietly rolls in. In today's world where efficiency is valued, this idyllic rhythm of ``local trains'' is a reminder that the essence of travel is the essence of travel.

text_en:
Funato. Among the Gomensen lines that cross the plains of Otsu, Kochi City, this is a stop where the old pilgrimage route intersects, and is a place where faith and wanderlust are mixed. Since its opening in 1902, the station has continued to transport pilgrims to the 88 places in Shikoku as well as local residents carrying agricultural products, and is proof that it supported the modernization of Tosa.

As you stand at the bus stop, the gentle flow of the Funairi River, from which the train takes its name, brings back memories of a time when water transportation was popular. During the heyday of the Showa era, a direct train from here to Aki ran through the area, giving you a sense of its history and giving off a powerful sound that symbolized the vitality of the area.

Although it is currently located in a peaceful residential area, the fact that travelers can sometimes be seen wearing pilgrim hats is a testament to the eternity of this area. A train car rang its bell and slipped out into the dusk again. Its unpretentious driving conveys the obvious truth in this Reiwa era that traveling is not just about rushing to the destination.

text_en:
Kago. Located in the eastern part of Kochi City, close to the rich flow of the Kokubun River, this area is like a borderline where the tram leaves the hustle and bustle of the city and finally steps out into the countryside. Since its opening in 1902, this station has also played the role of a signal station to control the crossing of single-track sections, and there is a history where the brave trains that ran directly to the Aki Line would take a breather here before running eastward.

The Kokubun River lies right next to the stop, and you can feel the history of the river, which was once a key point where water and land transport intersected, quietly supporting the local economy. Even in the hustle and bustle of modern times, the sound of trains crossing the iron bridge remains the same, and at dusk, the lights of the trains reflecting on the river surface still convey the travel spirit of the Showa era. The moment when the silence after a train has left, mixed with the sound of a murmuring river, teaches us the most obvious truth in this Reiwa era: that traveling is not just about rushing to the destination.

text_en:
Tanabeshima Dori (Tabeshima Dori). After crossing the Kokubun River, the bus stop is located at the point where the JR Dosan Line's huge viaduct begins to run side by side, just before Kochi's urban area begins to increase in density. When it opened in 1902, it was a rural area, but today it is lined with houses and small factories, clearly demonstrating the strong growth of a local city.

If you look up, you'll see an express train rushing like a gale down a modern concrete elevated bridge, and a streetcar thudding beneath your feet, pressing its feet against the ground in a rhythm that hasn't changed since the Meiji and Taisho eras. The contrast created by this ``air and land'' railway gives us a sense of the unique scenery of Kochi, where the modern era, which seeks efficiency, and the past, which admires emotion, coexist.

I look for remnants of the time when this area was surrounded by flowing rivers like an ``island'' among the houses, and wait for the sound of the next train. These quiet moments bring back to us in the Reiwa era a glimpse of the ``journeys of thought'' that were loved by the Showa era's literary figures.

text_en:
Mizuho Street. The bus stop is located in the eastern part of Kochi City, on the boundary line where the urban area is about to increase in density, going around the foot of the Kazura Island mountain. Since its opening in 1902, this area has been a rich rice field, symbolizing the ``Mizuho no Kuni'' (the land of Mizuho), as its name suggests, and the golden ears of rice sway in the wind of the trains during the harvest season, giving you a sense of its history.

In the heyday of the Showa era, direct trains from the Aki Line proudly ran through this area, making it a thriving artery connecting the eastern part of the prefecture and the prefectural capital. Nowadays, commercial facilities and residences are lined up neatly along the national highway, and the former rural landscape has changed its appearance, but the humble yet resolute appearance of the bus stop shows that the streetcar is still the mainstay of daily life.

At dusk, in the midst of the waves of cars passing by, a train rolls in, ringing its nostalgic bell. If we listen to the sound of the unpretentious railway, we will rediscover the ``fertility of the heart'' that we have left behind in this era of efficiency, in this land that bears the name Mizuho.

Kochi Station, which stands ahead, is the gateway to the Pacific Ocean, and was once a hub where freight trains full of charcoal came and went, supporting people's lives. It has now been renovated into a beautiful station building, with smooth connections to the streetcar, and the sight of the Anpanman train departing to the cheers of children brings back the old and new travel sensations. There is a deeply moving scene where the history and future of this place intersect.

text_en:
Chiyocho 3-chome. This is a stop located at the forefront of crossing the Katsurashima Bridge and finally entering the urban area of ​​the prefectural capital, Kochi, with the damp breeze of the Kokubun River at your back. Since its opening in 1902, this area has served as a relay point connecting Gomen in the east and Harimaya Bridge in the west, and has played an important role as a throat support for people's lives.

In the Showa era, this area was once lined with factory chimneys, and the streetcars were busy transporting commuters and merchants. The reliability of the train as it steps into the hustle and bustle of the city, making a heavy rumbling sound, makes you feel the heartbeat of the city itself.

Nowadays, large stores are lined up along the national highway, and the appearance of the area has changed, but the brilliance of the rails buried in the asphalt still maintains the pride of the railroad that has remained unchanged from the past. Watching a train slowly drive away through the waves of cars passing by is a refreshing reminder of the ``richness that exists alongside the city'' that modern people have forgotten in their haste.

text_en:
Chiyocho 2-chome. The urban area of ​​Kochi, the prefectural capital, has become increasingly dense, and has become a strategic hub where streetcars proudly pass between the shops and buildings that line the national highway. Since its opening in 1902, this place has always been a gateway to the eastern part of the country and the center of local commerce, giving you a sense of its history as a place that has always received the enthusiasm of the people.

In the past, the company's headquarters and depot were located in the neighboring town of Chiyose, and it literally served as the backbone of Tosa's railways, with the constant sound of trains echoing day and night. During the high economic growth period of the Showa era, large commercial facilities were lined up, and citizens carrying shopping bags boarded and alighted the trains one after another, a lively scene that was commonplace.

Nowadays, the city has been given a new look and a modern look, but the sight of a single train vividly passing a line of cars waiting at a traffic light gives you a sense of the same robustness of the streetcar. At dusk, the building window lights reflect on the rails, and the chiming departure bell melts into the hustle and bustle of the city. The scenery presents a sense of urban travel that will never fade, even though it has been washed by the waves of time.

Chiyocho 1-chome. The stop is located along the national highway, where expectations for Harimaya Bridge, the heart of the prefectural capital, Kochi, are gradually rising. Since its opening in 1901, this building has a history of serving as a gateway to government offices and medical institutions, and playing an honest role in connecting the lives of citizens and government.

In the Showa era, the nearby Kochi Police Station exuded its majesty, and the sight of uniformed police officers and citizens busily climbing up and down the steps of the train comes to mind. The calm cityscape that still remains today gives us a sense that the tram was not just a means of transportation, but a part of the bloodstream that supported the order and peace of mind of the city.

Nowadays, the police station has been relocated, and the scenery is changing little by little, but the sight of a train crossing a traffic light with a jaunty bell ringing continues to present the same aesthetic of Tosa's daily life. Even though the number of skyscrapers increases, the creaking sound of the rails still resonates at the same frequency as it did in the Showa era, giving travelers an indescribable sense of relief.

Chiyori Town. It is a place where you can enjoy the exhilaration of finally stepping into the center of Kochi City, accompanied by the sound of trains passing through the streets. Since its opening in 1902, this area has been the first contact with the hustle and bustle of the city for travelers from the east, and has reigned as a lively hub where commerce and industry intersect.

The Tosa Electric Railway's headquarters and depot were once located near this stop, and it is literally the heart of the railway, giving you a sense of its history as the place where many trains were operating day and night. During its heyday in the Showa era, direct trains from the Aki Line proudly passed through it, fulfilling its mission as the main artery that supported the city's prosperity.

Nowadays, modern buildings are lined up along the national highway, and the appearance of the old days has changed, but the sound of a train rolling by with the nostalgic chime of its bell still gives us a sense of Tosa's daily life. Surrendering yourself to the sound of the railroad passing peacefully across the sea of ​​asphalt, here you can rediscover the ``breathing of the city'' that modern people, who only seek efficiency, have forgotten.

text_en:
Hoei Town. As the eastern gateway to the prefectural capital, Kochi, it is a stop that preserves the memories of a factory town that was once lined with chimneys and echoed with the sound of industrial hammers. Since its opening in 1902, this area has not only been a place for passengers to board and disembark, but also as a distribution center for goods, giving us a sense of its history as a strong driving force behind the modernization of Tosa.

In the past, there were large-scale sawmills and sake breweries in this area, and the fact that there was a siding line running from the main streetcar line into the factories is a testament to the golden age of the Showa era, when railways were the lifeblood of industry. The heat of those days, when large freight cars roared back and forth, is now hidden beneath the paved roads, but you can still feel that the pride of the city as a former ``industrial capital'' still lives on in the neatly organized areas surrounding the bus stop.

Nowadays, modern apartment buildings and offices are lined up, and the colors of the trains passing through the streets have become brighter, but at dusk, when a train carrying people rushing home rolls in with the sound of joints, it deeply conveys the preciousness of the ``railways of life'' that remain unchanged even as times change.

text_en:
Saienba Town. The name of the stop still retains the flavor of history, as the fresh vegetables that once graced the dining tables of the Yamauchi family, the lords of the Tosa domain, were nurtured in the rich soil of this area. Since its opening in 1901, the tramway has served as the kitchen of the east of the prefectural capital, Kochi, and a place of relaxation for the common people, and the tram has constantly carried the people's energy.

Right next to the stop is the Saienba Shopping Street, which has a strong Showa-era feel to it, and the sight of seasonal fish and wild vegetables lined up alongside the energetic chanting gives you a sense of the depth of Tosa's food culture. This area, where Horikawa's water transport and railway lines once intersected, had a unique atmosphere of swirling goods and information.

In the evening, housewives on their way home from shopping are wheeled by a train as they leave, chatting and laughing. This casual scene of daily life is proof that the streetcar continues to live as a capillary blood vessel in the city. Even though it is surrounded by buildings, when you get off at this station, you can feel the love of Tosa and the warmth of the Showa era comfortably on your skin.

name_en: In front of Dentetsu Terminal Building
text_en:
In front of Dentetsu Terminal Building. At the corner of the main street that leads to Harimaya Bridge, the heart of Kochi City, the bus stop stands proudly watching over you. Since its opening in 1902, this place has a history of serving as the ``front door of Tosa,'' a place where travelers from inside and outside the prefecture intersect with citizens heading out into the city.

Seibu Department Store, a symbol of Kochi's modernity, once stood here, and the peaceful daily life of the Showa era was filled with moments spent in the large cafeteria on the top floor and the smiles of people boarding the train carrying colorful wrapping paper. The contrast between the glamor of the department stores and the old trains that slide into the stops gives you a sense of the depth of the culture that this city has cultivated.

Nowadays, it has been transformed into a modern building with a bus terminal attached to it, fulfilling its function as a ``land port'' where express buses depart from and arrive at various destinations in Shikoku and as far away as Tokyo and Osaka. Still, the sight of a train car sliding through the valley between the buildings and the cool chime of its bells is a powerful reminder that no matter how modernized the city becomes, the main character of Kochi is the railway.

text_en:
Harimaya Bridge. In the middle of Kochi, Tosa, where the Gomen/Ino Line running east to west and the Sanbashi Line running north and south intersect in a criss-cross pattern, it is truly the heart of Japan's number one tramway kingdom. Since its opening in 1902, this place has become more than just a stop; it has boasted a magnificent presence as a hub of Tosa, where people from all over Shikoku and travelers from across the ocean always stop.

The sight of a train passing over Diamond Crossing, where the tracks intersect at right angles, with the sound of a heavy metal sound, conveys to the Reiwa era the strength of the Showa era, when mechanical civilization was integrated with the breathing of the city. Nearby stands the vermilion Harimaya Bridge, which is famous for the love story between Junnobu and a horse, and with the melody of Yosakoi Bushi, you can feel the unique traveling spirit of the Tosa people, mixing their passion and sadness.

The sight of trains arriving from all directions orderly replacing each other at the touch of a single signal under the endless blue sky of the southern expanse is a vivid reminder of the pride that the railway continues to play as the main character of the city, no matter how times change.

product_ja:
藁焼き かつおのたたき（明神水産）
東西南北が交差する、とさでんの心臓部。土佐に来たら、この香りを嗅がずには帰れません。本場の藁焼きは、一気に数千度の炎で表面を焼き固めることで、中に旨味を閉じ込め、藁の香ばしさを纏わせます。厚切りにした身に塩を振り、ニンニクを添えて。口に入れた瞬間に広がる「土佐の海」の力強さに、誰もが虜になるはずです。
product_en:
Straw-grilled bonito tataki (Myojin Suisan)
The heart of Tosaden, where east, west, north, and south intersect. When you come to Tosa, you can't leave without smelling this scent. Authentic straw grilling involves baking the surface of the food with a flame of several thousand degrees all at once, trapping the flavor inside and giving it the aroma of straw. Sprinkle salt on the thickly sliced ​​meat and add garlic. Everyone will be captivated by the power of the Tosa Sea that spreads the moment you put it in your mouth.
product_fr:
Tataki de bonite grillée sur paille (Myojin Suisan)
Le cœur de Tosaden, où se croisent l’est, l’ouest, le nord et le sud. Quand on vient à Tosa, on ne peut pas repartir sans sentir cette odeur. Les grillades authentiques sur paille consistent à cuire la surface des aliments avec une flamme de plusieurs milliers de degrés en même temps, emprisonnant la saveur à l'intérieur et lui donnant l'arôme de la paille. Saupoudrez de sel la viande en tranches épaisses et ajoutez l'ail. Tout le monde sera captivé par la puissance de la mer Tosa qui se propage dès que vous la mettez dans votre bouche.
product_tw:
稻草烤鰹魚鰹魚（明神水產）
東、西、北、南交會的土佐電中心。來到土佐，沒有聞到這種香味就走不了。正宗的稻草燒烤是用幾千度的火焰一次烘烤食物表面，將食物的味道鎖在裡面，散發出稻草的香氣。在厚厚的肉片上撒上鹽，加入大蒜。放入口中的一瞬間，土佐海的力量就蔓延開來，所有人都會被它所吸引。

text_en:
Horizume. If you proceed westward with the hustle and bustle of Harimaya Bridge behind you, you will arrive at this stop, which is the commercial center of Kochi. When it opened in 1902, this place was the starting point for the Ino Line and the starting point for journeys to the west of Tosa, so you can feel the weight of its history.

It is said that the area got its name from the fact that the moat of the Tosa clan once ran out here, and during the high economic growth period of the Showa era, financial institutions such as the Bank of Japan Kochi branch were lined up here, and businessmen in business suits quickly got on and off the trains, giving it the appearance of ``Tosa's Wall Street.'' On the other hand, the sight of people waiting for the train carrying heavy baskets of vegetables on their way to the Sunday market held in the nearby Otsusuji area gives a sense of the indigenous vitality of Tosa, even though it is located in the middle of the city.

If you listen to the sound of train bells chiming while being blown by the wind from the buildings, you will realize that this place, where an early modern castle town and a modern railroad intersect, is a symbol of Kochi's history.

text_en:
Ohashi Dori (Ohashi Dori). To the west from Harimaya Bridge, this place, where the vibrancy of the Otesuji street and the bustle of the arcade intersect, is the gateway to the ``stomach'' of Kochi citizens. Since its opening in 1902, this stop has a history of over 120 years of transporting people to the Sunday Market, one of the largest street markets in Japan, as well as the nearby Ohashi-dori shopping district.

As soon as you get off the bus, the aromatic smell of straw-grilled bonito wafts in the air, reminding you of the strength of Tosa's food culture, which has remained unchanged since the Showa era. In the past, the scene of housewives rushing to board the train with their shopping baskets in tow, and Tosa dialect being spoken in a lively manner, is still alive today in the hustle and bustle of tourists and locals heading to Hirome Market.

At the foot of Kochi Castle, this place where early modern emotion and modern vibrancy are connected by the thin thread of the tram, allows us to rediscover the joy of walking and the joy of eating in modern travels that seek only efficiency.

text_en:
In front of Kochi Castle. Looking up at the towering white castle tower that pierces the blue sky of Tosa, the stop is located in this area, where the dignity of the prefectural capital, Kochi, is most evident. Since its opening in 1902, this area has continued to serve as the gateway to the famous castle, as well as the political and administrative center where the prefectural and city halls are located, transporting the people who run Tosa.

When you get off at the stop and look up at the elegant castle tower towering over the Otemon gate, you will feel the perfect harmony between the early modern majesty built by Kazutoyo Yamauchi and the modern pulse of the streetcar. In the Showa era, during the summer ``Kochi City Summer Fireworks Festival'' and ``Yosakoi Festival,'' this tram stop was filled with people wearing yukata, gazing up at the large flowers bursting into the night sky, and the lively memories still blend into the sound of the rails.

The sight of a single train car moving leisurely with Kochi Castle in the background gives travelers the ``space in their hearts'' to reflect on the weight of history in a modern world that values ​​efficiency.

name_en: In front of the prefectural office
text_en:
In front of the prefectural office. Located south of Kochi Castle, at the entrance to the government district leading from Otesuji, this is the bus stop where you can hear the pulse of Tosa's politics and administration closest to you. For 120 years since its opening in 1901, it has carried people to the prefectural and city halls and continued to watch over the modernization of Tosa.

During the heyday of the Showa era, one can vividly imagine students in tight collars and petitioners carrying heavy furoshiki wrappers stepping powerfully onto the steps of streetcars and heading out into town. Even now, with the stately prefectural government building in the background, the sight of single-car trains regularly arriving and departing gives us a sense of the unique scenery of this city, where the strictness of government and the warmth of the streetcar intersect.

In a modern society that values ​​efficiency, looking out at the majestic government building from the swaying train window provides a luxurious moment to quietly reflect on the weight of Tosa's history.

text_en:
Grand Street. This stop is located where the train passes through the government district where the prefectural and city halls are lined up and finally enters a quiet residential area and a town full of academic buildings. Since its opening in 1901, it has played the role of a truly splendid link between Tosa's political center and a place for citizens to relax.

The ``Grand'' in the name of the stop originates from the Kochi City Sports Ground (Grand), which used to be located on the north side of this area. During the heyday of the Showa era, the lively sight of the cheers of baseball players chasing a white ball and the bustle of families gathering for a sports day could be heard even through the window of the train, and it still feels like it's blending into the sound of the rails. Although the playground has changed in appearance, the footsteps of students attending nearby schools remain the same, and the sight of an old train chugging along, carrying the memories of their youth, proves that the railway is the very memory of the town.

When you look at the headlights of a train passing through a tree-lined avenue at dusk, you are reminded of the very obvious truth that traveling is not just about rushing to a destination.

text_en:
Masugata. The stop is located at a historic strategic point, where the Masugata Gate, which served as a guard to the west of Kochi Castle and was built by turning the road into a crank shape to prevent enemy invasion, was once located. Since its opening in 1902, this place has quietly watched over the progress of Tosa as a nodal point where the dignity of a castle town and the lives of ordinary people intersect.

Once you get off the bus stop, you will find the Masugata Shopping Street, which still retains the atmosphere of the Showa era, and the liveliness of people coming and going in search of ingredients for evening appetizers will remind you of the warmth of those days when the streetcar was the main character of the town. There was once an infantry regiment located near this area, giving it the appearance of a military capital, but now it is a peaceful place where the laughter of students going to nearby schools can be heard mixed with the sounds of trains.

Watching a train leave with the echoing sound of its joints reminds us of the long history of railways that have remained close to the hearts of local people.

text_en:
Kamimachi 1-chome. To the west of Kochi Castle, this station sits quietly in a historic corner where former samurai residences and townhouses are mixed together. Since its opening in 1902, this place has served as the gateway to the Kamimachi area, known as the birthplace of Ryoma Sakamoto, and has seen off trains carrying the pride of Tosa many times.

As soon as you step off the bus stop and step into the alley, you can feel that the enthusiasm of the Meiji Restoration patriots is still alive in the stone monuments and old buildings. In the Showa era, the nearby shopping streets were filled with people preparing for dinner, and one can imagine a train car gliding through the downtown atmosphere, ringing a jaunty bell.

Nowadays, there are more modern buildings, but the way the rails glow dully under the streetlights at dusk still conveys a sense of travel that has not changed over time. If you surrender to the sway of the train as it slowly moves under the Tosa sky that Ryoma would have looked up to, you will be reminded once again that this is the place where the soul of Tosa was born.

text_en:
Kamimachi 2-chome. This bus stop is located just a few hundred meters from 1-chome, where Ryoma Sakamoto was born, in a place where Tosa's history is even more densely looming. Opened in 1902, this place is close to the site of the pawnshop and kimono shop Saitaniya run by Ryoma's ancestors, giving the impression that the footprints of young people who dreamed of the Meiji Restoration are still hidden beneath the cobblestones.

During its heyday in the Showa era, a single old train car carried people's daily lives and ran smoothly through the streets that had a downtown atmosphere. Today, it is a quiet residential area and lined with shops, but the sound of the brakes of trains sliding into the stop somehow brings back the nostalgic twilight of the Showa era. It makes us realize once again that this railway, which has continued to run through the ages under the sky that Ryoma would have looked up at, is the bond that connects the spirit of Tosa.

text_en:
Kamimachi 4-chome. This stop is located at a perfect spot, passing through the area associated with Sakamoto Ryoma to the west, where the vestiges of the castle town mix with the scent of daily life. Since its opening in 1902, this place has a history of quietly watching over the comings and goings of people as a key point in the west of the town, which bears the formal name of Kamimachi.

As you stand at the bus stop, you can almost hear the bustle of the Showa era, when there were many kimono merchants and rough goods shops, and the appearance of Tosa's traditional merchant houses remains even stronger than it is now, overlaid with the sound of the train bells in the distance. Although it has now turned into a calm residential area, the remains of the cobblestones that line the tracks and the shadows of the old buildings give us a faint sense of the glory of the past.

At dusk, a train emitting an orange light, making a joint sound, leaves in the direction of Kagamikawa. The unadorned appearance from the back represents the aesthetics of Tosa's daily life, which remains unchanged even with changing times.

text_en:
Kamimachi 5-chome. This bus stop is located at the western edge of the Kamimachi district, known as the place associated with Ryoma Sakamoto, where the atmosphere of a castle town finally blends with the scent of daily life. Since its opening in 1902, this place has played the role of an ``exit'' and ``entrance'' to the city, seeing off people heading west from the ``castle area'', giving you a sense of its history.

In the past, the area around this area had the name ``Mizudori-cho'' (Mizudori-cho), and the clear flowing water and the peaceful lives of the people who surrounded it blended into the scenery of running streetcars. In the Showa era, the sight of a train passing away with the lights pouring in from the rows of shops illuminating the rails at dusk, carrying the chatter of shoppers was the very aesthetic of Tosa's daily life.

Today, there are more modern buildings, but the sound of the departure bell still echoes as it did back then. Its unpretentious appearance reminds us of the origins of travel in today's world where efficiency is all we seek.

text_en:
Asahi-machi 1-chome. This is a stop located on the border of the train, which passes through the old streets of Kamimachi and finally heads west towards Kochi. As the name ``Asahi'' suggests, since its opening in 1901, this place has a history of playing an important role as a gateway to the western commercial hub, which developed with the force of the rising sun.

In the Showa era, the area was dotted with bases of the Ministry of Communications (currently Japan Post) and small factories, and the trams ran along with the energy of the working people. The vibrant colors of the store signs visible from the train window were the very heartbeat of a local city. Nowadays, large commercial facilities have been built nearby, and the scenery of the city has changed, but the sight of a train car leisurely passing in front of people waiting for a crosswalk signal still represents the aesthetics of Tosa's daily life.

At dusk, the headlights of trains coming from the distant Asahimachi 3-chome area dye the rails a golden yellow. This quiet scene suddenly reminds us of the passion of the Showa era, which we had left behind.

text_en:
Asahi Ekimae Dori (Asahi Ekimae Dori). The stop is located at a key point where land transportation intersects, where the streetcar travels west along National Route 33 and the road to Asahi Station on the JR Dosan Line branches north. Since its opening in 1902, this place has served as a relay point connecting the city center of the prefectural capital, Kochi, and the western suburbs, and you can feel the history of this place, which has watched over many travelers and students.

If you turn your gaze north from the bus stop, you will see a straight road leading to Asahi Station, which still retains the atmosphere of the old wooden station building, where you can still feel the lingering scent of the lively shopping district of the Showa era. It used to be crowded with people switching from trains to streetcars and vice versa, and it maintained its pride as a hub to the west of Tosa. Nowadays, it has the appearance of an educational district with Kochi University nearby, and the lively footsteps of young people harmonize perfectly with the old trains that look like old soldiers.

When a train car slides in with the sound of its joints bouncing, and the wind pressure of a JR express train in the distance caresses our skin, we can deeply experience the ``crossroads of travel'' woven together by two railroads here in the Asahi region.

text_en:
Asahimachi 3-chome. As a base in the west of Kochi City, it was once touted as the ``downtown district of the west,'' and the stop is located at the point where the city's vitality was most concentrated. Since its opening in 1902, this place has been the center of the Asahi district, and as a strategic point on the road leading to Ino, it has a history of watching over the comings and goings of people for nearly 120 years.

In the golden age of the Showa era, movie theaters were lined up around the bus stop, and the brightly colored signboards and bustling restaurants brought a unique atmosphere to the entire town. The streetcars constantly carried young people coming to enjoy the latest movies and housewives busy shopping for dinner, fulfilling their role as the ``heart of the West.''

Nowadays, the number of large stores has increased and the appearance of the town has changed little by little, but the sight of a train rolling in at dusk with the sound of joints echoing through the streets still gives us a sense of the aesthetics of Tosa's daily life. If you gaze at the glow of the rails while being blown by the breeze from the buildings, you can rediscover in this land of Asahi the ``city's body temperature'' that has been lost in today's pursuit of efficiency.

text_en:
Firefly Bridge. Passing through the bustle of Asahi Town, the bus stop with its elegant name stands at this point where the murmuring of the Kagami River begins to faintly reach your ears. When it first opened in 1902, as the name suggests, countless fireflies danced in the waterway that flowed around this area, creating a fantastic parade of lights on summer nights, giving you a sense of its history.

In the Showa era, the sight of students going to nearby schools getting off at this stop and walking across the bridge while chatting was a symbol of the peaceful daily life of a local city. Nowadays, houses are densely packed, and the former calm of the waterfront has been replaced by the hustle and bustle of the city, but when you feel the breeze from a train passing by a stop, you can still feel the faint lingering scent of Kochi, the City of Water.

From here on, the railway finally leaves the road and enters a dedicated track, and the feeling of traveling deepens even further. As we watch a train car run off to the west with the sound of its joints bouncing, the name Hotabashi reminds us of the ``heart of admiring the seasons,'' which we have almost forgotten in our modern era of efficiency.

text_en:
Kagami River Bridge. The key point is located at the point where the hustle and bustle of the city that started from Harimaya Bridge comes to a temporary end with the clear murmuring of the Kagami River. Since its opening in 1902, this railway has a history of supporting Tosa's railways, serving as a turning point for many lines and as an important node on the long journey to Ino in the west.

When you get off the bus stop, the Kagami River, also known as ``Tosa's River of Life,'' flows slowly in front of you, and the wind blowing across the surface of the river cools down the heat of the train. It vividly brings back to me the scene of the Showa era, when on holidays, families playing on the riverbank and big bosses casting their fishing lines would land one after another at this bus stop, enjoying a peaceful afternoon.

Although it has now been replaced with a modern bridge and the surrounding scenery has changed, the profound sound of a train approaching the bridge with its chiming bell still represents the same feeling of railway travel. Escape from the hustle and bustle of the city and listen to the sound of the clear stream as you wait for the next train. This quiet time allows us to rediscover the ``peace of mind'' that modern people, who seek only efficiency, have forgotten.
