text_en:
Kabe. After crossing the Kagamikawa Bridge, the spacious double-track section comes to an end, and the stop is located at the ``gate'' of the single-track section that finally leads to Ino. Since its opening in 1902, this place has a history of narrow streets and crowded private houses, providing a breath-taking ``life-style'' landscape that even non-tram fans can take their breath away.

The sight of the trains running past the eaves of houses, which has not changed since the Showa era, clearly shows that the city and the railway breathe in the same rhythm. The sight of oncoming cars and trains literally coming and going shoulder-to-shoulder presents a unique landscape that combines the robustness and emotion of the Tosa people, something that cannot be seen in today's well-organized city planning.

As we watch the single-track rails disappear into the dusk, in a modern era where only efficiency is pursued, it is these railways, where this spirit of ``compromise'' lives on, that makes us question what true wealth is.

text_en:
Akebono-cho Higashimachi (Akebono-chohigashimachi). After passing Kagamikawa Bridge, the track, which has changed from double track to single track, finally enters the heart of a residential area, and this humble stop appears as soon as it passes. Since its extension in 1900, this area has a history of being at the forefront of watching the process of the countryside on the western edge of the castle town evolving into a modern city.

The area to the north of this area was once the vast grounds where the 44th Infantry Regiment was stationed, giving it the appearance of the military capital of Kochi, where the sound of military boots echoed. After the war in the Showa era, when the site was transformed into Kochi University, the color of the town changed completely, and the cheerful voices of students carrying textbooks began to mix with the sound of train horns. The sight of a train moving cautiously along a narrow road, keeping in sync with oncoming traffic, makes us feel strongly that we are part of a big family, the local community.

In the evening, young people gather at the bus stop after finishing their lectures and are sucked into the old, pale cars. While this scene foretells the dawn of a new era, it also recreates the nostalgic after-school experience of the Showa era in the Reiwa era.

text_en:
Akebono-cho (Akebono-cho). Located right in front of the main gate of Kochi University, this bus stop is full of its own unique vibrancy as it serves as the gateway to the school where young academic students gather. At the time of its extension in 1902, the area north of here was the training ground of the 44th Imperial Army Infantry Regiment, and the sound of military boots once dominated this area, giving us a sense of the changes in history.

After the war, the site was transformed into Kochi University, and elegant school buildings replaced the boring barracks, and the streetcar came to play the role of a ``corridor of knowledge,'' transporting young people's dreams and heavy textbooks. Of particular note is the truly modest ``safety zone'' that is simply painted green on the road. The way an old train, cars passing by, and students chatting all coexist in perfect harmony on the narrow streets of the single-track section, and this is a true testament to the generous nature of the Tosa people.

At dusk, students walk up the steps of the train after finishing their lectures. This image reminds us that it is a sight of youth that has not changed since the Showa era, and at the same time, it is a railway of hope that continues into the future of Reiwa.

text_en:
In front of Asakura Station. Asakura Station on the JR Dosan Line is located between Shiko, and the stop is located at the point where the train tracks and tram tracks are closest to each other. Since its extension in 1901, this area has fulfilled its role as an important node for transferring to trains, which are responsible for wide-area transportation, on road trips connecting the prefectural capital, Kochi, and Ino in the west.

Once you get off at the bus stop and follow the few steps that lead to the JR station building, you'll be greeted by the unique excitement of the beginning and end of a journey, a feeling that hasn't changed since the Showa era. From the days when steam locomotives once emitted white smoke, to today's Reiwa era, when limited express trains rush by, the streetcars slide in front of this station at the same speed, giving us a sense of the history of welcoming travelers.

The cheerful footsteps of students attending nearby Kochi University, the stately JR station building, and a single train moving modestly along the road. These ``sceneries where trains blend into daily life'' will allow you to rediscover the ``joy of movement itself'' that has been lost in the efficiency-driven modern world, here in Asakura.

text_en:
Asakura. The single-track section that continues from Kagamikawa Bridge has been a temple town since ancient times and was once the center of Asakura Village, giving it an even deeper atmosphere. Since the extension of the line in 1900, this area has a history of protecting the pulse of the railway as an important exchange base that supports the operation of the Ino Line.

What is particularly eye-catching is the way the trains above and below face each other in the middle of a narrow road, passing each other with spectacular breathing. The town was once crowded with students commuting to school and visitors to the ancient temple Asakura Shrine, and the atmosphere of the Showa era, when the entire town was enveloped in the intimate atmosphere unique to streetcars, can still be felt in the creaking sounds of the rails. It is also the connection point with the JR Dosan Line, and the unique liveliness of the intersection of the two "iron roads" of trains and trains gives it a sense of pride as a transportation hub.

A train car slowly opens its doors, shoulder to shoulder with the cars. This scene is a powerful demonstration of the importance of coexistence between the city and the railway in this era of Reiwa, in a modern era where efficiency is all the rage.

text_en:
In front of Asakura Shrine. As the train leaves the hustle and bustle of Asakura Station and heads west along the narrower single-track section, the lush green forest of Asakura Shrine, famous as Tosa's Ninomiya shrine, approaches the train window. Since its extension in 1902, this area has served as an entrance to the sacred precincts and as a footpath to a quiet temple town, giving you a sense of its history of nearly 120 years.

When you get off the bus stop and look up at the torii gate, you will see a stately shrine designated as an important cultural property, and the ``modern railway'' of the tram transports travelers to a place of worship since the Middle Ages.The vivid contrast between these two is thrilling. During the Showa era, during the annual autumn festival, flags would be fluttered along the roadside, and the shrine grounds would be filled with energy as worshipers got off the train.The sights that still make you feel like they are blending into the creaking sound of the rails.

The former countryside has been transformed into a residential area, but the time spent waiting for the train with the silence of the old shrine in the background is a valuable place that brings back the ``calmness'' to our hearts in modern travels that seek only efficiency.

The inner part of the shrine. The stop is located in a place where, after passing the majestic forest of Asakura Shrine, the train finally cuts into the literal ``road of life,'' as if it were just passing by the eaves of a house. Since its extension in 1900, this area has been a sacred place and a means of modest living for the local people, giving you a sense of its nearly 120-year history.

During the Showa era, this area still had a rural landscape, with the wind blowing across the rice fields through the train windows in early summer, and golden ears of rice lining the rails in autumn, creating an idyllic scene. Today, the area is crowded with residential buildings, but the sight of a single-track train suddenly appearing at the end of an alley and a train sliding into it still conveys the ``intimate distance between people and the railway'' that modern urban planning has forgotten.

As dusk approaches and warm light begins to leak through the windows of the houses, watching the back of the train as it rolls away with the sound of joints reverberating through it will help you rediscover the completely natural psychology that traveling is not just about rushing to the destination.

text_en:
Inside the mouth. This stop, located near the top of a steep mountain pass that runs from Kochi City to Ino Town, has a strong sense of ``mountain tranquility,'' which is rare for a streetcar station. Since its extension in 1900, this area has quietly played a role as a boundary between two towns, watching over travelers crossing the difficult slope of Hamanai-zaka.You can feel the history here.

Once upon a time in the Showa era, the feeling of relief you felt at the moment you climbed the hill panting with your weak motor roaring, and finally pulled into this green stop brings back powerful memories of the days when railroads challenged the natural terrain. In the surrounding area, remnants of the roads of yesteryear still remain, and the sound of train horns echoing through the valley before disappearing gives us the illusion that time has stopped in this day and age, where efficiency is all that is sought after.

The moment when you start descending from the top of the mountain pass to the town of Ino, the feeling of anticipation for the new scenery that spreads out from the train window is the greatest gift that this land of Hamanai can give to travelers.

text_en:
Kitayama. This stop is located where the single-track rail finally approaches the outskirts of Ino town, looking towards Ino, the final stop. Since its extension in 1901, this area has a history of supporting the lives of local people as a quiet residential area nestled in the mountains to the north, as its name ``Kitayama'' suggests.

In the Showa era, clear waterways ran through this area, and people transporting raw materials for Tosa washi paper and students attending nearby schools can be seen anxiously awaiting the arrival of trains. Currently, a modest safety zone with only a painted road surface has been established in a limited space on the side of the road, but this ``close sense of distance between railways and daily life'' is the true essence of the travel spirit that Tosa's streetcars have preserved for over 100 years.

At dusk, the headlights of a train coming over the mountain pass of Konai in the distance paint a single line of rail a golden yellow. It is in these casual everyday fragments that the warmth of the Showa era that we are looking for is alive.

text_en:
Yashiro-dori Street. This stop is located in a quiet place where a residential area and a highway intersect, just before the town of Ino begins to reveal its core. Since the extension of the line in 1902, this area has quietly served as the ``inner entrance'' to Ino, the village of Tosa washi paper, and you can feel its history.

During the Showa era, residential land development progressed in this area, and in the morning and evening the single-track rails echoed with the cheerful footsteps of commuters heading to the center of Kochi City and students attending nearby schools. The modest and graceful appearance unique to streetcars, where the ``platform'' is simply a white frame line drawn on the road, clearly conveys the intimate sense of distance between people and traffic, which is not found in modern giant station buildings.

When you stand at the bus stop and look west toward Ino, the mountains become even closer, giving you the illusion that you can hear the bells of the horse-drawn carriages that used to transport kozo, the raw material for Japanese paper, mixed in with the train horns. In today's world, where only efficiency is valued, the sight of an old train car leisurely crossing the streets of daily life in Tosa is the most luxurious moment in daily life.

Nakayama. The town of Ino is finally approaching its center, and this stop is located along the way, where the single-track rails weave past the eaves of houses. Since its extension in 1900, this place has been located at the entrance to Ino, the village of Tosa washi paper, and you can feel the history of having continued to play a role as a link to the lives of local people for nearly 120 years.

Once upon a time in the Showa era, the smell of steaming raw materials for washi paper wafted through this area, and the sight of handmade washi paper drying through the window of a train coming through the back alleys was a common sight. This is a modest stop on a narrow road with just a painted color on the road. The sight of a single train car sliding into the space with the sound of its joints bouncing through it conveys the intimate ``temperature'' between people and the railway that modern railway systems do not have.

Recently, the surrounding houses have been given a new look, but at dusk, when you listen to the distant chiming of bells, you will be reminded once again of the beauty of Tosa's daily life, which remains unchanged no matter how the times change.

text_en:
In front of Ino Commercial. The town of Ino is finally nearing its final destination, and the stop is located at this point, where youthful energy is overflowing from the train window. As the former ``Washi Paper Town of Ino'' strengthened its character as a place of education and education after the post-war period of high economic growth, this bus stop has a history of continuing to transport young patriots and ``budding businessmen'' attending the local Ino Commercial High School.

During the Showa era, when it was time to go to school, I could vividly imagine the students who lined up on a single train, carrying large bags as they descended on this humble safe zone, and their lively laughter wafting through the streets. The peaceful atmosphere of the single track section and the passion of young people dreaming of the future. It is this contrast that creates the unique travel atmosphere of this place.

Lately, the sounds of the creaking rails have been echoed by the shouts of students engaged in extracurricular activities, and even as we move into the Reiwa era, the sight of streetcars that continue to protect our school buildings continues to present us with the unchanging glow of youth.

Kitauchi. As the final stop, Ino, approaches, this stop is located on the way as the single-track rail moves forward, shyly but proudly past the eaves of houses. Since its extension in 1900, this area has served as the eastern gate of Ino town, which flourished as the village of Tosa washi paper, and has a history of closely monitoring the daily lives of local people.

Back in the Showa era, the smell of drying washi paper wafted around this area, and streetcars ran between rows of houses with a downtown atmosphere, as if they were sewing. Even today, if you stand in a modest safety zone just drawn out on the road, the closeness to the people passing by will remind you of the warmth of a time when the railway was more like a ``family'' than a ``public tool.''

In modern travel, where efficiency is valued, a train car leisurely crosses the roads of everyday life, making joint noises. This casual daily life is the crystallization of the culture that Tosa's streetcars have preserved for over 100 years.

text_en:
Namikawa. A journey along this railway, which retains the scent of the Showa era, can be described as a time slip brought back to the present day. These lines, where the powerful roar of steam locomotives once echoed and supported people's lives and industry, still quietly weave memories of each region.

For example, that small station nestled quietly in the mountains. It used to be a bustling gateway to the region, carrying the hopes and dreams of many people. The nostalgic scenery depicted on the hanging paper of the station bento, the warm gaze of the station staff. It makes you feel that time is passing at a slower pace, which is a clear contrast to the fast-paced modern lifestyle.

The lives of the people connected by this railway, the lively festivals unique to the area, and the changes in the industries that support the local economy. While unraveling them, we carefully collect the stories that live at each station. Such journeys are the real pleasure of our goal of ``a railway travelogue that tells the story of the Showa era in the Reiwa era.''

text_en:
Ino. It is the final station full of atmosphere, where the journey on Japan's longest tram line, which continues from Harimaya Bridge, finally comes to an end. Since its opening in 1900, this place has been the center of Ino Town, known as the production area for Tosa Washi, one of Japan's most famous papers, and you can feel the history of the paper, which once played a key role in transporting raw materials such as kozo and mitsumata, and transporting finished washi to Kochi, the prefectural capital.

The sight of the train carefully following the single-track rails, passing through rows of old houses, and finally arriving at the train is filled with a sense of calm and relief, like a traveler quietly taking off his cloak after a long journey. With the clear waters of the nearby Niyodo River in the background, Niyodo River paper carp streamers float through the sky every May, and the entire town is enveloped in the joy of the festival, a symbol of Tosa's pride that continues to this day.

At that moment when we stare at the stop at the end of the train and see the glow of the rails fade, we can once again experience the depth of the 120-year story that a single train has told us here in Ino.

product_en:

Tosa washi paper made in the clear waters of the Niyodo River is thin, strong, and beautiful. The warmth and gentleness that can only be felt from natural materials as soon as you hold them in your hands resonates with your heart in this digital age. Send it to your loved ones along with the sound of Tosa's clear streams. It is a traditional craft that makes such luxury come true.
product_fr:

La chaleur et la douceur que l’on ne peut ressentir que dans les matériaux naturels dès que vous les tenez entre vos mains résonnent avec votre cœur à l’ère du numérique. Envoyez-le à vos proches avec le son des flux clairs de Tosa. C’est un artisanat traditionnel qui permet de réaliser un tel luxe.

The weight of history, where many patriots once dreamed of Japan's future from this land, can be felt in the vibrancy of today. The statue of Sakamoto Ryoma stands dignified in the station square, inviting travelers to the romance of the end of the Edo period.

In recent years, the railway has been elevated and the station building has become more modern, but once you step outside, you can see the liveliness of the Sunday Market held every week and the spirit of the Yosakoi Festival, which the whole town gets excited about in the summer, continuing to convey the vitality of this area. It is a land where the charms of old and new are exquisitely fused, giving visitors a deep sense of travel.

text_en:
Kochi Bridge. Every time I visit this place, the scent of the Showa era fills my heart. In the past, this station was a lifeline that connected the region's vibrant industry and people's lives. The warmth of the station building's old wooden structure and the unique tranquility that emanates from it give you a sense of the unique atmosphere of train travel, which remains unchanged even with the changing times.

In recent years, new initiatives have been implemented to make use of local specialties, such as selling fresh local vegetables and processed products inside the station, and mini-concerts are held on weekends.The station and the local area are deepening their interaction in a way that is completely different from its former vibrancy. Amidst these changes, it is very amusing to see a glimpse of the Showa era at a momentary moment.

text_en: Hasuikecho Street. This tram stop, which stands quietly on the Tosa Electric Railway tracks that run from east to west through the center of Kochi City, is a place that is like a microcosm of the times, where old townscapes and new breath intertwine. It once prospered as a center of commerce, retaining the vestiges of the feudal era, and you can still hear the hustle and bustle of the shopping street, which still retains its vitality. Every time the trams pass by with their rattling noises, it evokes a sense of nostalgia and makes you feel a deep sense of travel. There is also a road to Kochi Castle nearby, and it is very interesting to see Tosa's history and modernity coexisting together in the daily scenery of tourists and local residents coming and going. Especially during the summer Yosakoi Festival, this area is sure to be filled with excitement.

text_en: Ume no Tsuji bus stop. On the Sanbashi Line, which runs north-south through the city of Kochi, this stop has a unique ``corner'' feel to it. It was probably once a place to take a breather before crossing the clear stream of Kagami River. When a tram approaches a curve while shaking its body, the high-pitched ``squeak'' sound of the flange being scraped echoes around the street corner. It can be said to be the very everyday music played by urban transportation in the Showa era. When I look at the old merchant houses and calm rows of houses in the area, I am enveloped in a strange sense of nostalgia, as if the flow of time is becoming a little sticky here. As I stand at this crossroads, surrendering myself to the rhythm of Tosaden, I am reminded once again that trams are the blood vessels of the city.

text_en: Sanbashi-dori 1-chome. The tram that has traversed the city of Kochi slips into its final destination with the scent of the sea, and is the final stop on the Tosaden Kotsu Pier Line, a place where you can feel the beginning and end of a journey at the same time. This port town, which once flourished as the gateway to Tosa and a base for deep-sea fishing, still has a somewhat open atmosphere and is full of lively activities. From the Meiji period to the Showa period, many goods and people departed or returned from here, and the breath of history is still alive in the modern cityscape. The scenery of the old pier and the sight of the trams coming and going makes you feel the romance of a bygone era. It's also fun to stare blankly at the sea while being blown by the sea breeze.

As you watch the cars making their way to the port with their whistles blaring loudly, you can feel the sea breeze reliving the memories of those who boarded ships from this pier long ago.

This line, which was once a bustling gateway to Kochi Port and carried many goods and people, is now a leisurely route for tourists and citizens alike. product_ja:
土佐あかうし（精肉・ステーキ用）
高知港を望む南北線の終点。ここでご紹介するのは、年間数百頭しか出荷されない「幻の和牛」土佐あかうしです。黒毛和牛とは一線を画す、きめ細やかな赤身の旨味。脂が重すぎず、噛むほどに肉本来の濃厚な味わいが溢れ出します。ステーキで焼けば、その香りは甘く芳醇。土佐の豊かな山々が育んだ、美食家垂涎の至宝です。
product_en:
Tosa Akaushi (for meat/steak)
The terminal point of the Namboku Line overlooking Kochi Port. What we would like to introduce here is Tosa Akaushi, the ``phantom Wagyu beef'' of which only a few hundred cows are shipped each year. The delicate flavor of the lean meat sets it apart from Kuroge Wagyu beef. The fat is not too heavy, and the more you bite into it, the richer flavor of the meat overflows. When grilled with steak, the aroma is sweet and mellow. A treasure grown in the rich mountains of Tosa that will be coveted by gourmets.
product_fr:
Tosa Akaushi (pour viande/steak)
Le point terminal de la ligne Namboku surplombant le port de Kochi. Ce que nous aimerions vous présenter ici, c'est le Tosa Akaushi, le « bœuf Wagyu fantôme » dont seules quelques centaines de vaches sont expédiées chaque année. La saveur délicate de la viande maigre la distingue du bœuf Kuroge Wagyu. La graisse n'est pas trop lourde et plus vous la mordez, plus la saveur riche de la viande déborde. Lorsqu'il est grillé avec un steak, l'arôme est doux et moelleux. Un trésor cultivé dans les riches montagnes de Tosa qui sera convoité par les gourmets.
product_tw:
土佐赤牛（肉/牛排）
俯瞰高知港的南北線終點站。這裡要介紹的是每年只有幾百頭的「幻影和牛」土佐赤牛。瘦肉的細膩味道使其與黑毛和牛不同。脂肪不算太重，越咬下去，越濃鬱的肉味溢出來。與牛排一起烤時，香氣甜美醇厚。生長在土佐富饒山區的珍寶，令美食家垂涎欲滴。

name_en: In front of Uji housing complex
text_en:
In front of Uji Danchi. After passing through Edagawa, the town of Ino is finally starting to show its true potential, and we arrive at this stop whose name is reminiscent of the Showa era's period of high economic growth. When the railway to Ino was first opened in 1900, the surrounding countryside and the fields of kozo and mitsumata, which are the raw materials for washi paper, were the main characters.However, as the demand for housing increased after the war, a new town called ``danchi'' was formed in this hilly area.You can feel the history of this area.

When you get off the bus stop, you will see a number of houses lined up at the foot of the mountain, and the single-track rail that runs modestly between them, which clearly tells the story of Ino's history as a suburb of a regional city. In the past, trams continued to transport people who moved to this area with hopes for a new life in their hearts, even on rainy and windy days, and have played the role of literally ``travels'' that supported the lives of Tosa.

At dusk, when the lights begin to illuminate in the windows of the housing complex, a train makes a joint sound as it slides toward its final stop, Ino. This scene quietly conveys the warmth of people rushing home to their families and the strength of the Showa era to the present Reiwa era.

text_en: Edagawa stop. By the time you get to this point, the tram journey to Ino takes on an intimate atmosphere that is closer to that of a ``light rail'' than a ``trail''. The sight of a single track laid unreliably in one corner of the road still conveys the simple appearance of pre-war local private railways. The heavy rails of the JR Dosan Line run right next to it, but the tram runs at the same level as the people passing by, almost brushing past the eaves. At dusk, when the lights of the houses begin to come on, the sight of the single-track railway stretching forever gives travelers an indescribable sense of solitude and peace. In today's world where efficiency and speed are sought after, this ``gentle'' journey embodies the gentle nature of railways.

text_en:
Narutani. Just before entering the town of Ino, this humble stop is located next to a single-track track that skirts the foot of the mountain. Since its extension in 1900, this area has served as a quiet border of Ino, the village of Tosa washi paper, and has seen the comings and goings of many craftsmen and their families for nearly 120 years, giving you a sense of its history.

During its heyday in the Showa era, the area around here had a scene reminiscent of a ``craft town,'' with the sound of water washing the raw materials for washi paper echoing from somewhere, and paper glistening white as it dried in the sun from the train windows. Nowadays, the number of houses has increased and the town has taken on a new look, but the withered atmosphere created by the wild flowers blooming next to the railroad tracks and the well-worn overhead wire poles still conveys the ``weight of life'' that has been forgotten by today's sophisticated urban transportation.

The train rang a light bell as it began to slide towards the western terminus. If we look at their leisurely steps, we can quietly savor the ``time to appreciate the four seasons'' that we have almost lost in the efficiency-oriented modern world.

text_en:
In front of Ino Station. The station overlooks the JR Dosan Line's Ino Station building, and is located at such an intimate distance that the train tracks and tram tracks seem to be touching each other's body heat. Since its extension in 1900, this area has served as the main entrance to Ino Town, which flourished as the ``Tosa Washi Village,'' giving you a sense of its history as an important node connecting the trains that provided wide-area transportation with the trains that supported the region.

In the Showa era, the station was lined with wholesalers and shops selling Japanese paper, and the bustle of merchants and students carrying large luggage was the epitome of the vibrancy of a local city. Nowadays, the surrounding landscape has changed little by little, but the sight of a single train car sliding in with the sound of its joints bouncing and the wind blowing from the JR express train at its back shows the unique travel atmosphere created by the two railways.

In this town where you can feel the presence of the clear Niyodo River nearby and the history of paper making is still alive, the role of the tram continues to be the ``memory of life'' in Tosa.

text_en:
Sukumo station. The journey that begins at this terminal station overlooking Sukumo Bay on the western edge of Tosa is a continuation of the grand dream of the ``Shikoku Loop Railway,'' which was once envisioned by Japan National Railways but never realized. This railway, which was finally completed in 1997 as the Sukumo Line, runs smoothly over modern elevated bridges, giving us a glimpse of a time when railways tried to connect us to the future.

When the train crosses the iron bridge over the Shimanto River, which is famous as ``Japan's last clear stream,'' and passes through Nakamura and enters the Nakamura Line heading towards Kubokawa, the atmosphere outside the train window changes completely, and now we are greeted by a somewhat nostalgic rural woodland scene filled with history dating back to the days of Japan National Railways. On the other hand, if you turn your attention to the Gomen-Nahari Line, which stretches east across Kochi City, you will find a spectacular view of the rough waves of the Pacific Ocean up close, and a cheerful tropical atmosphere greeted by twenty people and twenty-colored characters. Elevated lines made with the latest civil engineering technology and the atmosphere of a good old regional railway. Tracing the railway that bears the name ``Kuroshio'' from end to end is a journey that reconsiders the passion of the railway workers who continued to challenge the harsh terrain of Shikoku, and the pride that the railway still has in working with the local community.

text_en:
Sukumo. It is the terminal station of the Tosa Kuroshio Railway Sukumo Line, and is the ``end of the land,'' so to speak, where the railway ends its mission at the southwestern tip of Shikoku. The grand dream of the Shikoku Loop Railway, which was once supposed to connect to Uwajima in Ehime Prefecture, has come to an end here as the elevated train reaches a dead end, but this creates an indescribable sense of travel that is unique to this terminal station.

Although it is a relatively new station, having opened in 1997, the moment you step onto the platform, you can feel the humid tropical breeze blowing through you, and feel the pride of a port town that once prospered through trade in Sukumo Bay. In winter, the ``Daruma Sunset'', in which the setting sun refracts over the ocean and forms a shape similar to a daruma doll, dyes Sukumo Bay vermilion and quietly touches the hearts of travelers who have made the long and arduous journey to reach the destination.

Around the station, the Sukumo Civic Festival is a lively event in the fall, conveying the passion and vibrancy of the people of Tosa to this day. If you look up from the elevated car stop to the space that seems to continue to the sky, you will feel that the end of the railway is actually the beginning of a new story that continues beyond the Bungo Channel to Kyushu.

Fillets and processed products of "Kibinago" from Sukumo Bay

Pickled in oil or dried overnight, the flavor of the small fish and the aroma of the ocean burst out the more you bite into it, making it the perfect accompaniment to local sake. This is a masterpiece filled with the passion of Sukumo, the rich sea where the sun sets.

Filets et produits transformés de « Kibinago » de la Baie de Sukumo
Sukumo, le point terminal du chemin de fer. Le « kibinago » pêché dans la baie de Sukumo est appelé le « joyau de la mer » en raison de sa beauté. Marinés dans l'huile ou séchés pendant la nuit, la saveur du petit poisson et l'arôme de l'océan éclatent au fur et à mesure que vous le mordez, ce qui en fait l'accompagnement parfait du saké local. C'est un chef-d'œuvre rempli de la passion de Sukumo, la mer riche où le soleil se couche.

When you arrive at the platform, you will see a calm cityscape that retains the vestiges of the castle town of the past. Higashi Sukumo is practically the center of the city, close to the administrative and cultural centers of Sukumo City. Hirata. It is an elevated station located approximately in the middle of the Tosa Kuroshio Railway Sukumo Line, which suddenly appears in the mountains at the western end of Kochi Prefecture. This area once had a prosperous history as a transportation hub connecting Nakamura and Sukumo, and with the opening of the entire line in 1997, it finally received the blessings of modern railways.

Akakameyama Enkoji Temple, the 39th sacred temple of Shikoku, stands quietly not far from the station. The sound of the sticks of pilgrims walking on the old pilgrimage route intersecting with the sound of the engine of a modern stainless steel vehicle creates a strange atmosphere in which old and new forms of travel intermingle. The idyllic countryside that surrounds the area is a testament to the rich soil of Hirata, which has long been known as a rice producer.

In autumn, the train quietly slides through the rippling golden ears of rice, and the view from the window reminds us of the original scenery of the Showa era that we have forgotten somewhere. In the mornings and evenings, the cheerful voices of local high school students echo through the platform, reminding us that this unmanned station is still an important hub of daily life that supports the pulse of the region. This place retains the atmosphere of a dignified climate that seems to have resisted becoming a flashy tourist destination.

Once you get off the elevated platform, you will see the Sukumo Industrial Park spreading out below you, as the name suggests, but it is by no means a noisy place, but rather a calm and quiet place surrounded by the mountains of Shikoku. The contrast between the station name, which pursues functionality, and the rustic countryside that surrounds it, makes travelers think deeply about the coexistence of modern society and nature.

In the neighborhood, when spring comes, the cherry blossoms along the Nakasuji River add color and gently envelop the concrete texture of the railway. Despite being shaken by the rebuilding issue of the former Japanese National Railways, the sight of this railway, connected by the passion of local people, still supporting daily life gives us an irreplaceable sense of travel.

This station, which was founded in 1997 when the entire Sukumo Line was opened to traffic, is a reminder that it was once a vantage point from which to watch over this rich land, as its name suggests, ``viewing the country.''

Once you get off the platform, you can see an unobstructed view of the countryside, and the scenery of Tosa's nature, which changes with the seasons, is a feast for the eyes of travelers. The grand dream once envisioned by the Japanese National Railways to circumnavigate Shikoku has now been entrusted to a one-car train that supports the lives of local people, and is being quietly but powerfully engraved.

In autumn, the golden ears of rice ripple, and the ridgelines of the mountains in the distance blend into the setting sun. This gives us a strong sense that there is indeed a depth of ``time'' that has been forgotten in the city. Although there are no flashy sights, this quietness and the view from the train window are the most luxurious aspects of traveling on the Sukumo Line.

When you stand on the platform, you can see the bustling cityscape lined with large commercial facilities and stores below, and you can see that the local economy is thriving. However, when you turn around, you can see the Shimanto River flowing leisurely and the deep greenery of the mountains approaching, giving you a sense of the original landscape of a regional city where city and nature coexist.

Stainless steel diesel cars now run along the footprints of pilgrims who once walked this land, making a gentle sound. text_en:
Nakamura. It is the gateway to this town, known as Tosa's Little Kyoto, and once served as the terminal station of the National Railways Nakamura Line, and currently serves as the core of the Tosa Kuroshio Railway, it is responsible for the tourist attractions of the southwestern tip of Shikoku. Since its opening in 1972, this station has welcomed and sent off travelers seeking the ``last clear stream'' of the Shimanto River.

When you step off the platform, the modern design, made with plenty of locally grown cypress, conveys the spirit of the Reiwa era, but behind it are the traces of the grand dream of a long time ago, the Shikoku Round Railway. In November, the city is lit up with lanterns for the ``Ichijo Festival'' in memory of Lord Ichijo, giving you a sense of the unique character of this area, where the elegance of court noble culture and the passionate spirit of Tosa are mixed.

If you take a short walk from the station and sit down on the banks of the Shimanto River, you will be able to feel the breeze crossing the surface of the river gently caressing your broken heart in the city. Civilization connected by railways and the silence of nature that will never be invaded. In this mysterious balance lies the essence of Nakamura.

Shimanto eel (kabayaki/shirayaki set)
“Little Kyoto” Nakamura. Shimanto eel, grown with the blessings of the Shimanto River, is characterized by its thin skin and surprisingly plump flesh. When you add wasabi and soy sauce to Shirayaki, you can directly feel the purity of the meat nurtured by the clear waters of Shimanto. It is truly a masterpiece worthy of being called the king of freshwater.
product_fr:
Anguille Shimanto (ensemble kabayaki/shirayaki)
"Petit Kyoto" Nakamura. L'anguille Shimanto, cultivée avec la bénédiction de la rivière Shimanto, se caractérise par sa peau fine et sa chair étonnamment charnue. Le kabayaki est grillé lentement avec une sauce secrète et fond en bouche, avec la douceur du gras élégant. Lorsque vous ajoutez du wasabi et de la sauce soja au Shirayaki, vous ressentez directement la pureté de la viande nourrie par les eaux claires de Shimanto. Furutsuga. This station, which appears at the east end of the city just after the railway starts accelerating again from Nakamura towards Kubokawa, is a relatively new ``Seikatsu Station'' that was born after the changeover in 1988. When the former National Railways Nakamura Line was reborn into the third sector, it was established in response to the urgent needs of local residents.

The platform is located on top of an embankment, surrounded by residential areas and schools, allowing you to feel the daily life of the citizens up close. Although there are no flashy tourist attractions, the lively voices of high school students commuting to and from school echo through the platform in the morning and evening, giving a strong sense that this railway is not just a means of transportation, but the heartbeat of the city itself.

If you look up while waiting for your train, you'll see the deep mountains of Shimanto in the distance, and realize that an unchanging natural environment is living right next to a modern residential area. In its simple structure, which excludes ornate decorations, the precious role that railways should play in ``bonding with the local community'' is quietly but surely engraved.

text_en:
West side. On the way back from Nakamura to Kubokawa, you can see the vast Pacific Ocean on the right side of the train window, and you will arrive at this unmanned station with no decorations. This station was founded in 1975 when the entire line of the National Railways Nakamura Line opened, and since then it has been a quiet stop where the sound of the waves and the sea breeze dominate, close to the sea of ​​Tosa where the Kuroshio Current dances.

When you get off the platform, you will see the magnificent sandy beach of ``Irino Kaigan'' on the other side of the windbreak pine trees. This place is famous as a surfing mecca where wave riders from all over the country gather, and the sight of young people carrying colorful boards disembarking at the station adds a modern touch to the old concrete structure. Nearby, there is also the ``Sand Beach Museum'', a stylish attempt to turn nature into art without buildings, and it gives you a sense of the deep respect and playfulness towards the sea that the local people have.

Where once smoke-belching locomotives ran through this land, now a single diesel car runs lightly through it. There, the eternal time, like the waves that come and go, and the small sense of travel carried by railways, which do not change even with the changing times, are still alive.

text_en:
Tosa Irino. As the train heads east along the Pacific Ocean from Shimanto City, spray from the Kuroshio Current dances as the train travels, and the scent of the salt creeps into the train. This station, which opened in 1972 when the entire National Railways Nakamura Line opened to traffic, was once the central station of Ogata-cho, and has taken on the heavy responsibility of supporting local industry and tourism.

The station building has a warm wooden design, and the atmosphere of the local people is still preserved here. As soon as you step out of the station, you will be greeted by the deep greenery of Irino Matsubara and the magnificent four-kilometer sandy beach that awaits you. Every May, a ``T-shirt art exhibition'' is held on the sandy beach, with thousands of T-shirts flapping in the sea breeze, and the unique philosophy of a ``sandy beach art museum'' without a building broadens and deepens the hearts of visitors.

Steam locomotives once ran through this area, leaving their soot in the pine forest, but now nimble diesel locomotives cut through the sea breeze. Young people with surfboards and families enjoying clam hunting breathe the same air, and the sound of the train blends into their daily melody. Even in the Reiwa era, this scene still retains the travel spirit of the Showa era, and makes us feel the richness of train travel.

product_ja:
天日塩「土佐の塩丸」
美しい入野海岸の砂浜のすぐそばで、火を一切使わず「風と太陽」の力だけで結晶させた、完全非加熱の天日塩。ミネラルがそのまま残った大粒の結晶は、単に塩辛いだけでなく、甘みと深いコクを感じさせます。お取り寄せしたお肉やトマトにパラリと振れば、素材の味が驚くほど際立つ。太平洋の潮風そのものを味わうような、贅沢な調味料です。
product_en:
Sun-dried salt “Tosa Shiomaru”
Completely unheated solar salt crystallized right next to the beautiful sandy beaches of the Irino coast using only the power of the wind and the sun, without using any fire. The large crystals, with their minerals intact, are not only salty, but also sweet and deeply rich. If you sprinkle it on the meat or tomatoes you have ordered, the taste of the ingredients will be amazing. A luxurious seasoning that makes you feel like you can taste the sea breeze of the Pacific Ocean.
product_fr:
Sel séché au soleil « Tosa Shiomaru »
Du sel solaire totalement non chauffé s'est cristallisé juste à côté des belles plages de sable de la côte d'Irino en utilisant uniquement la force du vent et du soleil, sans utiliser aucun feu. Les gros cristaux, avec leurs minéraux intacts, sont non seulement salés, mais aussi sucrés et profondément riches. Si vous en saupoudrez sur la viande ou les tomates que vous avez commandées, le goût des ingrédients sera étonnant. Un assaisonnement luxueux qui vous donne l'impression de goûter la brise marine de l'océan Pacifique.
product_tw:
曬鹽“土佐鹽丸”
完全不加熱的太陽鹽就在入野海岸美麗的沙灘旁結晶，僅利用風和太陽的力量，不使用任何火。這些大晶體中的礦物質完好無損，不僅鹹，而且甜，味道濃鬱。如果把它撒在你點的肉或西紅柿上，食材的味道會令人驚嘆。奢華的調味料，讓您彷彿品嚐了太平洋的海風。

text_en:
Floating whip. The station stands alone in a place where the railway curves gently along the coastline of Tosa, where the rough waves of the Pacific Ocean crash. This station, which was established in 1960 when the National Railways Nakamura Line opened, preserves the memories of the railway on the southwestern tip of Shikoku, where steam locomotives and diesel express trains once ran through while being sprayed by the Kuroshio Current.

When you land on the platform, you can hear the powerful roar of the ocean directly reaching your ears, beyond the pine trees that serve as windbreaks. The place name ``Ukibuchi'', which has a somewhat fantastical and literary sound, brings to mind the history that once flowed here, and the ephemeral yet beautiful scenes of travel, like the foam of waves that come and go. This area, once known as the base of Tosa whaling, has now transformed into a sacred place for surfing, where surfers from all over the country gather, and the sight of young people in wet suits sitting on the benches of unmanned stations gives us a sense of modern Kuroshio culture.

National highways and railways run right next to the station, and the endless Pacific Ocean. The view from the train window created by these elements is exactly what Shunzo Miyawaki loved, ``Japan beyond the train window.'' There are no luxurious station buildings or station lunches, but the smell of the ocean, the sound of train joints, and the railroad tracks that stretch to the horizon. That alone is more than enough luxury for those who love trains.

text_en:
Welcome to the sea king. The name of the station has such a majestic and poetic sound that it makes travelers want to straighten their heads. Although it is a relatively new station on the Tosa Kuroshio Railway's Nakamura Line, having opened in 2003, its name is rooted in a grand historical legend in which Shinno Kaneyoshi, the son of Emperor Go-Daigo, washed ashore in this area at the end of the Kamakura period and was warmly welcomed by the locals.

Once you step off the platform built on the elevated platform, you will be able to see the horizon of the Pacific Ocean washed by the powerful Kuroshio Current, beyond the pine trees that serve as windbreaks. A single-car diesel train now runs along the sandy beach where the imperial family might once have descended, echoing the sound of its light engine. There, medieval legends and modern railway structures create a mysterious harmony under the sunlight of Tosa.

The area around the station has been developed as a sports park and serves as a regional promotion base, but once you feel the sea breeze, you are transported back to a space dominated by the roar of the sea, which has remained unchanged since ancient times. Although it is a nameless stop, the pride of ``welcoming the king'' engraved in its name creates a dignified atmosphere suitable for the final stage of a journey.

text_en:
Tosakamikawaguchi. It is a small station in a fishing town that has the atmosphere of the remotest area, where the roar of the Pacific Ocean can be heard passing through the windbreak pine trees and reaching the platform. When the National Railways Nakamura Line opened its entire line in 1971, how much joy was there at having the railway brought to this area? This simple platform still quietly embraces the memories of steam locomotives venturing out soot as they braved Tosa's difficult terrain.

Near the station is the port of Kamikawaguchi, known as the town of bonito, and the faint scent of the sea wafting on the wind lets you know that this is a base for men of the sea. Every summer, the excitement of the Kamikawaguchi Minato Festival engulfs the city, and the fireworks that decorate the night sky paint the rails of the quiet, unmanned station in vermilion. The contrast between that moment of gaiety and the silence that follows the festival is what gives us the real pleasure of traveling by train.

In recent years, the number of visitors has decreased, and time has become quieter, but if you sit on the bench on the platform and listen to the sound of the waves, you will feel that your heart, worn out by the hustle and bustle of the city, is being healed by the deep compassion of Tosa. There is nothing here, but there is plenty of time here. I can't help but feel deeply moved by the fact that the thin thread of civilization called railways still connects this small port town to the rest of the world.

text_en:
Ariigawa. Even on the Tosa Kuroshio Railway Nakamura Line, it is a truly luxurious station where you can feel the presence of the sea up close and from a high vantage point. When the National Railways Nakamura Line opened in 1971, a railway was brought to the area near this cliff, and the view afforded by this station greatly surprised even railway fans at the time.

Once you land on the platform, you will be greeted with an unobstructed panoramic view of the Pacific Ocean, and the soothing rhythm of the sound of the powerful white waves of the Kuroshio grazing the rock surface. In contrast to the hustle and bustle of National Route 56, which runs directly below, this station on a hill is dominated by a luxurious silence, with only the sound of the sea and the wind. If you think about the history of steam locomotives that once braved this slope and were splashed by the waves as they headed for Nakamura, you will be reminded of the weight of the railway, which is more than just a transit point.

Although the area has become increasingly depopulated in recent years, just sitting on the old bench in the corner of the platform and gazing out at the rounded horizon will make you feel the fatigue of your travels fade away. There's nothing, just the sea, the sky, and the railroad tracks. This simple aesthetic is the greatest charm of Tosa's railways, which has remained to this day.

text_en:
Tosa Shirahama. It is a small station with a truly open feel, with the blue folds of the Pacific Ocean spreading out below you and the sound of the sea riding up to the elevated platform on the wind. When the National Railways Nakamura Line carved a railroad along this rugged coastline in 1972, the station that bore the name ``Shirahama'' was created as the perfect setting to capture the beauty of Tosa's sea from the train windows.

The station itself is located on an embankment, and there are only quiet villages dotted around it, but the vastness of Tosa Bay seen from the platform is powerful enough to make you forget the hustle and bustle of the city. The white-sand beach that gives it its name is a short walk away, but just sitting on a bench at the station and looking out at the rounded horizon makes you realize the significance of the railway's arrival in this area.

Steam locomotives used to cross this hill, spewing black smoke, but now only one diesel car runs lightly over it. Times have changed, but the scent of the ocean and the regular sound of the rails tapping remain the same. The melodies woven through these lines vividly provide us with the ``peace of mind'' that we seek when traveling by train, even in this Reiwa era.

text_en:
Saga Park. The stop is located between Tosa Saga and Tosa Shirahama, on a hill overlooking the Pacific Ocean, and is literally integrated with the park. This station, which was established in 1988, when the lifeblood of the railway was transferred from Japan National Railways to the third sector, was born with new expectations for connecting tourism and a place of relaxation for the local area.

When you arrive at the platform, the magnificent panoramic view of Tosa Bay spreads out below you. The rising and falling white wave crests of the Kuroshio Current reach your ears like the powerful heartbeat of Tosa. While the sea breeze occasionally carries the sounds of laughter from families visiting the adjacent Tosasaga Seaside Park, if you stand alone on the empty platform, the roundness of the horizon will quietly remind you of the size of the Earth.

Saga is a brave fishing town known for ``bonito pole-and-line fishing''. Today, only one diesel car runs lightly through this rich ocean, where whales once migrated. The blue sea reflected in the train window gives us the feeling that the ``traveling spirit at the extreme'' that Shunzo Miyawaki loved has been preserved in this Reiwa era.

There are no flashy station buildings or shops, but you can hear the sea breeze, the sound of waves, and endless rails. That alone is more than enough luxury for anyone who loves trains.

text_en:
Tosa Saga. This area, which was founded in 1966 as the terminal station of the National Railways Nakamura Line, still maintains its stately and dignified character as a key point on the railway that runs through southwest Shikoku. Once you arrive at the platform, you will be greeted by the unique breeze that mixes the scent of the ocean with the smell of deep greenery, which is unique to this town with mountains in the background and views of the ocean.

This is a town where you can enjoy pole-and-line fishing for skipjack tuna, which silences crying children. Every time a limited express train comes to a stop with the roar of its engine, the memories of the days when steam locomotives and diesel express trains used to cross these difficult points are brought back vividly under the Reiwa sky. In May, the ``Tosa Sagakatsuo Festival'' is held, and the fragrant smell of roasting straw and the energetic voices of fishermen echo throughout the town, giving you a sense of the profound passion of the people of Tosa.

I bought a ticket at the station counter and quietly waited for the train to arrive. This is where the weight of "time" that railways have shared with local communities, which has been forgotten by modern society in its pursuit of efficiency, is still alive and well. As you savor a piece of tataki and think about the future of the railway, you will be reminded that this journey is more than just transportation, it is a microcosm of life.

明神水産・藁焼き鰹のたたき
「カツオの町」として知られる佐賀。ここで水揚げされた一本釣りの鰹を、熟練の職人が豪快な炎で焼き上げます。藁の強い火力で表面を一気に炙ることで、皮目は香ばしく、中はとろけるような「レア」の状態に。お取り寄せの冷凍パックを解凍すれば、鼻を抜ける藁の香りと、溢れ出す濃厚な旨味が、自宅の食卓を一瞬にして土佐の漁師町へと変えてくれます。
product_en:
Myojin Fisheries Seared Straw-grilled Bonito
Saga is known as the "town of bonito." The pole-and-line caught bonito caught here is grilled over a powerful flame by skilled craftsmen. By searing the surface all at once using the strong heat of the straw, the skin becomes fragrant and the inside becomes melt-in-your-mouth rare. When you thaw the frozen pack you ordered, the aroma of straw that permeates your nose and the rich flavor that overflows will instantly transform your dining table into the fishing town of Tosa.
product_fr:
Bonite grillée à la paille poêlée de Myojin Fisheries
Saga est connue comme la « ville de la bonite ». La bonite pêchée ici à la canne est grillée sur une flamme puissante par des artisans qualifiés. En saisissant la surface d'un seul coup à l'aide de la forte chaleur de la paille, la peau devient parfumée et l'intérieur devient fondant dans la bouche. product_tw:

text_en:
Iyoki. With the Tosa-Saga sea at its back, the train passes through the Iyoshi Tunnel, which is over 1,600 meters long, and is suddenly enveloped in the silence of the mountains, where the station seems to be hidden. This station, which was built in 1965 when the National Railways Nakamura Line took its first steps, is a reminder of the struggle of our predecessors who sought a railway in the narrow valley where the end of the steep Shikoku Mountains drops into the Pacific Ocean.

Once you arrive at the platform, the roar of the Kuroshio Current disappears, and in its place all you hear is the sound of the wind passing through the valley and the chirping of nameless birds. Surrounded by deep greenery, this small station makes us feel more strongly than anything else the simple mission of railways, which is to ``cross mountains and connect villages.'' It makes you feel that the transparency of the air surrounding the station has not changed at all since the days when steam locomotives would pant through the tunnel and leave behind a trail of soot and smoke in this valley.

There are several private houses nestled quietly around the station, where the simple daily life of the mountain village of Tosa is alive and well. When a local train with just one car comes to a quiet stop while a limited express train zips by, we feel a strange sense of peace, as if we are disconnected from the modern world of efficiency. Although there are no flashy tourist attractions, this place, where expectations for the unknown that spreads out on the other side of the tunnel intersect with regret for the scenery that has passed, evokes an atmosphere that is perfect for the setting of a travelogue.

text_en:
Kaina. It is a truly modest, unmanned station that sinks into the deep greenery as you cross a steep mountain pass from Kubokawa to Tosasaga. In 1965, when the National Railways Nakamura Line attempted to climb this difficult area, a ``loop line'' was established that gained altitude while drawing a circle along the mountain surface, and this station was placed at the end of the spiral. The way the train moves as if chasing its own tail is the result of a tenacity that brought together the best of the civil engineering technology of the time.

Once you arrive at the platform, you will be greeted by the deep mountains blocking your surroundings and the cool breeze blowing up from the valley floor. The name of the station comes from an ancient place name, but it has a warm, human sound that makes it seem like it symbolizes the life of this quiet mountain village. In recent years, it has become a place where only limited express trains rush past, but the moment when you wait for the joint sound of a train passing through the loop line makes you reaffirm the ``strength to overcome hills'' that railways originally have.

In this space, away from the hustle and bustle of civilization, where only railroad tracks and mountains stand against each other, the simple travel spirit that we had almost forgotten is still alive.

text_en:
Wakai. Away from the urban area of ​​Kubokawa, it stands in the mountains overlooking the clear waters of the Shimanto River, serving as a practical turning point where the fates of the Yodo Line and the Nakamura Line diverge. This small station, which was founded in 1966 with the opening of the National Railways Nakamura Line, does not have an ornate station building, but it exudes a quiet atmosphere as a ``node of travel'' where two railway lines intersect.

When you arrive at the platform, the slow flow of the Shimanto River, the last clear stream, spreads out below you, and the wind blowing across the river carries the scent of Tosa's mountains. Fireflies dance in the neighborhood in early summer, and autumn leaves decorate the railroad tracks in autumn. Its tranquil appearance gives the impression that it has preserved the original scenery of good old Japan, as if it had been cut off from the modern railway network that emphasizes efficiency.

The Yodo Line runs from here to Uwajima in Ehime, or the Nakamura Line heads for Sukumo. No matter which train you wait for, a moment at this unmanned station with the breeze blowing through it has a mysterious magical power that makes you reaffirm the purpose of your journey. More than just a passing point, this small platform is filled with the sense of solitude and exhilaration that is unique to places where railways intersect.

text_en: Kubokawa Station. Located in the southwestern part of Kochi Prefecture, this station is the terminus of the Dosan Line and the starting point of the Tosa Kuroshio Railway Nakamura Line, and is truly a key railway hub and a gateway for travelers. Since its opening in the early Showa era, countless trains have passed through this area, and even though it changed form into the third sector in the Heisei era, it has continued to hold on to the dream of a line that continues to the Pacific Ocean. Upon landing at the platform, travelers are enveloped in a clean air that makes them feel the majesty of the Shimanto River flowing in the distance, and their hearts are filled with anticipation for the next adventure and nostalgia for the past. The station building is lined with shops selling locally produced ingredients, and although it is a small station, it conveys the vibrancy of the area. This is a rare space where the history of railways and the joy of traveling towards the future are condensed.

product_ja:
四万十ポーク 桜味噌漬け
予土線の起点、窪川。ここで育つ「四万十ポーク」は、四万十川の清流と豊かな自然の中で、芋を食べて育つ贅沢な豚です。その身は驚くほど白く、脂身の甘みが格別。特製の桜味噌に漬け込まれた肉を焼けば、香ばしい香りが鼻をくすぐり、口の中で肉汁がじゅわっと溢れ出します。四万十の滋味をそのまま凝縮したような、力強い味わいです。
product_en:
Shimanto Pork Pickled in Sakura Miso
Kubokawa, the starting point of the Yodo Line. The "Shimanto Pork" that is grown here is a luxurious pig that is raised on a diet of potatoes in the clear waters of the Shimanto River and in the rich nature. The flesh is surprisingly white, and the sweetness of the fat is exceptional. When you grill the meat marinated in the special cherry blossom miso, the fragrant aroma tickles your nose and the meat juices overflow in your mouth. It has a powerful taste that seems to have concentrated the flavor of Shimanto.
product_fr:
Porc Shimanto mariné au Sakura Miso
Kubokawa, point de départ de la ligne Yodo. Le « porc Shimanto » cultivé ici est un porc luxueux élevé avec un régime de pommes de terre dans les eaux claires de la rivière Shimanto et dans la riche nature. La chair est étonnamment blanche et la douceur du gras est exceptionnelle. Lorsque vous faites griller la viande marinée dans le miso spécial aux fleurs de cerisier, l'arôme parfumé vous chatouille le nez et le jus de viande déborde dans votre bouche. Il a un goût puissant qui semble avoir concentré la saveur du Shimanto.
product_tw:
櫻花味噌四萬十豬肉
窪川，淀線的起點。這裡種植的「四萬十豬肉」是在四萬十川的清澈水域和豐富的大自然中以馬鈴薯為食飼養的名貴豬。果肉出奇的白，脂肪的甜味也異常鮮美。當您燒烤用特製櫻花味噌醃製的肉時，香氣撲鼻，肉汁溢滿口腔。味道濃鬱，似乎濃縮了四萬十的味道。

text_en:
Gomen (sorry). The name of this station, located in the center of Nankoku City, where the JR Dosan Line and Gomen Nahari Line share a firm handshake, is engraved with its historic pride as a tax-free area dating back to the Edo period. At the end of the Showa era, the dream of a railway that was once interrupted came to fruition in 2002 as a magnificent elevated line, and this is the story of how it became the majestic starting point, and is truly a symbol of the restoration of railways.

At the platform, ``Gomen Ekio-kun'', created by Takashi Yanase, cheerfully welcomes travelers wearing a bright red uniform. In keeping with its name, the town is also home to many humorous cultural activities such as ``Sorry for the Postcard,'' which gives you a sense of the deep-heartedness and playfulness of the Tosa people.

Comparing the old platform of the Dosan Line, where steam locomotives would have once smoked, and the modern elevated platform where state-of-the-art diesel locomotives await, as passengers busily come and go to transfer trains, one can feel the connection of the past through the railways and the hope for tomorrow.

product_ja:
澁谷食品「高知特産 芋けんぴ」
「土佐の菓子といえば、これ」と誰もが口を揃える芋けんぴ。南国市の老舗・澁谷食品が作るそれは、契約農家で育てた黄金千貫を良質な油で揚げ、秘伝の砂糖を纏わせただけの潔い逸品です。ポリポリと噛みしめるたびに広がる、素朴な芋の甘みと香ばしさ。一度食べ始めたら、袋が空になるまで止まらない、土佐人の情熱を形にしたようなおやつです。
product_en:
Shibuya Foods “Kochi Specialty Imo Kenpi”
``When you think of sweets from Tosa, this is the one,'' everyone says. Produced by Shibuya Foods, a long-established store in Nankoku City, it is a pure and exquisite dish made by frying Kogane Sengan, grown by contracted farmers, in high-quality oil and sprinkling them with a secret sugar coating. The simple sweetness and aroma of sweet potato spreads with every bite. Once you start eating it, you won't stop until the bag is empty, a snack that embodies the passion of the Tosa people.
product_fr:
Shibuya Foods « Spécialité Kochi Imo Kenpi »
«Quand vous pensez aux bonbons de Tosa, c'est celui-là», dit tout le monde. Produit par Shibuya Foods, un magasin établi de longue date dans la ville de Nankoku, il s'agit d'un plat pur et exquis préparé en faisant frire du Kogane Sengan, cultivé par des agriculteurs sous contrat, dans une huile de haute qualité et en le saupoudrant d'un enrobage secret de sucre. La douceur simple et l’arôme de la patate douce se répandent à chaque bouchée. Une fois que vous commencerez à le manger, vous ne vous arrêterez plus jusqu'à ce que le sac soit vide, une collation qui incarne la passion du peuple Tosa.
product_tw:
澀穀食品“高知特產芋堅皮”
「當你想到土佐的糖果時，就是這個，」每個人都說。由南國市的老字號澀穀食品公司生產，將簽約農戶種植的小金仙岩用優質油煎炸後，撒上秘製糖衣而成的純正精緻的菜餚。甘藷的簡單甜味和香氣，每一口都瀰漫開來。一旦開始吃，就不會停下來，直到袋子空為止，這是體現土佐人熱情的零食。

text_en:
Gomen Town (Gomen Town). Deeply connected to Nankoku City, it is truly a wonderful juncture where the elevated diesel cars and the streetcars crawling along the road come together as if sharing memories old and new. The desolation of the day when the Tosa Electric Railway Aki Line disappeared in 1960 was replaced by the even more lofty sound of the railway with the opening of the Gomen-Nahari Line in 2002, making us feel the drama of history.

When you step onto the platform, you will be enveloped by the atmosphere of the town loved by Anpanman's father, Takashi Yanase, along with the smiling face of the station character Gomen Machiko-san. The sight of old Tosaden Kotsu trains ringing their bells as they head towards Kochi City from the tram stop under the elevated bridge gives you the illusion that you have been transported straight from the Showa era into the present day.

The sound of ``gomen'' derived from the place name gives the impression that the modesty of the Tosa people coexists with a sense of playful playfulness. Transferring to the tram at this station while feeling the breeze from the sea slows down your journey and gives you a luxurious sense of space.

text_en:
Tateda. Located on an elevated line that cuts through the peaceful rural landscape of Nankoku City, this station, which was once reborn in 2002 and bears the vestiges of the Tosa Electric Railway Aki Line, which was abolished in 1960, now plays the role of a node between the air and the land. When you land on the platform, the roar of jet planes taking off and landing right next to you splits the sky, making you very aware that you are in close proximity to Kochi Ryoma Airport.

The station character ``Tateda Sora-chan'' welcomes you with a refreshing appearance that symbolizes a yearning for the sky, while the wartime ``entaigo'' dotted around the area quietly convey the weight of history. The sky is filled with the latest aircraft, and the railroad tracks are chock-full of diesel cars. The scenes created by these contrasts remind us of the depth of travel, which is often forgotten in the changing times. In this land where the conveniences of civilization intersect, the nostalgic scent of earth wafting in the sea breeze gives you a sense of the travel spirit that is unique to Tosa.

text_en:
Noichi. This station, which is central to the bustle of Konan City, wonderfully connects memories of the days when the Tosa Electric Railway Aki Line ran leisurely to the present day. After suffering a profound loss when the line was closed in 1960, the heartbeat of the railway resounded in this area in 2002, which was truly the fulfillment of a long-cherished wish for the local residents.

As soon as you get off the platform, you can feel the vibrancy of families heading to the nearby Noichi Zoological Park or the Shikoku Automobile Museum, where famous cars from yesteryear are lined up, giving you a sense of a traveler's spirit. This is also the place where the ``Chindon Contest'', which is rare even in Japan, is held, and the station character ``Noichindonman'' welcomes you in a flashy costume, symbolizing the brightness of this town.

Beyond the mountains that spread out behind the modern station building lies the Ryugado Cave, which is full of ancient mysteries, and makes you feel that the railway, a tool of civilization, and the unchanging nature coexist with an exquisite sense of distance. The sight of a single diesel car hurriedly discharging passengers and running eastward once again conveys the strength of local private railways working together with the local community in this Reiwa era.

product_ja:
冬のスイカ「ルナ・ピエナ」
冬にスイカを食べる贅沢を。香南市夜須町を中心に栽培される「ルナ・ピエナ」は、一つの蔓に一個だけを残し、空中に吊るして太陽の光を全身に浴びさせた究極のスイカです。驚くべきはその糖度とシャリッとした食感。真冬の冷たい空気の中、こたつで味わうこの甘みは、まさに「満月（ルナ・ピエナ）」のような輝きを放つ、高知が誇る芸術品です。
product_en:
Winter watermelon "Luna Piena"
Enjoy the luxury of eating watermelon in winter. ``Luna Piena'', which is cultivated mainly in Yasumachi, Konan City, is the ultimate watermelon, with only one watermelon left on each vine and suspended in the air to bathe the whole body in sunlight. What is surprising is its sugar content and crisp texture. Enjoying this sweet treat under the kotatsu in the cold air of midwinter, it is a work of art that Kochi is proud of, and it shines like a full moon (Luna Piena).
product_fr:
Pastèque d'hiver "Luna Piena"
Profitez du luxe de manger de la pastèque en hiver. La « Luna Piena », qui est cultivée principalement à Yasumachi, dans la ville de Konan, est la pastèque par excellence, avec une seule pastèque laissée sur chaque vigne et suspendue dans l'air pour baigner tout le corps de soleil. Ce qui surprend, c'est sa teneur en sucre et sa texture croustillante. Savourer cette friandise sous le kotatsu dans l'air froid du milieu de l'hiver, c'est une œuvre d'art dont Kochi est fier, et elle brille comme une pleine lune (Luna Piena).
product_tw:
冬季西瓜“Luna Piena”
享受冬天吃西瓜的奢華。主要在甲南市安町種植的「Luna Piena」是終極西瓜，每根藤上只剩下一個西瓜，懸浮在空中，讓全身沐浴在陽光下。令人驚訝的是它的糖含量和鬆脆的質地。在隆冬的寒風中，在被爐下享受這甜蜜的享受，就像滿月（Luna Piena）一樣閃耀，是高知引以自豪的藝術品。

text_en:
Yoshikawa. A modern elevated station suddenly appears in the midst of the idyllic countryside of Konan City. The fact that this new railway, revived in 2002, is quietly carrying on the memories of the Tosa Electric Railway's Aki Line, which was once abolished in 1960, gives us a sense of the strange fate of railways.

When you arrive at the platform, you will see a group of plastic greenhouses soaking up the Tosa sun. This is a land where flower cultivation and vegetable production are flourishing, and the strong efforts of the region can be felt through the sound of the rails. As the station character ``Yoshikawa Unagi-kun'' shows off, the area has long been known as a famous place for eel, and the fragrant vestiges of history can be felt to whet travelers' hunger.

As I watched the only diesel car disappearing behind the rice fields and the wind was blowing on the quiet platform, I realized that the traveling spirit of that day in the Showa era is still alive on this elevated track.

text_en:
Akaoka. This area, located near the center of Konan City, was once known as the largest small town in Japan, and it is a town filled with a truly mysterious charm, where the passion of Kinzo, a maverick painter at the end of the Edo period, still lingers in the air. The Tosa Electric Railway's Aki Line was abolished in 1962, and in 2002, a modern elevated railway was reconnected to this area, which once fell into silence, giving us a sense of the reincarnation of railways.

Every July, the many folding screen paintings that appear in the evening light invite the viewer to a mysterious world and tell the depth of the passion and karma of the people of Tosa. In addition, the heroic scenes of people gulping down large glasses at the Dorome Festival held on the coast give us a sense of the region's vibrant spirit. As you listen to the sound of a diesel car passing away while being watched over by the station character ``Akaoka Ekin-san,'' you begin to think of the railway, a tool of civilization, as a thin thread that connects good old tradition and the present.

product_ja:
土佐名物 どろめ（生しらす）
「どろめ祭り」で有名な赤岡。ここで獲れる新鮮なカタクチイワシの稚魚は、銀色に光り輝き、驚くほどプリプリした食感です。お取り寄せでは、最新の冷凍技術により、獲れたての鮮度をキープ。特製のぬた（ニンニクの葉の酢味噌）をたっぷりつけて口に放り込めば、土佐の海の荒々しさと清らかさが一気に押し寄せます。地酒との相性は言うまでもなく「最高」の一言です。
product_en:
Tosa specialty Dorome (raw whitebait)
Akaoka is famous for the Dorome Festival. The fresh young anchovies caught here are shiny silver and have an amazingly plump texture. When ordering, we use the latest freezing technology to maintain freshness. When you dip it in your mouth with plenty of our special nuta (garlic leaf vinegar miso), you'll be instantly reminded of the roughness and purity of Tosa's sea. It goes without saying that it goes well with local sake, and it can only be described as "excellent."
product_fr:
Spécialité Tosa Dorome (appât blanc cru)
Akaoka est célèbre pour le festival Dorome. Les jeunes anchois frais pêchés ici sont argentés brillants et ont une texture étonnamment charnue. Lors de la commande, nous utilisons la dernière technologie de congélation pour conserver la fraîcheur. Lorsque vous le trempez dans votre bouche avec beaucoup de notre nuta spécial (miso au vinaigre de feuilles d'ail), vous vous souviendrez instantanément de la rugosité et de la pureté de la mer de Tosa. Il va sans dire qu'il se marie bien avec le saké local et qu'on ne peut le qualifier que d'« excellent ».
product_tw:
土佐特產Dorome（生銀魚）
赤岡因多羅姆節而聞名。這裡捕獲的新鮮鳳尾魚呈現銀色光澤，質地豐潤。訂購時，我們使用最新的冷凍技術來保持新鮮度。當您將其與大量我們特製的nuta（蒜葉醋味噌）一起放入口中時，您會立即想起土佐海的粗糙和純淨。不用說，它與當地酒很相配，只能用“優秀”來形容。

text_en:
Kagami. The elevated station stands at the intersection of Konan City's lush greenery and the sea breeze-scented coastline, with a cool look on its face. Its history as a stop for the Tosa Electric Railway Aki Line, which was abolished in 1960, lies underground, but it was reborn as a magnificent elevated line in 2002, giving us a sense of the indomitable railway spirit of this area.

When you land on the platform, you can almost feel the sweet and sour scent of Yamakita mandarin oranges, a specialty of this area, wafting up on the wind. When you look around, you can see the waves of the plastic greenhouse glistening in the sunlight, and beyond that the Mother Pacific Ocean stretches out in blue. The station character, ``Kagami Mikan-chan,'' welcomes you with a smile like a ripe fruit, symbolizing the warmth of humanity fostered by Tosa's warm climate.

Just looking at the horizon as the only diesel car disappears into the evening makes me think deeply about the luxury of train travel.
