The hustle and bustle where many people once gathered for the construction of the dam is now filled with quiet murmurings.

Shinano Shiratori Station. As the name suggests, the graceful flow of the Chikuma River fills the train window, making you wonder if swans once rested their wings. It is a place on the Iiyama Line where you can encounter a particularly lyrical scenery, and the way the sunlight reflecting off the river surface illuminates the old platforms makes you feel like you are looking at a painting. The surrounding villages also preserve the scenery of good old Japanese farming villages, giving the illusion that time has stopped. It makes me feel that the essence of traveling is just getting off at these stations and watching the river flow.

Hirataki Station. Even though it is located at the bottom of a deep valley, it has a somewhat dignified atmosphere. The surrounding villages are small, and the station looks quiet, as if it is waiting for someone who is not supposed to come. If you think that pilgrims and merchants who once passed through this area heard the same sound of the river, you can understand how deeply rooted the railroad, a tool of civilization, is in the strata of history. The sound of a railroad crossing alarm echoing in the silence seems to be the only signal that connects the present and the past.

Yokokura Station. As the Shinetsu border approaches, the terrain becomes increasingly harsh, and the railroad tracks cling to the mountainside. When we think of the hardships faced by our ancestors who had their way blocked by heavy winter snow, we cannot help but have a deep respect for the way modern diesel trains effortlessly climb hills. Although the structure of the station building is simple, it makes us feel that it is an inevitable way to survive in this harsh natural environment. When you look up at the sky from the platform, it feels somehow low and heavy, which is a characteristic of the snow country.

Morimiyanohara Station. In 1945, the snowfall recorded at this station was 7 meters and 85 centimeters, which has now reached the level of legend. As the last station in Nagano Prefecture, and as a symbol of one of Japan's heaviest snowfall areas, its presence is overwhelming, and the monument that stands in the corner of the station conveys the awe of nature to this day. This difficult passage, where steam locomotives once had to clear the snow and emit black smoke, is now filled with the quiet sound of melting snow, but the tension of crossing this station still makes us feel the pride of railway workers.

Ashitaki Station. Although this is the first station to cross the prefectural border and enter Niigata Prefecture, the scenery is still dominated by the deep valley of the Chikuma River, which changes its name to the Shinano River once it enters Niigata. However, it is not just my imagination that the air smells humid and gives off a heavy presence that is unique to Echigo. There are few private houses in the surrounding area, and the station stands surrounded by the roaring sound of the river, but I can't help but think that its solitary appearance embodies the strong vitality of the Iiyama Line.

Echigo Tanaka Station. It is a small station that quietly gives you the feeling that you have crossed the Nagano prefecture border and stepped into Niigata prefecture. The platform lies nestled in the bosom of the river terraces created by the Shinano River, retaining some traces of the days when it opened as Iiyama Railway. The area is surrounded by well-organized rice fields, and in autumn, golden ears of rice sway in the breeze, welcoming travelers to Echigo's fruitful landscape. In the past, agricultural products were transported from here, and the remnants of the time when it was a base for people's lives can still be seen faintly alive in the silence of the empty waiting room.

Tsunan Station. It is the gateway to the center of Tsunan Town, which is known as one of the heaviest snowfall areas in Japan. The current station building has a hot spring facility attached to it, where you can enjoy the luxury of submerging your frozen body in hot water, but it is also a product of wisdom to overcome the harsh winters of this region. It once had a prosperous history as a hub for shipping across the Shinano River, and since the arrival of the railway, it feels like the tenacity of our predecessors who overcame this steep terrain is etched into the slope of the railway. When you stand in front of the station, you are reminded once again how pure the air is in this basin surrounded by mountains.

Echigo-Kado Station. This station overlooking the rapids of the Shinano River is a place on the Iiyama Line where you can feel the ruggedness of nature up close. As the name ``Shikawatari'' suggests, it is easy to imagine that it was once a hidden area where wild deer would cross the river. When you stand on the platform, you find yourself in a world dominated only by the sheer cliffs on the opposite bank and the sound of the rushing river, and you feel as if you have been left behind by modernization. The strong livelihood of people who cultivate a small amount of arable land is felt in the small villages around the station, and it touches the hearts of travelers.

Echigo-Tazawa Station. It was once the main entrance to Nakazato Village, and is a place where you can take a breather, where the Iiyama Line peeks out from the mountainous area into a slightly open plain. The area around the station is lined with buildings that give a sense of daily life, reminding us that railways still play an important role as part of local life. In winter, this region is covered with several meters of snow, and the sight of trains running through walls of snow carved out by snowplows can be said to be the very lifeblood of this snowy country. The appearance of the old wooden station building connects the travel sentiment of the Showa era to the present day.

Echigo Mizusawa Station. When you get off at this station, the first thing that catches your eye is the rural landscape of Uonuma that seems to go on forever. As befits the land that was once called ``Mizusawa,'' the clear water moistens the land and makes you feel that this is where the roots of growing Japan's best rice lie. The simple structure with just one platform actually accentuates the surrounding landscape, allowing you to enjoy the luxury of having nothing to obstruct the changing colors of each season. You can almost hear the earthy stories of the people who once used this station as their base for farming.

Tsuchiichi Station. Even though it faces the national highway, it maintains a tranquility that feels like it is removed from the worldly world, probably due to the unique atmosphere of this area. While its name is imprinted with the history of once being a market and a place for people to interact, today it is a modest haven that welcomes commuting students and a few travelers. The old storehouses and private houses dotted around the station give a sense of the bustle of the highway in the past, and the silence after the diesel cars leave is the most luxurious time at this station.

Tokamachi Station. It is the largest hub on the Iiyama Line, and currently serves as a connecting station with the Hokuetsu Express Hokuhoku Line, giving the appearance of a modern elevated station. However, once you step out of the station, you will find yourself in a textile town that was once famous for its ``Echigo Chijimi'' technique, and you will find yourself surrounded by a cityscape filled with layers of history. In the past, many freight cars gathered at this station, and traces of its prosperity can be seen in the spacious grounds, where specialty textile products were transported all over the country. Behind the hustle and bustle of modern transfers, the pride of the ``Snow City,'' which developed through the struggle against heavy snowfall in the past, still lingers on.

Uonuma Nakajo Station. This station is located at the point where the train leaves Tokamachi and enters the quiet countryside again. The ridgelines of the surrounding mountains are beautiful, and it can be said that it is a place that embodies the image of rich nature that the name ``Uonuma'' conveys. Whether it was the days when steam locomotives spewed smoke and ran through the streets, or the days of quiet diesel trains, the same beautiful sunset scenery has always graced the platforms, and we are relieved by the unchanging nature of train travel. It is a station that reminds us of the richness of nothing.

Shimojo Station. The pronunciation is ``Gejo'', but the sound has a somewhat old-fashioned feel. The area around the station is dotted with private houses with gables, which are typical of Echigo, and the strong architectural style that withstands the weight of snow is a testament to the harshness of life in this area. It may have once been crowded with people crossing from here to the other side of the Shinano River, but now it's a peaceful time, with only the cosmos and rape blossoms along the railroad tracks announcing the season. It can be said that it is a station with a gentleness that makes you come back to your senses and remember the scenery of your hometown during your journey.

Echigo Iwasawa Station. It can be said that this is the base where the Iiyama Line leaves the Chikuma River and approaches the final difficult point as it attempts to cross the mountains to finally join the Joetsu Line. The campus, which once had exchange facilities and was lively with trains passing by, is now quiet, but its spaciousness silently speaks of its former importance. The cold wind blowing down from the mountains makes us feel the depth of autumn in the northern countries, but it also sounds like a prelude to preparing us for the ``wall of snow'' that lies ahead.

Uchigamaki station. Hidden away in a deep valley created by the meandering of the Shinano River, this station is the most isolated and beautiful station on the Iiyama Line. If you look at the surrounding steep terrain, you can clearly see how difficult it was to build a railway in the past. There are only a few private houses around the station, and all you can hear is the murmur of the river and the voices of birds. Stopping for a few minutes in this place, which feels completely isolated from the hustle and bustle of modern society, provides an irreplaceable spiritual cleansing experience for modern travelers.

Echigo Kawaguchi Station. This station, which is the last stop on the Iiyama Line and joins the main line called the Joetsu Line, is a sentimental place where the end and beginning of a journey intersect. This area, where the Uono River and the Shinano River converge, has prospered as a transportation hub since ancient times, and reminds us of the days when steam locomotives came and went with their heavy sounds. The sight of a small diesel train on the Iiyama Line pulling up to the platform of the vast Joetsu Line gives me a sense of relief, like a child returning home to his parents after a long journey. When I get off the train here and gaze out at the mighty river, my journey on the Iiyama Line from Nagano comes to an end as a solid memory.

The Tadami Line. Departing from the historic castle town of Aizu-Wakamatsu and delving deep into the rugged heart of Oku-Aizu, this iron path was originally carved for the heroic endeavor of hydroelectric power development—a utilitarian origin that has, over time, blossomed into one of the world’s most poetic railway journeys, as it were. As the train skirts the serpentine bends of the Tadami River, the traveler is greeted by a series of soaring iron bridges that seem to stitch the emerald mountains together, allowing one to feel a profound harmony between human engineering and the untamed wild.

One cannot help but admire the indomitable spirit of this line, which triumphantly overcame the devastating floods of 2011 to see its full length restored to the public. In an age of clinical high-speed transit, the leisurely pace through primeval beech forests and mist-shrouded gorges offers a rare luxury—the chance to simply "waste time" beautifully, which is exactly what lures the wandering soul to this hidden corner of Japan. To cross the border via the long tunnels of Rokujurigoe and descend into the fertile lands of Uonuma is to experience a transition of light and landscape that feels almost cinematic. It is a journey that reminds us of the quiet dignity of the Showa-era railwaymen who fought the heavy snows to keep this lifeline open, a sentiment that still vibrates through the rails today.

Aizu-Wakamatsu Station. The final destination of the long Tadami Line journey is the majestic gateway to a castle town that survived the flames of the Boshin War and inherits the samurai spirit. Stepping onto the platform, the heavy scent of history and the pride of the recovered city turn weariness into a sense of achievement.

Nanukamachi Station. This area, with its impressive retro Western-style station building, is a stylish gateway to Aizuwakamatsu where the castle town culture remains. As you walk through the streets crowded with tourists, you can feel the chic atmosphere unique to this city where tradition and modernity intersect.
Streetscape of Nanokamachi Street. For a moment, a retro townscape filled with Taisho romance will pass by. You'll feel like you've traveled back in time.

Tsuruga Castle. Famed in history as an impregnable fortress, this castle is a monument inhabited by the indomitable soul of Aizu. Looking up at the red-tiled keep against the blue sky, the spirit of righteousness protected in this harsh climate straightens the posture of those of us living today.

Nishi-Wakamatsu Station. Bustling as a junction with the Aizu Railway, the energy of the castle town begins to reach the traveler here. The figure of Mt. Bandai in the distance powerfully announces that the journey's climax is near.
Aga River Bridge.

Aizuhongo Station. This historic station, which opened in 1909, continued to carry the exquisite porcelain of Aizu Hongo ware, which boasts a 400-year history, and flourished as a logistics base that supported the handicraft town. You can appreciate the richness of the culture created by railways while thinking about the smoke from the ancient climbing kilns.
Ears of rice in the Aizu Basin. In autumn, you can see the golden sea outside the window. This is the hometown of delicious Aizu rice and the plains that nurture life.
name_fr: Épis de riz dans le bassin d'Aizu

text_en: Aizu-Takada Station. It was the first terminal station reached by the railway from Aizu Wakamatsu in 1923, and has a proud history of flourishing as a town in front of Isasumi Shrine. The footprints of worshipers that have continued since the heyday of the Showa era quietly tell us the weight of the years that railways and faith have walked together.
Aizu Takada curve. At the end of the large, arching railway, the mountains in the distance line up beautifully, like the plot of a stage play.
Shooting location near Negishi Station. Can you see the people holding cameras next to the railroad tracks? This is the best photo spot on the Tadami Line, which is sought after by enthusiasts.
name_fr: Lieu de tournage près de la gare de Negishi
name_tw: 根岸站附近的拍攝地點

text_en: Negishi Station. The Koan Stone Pagoda, which stands near the station, is a valuable heritage that conveys the folk beliefs of the Kamakura period to this day, and is a place where you can touch the abyss of history. The rustic appearance of the unmanned station and the surrounding golden countryside will calm the hearts of travelers.

Shintsuru Station. Since its establishment in 1922, it has a glorious history of supporting the modernization of the region as a shipping base for specialty apples and Takada plums. Even now that freight handling has disappeared, the view of the mountains and countryside from the platform gives us the feeling that the memories of the richness brought by the railway remain vivid.

Wakamiya station. This station, which opened in 1933, is a place that truly symbolizes the original landscape of Mizuho no Kuni, with a sea of ​​rice ears stretching as far as the eye can see. The memories of rural people who once carried sacks of rice and longed for the city are still alive in this Reiwa era, along with the trains sliding across the golden carpet.

Aizu-Bange Station. Located at the entrance to the vast Aizu Basin, there is a sense of liberation as the railway, which has traveled through mountains, finally takes a breath. The rich rural scenery is a "Golden Sea" won by overcoming harsh nature, reflecting the pride of the Aizu people.

Todera station. This station, which opened in 1930 with the extension to Yanaizu, is like a guardian at the western end of the Aizu Basin, heralding the beginning of crossing a steep mountain pass. In the past, many pilgrims would get off at this station and head to the nearby Eryuji Temple (Tachiki Kannon), which reminds us of a time when faith and railways were closely connected.
Shichiori Pass. Listen to the sound of the train engine. We will powerfully climb the seven-fold mountain pass.

Aizu-Sakamoto Station. In Taisho 15, a railway was extended from Aizu Sakashita to this area, and it has a hidden history of being used as an entrance to Oku-Aizu by horse-drawn carriages and travelers on foot. The breeze that blows through the platform brings back memories of a time when it flourished as a key hub for freight transportation.

Aizu-Yanaizu Station. The gateway to this town, thriving since ancient times as a place of faith, is solemn yet filled with nostalgic warmth. The Akabeko figures in front of the station convey legends of saving the land from hardship, welcoming travelers gently.

name_ja: 福満虚空蔵尊 圓蔵寺
text_en: Enzo-ji Temple. Built as if protruding from a sheer cliff, this famous temple is the spiritual pillar of Aizu, having gathered prayers for over a thousand years. The flow of the Tadami River viewed from here quietly watches over human affairs while marking eternal time.
name_tw: 福満虛空蔵尊 圓蔵寺

text_en: Godo station. It opened in Taisho 15, and once supported the industrial history of the early Showa era as a material transportation base for the construction of Yanaizu Dam. When the entire line opens in 2022, the moment when the train horns reverberate across the mountains once again makes you feel like it was a historic moment when time in Oku-Aizu started moving again.

Takitani station. It opened in 1920 as the terminal station of the extension from Aizu Sakashita, and was once the entrance to Oku-Aizu, full of life and bustling with people and goods. The famous Takitani River Bridge is a testament to modernization and remains a historical heritage that still speaks to the spirit of Showa era craftsmanship.
Takitani River Bridge. It is one of the highest iron bridges on the Tadami Line. The bottom of the abyss is far below our feet. Enjoy a thrilling walk in the air.

Aizu Hibara Station. When the line was extended from Yanaizu to Miyashita in 1942, this station was built in a steep valley, and now it is the starting point for pilgrimages to the Daiichi Tadami River Bridge, a dream destination for photographers from all over the world. The fact that we have overcome the suspension of service in 2011 and will be able to see travelers seeking spectacular views from this station again in 2022 is a reminder of the universal appeal of railways.

name_ja: 第一只見川橋梁展望台
text_en: First Tadami River Bridge Lookout. When the train crossing the iron bridge reflects its form on the water, this place transforms into a "miraculous landscape" longed for by travelers worldwide. The contrast between the iron arch in the steep valley and the mountains changing colors with the seasons is a masterpiece of Japan's beauty.
name_fr: 第一只見川橋梁展望台
name_tw: 第一隻見川大橋展望台

text_en: Aizu-Nishikata Station. Located as the train moves toward the next mystery after crossing the bridge, this station is a sacred site for passionate railway photographers. Within the nameless scenery viewed from the platform, one feels the essence of the Tadami Line story.

Second Tadami River Bridge. Among the many bridges that span the Tadami River, the beauty of the arch's curves and the surrounding strangely shaped rocks are truly a collaboration between engineering and nature. The spectacular view that can be seen for just a moment from the train window will add vivid colors to your memories of your trip.

Aizu-Miyashita Station. The entrance to the massive bridges crossing the majestic Tadami River is where modern architecture and nature merge most beautifully. The path from here to the lookout is a pilgrimage to admire the ultimate structural beauty drawn by the rails.
Miyashita dam. A steady water surface. The blue of the sky and the green of the mountains are so transparent that it seems as if they continue all the way to the bottom of the river.

Third Tadami River Bridge. This bridge, which spans rapids and cliffs, is a masterpiece of railway engineering that silently conveys how difficult the construction of the Tadami Line was. Looking down from the train window and looking down at the deep blue of the valley, it gives you a sense of mystical fear and beauty at the same time that draws you in.

Hayato Station. Known as a "secluded station among secluded stations," the nearby "Mugenkyo" ferry carries people through the mist-shrouded Tadami River into an ethereal world. Disembarking and staring at the river, a deep silence makes time feel still, enveloping the soul.

Misty Gorge. The sight of river mist gathering in the morning and evening of summer and a ferry boat sailing into a mysterious world is truly the ultimate in fantasy, so much so that you forget about the real world. Carrying the memories of a once abandoned village, this place still captivates people's hearts, giving the impression that the spirit of the land dwells there.
Eight arches are lined up like glasses.

name_ja: 会津水沼のリフレクション
text_en: Reflection of Aizu Mizunuma. On windless days, the river becomes a perfect mirror. It's such a strange sight that you can't tell which side is the sky above or below.

Aizu Mizunuma Station. This station, which opened in 1955 in conjunction with the Aizu Kawaguchi extension, was once a lively wood distribution area and a post station for people involved in power development. After being damaged by heavy rains in 2011, the entire line was reconstructed in 2022, which truly symbolizes the history of the Tadami Line's revitalization.

Fourth Tadami River Bridge. It has a distinctive structure with an aqueduct bridge, and its reflection on the water surface, known as an ``upside down bridge,'' never ceases to fascinate photographers. Now that the entire line has been restored, the sound of trains crossing this bridge can once again be heard, and it feels like a symbol of regional revitalization.

Aizu Nakagawa Station. It is the entrance to Taishi Village, which can be said to be the original scenery of Okuaizu, and a quiet atmosphere surrounds the entire station. Standing on the platform, the sunlight reflecting off the surface of the Tadami River and the colors of the mountains that change with the seasons give a deep sense of peace to travelers.

Taishi village. The colorful roofs lined up like a peninsula jutting out into the Tadami River are one of the most photogenic views along the Tadami Line. The sight of railways running along the edge of a village is proof that railways and people's lives are closely intertwined.

Panorama of Aizu Nakagawa. This is the angle where the village and the Tadami River overlap most beautifully. The Tadami Line is steeped in industrial history, with steam locomotives once running through it and materials for dam construction being carried there. The fact that this place overlooking Taishi Village is now known as the most beautiful railway in the world is a result of the accumulation of time.

Aizu-Kawaguchi Station. With the blue surface of the Tadami River pressing right up to the platform, this station is a stage for a breathtaking view fitting for the name "Station on Water." The shadow of the train reflected on the river and the colors of the opposite bank are etched into the traveler's eyes like a masterpiece.
Fifth Tadami River Bridge. A long, straight bridge. Don't you feel a sense of exhilaration as the path continues deep into nature?

Real name station. The huge Honna Dam dam is right behind the station, making this area a key location that conveys the rich history of power development along the Tadami River. With the resumption of all line operations in 2022, the heartbeat of the railway has returned to this quiet mountain area, giving us a true sense of the indomitable spirit of the railway.

No. 6 Tadami River Bridge. The bridge, which was once swallowed by muddy waters, has now been reborn. The shine of the iron looks like hope. The wall of the real dam. A huge dam wall that approaches so close that you can almost touch it. The sense of scale will take your breath away.

Aizukoshikawa Station. For this village, which was once closed off by heavy snow and turned into an isolated land island, the railway was the only link that kept it alive. As I stand on the platform surrounded by deep greenery, I can feel the weight of the railway, which overcame periods of suspension, quietly approaching my heart.
River mist in Aizukoshi. In the summer, this area is famous for its fog. Driving through the white, smoky scenery feels like heading to heaven.

Aizu Yokota Station. In ancient times, it flourished as a transportation hub within Kanayama Town, and the area around the station still has the lingering scent of the post town of bygone days. The view of the clear stream of the Tadami River and the ridgelines of the mountains that you can see from the train window gives you the feeling that you are traveling through the original scenery of Japan.
Seventh Tadami River Bridge. The rough rock surface approaches. This is the point where Tadami River's ``steepness'' and ``gentleness'' coexist.

Aizu-Oshio Station. Known as a mysterious land where carbonated springs emerge, the area around this station is a healing spot where one can feel the Earth's pulse. Tasting the blessings of this land during the journey provides a peace that purifies both mind and body.

Aizu-Shiozawa Station. Where the murmur of the Tadami River almost reaches the station building, this land symbolizes the spirituality of the Aizu people living with water. The green tunnel of beech forests offers a luxurious moment as the train breathes through nature.
No. 8 Tadami River Bridge. A bridge that blends into the forest. We pass through the deep greenery, the branches of the trees tapping against the windows.

Aizu-Gamo Station. With the brave figure of Mt. Gamo in the background, this platform placed simply within a rustic settlement is where daily life and the rails touch most purely. When the whistle announcing the train echoes, time in the mountain village seems to stop for a magical instant.

Tadami Station. Entering Fukushima Prefecture and standing amidst a vast snowfield, this station possesses a serene atmosphere fitting for a "Sacred Ground of Snow." The bond of the rails, which achieved full reopening through indomitable will after disasters, brings deep emotion to all visitors.

Tagokura Dam. This massive artificial lake damming a steep canyon is the crystallization of the tenacity of men who created energy to support Japan's post-war recovery. Holding memories of villages submerged beneath its surface, its form asks us about the light and shadow of civilization.
Lake Tagokura. Pay attention to the gaps in the tunnel. The emerald lake water will momentarily jump into your eyes.
Old Tagokura Station ruins. The remains of the platform of a discontinued station. It is green in the summer and buried in snow in the winter, quietly watching the end of history.
name_fr: Ruines de la vieille gare de Tagokura

text_en: Rokujurigoe Pass. This steep pass separating Niigata and Fukushima was once so difficult that travelers lamented a single "ri" felt like ten; even now, the railway through the tunnel does not let us forget respect for nature. The abyss of primeval forests viewed from the window is the entrance to a paradise far from the human world.

Rokujurigoe Tunnel. Four kilometers from now, after passing through the long darkness, you will find yourself in the neighboring prefecture. This mountain pass has supported travelers through the long winter.

Oshira-kawa Station. As the final station in Niigata before the steep Rokujurigoe Pass, this location holds the tension of a major railway point. The memory of steam locomotives catching their breath before crossing the hardship still drifts through the quiet platforms.
Remaining snow on Oshirakawa. The snow that remains even in May and the yellow-green beech trees that have just sprouted. This contrast is truly the brilliance of life.

Irihirose Station. As the mountains grow steeper and the rails weave through the valleys, this place is a hub of tranquility embraced by nature. The abundance of wild mountain plants around the station quietly appeals to the traveler's heart about the joy of living with the soil.
Rice terraces in Irihirose. Rice terraces with gentle curves typical of Niigata. The original scenery of Japan still remains here.

Kamijo station. This station, which was founded in 1955 when the Koide and Oshirakawa lines were opened, is a symbolic place where railways connect isolated islands surrounded by steep mountains. During the heyday of power development in the 1960s, many workers involved in dam construction disembarked at this station, and the village in the mountains became vibrant.

Echigo-Suhara Station. Around this station, which has lived through the severity of heavy snow country, the wisdom and strength unique to such regions are melted into the landscape. The rows of houses with heavy roofs seen from the window convey the indomitable spirit of the people who endure long winters.

Meguro Mansion. This important cultural property, showcasing the life of a wealthy farmer from the Edo period, is an architectural aesthetic crystallizing the history of snow country. The thick beams, polished black floors, and the scent of hearth smoke connect Japan's fading original scenery to the present.

Uonuma Tanaka Station. Since its opening in 1952, this station has been accompanied by the murmuring of the Hama River, and it has a history of being filled with timber cut from the surrounding mountains. Although it is now a quiet, unmanned station, you can still feel the vibrancy of the past in the sound of the wind passing through the platform.
The final bridge over the Hama River. The river widens and the journey nears its end. The color of the water gradually takes on the atmosphere of the city.
name_fr: Pont final de la rivière Hama

text_en: 越後広瀬駅。 There are still traces of the time when the station opened in 1950, when the wooden station building stood proudly in line with the expectations of the local community. Carrying the character of Uonuma's historic post town, its appearance as it quietly waits for passengers reminds us of the days when railways were the pride of the region.

Yabukami station. This station, which was built in 1952 with the extension of the Koide side, marks the first step on the journey from Uonuma to Oku-Aizu. The vast rural landscape of Uonuma tells the story of the ancient history of agriculture, and quietly watches over the journey over the mountains that is about to begin.
A distant view of Echigo Sanzan. Echigo Sanzan including Hakkaisan. The famous peaks with silver crowns welcome you.
The golden sea of ​​Uonuma. In autumn, Koshihikari trees bow their heads as far as the eye can see. The smell of Japan's most delicious rice seems to be carried on the wind.

Koide Station. Branching off from the Joetsu Line, this station where the Tadami Line begins its journey into the heart of Echigo is the launchpad into the unknown wilderness. Standing on the platform, the flow of the Uono River and the presence of the formidable mountains ahead ignite a quiet excitement in the traveler's heart.

Tadotsu Station. Branching off from the Yosan Line toward the deep heart of the Tosa route in Shikoku, this station is the sacred sanctuary where the railway adventure begins. Once the heart of Shikoku's railways with the Tadotsu Works, the heat of the golden age, when steam smoke proudly filled the sky, still drifts through every corner of the overpass.
