三条・マルナオの箸（黒檀・紫檀）
ものづくりの街、燕三条。三条市の職人が、希少な銘木を削り出し、手作業で仕上げる「マルナオ」の箸は、もはや体の一部。指先に吸い付くようなフィット感と、食べ物を美しく摘み上げる精緻な箸先。一度使うと、他の箸には戻れないほどの感動を覚えます。日本の食文化を支える「道具」の極致。毎日の食卓が、背筋の伸びるような特別な時間へと変わります。
product_en:
Sanjo/Marunao chopsticks (ebony/rosewood)
Tsubame-Sanjo is a manufacturing town. ``Marunao'' chopsticks, carved by hand from rare precious wood by craftsmen in Sanjo City, have become part of our bodies. The chopsticks have a fit that feels like they stick to your fingertips, and the precision tips of the chopsticks allow you to pick food beautifully. Once you use them, you will be so impressed that you won't be able to go back to using other chopsticks. The ultimate in "tools" that support Japanese food culture. Your daily dining table will turn into a special time that will make your spine stretch.
product_fr:
Baguettes Sanjo/Marunao (ébène/bois de rose)
Tsubame-Sanjo est une ville manufacturière. Les baguettes « Marunao », sculptées à la main dans du bois précieux rare par des artisans de la ville de Sanjo, font désormais partie de notre corps. Les baguettes ont un ajustement qui donne l'impression qu'elles collent au bout de vos doigts, et les pointes précises des baguettes vous permettent de choisir magnifiquement les aliments. Une fois que vous les utiliserez, vous serez tellement impressionné que vous ne pourrez plus utiliser d'autres baguettes. Le nec plus ultra des « outils » qui soutiennent la culture culinaire japonaise. Votre table à manger quotidienne se transformera en un moment privilégié qui étendra votre colonne vertébrale.
product_tw:
三條/丸直筷（烏木/紅木）
燕三條是一個製造業城鎮。由三條市的工匠用稀有的珍貴木材手工雕刻而成的「丸直」筷子已經成為我們身體的一部分。筷子的貼合感就像黏在指尖上一樣，精準的筷尖讓您可以漂亮地夾取食物。一旦你使用它們，你就會印象深刻，以至於你將無法再回去使用其他筷子。支持日本飲食文化的終極「工具」。你每天的餐桌將變成一段特別的時光，讓你的脊椎伸展。

text_en: Kita-Sanjo Station. From this elevated station in Sanjo's old town, one can see the echoes of its past as a post town and the afterglow of a golden age when hardware wholesalers lined the streets. In the cityscape viewed from the platform, the sound of hammers still rings in a pleasant rhythm, exciting the traveler's heart. The multi-layered beauty of history casts its shadow upon the town's current form.

Sanjo Kaji Dojo. In front of the sparking furnaces where craftsmen put their souls into every strike, this is a sanctuary where the will of iron takes shape. The pride of Sanjo blacksmithing, passed down from Japanese nails to kitchen knives, remains a never-dying passion, confronting visitors with the essence of manufacturing. The powerful resonance of striking steel is the very pride of the Japanese people that never fades.

Higashisanjo Station. When you get off at this station, where the Shinetsu Main Line and Yahiko Line intersect, you are enveloped in an air of pride as a key railway hub, where you can even feel the vestiges of soot emitted by steam locomotives. The many rails that line the vast premises are a quiet reminder that this was a distribution artery that shipped hardware products made by Tsubame-Sanjo craftsmen throughout the country. When you stand on a station platform and listen to the roar of heavy freight trains passing by, you can feel the weight of the railways that supported Japan's modernization directly through the soles of your feet.

An essential part of this station's history is its connection to the Yahiko Line, which runs to Yahiko Shrine, Echigo Ichinomiya. From the Taisho era to the Showa era, we can see devout worshipers and peddlers crossing the overpass at this station and busily changing trains. It's hard to imagine from its current quiet appearance, but the former station building was filled with the enthusiasm of the people and the unique business spirit of Sanjo. Amidst the chaotic atmosphere in front of the station, you can find some nostalgic vestiges of the Showa era, giving you a sense of the travel atmosphere that is unique to this station.

As soon as you step out of the station and head out into town, you'll find yourself in the ``sacred place for craftsmanship'' built by Sanjo's blacksmiths. Even now, I feel like I can hear the sound of a hammer hitting every tool that fits in my hand, such as knives and tools, from some back alley. During the period of high economic growth, Sanjo's hardware products spread all over the world, and this Higashi-Sanjo station was the starting point for their journey. The aesthetics of a ``working railway,'' covered in sweat and oil, is certainly alive here, which is a little different from Tsubame-Sanjo, a Shinkansen station where the best of technology is gathered.

At dusk, the sight of the train tracks dyed in madder red with a dull glow is a particularly moving sight for those who love railway travel. In the days when night trains passed through this station with a long horn, how many people felt at home in the light from these windows, or how many people strengthened their resolve to move on to a new world? Even though times have changed and the shape of trains has changed, Higashisanjo's mission as a transportation hub is still engraved on each rusted rail.

When I returned to the platform to catch the short train on the Yahiko Line, I found a line of local students and people on their way home from work. Echigo's everyday life, which has not been turned into a tourist destination, is here, and it has a strangely calming effect on travelers. A place where railroads intersect, people intersect, and the spirits of craftsmen intersect. Higashi-Sanjo Station still tells us a profound story that could be called the ``origin of railways.'' "

Matsumoto. As a key transportation hub in Shinshu and the gateway to the Alps, this station has always been the site of the swaying backpacks of mountaineers and the energetic voices of ekiben vendors. The premises, where the Shinonoi Line, Chuo Main Line, and Matsumoto Electric Railway (currently Aruden) all meet, has the feel of a railway intersection. In the past, the express trains ``Azusa'' and ``Alps'' would stop here to relieve the fatigue of long journeys, allowing the cool mountain air to flow into the platform. Even now, even though the station building has been transformed into a modern one, listening to the unique broadcast of ``Matsumoto, Matsumoto'' that overlaps with the departure melody gives you a strong sense that this is the heart of a mountainous city.

Kitamatsumoto. Just one minute after exiting Matsumoto Station, you can see the majesty of Matsumoto Castle, a national treasure, on your right.This station has a quiet appearance that gives you the feeling of being on the outer edge of a former castle town. Although the Oito Line platform is small, there used to be a depot nearby, and there is a history where steam locomotives and old national electric trains were resting their wings. Standing on the special platform for the Oito Line, which is close to the Shinonoi Line tracks but somehow maintains its own unique pace, you will feel like you are in the prologue to the ``Journey to Azumino'' that begins here. The tranquility of the area, which is one step lower from the hustle and bustle of the surrounding area, is the perfect place to calm the mind of a traveler.

On the island. This station makes you feel like you have stepped out of the city of Matsumoto and into the alluvial fan formed by the Azusa River. The area around the station is a mix of old houses and fields, and the atmosphere of Azumino life is very much present here. In the past, it also handled cargo, and the vestiges of agricultural products being transported from here to all over the country can be seen in the spaciousness of the premises. Looking north from the platform, the Northern Alps mountain range finally begins to reveal itself in its entirety, giving the impression that the railway is moving deeper into the bosom of nature.

Island Takamatsu. This small station, which appears to be nestled in the middle of a rural landscape, is a testament to the fact that the railway was built faithfully to the undulations of the land. In autumn, when the surrounding area is covered with golden ears of rice, the stationary diesel train blends into the scenery as if it were part of the scenery. Although there are no major facilities, the view of the mountain ridges from the train window stands out and evokes a sense of travel. As the modern buildings recede into the distance and the smell of earth and grass permeates through the platform, the original rustic charm of the Oito Line is revealed.

Azusa Bridge. As the name suggests, this station is located just before crossing the Azusa River, a famous river in Shinshu, and is a refreshing place where the sound of flowing water and the mountain breeze resonate. From the edge of the platform, you can see the clear flow of the Azusa River, which originates in Kamikochi, and the iron bridge that spans it. This station probably experienced the same wind in the days when literary figures admired the flow of this river and set their sights on the Alps. Once you cross the river, you will finally enter the real land of Azumino, making you feel like you are at a turning point in your journey.

One day market (Hitoichiba). The station's name comes from the fact that a regular market was once held here, and it conveys the history of the area as a trading hub from ancient times. Around the station, there are still buildings made of earthen storehouses and rows of houses that give you a sense of history, giving you a sense of the depth of Azumino's culture. It's fun to follow the remnants of the massive station building (though it has now been renovated) and imagine the bustle of merchants of the past. Apart from its appearance as a mountain route, it also gives a sense of its character as a lifestyle route that supports the lifestyle of the Satoyama area.

Nakagaya. This station, with a lone platform lying quietly in a field of fields, is a place that embodies the tranquility of Azumino. There are no obstructions to the surrounding area, so you can directly feel the harshness of the Alps blowing down in the winter, and the freshness of the highlands in the summer. The silence of the unmanned station, with only the sound of the alarm warning of an approaching train echoing in the distance, somehow reminds me of the nostalgic after-school days of the Showa era. This makes you feel that the essence of train travel resides in the unadorned scenery.

Minami Toyoshina. Lined with modern factories and hospitals, it is one of the most modern and lively stations in Azumino. It was probably once a quiet rural area, but now it supports the practical aspects of the Oito Line as a base for commuting to work and school. However, if you look to the west from the platform, you will see the unaltered majesty of Mt. Jonen, watching over the modernized cityscape. This gives you a sense of the unique balance of this place, where convenience and the majesty of nature sit side by side.

Toyoshina. This station, which is the central station of the former Toyoshina Town and where the limited express ``Azusa'' also stops, is an important base for sightseeing in Azumino. Taxis and buses are waiting in front of the station, and the bright colors of tourists decorate the platforms. The history of this town, which once flourished as a silk industry, is still alive in the calm atmosphere around the station. Although it is equipped with modern facilities, it has the deep sense of being able to capture the excitement of people heading to the mountains, giving it the feel of being a semi-main player on the Oito Line.

Kashiwaya Town. This station, located in a residential area, is surrounded by a calm atmosphere that symbolizes daily life in Azumino. The village of Kashiwayacho, from which the station's name originates, has been on a road for a long time, and has a history of people coming and going even before the railroad was opened. Upon landing on the short platform, travelers are greeted by the scent of daily life wafting from the neighboring houses and the flowers blooming in the gardens. It gives you a sense of a down-to-earth, indigenous travel experience that is far removed from the hustle and bustle of tourist destinations.

Hotaka. It is the highlight of Azumino tourism, and above all, it is a station in front of the Hotaka Shrine, so it has a sacred atmosphere. The temple-style station building is an eloquent testament to the fact that this is a place of faith, and the moment you step onto the platform, you feel your spine stretch. In summer, you can see climbers aiming for Mt. Tsubaku and Mt. Jonen from here, carrying heavy backpacks on their backs and moving forward resolutely. As you stand at this station nestled in the sacred forest, feeling the breeze of the wasabi fields on your cheeks, you'll be convinced that the climax of your journey is near.

Ariake. This station, located at the foot of Mt. Ariake, once known as ``Shinano Fuji,'' has long been known as the starting point for mountain climbing routes. As the name of the station suggests, the sight of the dawn light illuminating the mountainside is truly divine. On the premises, there are large vacant lots and traces of side tracks, and the remains of the area's heyday, when it was once a busy area for transporting lumber and other cargo, can still be seen. Although it is currently a quiet, unmanned station, the imposing feeling of the mountains in the background and the cold air blowing down from there make you feel that this is the entrance to the mountain realm.

Azumi Oiwake. It is a station that stands at a crossroads in history, as the main line heading towards Omachi and the Ikeda Railway that continued to Matsukawa Village once branched off. As the name suggests, the place name ``Oiwake'', where the road splits, is proof that it was an important transportation hub. Nowadays, the Ikeda Railway has been discontinued, and it is difficult to find traces of it, but you can trace the shadows of its former bustle within the spacious station premises. The mountains of the Northern Alps are getting closer and closer, and before the track gets steeper, it feels like a moment of calm and respite.

Hosono. This station marks the end of the plains of Azumino and is the gateway to the mountainous area of ​​Omachi. Surrounded by pine forests and fields, its appearance, with few people in sight, embodies the desolate beauty that spreads out at the foot of the Northern Alps. In winter, when you stand on a silver-colored platform, the only sound you can hear is the sound of the train being absorbed into the mountains, giving you the feeling of a lonely yet refreshing journey. It makes us realize once again how precious a single thin line called a railway is in the face of the overwhelming silence of Mother Nature.

Kita Hosono. This station is quietly located at the border between the peaceful countryside of Azumino and the land of the north. Surrounded by golden ears of rice and, in winter, a world of silver, this small station is a testament to the fact that the railway was built to follow the undulations of the land. When you stand on this undecorated concrete platform, the wind blowing down from the Alps touches your skin, making you realize that the air on your trip has become even cooler. Far away from the hustle and bustle of the city, the sight of a single railway line continuing northward gives us a sense of the solitary yet refreshing nature of train travel.

Shinano Matsukawa. This station, located in the center of Matsukawa Village, has a history of being a busy place for shipping agricultural products and for students commuting from nearby villages. There is a plaza in front of the station that is reminiscent of the bustling past, and the beautiful view of Mt. Ariake that can be seen from there instantly captures the hearts of travelers. The calm appearance can be seen everywhere, making you feel the pride of the Oito Line since its opening as the Shinano Railway. Although it is now a quiet, unmanned station, the spaciousness of its premises and the remains of the former freight sidings convey its pride as an ``iron bloodline'' that supported the local economy.

Azumi Kutsukake. The name of this station, which inherited the name of a former post station on the Chikoku Kaido, is a reminder of the people who came and went before the railroad was built. The area around the station is now a mix of quiet residential areas and fields, but it is fun to stand on the platform and imagine the scene where travelers of old would have taken a breather before crossing the mountain pass. The simple waiting room seems to be imbued with the warmth of the people who have used this station for many years, and somehow reminds me of the nostalgic after-school days of the Showa era. Even now, when modern vehicles are quietly rolling in, you can still feel that the good old days of Shinshu have lingered there like a stagnation.

Shinano Tokiwa. With the city of Omachi just around the corner, the train gradually climbs up the vast alluvial fan, gaining altitude. The area around this station is a rich grain region blessed with the pure snowmelt water of the Northern Alps, and the colors of the train windows that change dramatically with each season can be said to be the true essence of the Oito Line. Although the station itself has a highly functional structure, the majestic view of the Ushi-Tateyama Mountain Range that can be seen from the platform is truly the station's greatest luxury. Although overwhelmed by the majesty of the mountains, this place has a somewhat friendly rural feel, making it a comfortable and peaceful anchorage for travelers.

Minami Omachi. Located at the southern entrance to Omachi City, in an area where residential areas and schools are concentrated, this station truly has the face of a ``town station'' that is rooted in local life. Every time a train arrives from Matsumoto, the lively voices of young people echo on the platform, reminding us that railways are still the foundation of our lives. The remnants of the era when Omachi expanded as a distribution center for goods and as a base for mountain tourism can be seen in the dense townscape around the station. It makes us feel that the powerful heartbeat of the Oito Line is closely connected to people's daily lives.

Shinano Omachi. It goes without saying that it is the eastern gateway to the well-known Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route, and was once the base for the ``drama of men'' who transported vast amounts of materials and personnel in the great project of the century, the construction of the Kuroshi Dam. The solid wooden roof of the station building is a silent reminder that this area is one of the areas with the heaviest snowfall, and its style is truly befitting the central station of the Oito Line. The spring water known as ``Otoko-bai'' still flows through the platform, and the sight of former climbers quenching their thirst while carrying their backpacks on their backs can be visualized. This station, where the bright colors of tourists and the smell of local life mix, is the place where the history of the Oito Line is most concentrated.

Kitaomachi. This station, located just before the train departs from the hustle and bustle of Shinano Omachi and enters the heart of nature once again, has a somewhat desolate atmosphere that befits the outer edge of the city. From now on, the line will begin to make large curves to overcome the steep gradient, and will begin to show its true potential as a mountain line. The area around the station is dotted with small factories and residences, but behind them is an overwhelming mountain wall, giving the impression of the boundaries of a city under the control of nature. The wind blowing past the short platform is already imbued with the harshness of the mountainous region, as if urging travelers to prepare for the next difficult point.

Shinano Kizaki. This station, located on the shores of Lake Kizaki at the southern end of Nishina Sanko, is one of the most atmospheric places on the Oito Line. The station building is just a stone's throw from the lakeside, and it is reminiscent of the Showa era, when the area was once crowded with summer travelers and young people enjoying boating. As you sit on the old wooden bench with the wind blowing across the water's surface, you can feel the slow flow of time coming to an end in Azumino and the beginning of the mysteries of the lake. The cheers of people enjoying the camp are absorbed by the sound of the train running, and the deep silence returns to the station, and that transition is irresistibly endearing.

Inao. This station, located on the eastern shore of Lake Kizaki, on a small piece of flat land between the mountain and the surface of the lake, has the feel of a ``waterside station.'' The clear blue lake water spreads out in front of the platform, and the reflection of the greenery on the opposite bank on the water's surface is as beautiful as looking at a painting. In the past, it looked like a temporary boarding area for fishing and strolling visitors to Lake Kizaki, but its simplicity is the true value of this station. It gives us the illusion that only the sound of waves and the occasional railroad crossing alarm are telling us the passage of time in this world.

Uminokuchi. Although it is located in Shinshu, a mountainous country, this station, which has the name ``sea'' in it, is a somewhat mysterious place where ancient legends are passed down to the present day. Located at the northern end of Lake Kizaki, at the mouth where the water flows out, and surrounded by old villages, it feels like seeing a forgotten original landscape of Japan. The old atmosphere surrounding the station building (currently a simple waiting room) is a quiet reminder of the days when timber and fish were once transported here. The time spent waiting for the train to arrive while feeling the cold wind blowing across the surface of the lake makes us feel the essential solitude of travel and the warmth of the railway that accompanies that journey.

Yanba. It is located at the entrance to Sanozaka Pass, a difficult point in the operation of the Oito Line, and is a strategic station that connects Lake Nakatsuna and Lake Aoki. The excitement of the days when the platforms were overflowing with ski resort visitors and special trains arrived and departed frequently has been preserved within the spacious grounds. During the summer, the wind from the lakeside inns shakes the trees, creating a tranquil beauty as a summer resort. The slope of the track leading from the lake to the mountain pass is steep, and the struggle that the steam locomotives of the past struggled to gain altitude can still be seen in the shine of the rails.

Minami Kamishiro. This is the station that announces that you have crossed the Sanozaka Pass, a watershed, and entered the headwaters of the Hime River, which flows into the Sea of ​​Japan. Surrounded by a deep forest and sparsely populated with people, its appearance gives you the feeling of being in the ``world on the other side of the mountain pass.'' It has a history of once functioning as a signal station, and the long effective length for changing trains is a reminder of the long passenger trains of the past. In the mornings and evenings when the fog rolls in, it creates a dreamlike atmosphere, giving you the feeling that from here onwards you are in the harsh realm of nature, in contrast to the splendor of the mountain resort that is Hakuba.

Kamishiro. As a base for ski resorts such as Hakuba Goryu and 47, it is a busy station in the winter with young people dressed in brightly colored clothing. While once the center of Kamishiro Village, it would have had the atmosphere of a simple and sturdy farming village, it now has a sophisticated impression as part of an international tourist destination. However, if you go behind the station building, you will see the unaltered majestic shadows of the three mountains of Hakuba, reminding you once again that railways are a bridge that connects nature and humans. It is a station with a mysterious charm, where the bustle of tourism and the solemn atmosphere of the mountains coexist in an exquisite balance.

Iimori. One step before Hakuba Station, Hakuba Sanzan stands out like a folding screen over a vast rice field, making it one of the most scenic spots on the Oito Line. Seasonal flowers bloom profusely along the railroad tracks, and it's no wonder why there are so many train fans holding cameras. Although there are no special facilities, what is there is an unobstructed panorama of the Alps and a single railway that cuts through it, making it an extremely pure railway scenery. Although it is the entrance to a modern resort area, this place still has a strong smell of earth and grass, filling the hearts of travelers with a simple emotion.

Hakuba. It used to be called ``Shinano Yotsuya,'' and it was a station that had the atmosphere of a good old mountain inn where climbers to Mt. Hakuba took off their sandals. Nowadays, its name is known all over the world, and it has the appearance of being the northern emperor of the Oito Line, offering luxurious express trains and welcoming international tourists. However, in the shadow of the ornate station building, you can still feel the profound memories of the days when steam locomotives roared up white smoke as they tackled the mountain passes, still alive in the corners of the masonry platforms. Watched over by the mountain gods, this station is both the end of your journey and the starting point for reaching the next height, giving you a sense of exhilaration.

Shinano Morikami. Located at the northern end of Hakuba's urban area, it is a station with a practical atmosphere, and many mountain climbers used to enter the mountain from here. The clear stream of Matsukawa flowing in front of the station, and the harmony of the Hakuba Sanzan towering in the background, can be said to be one of the most ``Shinshu-like'' scenery on the Oito Line. Although it is currently a quiet, unmanned station, the spacious grounds still retain the echoes of the days when express trains took a break from their long journeys, giving us a sense of the enthusiasm of the mountain climbing boom of the bygone Showa era.

Hakuba Oike. Although the station name suggests a daunting climb to the alpine lake, the sound of the name alone has the power to uplift travelers. Although the surrounding area is a quiet rural area, when you get off the train, you notice that the wind blowing down from the mountains has become noticeably sharper. This simple platform with no facilities is a quiet prologue to the steep canyon section that is about to begin.

Thousand countries. The station's name reflects its history as a post town on the ancient Salt Road, and it is a rare space where modern railways and ancient history intersect. When you think of the hardships people once had to carry salt on the backs of cows and horses to cross steep mountain passes, even the sound of a diesel car's engine sounds somehow luxurious. Standing on a platform surrounded by deep greenery, the ruggedness of the mountain range, which remains unchanged through the ages, reminds travelers of their sense of humility.

Minamikotani. This station, which is the border between JR East and JR West and the end of the electrified section, is the most important strategic point on the Oito Line. It is a place where you can witness the ``disruption'' and ``rebirth'' of the railway, where the limited express ``Azusa'' has completed its journey, and from here on out, a single diesel car travels unreliably along the valley floor. As the roar of the Hime River gradually gets louder and I look around at the houses crowded in the narrow area around the station, I am finally prepared to step into a truly unexplored region.

Chuto. It was once a busy station where trains were exchanged, and many railway workers worked hard here, so it is a station that still retains strong memories of its prosperity. The appearance of the old wooden station building is beautiful, like a Showa movie set, and gives the illusion that time has stagnated there. Standing at this station, which is surrounded by overwhelming cliffs, you can feel the humble efforts of humans in response to the power of nature as both endearing and precious.

Kita Kotani. As the last station in Nagano Prefecture and just before the tunnel that crosses the prefectural border, this place gives off a feeling of being at the end. The Himekawa valley is even deeper and more sharply carved, and the railroad tracks desperately cling to the mountainside in search of a little flat ground. Considering the difficult history of the railway, which suffered devastating damage from the torrential rains of 1995 and was cut off, I can't help but think that the fact that trains are still running is a miracle in itself.

Hiraiwa. This station, located in Niigata Prefecture, once prospered as a base for power development, and even today, the huge power plant boasts of its grandeur. The muddy waters of the Hime River flowing right next to the platform and the rusted iron bridge that straddles it give us the impression that civil engineering technology has challenged nature. The abandoned houses in front of the station, which would once have been crowded with hot spring bathers and construction workers, emphasize the sense of desolation that has struck the hearts of travelers since the wave of modernization has passed.

Small waterfall. It is located at the confluence with the Kotaki River, which is known as one of Japan's leading jade producing areas, and the huge rock wall of "Jade Gorge" towers in front of the platform. The area around this station is right in the middle of Fossa Magna, a fissure in the earth, and the energy of ancient tectonic movements is etched into the rock surface. Even though you are in an inorganic concrete home, you can feel the heartbeat of the earth directly, giving you a sense of its overwhelming scale.

Root knowledge. It is a railway stronghold, with switchbacks and a history of steam locomotives accumulating power to tackle the slopes. Today, there are fewer remains of these structures, but with the two platforms facing each other, you can still feel the tension of overcoming obstacles. I'm sure I'm not the only one who gets the illusion that a railroad connects two masses of land in this area where the Fossa Magna fault line runs.

Ohno Kubiki. This station is located where the steep Himekawa Valley finally opens up and the wind that carries the hints of the Sea of ​​Japan begins to blow through. Rice fields spread out around the area, and the harsh landscape that had been there before was completely changed to the peaceful landscape of a rural village. However, if you look behind you, you will see the Hakuba mountain range that you have just passed through, fading in the distance, making you realize once again the weight of the distance you have covered on your journey.

Himekawa. With its final destination, Itoigawa, just around the corner, it is a small station where you can quietly watch the flow of the river that gives it its name. This station, which was once the Himekawa Signal Station, has only one platform that has been stripped down to its functional beauty, but on the contrary, it clearly symbolizes the story of the Oito Line, which has walked alongside the river. As I look at the sunlight reflecting off the surface of the river, I have a feeling that my journey will finally reach the sea, and I am overwhelmed with emotion.

Itoigawa. This station, which is the terminal station of the Oito Line and faces the rough waves of the Sea of ​​Japan, once boasted a vast campus with a locomotive depot and served as a junction with the Hokuriku Main Line. Nowadays, the elevated Hokuriku Shinkansen line is towering over the area, giving it a modern look, but it is the nature of those who know the Showa era to seek out remnants of brick garages. The sea seen from here is deep and blue, just like the mountains we saw in Azumino, and it feels like a quiet celebration of the end of the railway journey.

Tokushima line. From the quiet junction of Tsukuda, which separates from the Dosan Line, to Tokushima, the capital of Awa, this railway line, also known as the Yoshinogawa Blue Line, is a blissful path that continues to follow the flowing flow of the Yoshinogawa River, also known as Shikoku Saburo. Once founded as the Tokushima Railway, it served as a logistics hub for transporting Awa's specialty products, indigo and tobacco, and you can feel its historical weight as it supported the prosperity of this area.

As the train leaves Tsukuda and turns east, listening to the hustle and bustle of Awa-Ikeda in the distance, a gentle plain with views of the Shikoku Mountains on the right and the Asan Mountains on the left opens up, inviting us travelers to a somewhat nostalgic picture of Japan's original scenery. Surrender yourself to the pleasant vibrations of the diesel car as you look out the window at the townscapes of Wakimachi and Awayama River, where the udatsu (udatsu) roofs still bear witness to the prosperity of the indigo merchants of the past. It is a luxurious journey where you can enjoy an eternity of time, similar to the flow of a great river, which sets it apart from modern railways that only pursue speed. As we approach the final destination, Tokushima, and the graceful appearance of Mt. Bizan comes into view, I feel as though the lives and thoughts of the people this railway has connected are slowly coming through through the joints of the rails.

Tsukuda. This branch point, where the Tokushima Line separates from the Dosan Line, is a kind of sanctuary for railway enthusiasts. Its stoic origins, which once existed as a signal station for the purpose of allowing trains to pass and connect, are still evident in its functional wiring. With the wide banks of the Yoshino River in the background, the sight of the two railways quietly but decisively parting will inevitably heighten the emotion of the journey. When the sound of a diesel car's engine approaching from a distance echoes in the silence of the unmanned station, it reminds us that this is a key point on the Awa railway.

Tsuji. Located next to Awa-Ikeda, this station has functioned as a transportation hub since ancient times, and even today it still has the calm appearance of a post town. Once you get off the station, you will find rows of old houses dotted around the area, reminiscent of the days when the area was rich with the tobacco industry, testifying to the richness of this area. The view of the mountain ridgeline from the platform gives you the feeling that the Yoshino River valley will gradually expand from here, and as the train accelerates, you can feel that the scenery of your journey will begin to change dramatically. It may not be flashy, but the scent of a down-to-earth lifestyle warms the hearts of travelers.

Awa Kamo. Located in the center of Higashi Miyoshi Town, this station, where express trains once proudly stopped, still maintains its majestic appearance. The premises are spacious, and memories of the days when it was once a busy area for freight transportation are etched in the rusted side tracks and vast vacant lots. The old townscape surrounding the station is a reminder of the days when water transport along the Yoshino River and railways coexisted, and you can feel the depth of history firsthand. At dusk, the sight of students gathering at the platform after returning from school quietly speaks to us of the preciousness of everyday life that has remained unchanged since the Showa era.

Mikamo. This station, with its lone platform lying quietly in the middle of a rural landscape, is filled with the simple charm of a rural stop. There are vast fields surrounding the station, and you can enjoy the view of Awa's nature that changes with the seasons from a special seat. In the past, agricultural products harvested here were transported to the outside world via railways. Although it doesn't have a modern station building, its appearance blends in with the surrounding greenery, making you feel that the railway is a completely established part of the landscape. The smell of earth carried by the wind deepens the feeling of traveling.

Eguchi. This station is located in the middle of a railway that weaves through the mountains to follow the meandering of the Yoshino River, and is a tranquil place where you can hear the murmur of the river all the way to the platform. The area used to be a transport hub for forestry resources, with freight cars loaded with wood lined up, but now it is a relaxing space dominated by deep greenery and the sound of water. When you stand on the short platform and look at the smoke rising from the village on the opposite shore, you get the illusion that time has stopped. This simple station gives you the feeling that you have stepped deeply into the heart of nature.

Awahanda. When you hear the name, everyone thinks of the white, pure flow of ``Handa Somen.'' When you get off the station, you can still see people drying noodles in houses all over the place, and this is a town where tradition and life are closely tied to the railway. A merchant town that once flourished through water transport utilizing the rapids of the Yoshino River, entered a new era with the opening of the railway, and the history of its transformation can be seen in the appearance around the station. Even the sound of trucks carrying noodles coming and going at this station has a somehow proud resonance that reaches the ears of travelers.

Sadamitsu. As the gateway to the magnificent townscape with its two-story udatsu, this station exudes a unique atmosphere. The platform, which was once filled with climbers climbing Mt. Tsurugi and merchants visiting for business meetings, still has a calm atmosphere reminiscent of the glory days of those days. Each and every feature of the station building shows pride in the local culture, giving us a sense of its pride as not just a transit point, but as the face of the city. If you stand on this platform after strolling through the rows of houses with raised udatsu trees, you will be able to appreciate once again the richness of the culture that the Tokushima Line has fostered.

Kojima. As the name suggests, the station has a strong waterside feel, making you imagine that it was once a place like a sandbar on the Yoshino River. Although it is located in a narrow area surrounded by mountains and rivers, there is a certain amount of human activity there, and the memories of the days when the railway was the only lifeline are still alive. The simple concrete waiting area is built to block out the strong Shikoku sun, and while it has a somewhat practical feel to it, it also gives travelers a small sense of peace. Although the number of trains that come and go has decreased, the brightness of the rails still seems to connect the hope of this village.

Anabuki. This station is the central station of Mima City and was once the base of the ``indigo merchants'' who made a huge fortune through the indigo trade, and is one of the most important stations on the Tokushima Line. The anabuki blue color applied to the roof of the station building symbolizes the flow of the Yoshino River and the history of indigo, and it catches the eye of travelers. The spacious premises and the character of the former express stop still remain in this area without fading. When the wind from across the Yoshino River blows through the platform and you can see Mt. Tsurugi, a mountain worshiped in the mountains, in the distance, you can feel the depth of this station where nature and history intersect in Awa Province.

Kawada. This station is located at the point where the flow of the Yoshino River begins to change its appearance from the mountains to the plains, and the massive wooden station building is still in use today, making it a truly valuable place. Fragments of history, such as the idea that a dedicated line for a textile mill was once considered, are hidden in the hints of industry that hang around this station. If you sit down at the well-used ticket gate or on the amber-colored bench, you will be vividly reminded of the scenes of Showa travelers waiting for their trains to arrive. It can be said to be a valuable heritage that conveys warm memories of a time when railways were the mainstay of civilization.

Awasan River. Located at the foot of Awa's sacred mountain, Mt. Takaetsu, this station has a history of flourishing in the manufacturing of Japanese paper and sericulture. The reason why the station name was changed from ``Yudate'' is that we can't help but feel the passion of our predecessors for the development of the region. The divine view of Mt. Takaetsu seen from the platform elevates this station from just a stop to an entrance to a sacred space. Even though the station building has been transformed into a modern one, the freshness of the air around the station remains unchanged, quietly conveying to travelers the pride of the traditional industry that this area has nurtured.

Yamase. The journey on the Tokushima Line has finally come to a climax, and although you can feel the expanse of the plains, the station is in an exquisite location, with steep mountains still looming in the background. Indigo cultivation was once popular in this area, and imagining how the platform would be filled with activity during the harvest season is one of the great pleasures of railway travel. Nowadays, the area around the station has been transformed into a quiet residential area, but as I gaze at the railroad tracks in the evening light, I feel as if the traces of the countless dreams and hopes that these railroads once carried emerge in the dim light. The sight of the rail that leads to Tokushima being sucked into the evening darkness is a quiet signal that the end of the journey is near.

Science. The station's elegant one-letter name originates from the fact that there was once an academic institute founded by Confucian scholars from the Awa clan in this area. In modern times, it is considered an auspicious station that leads to ``matriculation'', and during exam season it is crowded with people seeking a set of five admission tickets, so-called ``matriculation'', which makes us feel that the railway is still a device that carries people's wishes. When I stand on the platform, there seems to be a dignified and intellectual atmosphere, and I feel like I can hear scenes from the past, which students of the past would have debated, mixed in with the sound of the wind.

Awakawa Island. It is a station that carries the castle town that juts out into the Yoshino River and still conveys its pride as a castle town in the past. The reconstructed castle tower of Kawashima Castle can be seen from the train window, eloquently proving that this area was once a strategic and transportation hub. The old townscape around the station is steeped in the strength of the people who fought against the flooding of the Yoshino River and made the most of its blessings. Standing in the spacious grounds, you can feel the weight of Awa's history quietly approaching your heart along with the brilliance of the rails.

Nishima Ue. As the name suggests, this area is said to have been planted with hemp, a specialty of Awa, and has a rich history in the textile industry. Although it is currently an unmanned station located in a quiet residential area, you can still feel the remnants of the industry of the past in the surrounding fields and old storehouses. When you disembark on the short platform, the humid breeze from the Yoshino River blows through you, giving you the illusion that you can hear the singing voices of the people who once spun linen in this area. It may not be flashy, but it makes you feel the dignity of a down-to-earth lifestyle that is connected by a single line called the railway.

Kamo Island. It is the center of Yoshinogawa City and one of the busiest major stations on the Tokushima Line. It was once lined with textile factories and commercial facilities, and the excitement of the days when the platform was filled with people and goods headed for Tokushima city is still preserved within its stately grounds. The vibrancy of life emanating from Ekimae Street strongly asserts that this is not just a transit point, but the heart of the area. When the powerful engine sound of a limited express train echoes on the platform, the pride of this station that has continued to support Awa's industry is felt passionately in the hearts of travelers.

Asauezuka. Surrounded by houses and fields, the place has the feel of a small station on a local line. There used to be many ``mounds'' in this area, and the station name quietly conveys the history of people's activities since ancient times. Sitting in the simple waiting room and waiting for the sound of the railroad crossing announcing the approach of the train, I feel as if time has stopped in the Showa era. Although there are no special tourist spots, this station teaches us that the casual scenery of a rural village that can be seen from the window is the luxurious margin of a train journey.

Ushijima. As the name suggests, it is located on the middle of the Yoshino River, and is a quiet station that gives you the feeling of being near the water. There was once a vast pasture where you could see cows grazing, and the air around the station still has a pastoral gentleness to it. Perhaps it's a vestige from the days when express trains passed easily, but the effective length of the platform is generous, which makes the current tranquility stand out. In this place, which seems to have been left behind by the speed of the city, the time spent just being blown by the wind gives travelers the ultimate sense of rest.

Shimoura. It's a small station that is so small that it's easy to overlook it, as the railroad tracks weave through the back of a residential area. However, these stations are indispensable "gateways" for local residents, and have a history of watching over the beginning and end of each day. Although specific historical data is lacking, the truth of Awa's daily life is hidden behind the narrow alleys around the station and the laundry hanging out to dry in the gardens. This simple platform quietly embodies how railways are completely integrated into everyday life.

Ishii. It is the central station of Ishii-cho, which has developed as a commuter town in Tokushima City and is transforming from a former farming village into a modern city. However, the area around the station building still retains the tranquility of the times when it flourished as a center for the timber industry and agricultural products, giving the impression that old and new are intertwined in layers. Although it maintains its dignity as a stop for limited express trains, it still retains a somewhat friendly atmosphere, which is probably the result of the humanity that this area has cultivated. You can feel the steady progress of the country of Awa in the footsteps of people passing by.

Fuchu (Kou). As the name suggests, this station has a thousand-year history and was once the seat of the national capital of Awa Province. Compared to the profound history implied by the station's name, the current station building has a surprisingly quiet appearance, but this actually makes us feel the principle of ``all that rises and falls'' and the impermanence of the passage of time. Once you get off the station, the road continues to Jorakuji Temple, the 14th sacred temple in Shikoku, and the sight of people in pilgrim costumes overlaps with the scenery of the railway. While the ancient glory is hidden underground, modern railways run over it, making it feel like you are traveling through the strata of history.

Sweetfish. This station, located at the entrance to Tokushima city and close to the embankment of the Ayuku River, gives you a sense of exhilaration as you approach the end of your journey. Sweetfish fishing in the river was once popular, and I can't help but think that the name of the station reflects a longing for a time when people enjoyed the blessings of nature. Currently, the line is about to merge with the Kotoku Line, giving off a moment of tranquility before the line becomes denser. The sound of the train crossing the river gives you a sense of the freshness of the waterside, just before it starts to mix with the hustle and bustle of the city.

Kuramoto. The Tokushima University School of Medicine and Hospital are adjacent to the station, giving it a uniquely lively atmosphere filled with young people in white coats and people going to the hospital. There used to be a modern corner lined with brick buildings, and the area around the station has an academic and intellectual atmosphere. Lines of cherry blossom trees line both sides of the railway that leads to Tokushima city, and in the spring, the train appears to be passing through a tunnel of flowers, creating a fantastical scenery. The lives of people battling illness and those working hard at learning intersect on this platform, giving us a sense of the diversity of things that railways transport.

Sako. The Kotoku Line and the Tokushima Line converge, and the elevated track is the final barrier leading to Tokushima Station. There was a time when trains ran on the ground and separated the city with many railroad crossings, but now they are lifted into the sky and boast the functional beauty of an urban railway. The way trains on the two lines run side by side or move apart is a testament to the precision of the railway network. The view of Tokushima's cityscape from here not only tells you that the end of your journey is just around the corner, but also brightens the finale of the story of Awa that has been woven by the railway.

Takamatsu. This station, which has long been the gateway to Shikoku and connected to ferry boats, has now transformed into the modern Sanuki Takamatsu Udon Station. However, if you stand on the dead-end platform, you can still feel the faint atmosphere of travel from the past, when steam locomotives emitted black smoke and the whistle of the Udaka ferry echoed through the port. The stone wall of Takamatsu Castle that stretches out in front of the station quietly tells us that this area has been a strategic and transportation hub since ancient times. As you bathe in the gentle light of the Seto Inland Sea, you can't help but feel excited about the story of the railway that begins here.

Showa town. As its name suggests, this station, which bears the name of the Showa era, is an unmanned station located quietly in a school town near Kagawa University. It is located on the railroad tracks that weave through the back of a residential area, creating a strange harmony between the fresh energy of the students and the tranquility of the ancient alley. Although there are no special historical remains, the nostalgic sound of the station name seems to transport travelers back to that peaceful era of the Showa era. Every time a modern stainless steel vehicle arrives, we are reminded of the changing times and the unchanging preciousness of everyday life.

栗林公園北口。 This station serves as the back entrance to Ritsurin Garden, a scenic beauty comparable to Japan's three famous gardens, and is a stop on an elevated railway line with a truly spectacular view. If you look down from the platform, you will see the deep greenery of the park that blocks out the hustle and bustle of the city, giving you the feeling of an oasis in the city. There used to be a signal station near this area, and the structure, which made effective use of the limited site, reflects the hardships of building the railway. As soon as you step out of the station, a tranquil space filled with the scent of pine trees awaits you, promising a little rest during your journey.

text_en: Kuribayashi. It is a central hub in the southern part of Takamatsu City, and is a station that boasts a rich history of once handling freight. Now that it has been elevated, it has a modern look, but the pride that it has taken in supporting regional logistics is still alive in the spacious premises and the calm cityscape that surrounds it. The view of Mt. Shiun from here reminds us that Takamatsu is a rich land surrounded by mountains and the sea. The sight of express trains making a grand stop and people rushing back and forth makes us feel strongly that this station is still an important bloodline of the Kotoku Line.

Kita town. It is located in an area that has developed as a commuter town in Takamatsu, and the platform built on top of the embankment looks over its surroundings. Its appearance, surrounded by houses and shops, tells us that the railway is close to people's lives. It may have once been a rural area, but now it is used as a means of commuting to work or school, and has a practical look to it, watching over the start and end of each day. Although there are no special decorations, watching from the platform as the lights of the houses start to come on at dusk gives you a warm feeling that is unique to train travel.

text_en: 屋島。 Located at the foot of Yashima, which is famous for being the site of the Genpei War, the station retains memories of its glory days when it was once a connecting station to the cable car and overflowing with tourists. There is a truly intricate feeling in imagining the scene in which travelers of the past headed for the mountains, carrying heavy luggage, while following the remains of the old station building (currently renovated) that exudes a Western-style atmosphere. Looking up from the station, the flat peak of Yashima towers like a folding screen that conveys the eternal history of Japan, making us once again feel the profoundness of this place where myth and history intersect.

Old Takamatsu South. Located in a corner of a high-density residential area, it is a small station with the atmosphere of a stop for residents. As the name of the place, Old Takamatsu, suggests, this area has a hidden history dating back to before the center of Takamatsu was formed, and the back alleys around the station have a hint of the past. Although it is a simple structure with only one platform, there is the sound of trains arriving at a fixed time every day, and the rhythm of people's lives is engraved there. It makes you feel like you are at a turning point in the beginning of your journey, when the modern buildings recede and the indigenous way of life becomes more apparent.

text_en: Yaguriguchi. This station has a history of being used by pilgrims to get off on their canes as the entrance to Yakuri-dera Temple, the 85th temple of the Shikoku Sacred Site. Yakuriyama, which stands behind the name of the station, has a majestic appearance that has made it an object of worship, and you can feel a sacred atmosphere just by standing on the platform. The fact that it was once built as a signal station and later upgraded to a station shows how much demand there was for this area. The quiet prayers that people on the pilgrimage sometimes show add a deep sense of spirituality to the railway scenery.

Sanuki Mure. It is the gateway to Mure, the stone town loved by world-famous sculptor Isamu Noguchi, and the area around the platform is dotted with factories that process the famous Aji stone. This station, where you can hear the dry sound of stone being cut on the wind, is a rare place where industry and art are connected by railway. In front of the station, old train cars that once ran on the Shido Line are preserved, making it a quaint spot where memories of old and new railways intersect. The unique atmosphere of this place, where the coldness of the stones and the passion of the people mix, gives a quiet stimulation to the hearts of the travelers who disembark.

Shido. It is a town in front of Shido-ji Temple, the 86th sacred temple in Shikoku, and was once a town with a rich culture that nurtured a rare genius named Gennai Hiraga. Kotoden Shido Station is right next to the Kotoku Line station building, which tells the story of the history of the two railways supporting each other in the development of this city. The scent of the Seto Inland Sea carried by the sea breeze and the appearance of the old temple town create a perfect harmony, and your love for traveling will deepen even further here. When you stand on this platform after visiting Gennai's grave, you can feel for yourself the intellectual curiosity and vitality of this area that has continued since the Edo period.

orange town. It is a new town station that was born in the Heisei era, and its modern name stands out among the old-fashioned Kotoku Line station names. However, this station, which was developed along with a large-scale housing development, is a place that symbolizes the future of railways in the sense that it has established a new way of life for people here. Modern roundabouts and well-organized streets have transformed the once quiet mountain setting into a new vibrancy. The appearance of the station changes with the changing times, but what we see here is also a record of the seriousness of life in the modern era.

Zoda. As the name suggests, the station is surrounded by rich rice fields, giving it the feel of a rural station. Every season, the golden ears of rice and the mirror-like surface of the water decorate the train windows, providing travelers with the original scenery of Shikoku. There was once a time when the platform was a lively gathering place for agricultural products, and during the harvest season. Currently, the station is quiet and unmanned, but as you listen to the sound of the wind blowing across the ridge while waiting for the train to arrive, you can feel the strength of the people who live with the soil, and it gives you a feeling of cleansing.

Kanzaki. This station, nestled in a small village, is a place that makes you realize that the railway was built faithfully to the undulations of the land to connect people's lives. Although no special historical data stands out, this simple station makes us think about how many people have flown to the outside world and returned to their hometowns. Waiting alone on a station bench at dusk for a train feels like a precious ritual for coming face to face with oneself. The truth about train travel is hidden within the simple scenery.

Sanuki Tsuda. It is the station to get off at Tsuda no Matsubara, known for its beautiful white sand and green pine trees, and is steeped in memories of summers when the platform was once filled with beachgoers. The wind blowing through the pine forest carries the scent of the sea, and the station building has an air of openness, reminiscent of a summer resort. The bustle of the past, when express trains proudly stopped and the cheers of young people echoed through the air, still blends quietly into the sound of the waves. The contrast of colors between the blue sea, green pines, and rust-colored railroad tracks creates a sense of sad beauty, as if regretting that the end of the journey is near.

Tsuruha. This station, located at the point where the train approaches the sea again after leaving Sanuki Tsuda, has a truly open atmosphere with the calm Seto Inland Sea spreading out just behind the platform. In the past, it served as a port for shipping high-quality stones and agricultural products from the surrounding area, and it had a unique sense of life, with the scent of the sea mixing with the smell of the earth. Although it is currently a quiet, unmanned station, the time you spend waiting for your train to arrive while listening to the sound of waves crashing is a blissful moment that will help you forget the hustle and bustle of everyday life. The contrast between the endless blue sea and the rusted rails evokes a faint sense of nostalgia in the hearts of travelers.

Nibu. The quaint-sounding name of the place hints at the history of minerals such as mercury being mined here in the past. Today, it maintains the appearance of an exchange station with two platforms facing each other in a peaceful rural landscape, but you can still feel the vestiges of the spacious premises of the days when long passenger trains passed each other. The rows of old houses surrounding the station and the scenery of the fields that change color with the seasons are reminiscent of the original landscape of Shikoku. Although there are no special sights, if you place yourself in the regular flow of time carved by the railway, you can feel the steady progress of this area.

Sanbonmatsu. It is the central commercial hub of Higashi-Kagawa City, and as the main station on the east side of the Kotoku Line, it is a lively station where limited express trains proudly stop. The city's history as a port town, rich in industries such as tobacco and salt production, is still reflected in the lively appearance in front of the station. When you stand on the platform, you will see businessmen and students bustling about, reminding us that this is an important node that supports the local economy. Although it has modern conveniences, there is a nostalgic feeling of a Showa shopping street behind the station, giving you a unique sense of energy that mixes the vibrancy of old and new.

Sanuki swan. This station has made its name known throughout the country as the station in front of Shiratori Shrine and as the town of the glove industry, which boasts the largest market share in Japan. A monument of gloves stands in front of the station, quietly telling the story of the pride of the industry that local craftsmen have maintained. The atmosphere on the platform, where the sacred wind blowing from the shrine's forest and the faint sounds of factory machinery mix, provides a rare sight where faith and industry are connected by railway. It is the nature of travel writers to seek out the bustle of the past, when it would have been overflowing with worshipers, in the shadow of the stately station building that still remains.

Hikita. It is located at the eastern end of the country of Sanuki and is the gateway to a historic city that once flourished as a port waiting for the wind. The old townscape with its red tiled roofs and its quaint scenery lined with soy sauce warehouses conveys the rich culture that existed before the railroad was built. The station itself used to have many turnaround trains, and the station still maintains its character as an operational hub within its spacious grounds. Once you pass this point, the difficult Osaka Pass awaits you, giving travelers a quiet sense of tension that is unique to border stations, encouraging them to rest for a while and prepare for the next mountain pass.

Sanuki Aioi. It is the last station in Kagawa Prefecture, and the station is at the entrance to a mountain pass, with the Sanuki Mountains rising in elevation like a wall in the background. Surrounded by deep greenery, the home is surrounded by silence, unrelated to the hustle and bustle of the city, and the only sounds you can hear are the chirping of birds and the sound of the wind rustling through the trees. There must have been a history of locomotives taking a breather at this station and tackling the steep slopes, and there is still a solemn presence in the air as the tracks are sucked into the mountains. From this point on, the train enters the tunnel at the prefectural border and heads towards the land of Awa.

Awa Omiya. This station, located just after passing through a long tunnel that passes through Osaka Pass and entering Tokushima Prefecture, is nestled deep in the tranquility of the mountains. In the past, it had a heavy role as a signal station, and was a place where trains could breathe a sigh of relief after crossing a difficult point. The view of the mountain ridges seen from this high-altitude platform is a complete change from the previous scenery of the Seto Inland Sea, and once again reminds us of the depth of the mountains in Shikoku. In this area where human habitation is rare, the sound of diesel car engines echoing through the valley and disappearing makes you realize that the railway is deeply woven into the bosom of nature.

Itano. This is the main station that announces that you have passed through the mountainous region and finally landed on the plains of Awa. It was once a key transportation hub, with a branch line to the Tokushima Main Line (currently the Tokushima Line) being planned, and the vast campus that bears witness to that history quietly tells the story of the dreams of yesteryear. It is also close to Kinsen-ji Temple, the third sacred temple in Shikoku, and the sight of pilgrims taking a break on the platform reminds us that this is an ancient route. The time spent waiting for the next train under the open sky, free from the tension of crossing the mountain, provides a pleasant break towards the second half of the journey.

Awa Kawabata. It is a small station quietly located in a peaceful rural landscape where residential areas and fields coexist. Although there are few special historical remains, the roads around the station run close to the railroad tracks, and it can be seen that the railway has completely blended into people's daily lives. The simple waiting area is steeped in warmth that has been cherished by the local people, and somehow reminds us of the nostalgic evenings of the Showa era. The sight of modern stainless steel cars sliding onto a platform smelling of earth gives us a sense of the sincerity of the railway, which is in step with the unchanging climate.

Bando. When you hear the name of this station, you can't help but think of the episode in which Beethoven's "Ninth" was premiered in Japan in a German prisoner of war camp during World War I. This is a place where stories of human love that transcend national boundaries are passed down from generation to generation, and there is a dignified, refreshing atmosphere around the station. It is also the closest station to Ryozenji, the first temple on the Shikoku 88-point pilgrimage, and the platform is filled with the elation of pilgrims as they prepare for the start of their journey. This station, where the multilayered history intersects with the premonition of a new journey, is one of the places on the Kotoku Line that gives you a sense of spiritual depth.

Ikeya. The V-shaped platform that clearly separates the Kotoku Line and the Naruto Line attracts even non-railway fans with its unique design. A stately brick station building once stood here, and it brings to mind the scene of a bygone era, when steam locomotives shared smoke on their way to their destinations. This branch station, which suddenly appears in a vast lotus root field, boasts a functional beauty worthy of being called a ``railway intersection.'' The sight of trains on two lines entering the line at the same time and then dispersing on their respective journeys seems to symbolize the encounters and partings of life, and no matter how long you watch it, you will never get tired of it.

Katsuzui. Located right next to the ruins of Shozui Castle, which was the political and cultural center of medieval Awa, it is a historical station that hides the prosperity of the Miyoshi clan, who once ruled this area, underground. Although the area is currently more of a residential area, the remains of the moat and temples and shrines around the station still retain strong traces of its former status as the ``capital of Awa''. When the express train slows down to a stop, the greenery of the historic site visible from the train window quietly reminds us that a modern railway is running on top of a layer of history. If you stand on the platform imagining what the city would look like as dreamed of by the powerful people of old, the atmosphere of your trip will become even more profound.

text_en: Yoshinari. With the city of Tokushima just around the corner, the station is surrounded by rich farmland and brand new homes, giving the station a calm, suburban feel. It has a history where the old Kotoku Main Line once branched from this area, and it is also a place that has watched over the evolution of a complex railway network that is hard to imagine from its current peaceful appearance. This station is located in the vast delta area of ​​the Yoshino River, and the faint smell of the river wafts in the wind, creating a pleasant sense of tension that suggests that the final station is near. Just before the hustle and bustle of the city begins, the calm before a storm calms the mind of the traveler.

Sako. It is the entrance to the elevated section where the Kotoku Line and the Tokushima Line converge, and the three lines continue to Tokushima Station. This station, which once ran above ground and was surrounded by the hustle and bustle of a series of railroad crossings, has now been elevated to give it the appearance of a sophisticated urban railway. The sight of trains on two routes running side by side or crossing each other vividly embodies the precision and strength of railway transportation. The view of Tokushima's cityscape from here, with the graceful ridgeline of Mt. Bizan in the background, makes for a gorgeous end to your trip. You can feel the countless stories connected by Awa's railway converging in modern facilities.

Tokushima. As the terminal station on the Kotoku Line and the base for transportation across Awa no Kuni, it is always full of enthusiasm and vibrancy. The dead-end platform brings together the heartbeats of railways from all over the prefecture, and from there a new journey begins again, giving the station a profound sense of travel that can only be found at a terminal station. The sounds of ekiben vendors and the smell of soot from steam locomotives have disappeared, but as you stand on this platform overlooking Mt. Bizan, the longing for the railway that connects Tosa, Iyo, and Sanuki still comes and goes in the hearts of travelers. This station quietly and dignifiedly marks the end of a long story woven by the railways of Shikoku.

Tokushima. It is the starting station for the Mugi Line, and the starting point for journeys to the southeastern part of Shikoku. The excitement of arriving at the end of the Kotoku Line still hasn't faded, and from here on out, a more lonely and powerful railway begins, heading for the rough waves of the Pacific Ocean. If you stand on a dead-end platform, you can't help but feel that the memory of the black smoke spewed out by the steam locomotives of old, even now surrounded by modern station buildings, is rising from beneath your feet. While being embraced by the climate of Awa, I am filled with anticipation for my next journey.

Awa Tomita. Although it is located in a corner of the city near government offices such as the prefectural office, it is a quiet station that feels like a hideaway. Its simple structure reflects the fact that it was built at the request of the people in a place where there was once no station and trains were just passing through. It's probably crowded with commuters in the morning and evening, but in the afternoon the platform has an atmosphere that embodies the calmness of Tokushima town. It makes you feel the fine line between the hustle and bustle of the city and the tranquility of travel.

Two houses. Once you get off the station, you'll be greeted by a quaint townscape lined with old townhouses, and you can feel that the vibrancy of Awa's former merchant houses is still alive and well. Remnants of the days when it once had two-way platforms and many trains came and went, still remain quietly within the spacious premises. If you sit down on the edge of the stone platform, it gives you the pleasant illusion that you can hear the sound of old train whistles echoing down the back alley. It does not resist the changes of the times, but its dignified appearance gives off the dignity of a long-established store.

Cultural forest. Although it is a new station that was born in the Heisei era, as its name suggests, it has a heavy responsibility as the gateway to Tokushima's intellectual and cultural hub. Its appearance, located at the foot of a lush mountain just before crossing the Sonose River, presents a complete landscape where a modern railway tries to harmonize with the bosom of nature. The sight of people visiting libraries and museums standing on platforms with books under their arms makes us realize once again that railways are devices that transport knowledge and culture. This makes us realize that a new history is being carved into the new station.

Jizo Bridge. As the name suggests, a Jizo statue that has been watching over people passing by since ancient times is enshrined near the station, and the railway is so peaceful that it seems as if it is surrounded by its benevolence. As you leave the city of Tokushima, you can see the expanse of rice fields outside the train window, and this area retains the strong memory of a farming village that once prospered by shipping agricultural products. The way the simple concrete station building casts a shadow under the setting sun somehow reminds me of the nostalgic summer holidays of the Showa era. The people's simple faith and the daily life of the railway blend together to create a truly Tokushima-like landscape.

Chuden. When talking about this place, it is impossible to ignore its history as a turning point for the Komatsushima Line, which used to be known as ``Japan's shortest national railway line.'' Nowadays, it stands quietly as an intermediate station on the Mugi Line, but if you look at the vast ruins of the site where the tracks that led to the ferry used to split, you can clearly see the footprints of a giant who supported Shikoku's logistics. Overwhelmed by the waves of time, the line of track has disappeared, but the pride that this station has as a ``crossing point'' is still evident in the dignified atmosphere.

Minamikomatsushima. In the days when Komatsushima Port reigned as the sea gateway to Shikoku, this station served as a key point connecting the port and the inland, witnessing the joys, angers, and sorrows of the people that cannot be described in words. Now that the Komatsushima Line has been abolished, this station has taken over its role as the city's central station, but the desolation and liveliness that is typical of a port town still tickles the noses of travelers. As I stand on the platform, where the smell of salt carried by the sea breeze and the smell of train oil mix, I can't help but think about the long story of the railway that connected to the other side of the sea.

text_en: Awa Akaishi. It is the southernmost station in Komatsushima City, which gives you a feeling that you are finally approaching the coastline after crossing the Katsuura River. The area around the station is dotted with small factories and residences, and it must have once served as a strong industrial base. The simple exposed concrete station building is exposed to Shikoku's strong sunlight, giving a sense of practical beauty and functionality. As the train accelerates, just before the faint blue color of the sea begins to appear in the train window, the station is filled with an expectant silence.

Tachie. It is a station in front of the gate of Ritsukoji Temple, the 19th sacred temple in Shikoku, and is feared and respected by pilgrims as ``Sekishoji'', and has a sacred atmosphere. As you get off the station and walk down the road leading to the temple, you can feel the history of ancient pilgrimages engrained in each cobblestone. There was probably a time when passenger trains carrying worshipers would huddle on the long platform. Although it is currently a quiet, unmanned station, the sight of pilgrims bowing and leaving the platform is a quiet reminder that the railway is still part of the ``Path of Prayer.''

Hanoura. This station has a history as a transportation hub, as there was once a plan to pass through the mountains of Anan from this area. Currently, as the northern gateway to Anan City, it is a lively station where the hustle and bustle of commuters echoes every morning and evening. A calm residential area spreads out around the station building, making you realize how central the railway is to people's lives. This station warmly welcomes you as a temporary respite on the flat land as the railroad heads over the mountains to the sea.

Nishihara. If you look around you, you can see vast rice fields stretching on forever, making this a quiet station that symbolizes the richness of the Anan Plain. Although no special historical data stands out, we can't help but think about how many lives were nurtured and departed due to the presence of this ordinary rural stop. In autumn, the golden rice ears wave and the diesel cars parked look like a stroke of color in the landscape. It makes you feel that the true face of Awa is hidden within the unadorned scenery.

Awa Nakajima. Located on the north bank of the Nakagawa River, one of the largest rivers in Shikoku, it is a place where you can feel the tenacity of the railroad workers who once fought the difficult construction work to cross this river. The huge iron bridge that awaits you as soon as you exit the station is the crystallization of human wisdom and courage in the face of the fury of nature. The area around the station is a quiet village, but this place, where you can always hear the murmuring of the river carried by the wind, quietly tells the story of the history of the Awa people who have lived with water. The roar of the train crossing the bridge echoes like a signal gun announcing a new phase of the journey.

Anan. It is the central station of Anan City, which is known as the city of bamboo groves and is also famous as the city of LED technology in modern times. It was once called "Tomioka Station" and boasts an immeasurably active history as a distribution center for goods in the Naka River basin. Even though the current station building has been changed to a modern one, the calm atmosphere of a castle town that surrounds the station has not been lost, and it fully shows off its character as a city representing the southern part of Awa. From here on, the Mugi Line finally enters the full-fledged coastal section, giving us a sense of the dignity of being the last major base on the journey towards the majestic panorama of the Pacific Ocean.

Kenorin. This station, located at the entrance where the train passes through the city of Anan and once again enters the bosom of nature, is in a unique location where a residential area and a mountainside collide. In the past, many forests spread around this area, and the area was probably a thriving area for lumber production, which is reflected in its name. Currently, it is a quiet unmanned station, quietly watching over the daily activities, but it also plays a role in increasing the anticipation of the journey, as once you pass through the mountain you will finally be able to see the ocean. The time I spend alone waiting for the next train on this platform, where the smell of earth is strong, makes me feel like I'm getting in touch with the essence of travel.

Awa Tachibana. This area, which overlooks the intricate Tachibana Bay beyond the city center of Anan, still tells the history of Tachibana Port, which once prospered for the sea transportation of coal and other goods. From the station, you can see the chimneys of a huge thermal power plant, and the combination of the quiet scenery of a fishing village and the majesty of modern industry creates a unique sense of tension.
