Remnants of the past, when freight sidings were wide and the heartbeat of industry could be heard directly, can be found within the spacious premises. More than just a transit point, the pride that has supported Awa's industry at its core is reflected in the dignified appearance around the station.

Kuwano. This station, located on a quiet flatland in the mountains, once served as a relay point for transporting lumber from the upper reaches of the Naka River, and was at the height of its forestry industry's heyday. Today, it is a quiet exchange station where limited express trains stop quietly, but the old stone platform still retains the strength of the days when freight cars laden with heavy timber were lined up. The depth of the surrounding greenery enhances the atmosphere of your journey as you delve into the depths of Awa. The smell of earth and the faint scent of wood welcome travelers.

Niino. It is home to Tokushima Prefectural Shinno High School, and is a lively school station where the voices of tenacious young people echoed, like the ``Shinno Take'' that once rocked Koshien. The basin-like topography, surrounded by mountains on all sides, exudes a tranquility that is somehow out of this world, and it speaks to the importance of the era when railways were the only window to the outside world. The wind blowing through the simple station building is laced with the scent of the rich countryside, giving travelers a sense of tranquility as if they were back home. It is a truly quaint stop where the fresh energy of students and the tranquility of an ancient farming village create a strange harmony.

Awa Fukui. This station, located just before the line rises in altitude and tackles an increasingly steep watershed, symbolizes the ruggedness of the Mugi Line as a mountain line. Surrounded by deep forests and sparsely populated, its appearance quietly conveys the tenacity of our predecessors who overcame difficult construction work to build the railway. From this point on, the train plunges into a long tunnel and rushes down to the Yuki coastline overlooking the Pacific Ocean, giving us a sense of the quiet determination just before that happens. The sound of a diesel car's engine echoing through the valley adds to the tension of the trip.

Yuki. The moment you step out of the long tunnel, everyone is astonished by the blue Pacific Ocean that catches your eye. This station is also known as the town of spiny lobster, and the sea breeze and the scent of the ocean fill the entire platform, giving you a sense of the powerful liveliness that is typical of a port town. Once upon a time, as the central station of Yuki-cho, it would have been filled with people involved in the fishing industry and peddlers, and it seems that the bustling atmosphere of the past is still somewhat visible within the renovated station building. The time spent waiting for the train to arrive while listening to the sound of the sea is nothing short of a treat known as traveling. It allows you to feel the heartbeat of a city that has lived with the blessings of the sea.

Tainohama. The existence of a ``temporary station'' that opens its doors only for beachgoers during the summer season is a fragment of the colorful memories of the Showa era, when railways were the main form of leisure. The sandy beach is literally right in front of the platform, and the sound of the sea breeze and crashing waves the moment the train doors open is a luxurious experience that cannot be experienced at any other station. The uninhabited homes that are now being quietly washed away by the waves seem to be quietly waiting for the joy of children to return once summer comes. You can't help but feel the traces of a railway dream in these phantom-like stops that appear and disappear as the seasons change.

Kiki. It's a stop in a small fishing village that clings to the rugged coastline. The close proximity of the tracks and houses, and the sight of people's lives visible from the train windows at arm's length, proves that railways are deeply rooted as a part of people's lives. The sight of a small boat rocking in a quiet cove and the white crest of a wave in the distance makes you completely forget the hustle and bustle of the city and allows you to hear only the sound of time passing. This unadorned yet beautiful station remains deeply etched in the hearts of travelers. Even the wooden utility poles, washed by the sea breeze, give off a painting-like atmosphere.

Kitakawachi. Just before entering the town of Hiwasa, this station is located in what looks like a cul-de-sac surrounded by mountains and rivers, and although it has the appearance of a practical exchange station, it somehow has the desolation of a mountain village. It may have once served as a transport hub for forestry resources, and there are some blank spaces within the premises that give the impression of vestiges from the past. The murmuring of the river is always nearby, and the shadow of the mountain covers the platform from an early age, making us realize once again the depth of nature in southern Shikoku. The sight of a limited express train cutting through this silence reminds us once again of the speed of modernization.

Hiwasa. It is the largest tourist base in southern Awa, home to Ohama Beach, where loggerhead sea turtles come to lay their eggs, and Yakuoji Temple, the 23rd sacred temple in Shikoku. The castle tower of Hiwasa Castle, towering above the station building, welcomes travelers, and the formal bustle of the town is reflected in the bustle of the platform. You can feel the history of the place, where many worshipers and beachgoers would have disembarked from the heavy passenger trains, and the unwavering pride of being a major station can be seen in the way the express trains proudly stop there. The sound of the pilgrim's bells and the lively atmosphere in front of the station mix together, giving you the most vibrant experience on the Mugi Line.

Yamakawachi. After passing through Hiwasa, this station is located on the way to the mountain pass again, and as its name suggests, it has the feel of an ``unexplored station,'' as if it were quietly hidden between mountains and rivers. Surrounded by overwhelming green walls, the only sounds you can hear are the sound of the wind shaking the trees and the chirping of birds in the distance. Considering that this single platform was once the only bridge of hope to the outside world for the people living in this area, even its simple appearance begins to feel divine. In this place, which seems cut off from modern conveniences, the time spent waiting alone for the train to arrive gives you a sense of the far north of your journey.

Byekawa. This station, located just before Mugi, at the point where you descend over a hill to the plains, is an extremely simple stop that is a direct representation of the daily life of a rural village. Although there are no special historical remains, the scenery created by the fields surrounding the station and the houses dotted there remind us of the original scenery of ``nostalgic Japan'' that is engraved in our DNA. I sit on a bench in an unmanned station, just waiting for the sound of the alarm to notify me of an approaching train. This station quietly teaches us that such casual moments are actually the best part of the most luxurious journey.

Mugi. This station, which bears the name of the line, still conveys the stately atmosphere of the days when it was the terminal station. The vast grounds that once housed the locomotive depot and the wiring that still functions as a base for operation today are filled with pride in having supported the railways in southern Awa. As soon as you step out of the station, you'll find yourself in a lively port town filled with the scent of saltwater and fish, and this is where your travel journey comes to fruition. From here on, you can feel that the story of the railway extending further south is finally approaching the heart of the Pacific Ocean, and it is truly worthy of being called the heart of the Mugi Line.

Sabase. Right next to the station is Yasaka-dera Temple, affectionately known as ``Saba Daishi,'' which has long been known as a resting place for pilgrims. The vast Pacific Ocean spreads out in front of the platform, and the sight of the railway running right next to the shore of the waves can be described as a spectacular view. As I gaze at the crashing waves while thinking about the legend that Kobo Daishi brought a mackerel back to life, I am once again reminded of the depth of the railway, where the wonders of nature and human faith intersect. The sound of the sea always echoes through the platform, and it feels like it deeply purifies the soul of the traveler.

Asakawa. It is a quiet fishing port town station located at the deepest part of the intricate Asakawa Bay and surrounded by mountains. The calm atmosphere of the premises is a reminder that in the past, much seafood was transported from here to consumption areas via railways. The narrow alleys around the station and the rows of old houses that stand up against the sea breeze still retain the original scenery of a fishing village in the Showa era, giving a quiet sense of peace to the hearts of travelers as they disembark. The silence that follows the roar of the train tells of the eternal history that this city has cultivated, and seems to quietly announce that the end of the journey is near.

Awa Kainan. Today, it has transformed into a station that is attracting worldwide attention as a connecting point for DMV (Dual Mode Vehicle), which has both rail and bus functions. It used to be a quiet intermediate station on the Mugi Line, but now it has become a key hub supporting the transportation system of a new era, with a state-of-the-art atmosphere. However, the tenacity of the railway that has led to the southern tip of Awa is still alive and well, and you can feel the passion of the railway workers who are trying to connect the journey even though the form has changed. From here on, the railway transforms into a road, giving us a sense of the dramatic turning point where a new story that continues to Muroto begins.

Uchiko. The gateway to the wealthy merchant town that flourished with white wax and Japanese umbrellas now has the appearance of an imposing elevated station, serving as a bypass for the Yosan Line. The history of this area, which was once the terminal station of the Cecal Line, transformed into a strategic hub where the limited express trains ``Shiokaze'' and ``Ishizuchi'' ran through with the opening of the short circuit line makes you feel the strange fate of railways. However, once you step out of the station, the townscape of Yokaichi and Gokoku, which has been designated as an Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, opens up, giving you the illusion that the prosperity of yesteryear has been encased in amber. The contrast between the mountain scenery seen from the new elevated platform and the old townscape is what symbolizes modern Uchiko.

Isozaki. When you get off at this station, which is nestled along the Odagawa River, you will be greeted with the magnificent sight of giant kites flying in the sky during Boys' Festival. Although it is located next to Uchiko Station, it retains the atmosphere of a quiet, unmanned station, and conveys the simple way that railways play a role in local life. It has a history that traces back to the flow of light railways that continued to Ozu, and I feel that the warmth of handmade washi paper, which was a local industry, is somehow seeping into the atmosphere around the station. The time you spend waiting for the next local train on this small platform while feeling the pressure of the wind as the express train passes relentlessly is a precious moment that makes you think about the speed of travel.

Mt. Kita. This station, nestled on a small piece of flat land in the mountains, is a reminder of the days when the Ehime Railway was a light railway, and its rugged topography is a reminder of the days when the Ehime Railway was a light railway. Surrounded by mountains, the sound of diesel car engines echoing through the valley and disappearing gives you the feeling of being at a train station in the mountains. Although there are no major facilities, the terraced rice fields surrounding the station and the changing colors of the mountains each season are full of beauty that resembles a landscape painting. This quiet home will teach you the real thrill of a solitary journey, far away from the hustle and bustle of the city, with only the rhythm of the railway as your companion.

Shintani. This area has a history of flourishing as a 10,000 koku jinyamachi of the Shintani clan, which was a branch of the Ozu clan, and there is a certain elegance and tranquility surrounding the station. The current track, which serves as a shortcut for the Yosan Line, looks different from the light rail tracks of the past, but the memory of the land cannot be rewritten. Listening to the murmuring of the Yarogawa River that flows by the station, and looking up at the mountain ridges that the feudal lords of yesteryear would have seen is one of the best parts of historical travel. Although it is a short-circuit line station that is a child of modernization, when you feel the lingering scent of the old Jinyacho in the wind, the depth of your trip becomes even deeper.

Ikeya. No matter how many times I visit this branch station, where the Kotoku Line and the Naruto Line split into left and right sides like a fan, I am captivated by its geometric beauty. Surrounding the station is a field of lotus roots, with large leaves swaying in the wind in the summer and waiting to be harvested in the cold wind in the winter, creating the original scenery of Awa. There was a time when this was the starting point of the Tokushima Line, and a complicated thread of history is intertwined with this V-shaped platform. While waiting for the connection, as I watched the two rails scatter from the wooden overpass on their respective journeys, I couldn't help but think of the strange fate of a device called a railway.

Awa Otani. As soon as you get off the station, you are immediately greeted by the smell of earth and the smell of smoke from the kilns. This area is the home of Otani ware, which is famous for its giant pots and pots, and the station's appearance also has the simple, sturdy, and calm atmosphere of a town of craftsmen. There is a history in which many pieces of pottery were once fired from here, loaded onto freight cars and shipped across the country. Although the station is currently quiet and unmanned, the sound of potter's wheels coming from the surrounding workshops and the occasional sound of train joints make you feel like a duet of local culture.

Standing road. This station, with its single platform appearing out of nowhere amidst the rural scenery as far as the eye can see, especially a vast lotus root field, maintains the purity of a rural stop. There is no station building, just a simple waiting area, but this actually makes the vast sky and mountain ridges of Shikoku stand out. In the past, much of the culture of ``entertainment'' still remains in this area, and it is also a place where the history of people has been carved out even before the railway was opened. The way the sunlight shines through the train windows and reflects off the rice paddies and illuminates the platform is a luxurious sight that you can never experience in the city.

In front of the church. It is rare to find a railway station in Japan with such a direct and poetic name. As the name suggests, there is a beautiful church built right next to the station, adding a touch of exoticism to Awa's Japanese atmosphere. The history of Christian evangelism once taking deep roots in the hearts of the people of this area is still engraved in the name of the station. Although there are no special tourist spots, the fact that a quiet place of prayer and a railroad are located next to each other gives travelers a refreshing feeling as if they have visited a nameless sacred place.

Before Konpira. Just a few hundred meters from Kyokimae Station, travelers are now greeted by the torii gate of Konpira Shrine, a shrine dedicated to Japanese gods.This contrast is truly interesting. The way Japanese and Western prayers are connected by railways is a symbol of the deep compassion of the Japanese people. The station itself is a simple structure nestled under an embankment, but during the New Year, the crowd of worshipers overflows onto the platform, demonstrating its true character as a small station beloved by the local community. Watched over by a shrine with a long history, you can feel that the railway is completely integrated into the daily scenery.

Muya. This is a station with a rich history, as it was once an important transportation hub where ferries to Awaji Island departed and arrived, and it was also the terminal station when the Naruto Line was launched as the ``Awa Electric Tramway''. In the past, great wealth was gathered in this area from the salt production and commerce, and there are still old buildings and warehouses around the station that remind us of the prosperity of those days. Although it still retains the character of the days when it was a terminal station, it is now a quiet corner of the city, quietly marking time. The sea breeze blows through the back alleys, and the hustle and bustle of the old port town is faintly mixed in with the breeze, giving you a strange sense of nostalgia.

Naruto. It is the last station on the Naruto Line, and beyond the rail where the cars are stopped, the Onaruto Bridge, where the Seto Inland Sea and the Pacific Ocean finally collide, and the whirlpool sea await. There was once a grand plan to connect the rails to Honshu via Awaji Island, but in the end, this dead-end platform ended up being the end of the journey. However, the traces of those ``unfulfilled dreams'' give this station a unique sense of melancholy and a sense of travel that is unique to a terminal station. Standing on the premises, where the scent of the sea is strong in the air, you can quietly feel the pride of being the northernmost point reached by the Awa railway and the endless longing for the sea.

Chayamachi. This station, where the Shimotsui Electric Railway branched off and the peaceful whistle of the light railway echoed, is now a modern junction with the elevated Seto Ohashi Line towering over it. The fact that it takes on the heavy responsibility of serving as the main artery connecting Honshi and Shizu in the midst of the expanding plains of Kojima Bay's reclaimed land is a symbol of the changing times. Although vestiges of the past as an above-ground station have faded, the sound of the footsteps of travelers changing trains still carries the same sense of excitement from the journey. It gives you a unique sense of tension, as if you're running towards the gateway to Shikoku.

Uematsu. This station, located on an elevated platform overlooking a residential area in the southeastern part of Kurashiki City, is a particularly practical stop on the Seto Ohashi Line that is rooted in daily life. From the unobstructed hill, you can see all the way to the mountains of Sanuki on a clear day, and it feels like a prelude to a journey across the ocean. Although there are few special historical remains, the sight of people heading out into the city as the sound of the train heralds the start of the day shows us that the railway is the very breath of the city. The truth about railways lies in the simple everyday life.

Kimi. This station is located between tunnels, slipping into a small gap in the mountains, and has a tranquil atmosphere that gives you the feeling of being in a ``unexplored region.'' The surrounding steep terrain speaks volumes about how difficult the construction of the Seto Ohashi Line was in the past. When you land on the sparsely populated platform, all you can hear is the sound of the wind rustling through the bamboo forest, making you forget that you are on the side of the main artery that connects Honshu and Shikoku. This tranquility nestled in the bosom of nature is another true face of the Seto Ohashi Line that cannot be seen from the window of a high-speed express train.

Upper town. This station, located in a high position overlooking the roofs of a residential area just before the tunnel that leads to Kojima, gives you a feeling that the Seto Inland Sea is finally near. The area around the station is dotted with factories for Kojima's specialty clothing industry, and the pride of Kojima as a textile town is still alive and well. The contrast between the silence beneath the elevated tracks and the occasional roar of high-speed trains passing overhead clearly demonstrates the power of modern railways. For the people of this city, which has many hills, this high platform feels like a special staircase leading to the sky.

Kojima. This station, which is the final hub on the Honshu side and is world-famous as a sacred place for denim, is a gathering place of anticipation and excitement as the journey reaches its climax, crossing the Seto Ohashi Bridge. While we are still searching for the ruins of the former Shimotsui Electric Railway, the beauty of the Seto Inland Sea islands that can be seen from the current gigantic elevated platform is a true example of the best of Japan's civil engineering technology. As you pass through the ticket gates, where the sea breeze blows through, you can feel the vibrancy of the people who have lived alongside the sea, and the fruition of the grand dream of the Showa era, when railways crossed the sea, still vividly alive today.

Utazu. This station, the first station that trains arrive at after crossing the Seto Ohashi Bridge, is a strategic point in a new era, built on the history of vast salt fields. The complex wiring of the Delta Line shows that this is the heart of the railway that connects Kagawa, Kochi, and Ehime. It is a traveler's privilege to look up at the Gold Tower towering in front of the station and think about the work of our predecessors who toiled in the Irihama-style salt fields of old. With its modern décor, the scent of the sea and the strata of history overlap, giving you a full sense of its status as the gateway to Shikoku.

Yosan line. Starting from Takamatsu, the ``gateway'' where travelers once took their first steps to Shikoku when they disembarked from the Utaka Ferry, this railway runs along the Seto Inland Sea to the end of Iyo and Uwajima, and boasts a grandeur worthy of being called the artery of Shikoku. Immediately after leaving Takamatsu, you can see the modern scenery of looking up at the huge steel frame of the Seto Ohashi Bridge across the Sanuki Plain, and the view of the calm ocean filled with beautiful islands as you emerge from the coastline after passing Tadotsu, tempts you to travel as much as it has in the past.

This railway line, where the limited express Shiokaze once roared with its heavy diesel sound, and before that, steam locomotives such as the C57 emitted white smoke, is now electrified with pendulum trains that zip through the area. However, as you pass Kannon-ji Temple and enter Ehime Prefecture, looking up at the majestic view of Mt. Ishizuchi, you can still feel the atmosphere of the former main route. In particular, the tranquil view of the Iyonada Sea that stretches out from the window of the old ``Umiwari'' line that branches off from Mukaibara via Nagahama quietly makes us question what is the essence of railway travel in this day and age where efficiency is valued. This long journey, passing through the golden yellow slopes of Mt. Mikan, towards the final destination, Uwajima, offers a luxurious feeling of unraveling the richness and history of the land of Shikoku with each stop.

Takamatsu. All of Shikoku's railways converge here and start from here, and the style of the dead-end platform is truly worthy of the name ``gateway.'' The hustle and bustle of travelers disembarking from the Udaka Ferry and crossing the overpass carrying heavy luggage still lingers faintly in the sea breeze, even now that the station has been transformed into a modern station building. The scent of udon soup wafting at the edge of the platform is the best hospitality for travelers and makes them realize that they have arrived in Shikoku. When you look at the stop at the end of the rail, you are reminded that this was once the final destination of a dream that crossed the ocean.

Kozai. This station, located just as the train begins to accelerate after passing through the city center of Takamatsu, is a mix of residential and industrial areas, giving it a somewhat practical calm. Kosai Castle once stood near here, and if you think about the history of medieval samurai gazing at the Seto Inland Sea, the current appearance of the quiet, unmanned station makes you feel like it's just another layer of history. When you look out over the roofs of the houses from the platform on top of the embankment and feel the hint of the Seto Inland Sea in the distance, you are once again reminded that you are on the outer edge of the port town of Takamatsu.

Kinashi. This station is known as the place of the legend of Momotaro, and the stone statue placed on the platform attracts the attention of travelers, but it also has the face of a world-renowned bonsai village. The greenhouses around the station are lined with meticulously grown pine bonsai, and you can admire the deep greenery from the train window. There used to be a freight siding, and you can feel the traces of the bonsai from this area being transported to enthusiasts all over the country in the margins of the premises. The legendary romance and the breath of traditional industry are quietly blending into the noise of the railway.

Hataoka. It is said that there were once plans for a line to branch off from this area, and the station has the potential to become a transportation hub. The spacious grounds and long platforms are remnants of the days when passenger trains were proudly passing by, and today it is still a key location for trains to take shelter and cross paths. The area around the station is dotted with stone stores that sell Kokubunji stone, a specialty of Kagawa Prefecture, and you can sometimes hear the sound of stone being carved on the wind. It is a simple and sturdy stop in the middle of the Sanuki Plain that gives you the purest sense of the regular rhythm of the railway.

Kokubu. It is located in front of the gates of Sanuki Kokubunji, one of the Kokubunji temples built by Emperor Shomu throughout the country, and the station has a tranquil atmosphere that feels like thousands of years of history has enveloped the entire station. Standing on the platform, you can see the majestic forest of temples up close, and the stone lanterns standing right next to the railroad tracks quietly announce that this is a place of worship. In the past, pilgrims would have disembarked at this station to rest their heavy legs. Even today, when modern trains run through the station, the atmosphere that flows through the station is somehow removed from the worldly world, giving travelers a moment of peace.

Sanuki Fuchu. As the name suggests, this station is the ancient political center where the capital of Sanuki was once located. Washed by the turbulent waves of history, its former glory has been buried underground, but you can still feel a bit of the dignity of the past in the calm appearance of the village around the station. When you get off the short platform, you can see the beautiful ridgelines of the surrounding mountains, which tell us that this place was a natural stronghold. The real pleasure of traveling is thinking about the contrast between the times when railroads now run straight through the roads that ancient officials would have walked.

Kamogawa. Located just before crossing the Aya River, this station is blessed with abundant water and greenery, and still conveys the atmosphere of a rural station. The sight of a limited express train taking a break on the siding track and giving way to the following limited express gives you a sense of the functional beauty that is unique to the Yosan Line, which has a mix of single and double tracks. In the past, water transportation and the flour milling industry used this river to prosper, and the opening of the railroad has a history of completely changing the landscape. When the fresh breeze from across the river blows through the platform, you can feel for yourself the eternal nature that Sanuki's nature has nurtured over time.

Yasoba. This area is known for the legend of the Retired Emperor Sutoku and its thirst-quenching spring water, and although the station itself is small, the aura that wafts through it is extraordinary. Right next to the station is a shop that serves the famous Tokoroten, giving the illusion that the summer of the Showa era, when travelers once stopped to cool off, is still intact. Even though it is an inorganic platform without a station building, the richness of the legends surrounding it arouses a sense of awe in those who stop by. The mysterious sound of the spring, combined with the sound of the rail joints, creates a mysterious sense of travel.

Sakaide. This area, once home to vast irihama-style salt fields and a mountain of white salt that symbolized the city, has now been transformed into a modern elevated station, serving as a branch point on the Seto Ohashi Line. The hustle and bustle under the elevated tracks and the modern buildings testify to the strength of post-war reconstruction, when the former salt fields were transformed into industrial areas. From the platform, you can see the huge truss structure of the Seto Ohashi Bridge in the distance, and witness the realization of the Showa era dream of a railroad crossing the sea. Even now, when the smell of salt has been replaced by factory smoke, this station remains the heart of Shikoku's logistics.

Utazu. This station, where trains from Honshu first set foot on Shikoku soil, is a crossroads of time, where the old townscape coexists with the brand new urban landscape that spreads out on reclaimed land. In the past, salt fields spread out and trains ran leisurely above ground, but now the complex wiring of the Delta Line has been laid out on an elevated platform, and it has become a symbol of the precision of railways. When you step into the old village hidden in the shadow of the station building, you will find that the memories of the wealthy salt merchants are still alive, and you will feel the layers of old and new.

Marugame. The station boasts a truly luxurious view, as you can look up at Marugame Castle, one of the 12 existing castle towers, from the station platform. The port used to be a busy gateway to the Konpira Shrine, and has a history of being crowded with people transferring to the railway from there. The sound of cracking bamboo to make the famous fan could once be heard from all around the station. Now that it has been elevated, it gives a sophisticated impression, but the calm atmosphere in the plaza in front of the station shows that it has not lost its pride as a castle town. The majesty of the stone walls makes you feel like you are traveling even more deeply.

Sanuki salt shop. As the train passes through the city of Marugame and approaches the coastline again, this station is quietly located, and as its name suggests, the station's name refers to the vestiges of the salt pans of the past. A single home nestled in a residential area exudes the scent of a down-to-earth lifestyle, unrelated to the glamor of tourism. Although specific historical data is lacking, watching from the platform as the lights of the houses start to come on at dusk is a warm feeling that can only be achieved by traveling by train. Amidst the ever-changing cityscape, the only constant is the sea breeze blowing through the platform.

Tadotsu. It is the birthplace of Shikoku's railways, and the fateful turning point where the Yosan Line and Dosan Line diverge. The brick water tower and old rolling stock factory buildings still remain, and the city's character as a ``sacred place for railroads'', with its smell of sweat and oil from railroad workers, is overwhelming. You can feel the excitement of the past, when steam locomotives used to refuel here with coal and set off on their respective journeys in every corner of the spacious grounds. The voices selling ekiben have long since disappeared, but if you listen closely to the sound of train joints, you can almost hear the heartbeat of our predecessors who built the railways of Shikoku.

Coastal temple. As the name suggests, this station is located right next to Kaiganji Temple, a famous temple said to be the birthplace of Kobo Daishi, and the train windows that run along the shore of the Seto Inland Sea are beautiful. The station building has a calming appearance that reminds you of a temple, and when you step onto the platform, the scent of the sea and the smell of incense intertwine, giving it a unique sense of travel. It feels like the memories of summers when the platform was once overflowing with beachgoers and worshipers are etched into the grain of the old benches. The scenery created by the blue sea, ancient temples, and railways quietly but powerfully tells us about the quiet time Shikoku has lived through.

Tsushimanomiya. It is truly a ``phantom stop,'' with trains only stopping for two days a year during the summer festival of Tsushima Shrine, the guardian deity of children. This short platform continues to quietly wait for people to cross the bridge that leads to the shrine floating in the sea. On non-business days, the trains pass by at breakneck speed on the empty platforms, but on festival days you can feel the cheers of children floating in the air, as if trapped in amber. At this station, which condenses the memories of the ``hare'' days of the railway, we can see the happy relationship between simple, warm faith and the railway that has remained unchanged since the Showa era.

Takuma. This area, which is the entrance to the Shonai Peninsula and where the legend of Urashima Taro lives on, is quietly steeped in history as it was once the base of the Naval Air Corps. When you get off the station, you can feel the gentle sea breeze of the Seto Inland Sea, and the heartrending memories of the young crew members looking up at the sky can still be felt in every corner of the city. Although it is now a modern station building where limited express trains also stop, the view of the Mitoyo Mountains from the platform still greets travelers with its gentle gentleness, giving a sense of the depth of this place where myth and history intersect. When I look at the road that leads to the peninsula, drawn by the scent of the sea, I can't help but think that the countless fragments of life carried by the railway are shining in the waves.

Mino. Established in 1994, this station, the first in Shikoku to have a hiragana station name, plays the role of connecting the memories of the old Shimotakase to a new era. Surrounded by gentle hills, with orchards and fields, its appearance truly embodies the original landscape of Sanuki's Satoyama. The liveliness of Fureai Park, which is adjacent to the station, is proof that the railway has created a new gathering place for the community, and it gives us a sense of a modern public transportation system that is different from the old Showa era station buildings. The breeze blowing through the short platform is tinged with the faint scent of local tea, adding a warm feeling that reminds you of your hometown during your journey.

Takase. Located in the center of Mitoyo City, it boasts an immeasurably vibrant history as a distribution center for the finest tea and agricultural products produced in the area. A calm streetscape spreads out in front of the station, conveying the dignity of the days when it was an ancient highway. The spacious premises retains the vestiges of the days when freight trains were frequently shunted, reminding us of the golden age of the Showa era, when railways were a powerful driver of local industry. The powerful sound of a limited express train sliding onto the platform proudly conveys the fact that this town is still a key transportation hub in Seisan.

Hijidai. Surrounded by rich rice fields and with a single platform quietly placed on top of a mound, this station is the perfect example of the simplicity of a rural stop. Although there is little specific historical data, one cannot help but think about how many lives were nurtured and spread out into the outside world because of this station. At dusk, the sight of a train cutting through a sea of ​​golden rice ears is as beautiful as a landscape painting. Sitting alone in a simple waiting area, listening to the sound of the railroad crossing announcing the approach of a train, it makes me feel deeply the preciousness of the regular time that trains keep.

Motoyama. As the station in front of the gate of Honzan-ji Temple, the 70th temple of the Shikoku Sacred Site, it has a history of many pilgrims getting off here and walking on their canes. The appearance of the station building gives you a sense of the calm characteristic of a temple town, as well as the deep sense of compassion that has watched over countless travelers. When you look up at the majesty of the five-storied pagoda that towers over the temple grounds in the distance, you realize that timeless faith and the railroad, a symbol of modern civilization, are in happy harmony here. Standing on the platform where the sound of the pilgrim's bells and the sound of the train's joints mix together, I feel as if I am being asked anew the essential meaning of travel.

Kannonji Temple. It is the main station representing Nishisan, and the gateway to Ariake Beach, which is known for its huge sand paintings by Kan'ei Tsuho. In the past, a lot of freight and passengers came and went here, and the bustling atmosphere of the Showa era, when movie theaters and restaurants lined up around the station, still remains in the atmosphere of the town. The vast grounds are engraved with memories of locomotives resting in preparation for crossing difficult passages, and you can feel the pride of the place as a key railway hub. The panoramic view of the city nestled between the mountains and the sea that can be seen for a moment from the window of a limited express train is sure to heighten your travel spirit to its peak.

Toyohama. Located in the westernmost part of Sanuki, this town is known for its extravagant Chosa (Taikodai) festival, and even the appearance of the station building gives the impression of a quiet pre-festival atmosphere. The area once prospered for trade in salt production and cotton, and the prosperity of the past, when rich seafood was transported through the railways, can be seen in the old warehouses and rows of houses. Looking up at the ridgeline of the Sanuki Mountains from the platform tells you that you are finally nearing the border with the country of Iyo, and gives you a feeling that the landscape of your trip is about to change dramatically. In this area where the scent of the ocean is strong, you will once again realize the strength of the regional bonds that have been forged by the railways.

Minoura. This station is the last station in Kagawa Prefecture, and is located in a scenic area where the railway line is closest to the sea, and it is filled with the desolation and beauty of a ``boundary station.'' The Seto Inland Sea stretches out in front of the platform, and the sight of a limited express train running right by the water's edge is one of the most dynamic scenes on the Yosan Line. In the past, it had a heavy role as a signal station for crossing prefectural borders, and there was a time when trains used to take a breather after passing through difficult passages. Today, travelers are greeted by a waiting room made from an old freight car, giving a sense of tranquillity, as if left behind by the waves of modernization.

Kawanoe. This station, which is the first to greet you upon entering the country of Ehime, tells the story of its history as a strategic and transportation hub since ancient times, as well as the majesty of Kawanoe Castle towering in the background. As soon as you step out of the station building, the tall chimneys of the paper mill pierce the sky, and the nostalgic smell of paper wafts on the wind. The vibrancy that once supported Japan's rapid growth as a "paper town" is still reflected in the dignified appearance around the station. The contrast between the calm sea of ​​Seto Inland Sea and the powerful industrial area symbolizes the diverse expressions of the country of Iyo, and gives us a strong sense of new developments in our travels.

Iyo Mishima. The station of this city, which plays the central role of Shikoku Chuo City and is world-renowned for its paper and pulp industry, is the lively ``industrial heart'' where large freight trains always arrive and depart. The pipelines of a huge paper mill run crisscrossing the premises, and the heartbeat of the mill can be heard day and night, making it a living witness to the era when railroads were directly connected to industry. The scene of the Showa era, where the smoke rising from the many chimneys was once a symbol of affluence, is still preserved in its overwhelming scale. Even though a station building is highly functional and beautiful, the pride of its workers and the weight of the economy supported by railways can be felt all too clearly.

Iyosangawa. Located a little away from the hustle and bustle of heavy and chemical industries, this station is located on a narrow plot of land where the ocean and mountains once again approach, giving it a peaceful atmosphere that makes you feel like you have regained a moment of tranquility. In the past, there was a history of many agar-manufacturing factories in this area, and the word ``Kan'' engraved in its name tells us about the activities of our predecessors who took advantage of the cool climate. The view of Hiuchinada from the platform is beautiful, and the sight of the nature of Setouchi, which had been hidden in the shadow of factories, peeking out once again is a soothing sight for travelers. In the unpretentious appearance of a local station, you can feel that the unique time of the land is quietly passing by.

Red star. Its poetic name comes from the majestic figure of Mt. Akaboshi rising in the background, and there is a legend that ascetics once looked up at the bright star at the peak of the mountain. The station itself is a simple structure facing the national highway, but the view of the Ishizuchi mountain range seen from here is divine and makes you realize that the railway is running at the foot of sacred territory. The name is said to be filled with people who would have come to see the katakuri flowers on Mt. Akaboshi in the spring. The time spent waiting for the next train, surrounded by the hustle and bustle of modern asphalt, while being watched over by the gods of the mountains, gives us a strangely refreshing feeling.

Iyodoi. This station has a history as a post town where the Tosa Highway branched off and travelers heading to various parts of Shikoku took off their sandals. The area around the station still retains the appearance of an old village, and retains a trace of its character as a transportation hub that existed even before the railroad was opened. The spacious interior gives a sense of the spaciousness of the days when the station was busy with cargo shipments and train exchanges, and as modern express trains pass by without slowing down, you can't help but feel the ruthlessness of the passage of time. However, this single home, which connects the unchanging shadow of the mountain and the lives of the local people, continues to create a stable rhythm for the journey.

Sekikawa. The train tracks run behind a residential area, and the station is surrounded by deep greenery and a stream. Although it doesn't stand out on the Yosan Line, it has the tranquility of a hideout. Although there are no special historical remains, as the name of the station suggests, there is a certain harshness to the topography that makes one imagine that there may once have been a ``checkpoint'' in this area. Standing on a single platform with no major equipment and listening to the chirping of birds in the distance, you can feel the purest way the railway blends into nature. This quiet station gives us a sense of the quality of a lonely journey, freed from the speed of the city and simply staring at the railway line.

Takihama. It is a stately station with a history of being home to the Takihama Salt Farm, once the largest in the East, and mountains of white salt coloring the railway. Today, large-scale factories are built on the site of the former salt fields, and although the form of industry has changed, its importance as a logistics base has not changed. When you look at the spacious grounds and the remains of the siding where freight cars were once lined up, you can't help but think about how much this area has contributed to Japan's modernization. The unique atmosphere, where the scent of salt and oil mix, eloquently tells the story of the history of sweat, tears, and prosperity that the land of Takihama has carved out.

Niihama. It is a well-known company castle town for Sumitomo, and it is also a symbolic station of the ``Koryo'', which has been a strong driving force behind Japan's modernization since the opening of the Besshi Copper Mine. A unique railway called the Besshi Mining Railway once ran here, and copper mined from the mountains traveled to the world from here, making it the stage of a magnificent history. Even though the station building has changed to its current modern form, the unique vibrancy surrounding the station and the majestic view of the huge smelter are testament to the overwhelming energy of this city. The sight of express trains proudly stopping and throngs of businessmen and workers passing by gives us a strong and passionate feeling that railways are still at the forefront of industry.

Nakahagi. It is a station located at the border where the train slips into the rich rice paddies of Saijo, while retaining the lingering impressions of the industrial area of ​​Niihama. There used to be many munitions factories scattered around this area, and there is a history of railways transporting the tense atmosphere during wartime. Currently, it is located in a quiet residential area, but once you stand on the platform, you can see the Ishizuchi mountain range rising even closer behind you, giving you the strong feeling that you are traveling along the spine of Shikoku. The sight of a modern stainless steel train gently sliding onto a platform filled with the smell of earth is a quiet testimony to the changes of the times.

Iyo Saijo. It is the starting point for climbing Mt. Ishizuchi, and above all, it is the gateway to the City of Water, where artesian water fountains called ``Uchinuki'' water the city. The ``Shikoku Railway Culture Museum'' is located next to the station, and the 0-series Shinkansen trains and other cars that convey the glory of the past make it a place worthy of being called a sacred place for railways. It was once the site of a locomotive depot, and you can still feel the history of the locomotives resounding as they tackled the difficult crossing of the Sekigawa River within the spacious grounds. Just a sip of the cool water flowing from the faucet on the platform will make you feel as if the fatigue of your journey is quietly relieving.

Mt. Ishizuchi. It is a station in front of the gates of Ishizuchi Shrine, overlooking the sacred mountain of Shikoku, Mt. Ishizuchi, and is a tranquil place where a sacred atmosphere envelops the entire platform. Although the station building has a simple appearance, it bears the burden of a history in which religious people from all over the country once made their way to the top of the mountain. Although there are no major facilities, the deep forest surrounding the station and the occasional sound of train horns make you feel strongly that you are on the border between the mundane and the sacred. The time spent waiting for the next train while being watched over by the gods of the mountains gives travelers a refreshing feeling, like a kind of training.

Iyo Himi. This station, which passes through the city of Saijo and is quietly placed in a tranquil rural landscape, is a stop that conveys the peaceful daily life of the country of Iyo in the past. Although specific historical data is lacking, the scenery created by the green fields surrounding the station and the ridgeline of the mountains beyond is full of beauty, like a landscape painting. Sitting in the simple waiting area of ​​an unmanned station and listening to the chirping of birds in the distance, you can really feel how the railway is quietly integrated into nature. It shows us that the true expression of Iyo is hidden in the unadorned scenery.

Iyo Komatsu. It was once a castle town of the Komatsu clan with a 10,000 koku estate, and is a historic station that still retains the vestiges of samurai residences. It is also the station for getting off at Koonji Temple, the 61st temple of the Shikoku Sacred Site, and the sight of pilgrims and local students lined up on the same platform creates a mysterious sense of travel where ancient faith and modern life intersect. The railroad tracks run along the route that feudal lords would have once walked on their sankin shifts, and the pride of the Showa era, when railways became the main character of a new era, can be felt in the calm rows of houses around the station. It gives a feeling of comfortable silence, as if time is slowly stagnating.

Tamanoe. If you look around you, you will see lush rice fields, and this is a small station that has the feel of a ``stop in a rice field.'' Although it is relatively new, opening in 1952, its simple structure allows you to directly feel the undulations of the land and the breath of nature. In autumn, the golden rice ears are waving, and the stationary diesel cars look like a stroke of color in the landscape. Although there are no special tourist attractions, this station teaches us that the simple changes of the four seasons in a rural village that can be seen from the window are the luxurious margin of a journey on the Yosan Line.

Mibu River. As the central station of Toyo City, it was once a connection point with the Seto Inland Sea route, and boasts an immeasurably vibrant history as a distribution center for goods. Even today, the limited express trains park here and the station is bustling with people commuting to the nearby industrial area, proving that this station is still an important base that supports the local economy. Looking at the spacious premises and the remains of the former freight sidings will remind you of the golden age of the Showa era, when railways were at the forefront of industry. The unique atmosphere, where the scent of the sea and the smell of oil mix, quietly tells us about the history of sweat and tears that the port town of Mibu River has carved out.

Miyoshi Iyo. It is located in the middle of a railway line that cuts straight through a vast plain, and as its name suggests, it is a quiet station blessed with rich farmland. The premises, which was once bustling with shipments of agricultural products, is now filled with nothing but a gentle breeze. There is a historical straight section here that was once the stage for high-speed railway tests, and the traces of the passion of engineers pursuing their dreams are hidden in the shine of the rails. As I watch modern express trains pass by like arrows, I am deeply moved by the contrast between the evolutionary history of railways and the unchanging landscape of Satoyama.

Iyo Sakurai. It is located at the southern end of Imabari City, and is a station in a traditional town that has long been known as the production center for Sakurai lacquerware. Once you get off the station, you will see rows of old houses that have withstood the sea breeze, and you can feel the calmness of the days when craftsmen competed to show their skills. The station building's appearance gives it a sense of pride that it has continued to support the local culture, and it has the dignity of being not just a transit point, but an ``entrance to the city's history.'' If you stand on the platform while thinking of the pine forest of Shijimagahara, a scenic spot near the coast, you will be reminded of how precious it is that the sea and culture of Iyo are connected by railway.

Iyo Tomita. The station is right in front of the city center of Imabari, and is surrounded by brand new houses and old villages, giving the station a calm, suburban feel. The name of the station hints at the history of the vast salt fields that once existed in this area, and tells us that the appearance of the town has changed greatly over time. The view from the platform is calm, but in the distance you can see the cranes of Imabari's huge shipbuilding dock, giving you a sense that your trip will finally enter the "city of shipbuilding." A single platform that quietly watches over daily activities creates a stable rhythm on the journey.

Imabari. It is a world-renowned towel industry and shipbuilding town, and now that it has been elevated, it boasts the appearance of a sophisticated city station. However, as you stand on the platform, you can still look up at Imabari Castle and feel the strong liveliness unique to the Showa era port town where travelers first arrived after crossing the rough waves of the Seto Inland Sea, mixed in with the breeze. The breeze blowing through the premises has a gentle scent, like towel fabric softener, mixed with the smell of welding from the docks, which speaks to the diverse vitality of this city. As the starting point of the Shimanami Kaido, which connects Shikoku and Honshu, it gives us a sense of the trends of a new era.

Hatohama. Although it is located next to Imabari Station, everyone is surprised by the dramatic changes in its landscape. There is a huge shipyard right behind the platform, and the huge hull of the ship, which is still under construction, looks down on the station like a skyscraper. This area, which once made a huge fortune through salt fields and shipbuilding, has a hidden dynamism that rivals even the mountainous scenery of the Oito Line, where you can truly witness an ``industrial panorama.'' The sounds of hammers hitting and cranes driving resonate perfectly with the sounds of train joints, giving you a real sense of the energy that continues to support Japan's post-war rapid economic growth.

Wave direction (Namikata). It was once known as the ``City of Sailors,'' and is the hometown of men of the sea who have produced many talented sailors. The station is surrounded by a calm inlet, and the smell of the sea is strong in the air, which is proof that the railway has lived in harmony with the sea. Although there is no large station building, the view of the calm sea from the platform and the sight of the numerous ships floating there testify to the profound history of this area. In this place where land railroads and sea routes intersect, I can't help but think of the stories of farewells and reunions of sailors of the past who left their hometowns by train.

Onishi. As soon as you step out of the station building, you will be overwhelmed by the majesty of the huge shipbuilding dock right in front of you. This area, which was once famous as the ``Kurushima Dock'', continues to produce gigantic ships that bring together the best of Japan's shipbuilding technology today as the ``Shin Kurushima Dock''. Just by standing on the platform, you can feel the sound of the steel being struck beneath your feet, giving you a sense of the exhilaration of being at the forefront of industry. There was once a time when the prosperity of this town supported the transportation of freight by rail, and the Showa era scene, where smoke rising from factory chimneys was a symbol of affluence, is still preserved in its overwhelming scale.

Iyo Kameoka. This station is located at the point where the hustle and bustle of the shipbuilding town recedes and the trains begin to run along the coastline of the Takanawa Peninsula. There is a calm village in front of the station, and a beautiful sandy beach in the background. There is a history in the past where clay, the raw material for Kikuma tiles, was collected in this area, and you can feel that the memory of the area is ingrained in the old buildings around the station. The sunlight from the sea shining through the train windows illuminates the platform, and from here on, you can feel your travel mood once again change to a calmer one, admiring the beauty of the islands of the Seto Inland Sea.

Kikuma. It is a town known for its ``Kikuma tiles'', which boasts a history of 700 years, and the sight of the roofs of the houses flowing through the train window filled with heavy silver tiles is truly a sight to behold. The huge oil storage tanks lined up next to the station symbolize the strength of Iyo, where traditional industry and modern energy bases coexist. You can feel the history of freight cars loaded with roof tiles traveling all over Shikoku from here in the calm atmosphere of the premises. Standing on the platform where the smell of smoke from burning tiles mixes with the sea breeze, the pride of the people who have lived with the earth warms the hearts of travelers.

Asami. As the name suggests, it is one of the most beautiful small stations on the Yosan Line, with the shallow, clear sea approaching right next to the platform. It is located on a narrow strip of land surrounded by mountains and the sea, and the sight of a short diesel train parked there is full of the emotion of a landscape painting. Although there are few special historical remains, waiting for the train to arrive while listening to the sound of the waves is a blissful moment that makes you forget the hustle and bustle of everyday life. I would like to strongly assert that even before Shimonada Station was known as the ``station near the sea,'' this shallow sea was also a hidden gem that filled the hearts of travelers with the sounds of the sea.

Oura. This station, nestled in a quiet cove before crossing the final mountain pass to Matsuyama, is full of tranquility, like a temporary respite before the journey finally heads to the prefectural capital. In the past, there were many fishing boats lined up in this area, and the remains of seafood being transported via railway can be seen in the old stone walls and alleys around the station. When you stand on the platform, you can see the beautiful shadow of the mountains of the Takanawa Peninsula falling into the sea, making you feel that you are deeply immersed in nature. Just before the speed of the city approaches, the tranquility that feels like the end of this world calms the mind of the traveler.

Iyo Hojo. Once the center of Hojo City, this station overlooks the scenic Kashima Island floating off the coast, and the gentle sea breeze of Nishiseto always blows through the platform. The atmosphere of the Showa era, when express trains once proudly stopped here and the area was crowded with vacationers heading to Kashima, is still vividly remembered in the spacious space in front of the station. This place, where the maritime history preserved by the descendants of the Iyo Navy and the modern railroad intersect, is more than just a transit point; it is full of local pride. Looking at the glow of the rails as the express train accelerates, it quietly but powerfully tells the traveler that they are finally near the prefectural capital, Matsuyama.

Yanagihara. It is a station with a single platform quietly placed in a quiet landscape with a mixture of countryside and residences, passing through the urban area of ​​Hojo. Although there is a lack of specific historical data, these ordinary small stations are proof that railways have continued to follow the ups and downs of the land and continue to support the delicate daily lives of people. Sitting in a waiting area with no major facilities, waiting for the sound of the railroad crossing announcing the approach of a train, it feels as if time has stopped in the Showa era. This station quietly reminds us that the luxurious margins of train travel are hidden within the unadorned scenery.

Awai. It is a historical place close to Kono Beppu, which was once the residence of the Kono clan, and the calm rows of houses around the station give it a sense of dignity that is typical of a samurai town. In the past, the shipping of agricultural products was popular in this area, and the silence of the premises is a reminder of the vestiges of the past, when the platform would have been full of energy during the harvest season. The view of the Takanawa Mountains from the edge of the platform is beautiful, and while being surrounded by nature, it makes you realize how railways run right through the heart of people's lives. The sight of modern stainless steel cars sliding onto a platform smelling of earth gives us a sense of the sincerity of the railway, which is in step with the unchanging climate.

Koyodai. It is a new town station that was built in 1986 and symbolizes the end of the Showa era. As the name suggests, the platform, located on a hill, offers a panoramic view of the blue waters of the Seto Inland Sea, giving us a sense of a new layer of history that began to evolve alongside modern residential development. The bright and open atmosphere, which is different from the heavy history of the former Yosan Line stations, is proof that the railway has brought a new breath of life to the city. At dusk, the sight of the sun setting over the sea painting the platform a golden hue is a vivid reminder that even if the station is new, it still retains the same sense of travel.

Horie. When talking about this place, it is impossible to ignore the history of the ``Nibori Ferry'' that once departed and arrived at Nikata in Hiroshima Prefecture. Although it was hidden in the shadow of the Udaka Ferry, the dream of a railway connecting across the sea to Honshu is clearly engraved in this small station. Although the station is currently quiet and unmanned, I can't help but feel like I can hear the faint whistle of a ferry mixed in with the sea breeze. The appearance of the old port in front of the station and the old warehouses that watched over the bustle of the past still quietly tell the story of a time when railways and shipping coexisted.

Iyo wake. Located on the outer edge of the city of Matsuyama, this station serves as a gateway to Taizan-ji, the 52nd sacred temple of Shikoku, and Enmyo-ji, the 53rd temple. When you get off the station, you can see pilgrims walking with canes, demonstrating the perfect harmony between the ancient religious path and the modern railway. In the past, travelers were welcomed by a solid wooden station building, and there was probably a calm atmosphere typical of a temple town. Even today, despite its modernization, the time passing around the station feels somehow removed from the worldly world, giving travelers a moment of peace. It gives you a sense of the depth that is unique to Iyo's railways, where the sacred and the profane intersect.

Mitsuhama. As Matsuyama's gateway to the sea, it is a historic station that has long been vibrant as a port town. The memory of the previous station building, which was built in 1927 and retaining its half-timbered style, seems to be echoing in the current station building, giving it a truly high-class atmosphere. When you get off the station and walk down the road that leads to the port, you feel like you can still hear the heartbeat of the city that Soseki and Shiki once followed. The scenery lined with shipyards and old merchant houses is proof that the port town has strongly responded to the waves of modernization brought by the railway. Standing on the platform where the scent of the sea and the smell of oil mix together, your travels will reach their peak here.

Matsuyama. It is the gateway to Matsuyama City, one of the largest cities in Shikoku, and has been synonymous with travel sentiment since the days when Natsume Soseki's ``Botchan'' got off the train. The appearance of the Showa station building, with its impressive triangular roof, is about to change due to modern elevated construction projects, but the ``Iyo atmosphere'' that exists there remains unchanged. As you stand on the platform, you can hear the sound of the engine of the diesel express train heading towards Uwajima, making you realize that this is the heart of western Shikoku. The sight of large numbers of travelers coming and going with great anticipation for Dogo Onsen shows that the railway is inseparable from the city's culture.

Ichitsubo. Located in the delta area between the Ishite River and the Shigenobu River, this place, which was once a quiet rural station, now lives as a stop for getting off at Botchan Stadium, next to a gorgeous sports hall. On days when there are big matches, the city is noisy like never before, but the silence during the day has a special charm. The scenery created by the modern structures and the wind blowing across the river gives you a sense of dynamism that can only be experienced on a suburban railway. It's truly heartwarming to see the enthusiasm for baseball, a game Soseki loved, taking root in this area along with the rhythm of the railway.

Northern Iyo. This station is located at the point where you leave the city center of Matsuyama and the rich rural scenery of the Iyo Plain begins to spread out again. In the past, the shipment of agricultural products was popular in this area, and the weight of the era when the railway was the only artery supporting the local life can be felt in the spacious premises. In recent years, large-scale commercial facilities have been built nearby, and the appearance of the town is changing, but the shadow of the Ishizuchi Mountains seen from the platform remains unchanged, quietly preserving the memory of the land. This makes us realize once again that the preciousness of time created by railways is hidden in the casual scenes of daily commuting to work and school.

Minamiiyo. It is one of the newest stations on the Yosan Line, opened in 2020, and is a place that truly symbolizes the ``future of railways'' as it was developed along with the relocation of the Matsuyama train station. The appearance of a station equipped with the latest equipment in the middle of what was once a rice field clearly shows the speed of modernization. However, the sight of trains waiting for their turn at the adjacent depot is an irresistible sight for railway fans, and makes you feel that the "heartbeat of iron" is still beating at the new station. I want to see what kind of history this new station, full of pioneering spirit, will have in the future.

Iyo Yokota. Surrounded by rolling fields, this station has a single platform that suddenly appears, giving it the feel of a ``Nonaka Station.'' Although no special historical remains stand out, you can't help but think about how many lives were nurtured and sent out into the outside world because of this station's presence. The wind blowing through the simple waiting area is laced with the seasonal scent of earth, gently soothing the hearts of travelers tired of the speed of the city. This makes us realize once again how precious it is that a single, thin line called the railway connects these quiet villages to the rest of the world.

Torinoki. Although it is a relatively new station, established in 1986 and located in the middle of a residential area in Iyo City, it can be seen that it has completely integrated into the local life. In the mornings and evenings, the lively voices of students commuting to the railway echo on the platform, reminding us that railways are still an active part of our daily lives. The unique balance between the orderly streetscape around the station and the atmosphere of an old farming village is like a microcosm of a modern regional city. You can feel the steady progress of this place in the nods and footsteps exchanged during the short time the train stops.

Iyo city. It is the center of Iyo City, which was once called ``Gunchū,'' and is a key transportation hub located across from Gunchu Port Station on the Iyo Railway. As soon as you step out of the station, you will be greeted by a calm townscape from an era when seafood and goods were transported from Gunchu Port, giving you a sense of the richness of its history. The spacious premises and the character of the former express stop still remain in this area without fading. Standing on the platform where the smell of salt carried by the sea breeze mixes with the smell of oil from the train, your sense of travel deepens even further, and it makes you look forward to the next steep mountain pass.

Mukaihara. This is the ``crossing point of fate'' on the Yosan Line. Even if you're not a railway fan, the sight of the old ``Umi-mawari'' line passing through Iyo-Nagahama and the new ``Yama-mawari'' line passing through Uchiko separating vividly but sadly is something that touches the heart. These two rails are a fragment of history, from when all trains ran along the coast to a new line that ran through the mountains to increase speed. As I look back at the old railroad tracks that quietly head towards the sea from the current elevated platform, I am deeply moved by the contrast between the evolution of the railway and the sense of travel that has been left behind.

Takano River. This is the first station where the old line, which split at Mukaihara, finally begins to confront the blue waters of the Seto Inland Sea, especially the Iyonada Sea. This station, located in a narrow area of ​​land between the mountain and the sea, is a refreshing prologue to the ``sea journey'' that is about to begin. The sound of the Takano River flowing into the sea, which gives the station its name, and the sound of waves crashing against each other create a duet on the platform. When the sound of a diesel car approaching from afar echoes in the silence of an unmanned station, we are convinced that we have truly stepped into the ``abyss of travel''.

Iyo Kaminada. This station is the first place that tells travelers of the pride that the town of Futami holds as the ``Town of the Sunset.'' From the platform, you can see the calm waters of the Iyonada Sea, and the wooden station building, washed by the sea breeze, gives you a sense of the deep compassion that has been watching over travelers since the days when ferry boats were connected. In the past, a lot of agricultural products and seafood were shipped from here, and the peaceful size of the premises preserves that memory. Standing on this platform in the evening, when the horizon turns red, gives travelers a sense of supreme luxury.

Shimonada. This place, once known as ``Japan's closest station to the sea,'' has now become a sacred place on the Yosan Line, where travelers from all over the world gather. When you sit on the bench on the platform, the unobstructed view of the Seto Inland Sea spreads out in front of you, and the gradation of blue that blends the sky and sea will leave you speechless. The roughness of the days before national highways were built, when the shoreline was just a stone's throw away, has disappeared, but the quiet enthusiasm of people waiting for the sun to set on the horizon reminds us of the romance of railroads. It is a pure stop that exists just to look out at the sea.

Skewers. This station, which is located past the Shimonada Sea and clinging to a small gap between the steep mountainside and the sea, has a tranquil atmosphere that gives you the feeling of being in a ``unexplored region''. When you look down from the platform, you can almost hear the sound of clear seawater chewing on the rocks, giving you a sense of the fragile yet strong symbiosis between the harshness of nature and the railway. There is no special station building, and the single platform with nothing to block the sea breeze teaches travelers the luxury of being alone. After the wind pressure of passing express trains has passed, the silence dominated only by the sound of the waves is the true image of this station.

Kitanada. It is located astride the border between Iyo City and Ozu City, and has a history of being a border station with a delicate sense of tension. Although it is currently a quiet and unmanned station, the panoramic view of the Iyonada Sea from here boasts a beauty comparable to that of the Shimonada Sea. Considering the history of citrus fruits picked from the surrounding mountains traveling all over the country from this small station, the scent of this station, which mixes with the smell of earth and sea breeze, is truly endearing. It's the perfect place to appreciate the steady progress of your journey while looking at the signs that mark city boundaries rather than prefectural boundaries.

Iyonagahama. Located at the mouth of the Hijikawa River, it was once a key transportation hub where water transportation and railways intersected, and it has watched over the lives of people that cannot be described in words. When you get off the station and look up at the red color of Nagahama Ohashi Bridge, Japan's oldest operating bridge, you can feel the traces of modernization from the Meiji to Showa eras still being reflected on the surface of the river. The area around the station, which was once home to the hustle and bustle of many fish markets, has both the pride of a port town and a somewhat nostalgic sense of solitude. On winter days when the cold air from the Hijikawa storm envelopes the home, my love for traveling deepens even more.

Iyo Izushi. This station is located at the point where the train finally bids farewell to the sea and enters the mountain scenery along the flow of the Hijikawa River. Surrounded by deep greenery and surrounded by the constant sound of the murmuring river, its appearance symbolizes the modest lifestyle of the people of Iyo, who have lived in harmony with water. Although there are few special historical remains, I can't help but think about how many lives were nurtured and spread out into the outside world because of this station. This simple platform quietly embodies how the railway is completely integrated into nature.

Iyo Shirataki. As the name suggests, it is the stop for getting off at Shirataki, the famous waterfall behind the station, and has a history of being crowded with tourists who enjoy the contrast between the autumn leaves and the waterfall in autumn. I feel that the bustle of the past, when special trains ran and many people cheered on this platform, is still etched in the grain of the old waiting area. The Yosan Line, which has begun to take on the character of a mountain line, has a unique atmosphere of both harshness and gentleness. The time you spend waiting for the next train while listening to the sound of the waterfall is a refreshing experience that will help you wash away the grime in your heart.

Yataki. It is a simple stop that is nestled in the gentle meandering of the Hijikawa River, and is a reflection of the daily life of a rural village. It has a history of descending from a light railway called the Ozu Line, and the hardships of our predecessors can be seen in the way the tracks are laid, faithful to the undulations of the land. The wind blowing through the simple platform is laced with seasonal mountain scents, gently soothing the hearts of travelers tired of the speed of the city. This casual scenery shows us the preciousness of the mere existence of a railway.

Haruga. It is a small station that overlooks the village on the other side of the Hijikawa River, and is located on the way where the railway line winds its way through the foot of a quiet mountain. Although specific historical data is lacking, the presence of this casual station makes us realize once again the preciousness of how life in the mountains is connected to the rest of the world. At dusk, the sight of train lights approaching amidst the river mist is as beautiful as a landscape painting. This station quietly tells us that the essence of railway travel lies within its unadorned scenery.

Goro. It has a history of being a branch of the Uchiko Line, and was once an important transportation hub, which is hard to imagine from its current simple appearance. The fields of rape blossoms and cosmos that spread around the station were cultivated by local people out of their love for the railway, and symbolize that the railway is still loved today. The pride of being a former branch station is conveyed through beautiful flowers, and its gentle appearance warms my heart. You can feel the happy relationship between people and the railway from this small station.

Iyo Ozu. It is the gateway to Iyo's Little Kyoto, nestled along the Hijigawa River, and the station has a rich history, with the tower of the reconstructed Ozu Castle proudly visible from the platform. In the past, wealth was transported by waterways and railways, and many merchants took off their shoes at this station, and the lively atmosphere still resides in the calm appearance of the station building. Even in modern times when limited express trains come and go frequently, the elegant tranquility that pervades this station proves that it has not lost its pride as a castle town. At night, when cormorant fishing bonfires illuminate the river surface, the entire station is enveloped in a mysterious atmosphere.

West Ozu. It is a small station located on the edge of Ozu's urban area, in a peaceful area where residential areas and farmland coexist. This area, which once tended to be hidden in the shadows of the history of the Ozu clan, now continues to support people's down-to-earth lifestyles as a base for commuting to work and school. The wind blowing through the single platform is mixed with the refreshing feeling of crossing the surface of the river, making you feel that the speed of your journey slows down just a little. I can't help but think that the concrete structures without any special decorations actually highlight the honest way of life in this area.

Iyo Plain. It is a rural station that offers a moment of peace before passing through the Ozu basin and finally crossing the steep mountain pass that leads to Uwajima. It was once used as a distribution center for agricultural products, and you can feel the vibrancy of the past, when oxcarts and trucks gathered there, in the spacious wiring within the premises. Although there are no major facilities, the ridgeline of the surrounding mountains is beautiful and gives us a sense of the sincerity of the railway, which has been in harmony with nature. Not just the calm before a storm, but the calm before crossing a mountain pass, which provides a quiet rest to the soul of a traveler.

Senjo. This station, located right in front of the port of Yawatahama and surrounded by steep Mt. Mikan, is a place that symbolizes the rich blessings of the country of Iyo.
