The sight of the stone terraced fields stretching to the sky is truly a sight to behold, and there is a history in which many mandarin oranges were once transported across the country from this station, spreading their sweet fragrance. Currently, it is a quiet and unmanned station, but during the harvest season, the smell of soil and fruit fills the entire platform, intensely stimulating the five senses of travelers. I can't help but pay respect to the history of how the sweat and tears of pioneering painted this steep slope a golden color.

Yawatahama. As a port town on the western tip of Shikoku and a node on the sea route that leads to Kyushu, it is a station that is always filled with the excitement of people and the scent of the sea. In the past, commerce flourished to the point that it was called the ``Osaka of Shikoku'', and the heavy wooden station building was filled with merchants and travelers.The thickness of the beams still reflects the enthusiasm of the past. The liveliness of the port in front of the station and the somewhat exotic townscape are proof that the railway has embraced the culture that has crossed the seas. When you stand on a platform where the scent of the sea and the smell of fish mix together, your travel spirit reaches its peak.

Futaiwa. This station is located at the point where the train leaves the hustle and bustle of Yawatahama and once again enters the rugged mountain road. As the name suggests, it is a station with a somewhat tense atmosphere, where railroad workers of the past would have taken a breather before crossing a difficult point, with the shadow of a mountain topped with strangely shaped rocks. Silence reigns now, but as you stand on the fog-shrouded platform, you can almost feel the smell of burning iron and soot from the days when steam locomotives would pant over mountain passes. It makes us realize how precious the single line of railway is in front of the majesty of nature.

Iyo Stone Castle. We arrived at the Uwa Basin, which is nearly 300 meters above sea level, where we found a surprisingly peaceful and vast rural landscape. The sight of straw mammoths and other straw crafts lined up in rice fields gives us a sense of the humor and strength of the people who live with the soil. In the past, rice from this basin was transported via railway, and there is a history of it sustaining people's lives. Despite being surrounded by high mountains, this station has a wide sky and is full of light, making it feel like the perfect treat after a long tunnel journey. The peaceful rural time passes slowly along with the sound of rail joints.

Kamiuwa. This station, located at the northern end of the Uwa Basin, is located on a hill about 200 meters above sea level, yet a spacious rural landscape welcomes travelers. In the quietness of the premises, you can feel the vestiges of the past, when it was once a gathering and distribution center for agricultural products, taking advantage of the cool climate, and would have been full of energy during the harvest season. The ridgelines of the surrounding mountains are beautiful, and this area offers a moment of peace after the rigors of Shikoku's mountain routes. It is in this unpretentious scenery that we can feel the sincerity of the railway, which lives together with the land.

Uno Town. It is the entrance to the townscape, which has been designated as an Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, and is a station that still conveys the dignity of being the cultural center of the Uwajima clan. The Meiji Kaimei school and the rows of old merchant houses give you a sense of the rich history that dates back to before the railroad was built. The sight of the express train quietly stopping and intellectually inquisitive travelers getting off the train tells us that this station is not just a transit point, but a doorway to history. The smell of old wooden school buildings wafting on the wind brings back memories of school buildings from the Showa era, or even the Meiji era.

Shimouwa. It's a quiet station, like a temporary respite, before crossing the steep mountains that lead to Uwajima, at the southern end of the basin. The space in front of the station, where oxcarts loaded with agricultural products would once have gathered, is now filled with a gentle breeze. Although there are no major facilities, the scenery of the surrounding mountains and fields highlights the sincere way of life of the people who have lived with the soil. This makes us realize once again the quiet history of railways. Once you pass this point, the steep slope of Hokketsu Pass awaits you, and you can feel the calm just before that.

Tachima. This station, the first station that trains arrive at after descending from Hokketsu Pass, is one of Shikoku's leading producers of mandarin oranges, and is surrounded by terraced fields that dye the mountain surface a golden yellow. It was once nicknamed ``Mikan Station,'' and you can feel the excitement of the days when wagons waving sweet scents lined up during the harvest season in every corner of the spacious grounds. Although it is currently an unmanned station, standing here, where the sea breeze and the scent of mandarin oranges mix, will give you a keen sense of the history of transporting the rich blessings of Iyo country by railway. The terraced fields of stone masonry extending to the sky are the result of the sweat of pioneering efforts.

Iyoyoshida. It is a historic station that was once the Jinyacho of the Yoshida clan's 30,000 koku clan, nestled in a scenic cove overlooking the Uwa Sea. Once you get off the station, you will see rows of old houses that have withstood the sea breeze and still retain the vestiges of the samurai residences of the past. When a limited express train slows down to a stop, the calm sea surface visible from the train window seems to be a silent warning that the end of the journey is near. This is a truly enjoyable stop that blends the richness of history with the atmosphere of a port town. The scent of the ocean fills the home, giving us a sense of Nanyo's rich seafood.

Takamitsu. Before taking the final step to Uwajima, this somewhat modest station is located where the residential area and the mountainside meet. Although there are few special historical station remains, the view of the city of Uwajima from here gives travelers the feeling that they have arrived at a haven after a long journey. The wind that blows through this single platform with no major facilities seems to be starting to mix with the hustle and bustle of the final station, giving us a strange sense of travel where expectations and regrets intersect. It embodies the kindness of local railways, where railways are close to everyday life.

Kitauwajima. Although it is a key transportation hub where the Yosan Line and Yodo Line meet, what makes this station so special is that it maintains a somewhat practical tranquility. As the two railways come together and make their final journey to their final destination, Uwajima, it feels like watching the stories of the railways that traveled around Shikoku converge into one. There used to be a train yard near this area, and you can feel the energy that steam locomotives used to prepare for their respective journeys in the functional wiring that exists today. It gives us a sense of the philosophy of railroads, where a divided road becomes one again.

Uwajima. This station is the terminal station of the Yosan Line and is located at the end of the railway that leads to the southwestern part of Shikoku.Beyond the rails covered with bollards, you can feel the bottomless depths of the country of Iyo. As a former castle town of the Uwajima domain's Date 100,000 koku clan, this station is home to bullfighting and the majesty of Uwajima Castle, and it has a profound travel atmosphere that is unique to a terminal station. From here on, the rails stop, but I can't help but think of this as a powerful starting point for the journey that continues further south to Sukumo and Nakamura. The open feel of the station plaza lined with palm trees is the perfect finale to your trip to Nanyo.

text_en: Sheng. This is the starting point of the Sanriku Railway Rias Line, and was once a busy transportation hub connecting with the National Railways Ofunato Line. The sight of the platform of the Ofunato Line, now known as the bus rapid transit system (BRT), and the Iwate Development Railway, which specializes in freight, is an illustration of the diverse nature of railways. The scent of the sea wafting in front of the station and the heavy sound of freight trains. They resonate in the hearts of travelers like the powerful heartbeat that supports Sanriku's recovery. When you witness the beginning of the railway extending north from here, you can feel that the dream of the ``traversing railway'' of the past is still alive in this area.

text_en: Rikuzen Akasaki. This station, located deep in Ofunato Bay and overlooking the calm sea surface, overcame severe damage from a previous earthquake and relocated to higher ground. Looking down from the platform, you can see the neatly divided seawall and the silver roofs of the fish processing plants that have regained their vitality and shine beautifully in the afternoon sunlight. The force of nature and the indomitable spirit of the people who live together with it, living together with it, are alive and well in the atmosphere of this quiet, unmanned station. The moment you wait for your train while being blown by the sea breeze makes you feel as if you are standing at the crossroads of reminiscing about a lost landscape and creating a new history.

text_en: Ayari. It was once the center of Ayari Village in Kesen District, and the station, along with its stone monument, continues to quietly preserve the memories of the Meiji and Showa tsunamis that hit this area. Standing on the platform, you can get a sense of the depth of the intricate ria coastline and the richness of the seafood that comes from it. The somewhat nostalgic appearance of the station building shows how the railway was a hope for people's lives in the harsh nature of Sanriku. A landscape of steep mountains plunging into the sea, just like when literary greats once traveled. It reaffirms that the narrow railway that is laid between these areas is the lifeline of this land.

text_en: Koishihama. It used to be called Koishihama, and as the name suggests, it was a station in a quiet fishing village where small stones were rolling. Nowadays, the station has transformed into a ``sacred place for love'' that many travelers visit, attracted by its romantic station name. The dry sound of the numerous scallop shell votive tablets hanging in the waiting room of the platform swaying in the sea breeze sounds like a melody carrying people's wishes to the sea. Changing the name of the station, a smart move unique to the railways, has brought a moment of comfort to the harsh disaster-stricken area. When you ring the bell on the platform overlooking the sea, you can feel the sentimentalism of train travel deepening even more.

text_en: Horei. Although it is located close to the sea, this station has the tranquility of a mountain village, and is a place on the Sanriku Railway where you can feel time passing more slowly. The calm blue of Hirota Bay spreads out on the other side of the seawall. It is the very scenery of Sanriku that was once loved by literary greats, and it allows you to forget the hustle and bustle of modern times. Sitting on a bench at an unmanned station, I wait for the next train with the sound of waves in the background. Such luxurious boredom is the true value of this route. The agriculture and fishing that once supported this area are still reflected in the small fields and fishing boats around the station, providing a calming and calming experience for travelers.

text_en: Sanriku. It was once the gateway to Okirai Village, and is the central station of the area that was renamed Sanriku Town after the merger of towns and villages in the Showa era. Although the cityscape surrounding the station has been completely renovated through large-scale elevation work after the earthquake, the ridgeline of the mountains in the background remains as rugged as ever. The weight of the word "Sanriku" that this station name is attached to. It makes us feel the pride of the people who have overcome repeated disasters and kept this railway connected. When you come into contact with the displays of local culture and history displayed inside the station building, you realize that the railway is not just a means of transportation, but the pride of the region itself.

text_en: Yoshihama. The village where this station is located is known as a ``model of disaster prevention,'' as it was one of the first to move to higher ground, drawing on the lessons learned from past tsunamis. The spectacular view of Yoshihama Bay that opens up the moment you exit the tunnel is one of the most beautiful on the Sanriku Railway. The wisdom of the Japanese people to coexist with the harsh nature, as written down by the writers of the Showa era, pervades every corner of the well-ordered streets. The calm sea seen from the train window quietly but powerfully conveys the awe of nature that sometimes shows its fangs. As you pass through this station, you are convinced that the railway carries more than just passengers, it carries hope for the future.

text_en: Tangtan. The contrast between the row of cherry blossom trees and the tsunami monument that can be seen from the station platform speaks silently of the depth of history that this land has carried. In spring, the cherry blossom petals bloom, as if to soothe the tragedy of the past, painting the railroad tracks a pale red. Hidden deep within the ria coastline, this station is surrounded by silence, as if isolated from the open sea, and travelers spend time there facing the laws of nature. Memories of the mine transportation of the past are long gone, and the scene where only the sound of the sea remains on the platform gives us a sense of emotion that would be suitable for the setting of a ``travel story''.

text_en: Hirata. This station, which appears between tunnels just before the city center of Kamaishi, feels like it somehow still conveys the heat that was emitted by the former steel mill. The Kamaishi Great Kannon is enshrined nearby, and its benevolent figure overlooking the sea continues to pray for safe voyages and peace in the area. It has both an industrial city and a religious place. A mysterious atmosphere that combines both of these aspects hangs around this small station. When you look at the houses that cling to the steep slopes, you can clearly feel the strength of the people who worked hard to survive in this harsh terrain.

text_en: Kamaishi. This is the largest base station in Sanriku, which flourished as the ``Iron Town.'' The premises where the JR Kamaishi Line and the Sanriku Railway converge are criss-crossed by railroad tracks leading to Japan's oldest steelworks, reminiscent of the days when the sky was covered in smoke from steam locomotives. Even today, this city, where the enthusiasm for rugby and the pride of steel manufacturing still lives, still conveys the weight of ``modern Japan'' that was brought to Japan by railways. Standing in front of the station, you can feel the faint smell of iron in the sea breeze. This is Kamaishi's identity, and it gives us a sense of the unwavering confidence of this city, which has overcome many hardships.

text_en: Both stones. This station, which appears when you exit Kamaishi and pass through the first tunnel, is located in a location that can be described as a ``fishing village station.'' The view from the platform overlooks the inlet of Ryoishi Bay, where small fishing boats are tied together shoulder to shoulder, giving you a tangible glimpse into the daily activities of the people. Sanriku appears as it is, as if refusing to become a large-scale tourist destination. By immersing themselves there, a traveler can return to his or her origins as a wanderer rather than a tourist. The fact that a railway still runs through a terrain where mountains and the sea compete for narrow flat areas. That in itself seems like a kind of miracle.

text_en: Cormorant residence. When you get off at the station with this unusual place name, you can feel the enthusiasm of the ``Rugby City,'' which has overcome the scars of the previous earthquake and has rebuilt itself strongly. The grandeur of the stadium in front of the station is truly a symbol of reconstruction. However, when you look out at the calm sea that stretches out behind it, you can feel the weight of the history carved by the old railway along with the sea breeze. A modern station building and the mountain ridgeline that has protected this area since ancient times. This contrast shows us the changing trends of the times. Whether it's days filled with the cheers of sports or days dominated by the quiet sound of waves, this station remains an immovable coordinate that continues to gaze upon Sanriku's future.

text_en: Sledgehammer. This town overlooking Horai Island, which is said to be the model for Hyokkori Hyotan Island, is a town of proud fishermen who have lived with the sea and overcome hardships together with it. The design of Hyotan Island, which sits on the roof of the station building, conveys the dreams of the Showa era, when children were glued to their television sets. When you stand in front of the station, the scent of the sea and the ocean floats in the air, making you feel confident that the rich blessings of Sanriku's sea are just around the corner. If you walk through the newly renovated station plaza while thinking about the lost cityscape, you can quietly savor the hope of ``rebirth'' brought about by the accumulation of time.

text_en: Kirikiri. The name of the station, which has a unique sound, is reminiscent of the independent nation once depicted by Hisashi Inoue, and greatly stimulates the imagination of travelers. With the beautiful coast known for its singing sand in the background, the area around the station has a somewhat distant, yet nostalgic smell that wafts through the air. The overlapping roof tiles of the village that you can see from the platform give you a sense of the unique culture that this area has nurtured and the strong unity of its people. The passion for railways that connects Sanriku's difficult spots, which has continued since the days of the Japanese National Railways, is still alive in the appearance of this small station. It is not just a transit point, but a punctuation mark on a journey that even has a literary flavor.

text_en: Namiita coast. This beach, known for the legend of ``one-sided waves'' that never come back, is a scenic spot that represents Sanriku, and was once a place where many writers and artists admired its beauty. If you stand on the station platform and look out at the Pacific Ocean spreading out below you, you will be overwhelmed by the circularity of the earth and the majesty of nature as depicted by the horizon. After the earthquake, the beach's former appearance has completely changed, but the sound of waves crashing on the beach continues to mark eternity. Waiting for a train with the sound of the ocean at your back offers a kind of meditation time, isolated from the hustle and bustle of modern society.

text_en: Iwate Funakoshi. This station, which has the honorable title of being the easternmost station on Honshu, is both a destination for travelers and a starting point heading into the abyss of Sanriku. The Whale and Sea Science Museum is located near the station, preserving the memories of a time when this area once flourished as a whaling base. The activities of people who have firmly planted their roots in this narrow land where the sea and land collide. The railway that runs through its center carries the weight of being the lifeline of the region in each rusted rail. If you imagine the black smoke spewed out by an old steam locomotive blowing in the easternmost wind, your love for traveling will deepen even further.

text_en: Orikasa. This station, located near the mouth of the Orikasa River, was moved to higher ground after the earthquake and has been given a new look. However, in the cityscape overlooking from the station building and the calm waters of Yamada Bay in the distance, you can feel the warmth of this land that has not changed since then. A new history since it was transferred to Sanriku Railway, and an old history built by the former JNR Yamada Line. Both of these coexist with the scent of wood in the new station building. Just as a river flows into the sea, people's lives are also gently flowing into a new era. It gives us a sense of the breathing of a city in the process of revitalization.

text_en: Rikuchu Yamada. As if to symbolize the rich blessings of Yamada Bay, the station building was rebuilt with an elegant Dutch-style design, making a powerful declaration of the city's revival. This town, which once suffered severe damage from fires and earthquakes, is beginning to take on a new charm thanks to the systematic reconstruction centered around the station. The aroma of oysters and scallops wafting from the market around the station speaks volumes about the richness of Sanriku's food culture. The excitement of people gathering as the train arrives. This reminds us that the railway is the heart of the city and the base for people's exchanges. It is the perfect place for an adult journey, one that mourns the lost past while affirming the new form of the city.

text_en: Toyoma root. This station, located on the Sanriku Railway, is located in a rural area where the train passes through rugged terrain along the coast and provides a moment of calm, giving it a calm, inland-like appearance. The mountains surrounding the station and the green fields spread out at their base. This is an original landscape that once existed everywhere in Japan, and it deeply soothes the hearts of travelers. Since the days of the Japanese National Railways, this area has been a staple of daily life, supporting local people's commute to school and hospital. This station teaches us that even if there are no flashy tourist attractions, the everyday scenery that exists there is the most luxurious travel treat.

text_en: Hokkaido. This station, which was newly built in conjunction with the opening of the entire Sanriku Railway Rias Line, is an unmanned station, but it is a ``station of hope'' that has given shape to the long-cherished wishes of the local people. It is surrounded by mountains and has a quiet appearance, but its very existence proves the significance of continuing to connect railways. Standing on the simple platform, I wait for the sound of the train passing through the mountains. It reminds us of the richness of waiting in a modern world where convenience is the only pursuit. Although it is a new station, it feels like it has been there for a long time, and it may be the magical power of the local atmosphere that gives it a sense of intimacy.

text_en: Tsugaru stone. This station, located on the banks of the Tsugaru Ishikawa River, is a lively place where you can feel the dynamism of life as salmon come upstream in the fall. This area, which once made a name for itself in history as the gateway to Miyako and as a strategic military center, still retains a somewhat solemn atmosphere. The profound sound of trains crossing the iron bridge has not changed since the days of old wooden station buildings. The way it reverberates in the surrounding mountains is exactly the scenery of a Showa era railway travelogue. Just like a salmon moving up a river, following the laws of nature, the railway has overcome many hardships to return to this land. I cannot help but express my respect for their tenacious steps.

text_en: Yagisawa/Miyako Junior College. This new station, named after Gakusha, marks a new chapter for Sanriku Railway as a means of transportation for young people who will lead the future. The platforms are arranged to blend in with the residential area, showing how closely railways are connected to people's daily lives. The sounds of students' laughter echoing during school hours. This is the brightest tone of a region that still carries memories of the earthquake, but is steadily moving toward the future. This station, which is different from the former base station with its vast station building, has modern rationality and careful consideration for the local community, and I feel like I see a new path for the survival of the railway.

text_en: Iso chicken. Just before you enter the city center of Miyako, you can see the chimneys of Rasa Industries in the distance, and you can still see the image of a paper mill where freight transportation was popular. After the earthquake, this section was transferred from the JR Yamada Line to the Sanriku Railway, and has truly made a fresh start as a means of transportation for the region. In a landscape where houses and small factories coexist, the gentle sound of the rails carving gives us a sense of the steady progress that a local city had in the Showa era. The simple and sturdy atmosphere, where the scent of saltwater and the smell of oil subtly mix, is the true essence of Isogei Station.

text_en: Miyako. It is the easternmost city in Honshu, and was once a strategic point on the Japanese National Railways Yamada Line, and is currently the center of the Sanriku Railway Rias Line, so the entire station is filled with the pride of the railway workers. The stately appearance of the station building has a dignity befitting the gateway to Kita-Sanriku, and while it makes travelers wonder about the fate of the railways branching off from here, it also arouses a sense of exhilaration among travelers. The idling sound of a diesel engine echoing on the platform is like a heartbeat preparing to take on the harsh ria coastline, and even the bustle of tourists heading for the white rocks of Jodogahama Beach has a deep sense of belonging that swallows it up as a part of history.

text_en: Yamaguchi housing complex. The station is located in a residential area just before the train passes through the city center of Miyako and approaches a steep slope. The way stations are closely connected to daily life, which was unthinkable in the days of JNR, is proof that the railway has transformed from a ``special vehicle'' to an ``everyday tool.'' At dusk, the sight of students gathering at the platform after returning from school gives us a sense of warmth, like a cradle in which Sanriku's future will be nurtured. It embodies the form of modern railways, with a simple structure that pursues functionality and a strong desire to support the local community.

text_en: Ichi no Watari. This station, which appears at the end of the deep green tunnel that is the first difficult part after leaving Miyako, is a place that truly symbolizes ``tranquility in the mountains.'' There were no notable houses in the surrounding area, just a valley with the sound of the rushing water and a steep mountain looming over it. It feels like the hardships of the days when steam locomotives struggled to climb these slopes are still etched in the joints of the rails. This slow flow of time seems to have been abandoned by modern high-speed travel. This is a luxurious introduction to understanding the depths of Sanriku.

text_en: Sabane. Surrounded by lush trees, the station creates the illusion that the scent of the forest washes over your lungs as you step onto the platform. The pioneering spirit of the time when the line opened as part of the former Japanese National Railways Miyako Line is still alive in every moss-covered concrete corner. Although the station is far away and the number of users is limited, the continued maintenance of this station itself is an expression of the tenacity to connect railway lines. If a traveler waits for a train on a platform in the afternoon when nothing can be heard except for the sound of the wind rustling the branches, it has a magical power that makes the traveler suddenly forget what era he or she is in.

text_en: Taro. In the shadow of a huge seawall that was even called the Great Wall of China, this city has a history of living both with and against the sea. The cityscape seen from the station platform is a rebirth that has overcome past tragedies, and the neatly lined houses reflect the indomitable will of the people. Time has changed since that day when writers from the Showa era marveled at the area's preparations for tsunamis, but their reverence for nature remains unchanged. While listening to the voices of seabirds mixed in with the sea breeze, I think about the role played by the seawall in the past. It is a journey to learn about the weight of life.

text_en: Old Nitta. This station is located at a high altitude and was built by Sanriku Railway to take a new step forward in response to the move to higher ground after the earthquake. The view overlooking the sea from a higher point than the old Taro Station is a symbol of modern wisdom and determination to never repeat the same tragedy. The dazzling white concrete platform offers a panoramic view of the newly reborn Taro, providing a scene where memories of the city's past intersect with steps toward the future. The appearance of this station, which combines convenience and safety, has already become familiar to the area as part of Sanriku's new landscape.

text_en: Providence. If we look back at its history, it is a station with a name that evokes a sense of travel, as it comes from the ``hospitality'' of providing lodging and meals to pilgrims and travelers in the past. Its appearance, nestled in a small village in the mountains, still conveys the quiet and modest beauty of the rural landscape of Tohoku in the past. The fields surrounding the station and the deep blue of the mountains in the background. The contrast is exactly the same as the nostalgic ``original landscape of Japan'' that I used to see vaguely from the window of a long-distance train. This station teaches us that even if there are no special landmarks, the everyday scenery that exists there is the most luxurious travel treat.

text_en: Iwaizumi Komoto. It is also the place where the dream of the Iwaizumi Line, which was once known as Komoto and branched off from here and headed for Ryusendo Cave, was lost. Today, there is a magnificent station building serving as the gateway to Iwaizumi Town, but the sadness of the disappearance of the old railroad still lingers in every corner of the station. The sight of trains and buses working hand in hand to support the transportation of local communities alongside the clear waters of the Omoto River flowing into the sea shows us the front lines of local transportation in the face of the harsh reality of depopulation. This station shows us the strength of the Sanriku Railway, which continues to run even today, with a sense of longing for the lost railway.

text_en: Shimagoe. This station, nicknamed Carbonado Shimakoshi, suffered a cruel fate when the beautiful arch bridge and the station building were destroyed without a trace by the tsunami caused by the earthquake. However, it has now been beautifully rebuilt, and the station building, which resembles a chalk tower, warmly welcomes travelers as a ``lighthouse of reconstruction''. The beauty of Shimagoshi Bay seen from the platform is calm, as if hiding the tragedy of the past, and it confronts us with the cruelty and beauty of nature at the same time. Disembarking at this station is to offer a prayer for rebirth together, and it makes us believe once again in the ``power to connect'' that railways have.

text_en: Tanohata. This station is like a place of relaxation for trains that have passed through numerous tunnels through the steep cliffs of Northern Rias. In front of the station, the atmosphere of the rustic fishing village of the past remains, while the mountains rising in the background hint at the road to Kuji becoming even more rugged in the future. Those days when travel writers who visited this place were amazed at how ``a solitary land island'' it was. Nowadays, railways have overcome this problem, but the wild yet beautiful spirit of the land is still alive and well. The atmosphere at this station, where the sea and the mountains seem to be asserting their existence, foreshadows the climax of your trip to Sanriku.

text_en: Fudai. This place is known as the place of the ``miracle'' where a huge water gate saved the village during an earthquake. The station is located on a hill, and the view of the sea from there is endlessly calm, but the decisions of the people and the weight of history behind it are something that touches the hearts of travelers deeply. Local specialties are lined up inside the station building, making you feel that the lives of the simple people are closely connected to the railway. The pride of the Northern Rias Line, which once connected ``isolated islands'', continues to flow through this land of Fudai. The train heading further north from here will take us on a journey through even more rugged cliffs.

text_en: Shirai coast. This station, which exists between two tunnels as if sucked in, is truly one of Sanriku Railway's most ``unexplored stations.'' The road leading to the station is narrow and steep, and apart from the sound of waves and rustling trees, there is almost no sign of civilization in the surrounding area. When you arrive at the platform, you are alternately overwhelmed by anxiety about where you are and the pleasure of being completely separated from everyday life. If you imagine the sweat that the former builders put into laying the railway on this steep cliff, you can't help but be convinced that the very existence of this small station is the result of their tenacity in the name of railway.

text_en: Horiuchi. This station, which gained national fame as the setting for the TV drama ``Ama-chan,'' has a mysterious magnetic field that still attracts many fans. The spectacular view of the Pacific Ocean overlooking the Osawa Bridge near the station is the best view of the Sanriku Railway, and the moment when the driver slows down to provide service is the highlight of the trip. Blue sea, white foaming waves, and intricate coastline. The landscapes created by these scenes convey the image of the ``harsh and beautiful Tohoku'' that writers loved in the Showa era to this day. The time spent basking in the sea breeze while soaking in the afterglow of the story is truly bliss.

text_en: Noda Tamagawa. Manganese mines once existed underground in this area, and it has a history of being a bustling industrial hub. The view of Jufugaura from the station platform is a scenic spot that has been written about in ancient waka poems, and will continue to delight the eyes of travelers throughout eternity. The heavy breathing of the men who once worked to transport the mines has now faded into the roar of the sea, but the strong rock texture around the station is still engraved with the prosperity of those days. This station, where nature, industry, and history intertwine, has a unique atmosphere that symbolizes the depth of Sanriku.

text_en: Tofugaura coast. This new station, which was built at the end of the Heisei era, is an expression of the city's desire to create a new landscape of Sanriku while keeping the memory of the earthquake in mind. Jufugaura, a purple sandy beach that stretches out in front of the platform. The railway that has been laid along the fantastic coastline presents a new kind of coexistence with the landscape that was unimaginable in the days of Japanese National Railways. At dusk, when you look out from the platform at the ocean's edge turning a madder red, you are reminded of the peace of mind that railways bring. Even though the station is new, you can still feel the spirit of ancient waka poetry.

text_en: Rikuchu Noda. This place is known as the starting point of the ``Salt Road'' in the past, and is the gateway to the city where the culture of ``Nodashio'' continues since the Edo period. The station building, which is integrated with the roadside station, is a lively plaza where travelers and local people interact, demonstrating how deeply the railway is rooted in local life. When you arrive at the platform, the faint scent of the ocean will remind you of the history of salt, which was once carried across mountains on the backs of oxen. The good old Sanriku traditions are still alive within the modern facilities, giving us a sense of peace that feels like a ``hometown'' in a railway travelogue.

text_en: Rikuchu Ube. With the town of Kuji just around the corner, this station is surrounded by a peaceful rural landscape, and is a place that will give you a sense of relief as you suddenly relieve your tension during your trip on the Sanriku Railway. The daily scene of houses dotted around the area and local people waiting for trains gives us a sense of the sincerity that can be said to be the origin of railways, apart from the glamor of tourist routes. It's also fun to look for remnants of the past when it was called Kitakuji Station in its quiet appearance. The accumulation of history is hidden in the ordinary scenery. It is a modest and good station that will test your perspective as a travel writer.

text_en: Kuji. It is the northern terminus of the Sanriku Railway Rias Line, and is also a connecting point for journeys that continue to the JR Hakkado Line. This area is known for its production of amber, and the entire station has a somewhat mysterious and calming atmosphere, just like a jewel containing ancient memories. Sanriku Railway's red cars and JR diesel cars lined up on the platform. This contrast quietly speaks to us of the joy that railways have brought us together despite many hardships. The aroma of the famous ``uni bento'' wafting from the restaurant in front of the station tempts me to savor the end of a long journey. It is the ultimate luxury that can only be enjoyed by those who have followed a single line of railway.

text_en:
Oigawa Railway Igawa Line. This small railway from Senzu to Ikawa was originally created as a special railway for the power development of the Oigawa River, in other words, to transport Chubu Electric Power's dam construction materials. As you sink into the train, which is much smaller than other lines, and head deep into the mountains, it gives you a strange sense of intimacy, as if you were being swayed by a life-sized model train.

Along the way, on the steep slope between Abt Ichishiro Station and Nagashima Dam Station, Japan's only Abt-type locomotive pushes the train powerfully from behind, and the unique sound of the rack rails meshing lets you know that the railway is pushing its physical limits. The extraordinary appearance of Okuoikojo Station, as if it were floating on the surface of the lake, and its trajectory as it threads its way through the deep greenery of the Sapporo Gorge are a series of spectacular views worthy of the name ``Minami Alps Apto Line.'' The sweat of the people who worked on the dam construction in the past and the pride of this small railway that continues to work today blend into the quiet atmosphere of Senzu. For those who love railways, it can be said to be a moment of bliss for those who love railways to aim for the final destination, Igawa, while appreciating the accumulation of history.

text_en: Thousand heads. The Oigawa Railway's main line is coming to an end, and the Minami Alps Apto Line is the key point where its journey begins. When you arrive at the platform, you will see the steam locomotives that once served as supporting players on the Tokaido route or as the main transport for lumber deep in the mountains, still in active service today. The scent of tea wafting from the plaza in front of the station and the bustle of tourists. The way these things mix together is a modern-day recreation of the "bustling of terminal stations" that was common throughout the Showa era. The moment you untie your ekiben while waiting for the train to take you further into the rugged mountains is the real thrill of traveling by train.

text_en: Kawane Ryogoku. This station, located just a few minutes after leaving Senzu, at the end of a long iron bridge that crosses the Oi River, is not just a stop, but a ``factory station'' that keeps the railway alive. There are maintenance vehicles lined up next to the train window and a somewhat rustic storage area for materials. They give us a sense of the discipline of the men who protect the railway, which lies behind its glamor as a tourist railway. The pride of the time when the area once served as the starting point for the forest railway and was reliant on the blessings of the mountains is still ingrained in every rusty track. The sound of the river and the sound of metal echoing from the vehicle area. That dissonance is what speaks to the rich history of this station.

text_en: Sawama. Along the Sumata River that flows behind this station, there used to be a long line called the Senzu Forest Railway. The abandoned railroad tracks, now covered in deep greenery, were once filled with trolleys laden with high-quality wood. When you stand on the platform and look out towards the mountains, you get the illusion that you can hear the lively voices of people reloading wood, mixed in with the sound of the wind. The current silence is like a device that makes the industrial glory of the past stand out even more, and travelers can't help but feel the sadness of civilization returning to nature.

text_en: Tsuchimoto. Surrounded by steep mountains, this station has several private houses huddled together, giving it an appearance that is truly worthy of the name ``Unexplored Region.'' What is surprising is the fact that most of the residents of this village share the same surname, Tsuchimoto, making us realize that the land and bloodline are connected by a thin thread called the railway. It has an intimate feel, as if the train were stopping in your garden rather than a station. There, the form of happy coexistence between people and railways that has been left behind by modern society in its pursuit of efficiency and speed still lives on quietly.

Now, that hustle and bustle is a thing of the distant past, and after the train leaves, only the deep silence and the sounds of birds remain on the platform. However, the power generation equipment scattered around the station and the texture of the concrete structures still convey the will of steel that supported Japan's modernization in the past. As you listen to the roar of diesel locomotives tackling the mountainside, you will be reminded of a bygone era of development. It is the multilayered history

text_en: Okuizumi. This is a strategic point on the Oigawa Railway, and serves as a junction for travelers heading to Sumatakyo Onsen to transfer to buses. The appearance of the station building is a reminder of the days when this area was once a hub of power development and the export of forest resources. The mountains you can see from the platform are somehow steep, giving you a sense of tension as you head into an even deeper canyon. After the tourists have left, the cool mountain air that wafts in silence gives you a sense of the dignified atmosphere that befits the gateway to the Southern Alps.

text_en: Abt Ichiro. This station, which was once called Kawane Ichiyo, overcame its fate of being submerged under water due to the construction of the Nagashima Dam, and has now been revived as a connecting base for the Abt Railway. The series of operations in which a heavy electric locomotive is connected to the rear of a train is a moment that reminds us that railways are "machines." The sight of the old railway tunnels remaining as promenades allows us to feel both the changing trends of the times and the unwavering passion for railways. The challenge of climbing a steep slope that begins with the sound of a powerful motor will carve a new page in your travel passion.

text_en: Nagashima Dam. The gigantic concrete wall that stands in front of the station is the culmination of a history of human wisdom that challenged Mother Nature. From the modern station building, the scenery has changed so much that it is hard to imagine that a village once existed at the bottom of this valley. However, the roaring sound of the water being released has a power that somehow evokes memories of the rapids of the past. The sight of the train detaching from its auxiliary locomotive at this station and starting to move on its own again seems to symbolize the spirit of the Japanese people who have carved out a path through difficult times.

The sight of the surface of the dam lake calmly approaching the station below gives you a sense of freedom on a train journey deep in the mountains. The silence that spreads around the station quietly speaks to us of the sadness of how our former lives have sunk to the bottom of the water. A sense of longing for lost landscapes blends into the peaceful landscape of modern times, where the shadows of people rowing kayaks can be seen in the distance. So

text_en: On Okuoi Lake. This station, which sits on a cape floating in the middle of a lake, boasts an unrealistic landscape that makes you feel like you're looking at a modern-day ukiyo-e print. Its appearance, sandwiched between two large iron bridges called Rainbow Bridge, may have been the future that railroad workers dreamed of in the past. You can see the emerald green lake surface and the surrounding steep mountains from the platform. This contrast shows the depth of the nature of the Oigawa River and the tenacity of the people who have continued to challenge it. Stepping off the train here feels like a ritual of disconnecting from the shores of everyday life and stepping into the heart of pure travel.

text_en: Chikukyo Onsen. This station, which used to be called Kawane-Nagashima, changed its name with the completion of Nagashima Dam and assumed a new role. Once you get off the station, you can see the sheer cliffs of the Chiku Gorge, and you can feel the history of this deep gorge carved by the torrents of the Oigawa River. The steam from the hot springs is where workers who once worked on dam construction would have soothed themselves after a hard day's work. Nowadays, it has become a place that warms the hearts of travelers. The moment you see off the red trolley train while listening to the sound of the sound echoing in the silence creates an atmosphere befitting a hot spring inn in the mountains.

text_en: Omori. This is now a true "unexplored station" that seems to have been forgotten on modern maps. There is no road leading to the station, and the only connection with the world below is the railway. This area was once lined with dam construction materials storage areas and worker quarters, and where you could even hear the cheers of children, but now the deep forest is swallowing everything up. When you arrive at the platform, the only sounds you hear are the sound of the wind and the chirping of birds, as if mourning the lives of people of the past. This unique feeling of loneliness, as if left alone at the edge of civilization, is the station's greatest charm.

text_en: Quiet storehouse. This station, which makes you feel that the density of the air has become thinner as the altitude has increased, was once an important gateway to Ikawa Village. Right next to the station stands the Sekinosawa Tetsu Bridge, which was once the tallest private railway in Japan, and the thrill of peering into the abyss chills the souls of travelers. In this area deep in the mountains, the hardships of our ancestors who worked hard to transport lumber and daily necessities are etched into the stonework of old platforms. From here, the journey by bus to deeper villages feels like a pilgrimage through the original landscape of Japan.

text_en: Igawa. It is the final station where the long journey towards the source of the Oigawa River finally comes to an end. The tenacity of the railway, which has overcome this steep terrain with pride as the former Chubu Electric Power Railway, is summarized in this dead-end track. The majestic Igawa Dam towering behind the station looks like a grand monument to the energy development that supported post-war Japan. As you step off the train and walk in front of the quiet station, you will be enveloped by the quiet breathing of people who live in the mountains and the scent of deep greenery. The somewhat lonely, yet satisfying aftertaste that is unique to a terminal station is deeply ingrained in your heart.
