text_en: Kushiro. As the gateway to eastern Hokkaido, it was once a vibrant capital filled with smoke from coal, fisheries, and paper manufacturing. The station building is made of dignified reinforced concrete, and the sound of diesel engines lined up on the dead-end platform enhances the journey to the farthest reaches. There is a history of many night trains arriving at the end of their long journeys on this platform. When I stand on the platform, I can't help but feel that the afterglow of the steam from which C11 once departed is lurking somewhere. As it is known as the town of fog, the white, hazy air invites a sense of travel and increases expectations for the Senmo Main Line, which begins here.

East Kushiro. This is a turning point that railway enthusiasts cannot overlook, where the Nemuro Main Line and the Senmo Main Line separate. The huge chimneys of a paper mill tower in the background, giving off the somewhat inorganic aroma of an industrial area, but the single-track railway that extends north from here suggests that this is the real entrance to the northern wilderness. Although the station structure is simple, there is a somewhat unsettling yet solemn atmosphere that is characteristic of a place where two main lines intersect. One of the hidden pleasures of traveling is to take a moment to reflect on the hustle and bustle of the days when freight trains came and went during the short breaks between transfers.

Toya. This station is like a boundary line where you finally pass through the city of Kushiro and step into the bosom of the wetlands. This place, whose name comes from the Ainu word "to-ya" (shore of the lake), quietly arouses expectations for the city of water that we will soon encounter. Although the smell of people's daily lives still lingers around the station, the wind blowing against the train windows has become unbearably cold, and the coniferous trees outside the train windows are growing greener. This station exists in a delicate balance where the everyday and the extraordinary intersect. From this point forward, this station is responsible for the run-up period into the wilderness, when human habitation becomes scarce.

Kushiro Marsh. This station, which opened as a temporary station in 1988, has now become the center of attraction for wetland tourism. The log house-style station building blends seamlessly into the surrounding landscape, watching over trains as they stop. If you climb the steep stairs from the platform, you will find a vast sea of ​​green that has remained unchanged since time immemorial, and we travelers can do nothing but stand still in front of the overwhelming mass of nature. It is crowded with tourists when trains arrive and depart, but once the train leaves, only silence and the sound of the wind reigns. It can be said that this station embodies the modern challenge of coexistence between nature conservation and railways.

Hosooka. This small station appears as the train creeps along the eastern edge of the wetland. It is said that it was once used to handle cargo, so the weight of its pioneering history cannot be underestimated. There was a time when the station building was a reused old freight car, but now it is a calm building that welcomes travelers. The Kushiro River winds gently right next to the station, and you can often see people enjoying canoeing. However, if you are left alone on the platform, you will feel the illusion of the silence of nature piercing your skin. It is the closest station to the abyss of the wetlands, making it the perfect station to experience the true solitude of the northern land.

Toro. This station is conveniently located on the shores of Lake Toro, which forms the core of Kushiro Marsh. The station building, which was once a busy place for transporting lumber, now quietly welcomes tourists and conveys the warmth of the good old wooden structure to the present day. While waiting to change trains at this station, when I step onto the platform, the wind blowing in from the lake carries the scent of the wetland. It would not be an exaggeration to say that the sight of an oncoming train sliding into the train while spewing white diesel smoke is truly a railway scene from the Showa era. This is a station that will leave you immersed in the feeling that nature, humans, and railways coexist with just the right amount of distance.

Kayanuma. When you hear the name of this station, you are sure to imagine an elegant red-crowned crane. This story, which began when a former stationmaster started feeding the cranes, has now become synonymous with the station, and has created the rare sight of cranes flying right next to the platforms. A simple home set alone in the middle of a field is surrounded by silence, as if it had no connection to the conveniences of civilization. In winter, the white wings dancing on the snowy fields gently soothe the loneliness of travelers. This small, unmanned station teaches us through the sight of cranes descending silently that trains are not just a means of transportation, but a point of contact with all living things.

Shibecha. This station once branched off from the Shibetsu Line and has a prosperous history as a key logistics hub in eastern Hokkaido. The spacious grounds still bear the traces of that past, and it is also part of the nature of railway enthusiasts to look for the remains of the turntables where steam locomotives were once converted. As soon as you step out of the station, you will find yourself surrounded by a somewhat fertile yet simple and sturdy townscape, typical of a dairy farming town. From here on, the track leaves the marshland and finally enters the Konsen Plateau. As if to solidify their resolve, the diesel car waits for departure with a particularly high-pitched engine sound. One of the tastes of traveling as an adult is to imagine the hustle and bustle of the past while admiring the quiet appearance of the present day.

Within Isobu. Passing Shibecha, this station has an impressive silver milk tank that suddenly appears in the pastoral scenery that spreads out from the train window. A huge dairy factory is located next to the station building, which eloquently proves that dairy farming is the main industry of this area. Although the station building has been unmanned for a long time, I can't help but feel that the excitement of the days when milk collection trains came and went is still seeping into the joints of the railway. Wide skies and endless meadows. When you open the train window, you can feel the very vitality of Hokkaido, with the scent of grass and the presence of cows. Although it is not flashy, it is a station that has a lot of weight to it, allowing you to touch the roots of life.

Mashu. This station, which was once called Teshikaga, has now given its name to the mysterious lake and has established itself as a tourist hub. There is a footbath next to the station building, and you can see travelers warming up their cold bodies, which is a typical sight of this place. The somewhat refined atmosphere in front of the station suggests that this is the entrance to Lake Mashu, which continues to attract many poets and literary figures. However, when we stand on the platform, we are still on a rugged railway in the north, and the view of Mt. Mashu in the distance reminds us of our humble hearts. On days shrouded in fog, the entire station becomes a fantastical stage setting, making your trip even more profound.

Miruwa. This small station stands quietly as the train passes Mashu and enters the deep virgin forest. The name of the station is said to come from the Ainu word ``bil wa'' (a place with spring water), and as the name suggests, when you step onto the platform, you can feel the pure air filling your lungs. There may have been a time when it was enriched by the export of timber, but now it simply blends into the breathing of the forest and silently welcomes visitors. There are few private houses in the surrounding area, and each time the train door opens, it gives the illusion that the silence of a primeval forest flows into the train. In this place, which seems to have been left behind by the waves of modernization, simply listening to the sound of the wind is a luxury of traveling by train.

Kawayu Onsen. It is a famous station that once served as the inner parlor of ``Senpoushi'' and later ``Teshikaga,'' and served as the gateway to Mt. Iou and Lake Kussharo. When you step into the stately log-built station building, the faint scent of sulfur wafting from somewhere makes you aware that you are at the foot of a mountain of fire. Soaking in the footbath inside the station while waiting for the next train is truly the best part of traveling north. The platform, which was once crowded with tourists and mountain climbers, has now regained its calm and still conveys the elegance of a good old mountain resort. It is rare to find a station on the farthest reaches of the railway that gives you such a sense of warmth and travel spirit at the same time.

green. As its name suggests, this station, surrounded by deep mountain greenery, was the base for tackling the most difficult point on the Senmo Main Line, the mountain pass that marks the border between Abashiri and Kushiro. In the past, when steam locomotives were panting uphill, they used this place to replenish water or connect auxiliary locomotives to prepare for difficult passages.There are traces of those days floating faintly in the spacious grounds. Although it is now an unmanned station in a quiet mountain setting, the steepness of Mt. Shari looming in the background remains the same as in the past. When we hear the sound of a train's engine getting louder as it crosses a mountain pass, we are once again reminded of the history of railways confronting the harshness of nature. Facing the silence for a while in this secluded place deepens the interest of traveling.

Fuda string. Located at the magnificent foot of Mt. Shari, it is an agricultural station that suddenly appears in the vast field of farmland that stretches out from the train window. The area around the station is lined with potato storage warehouses and chimneys from starch factories, eloquently testifying to the fact that industry in this area has evolved in tandem with the soil. In the past, many agricultural products were transported from this station to all over the country on freight cars, and the memories of that industry remain strong in the station's appearance. When you arrive at the platform, the smell of the soil and the sound of the wind mix together, and you feel as if you can feel the joy of the pioneers' hard work and fruitfulness. It's rare to find a station that is so well-suited to the words "simple and sturdy," and when you stand on the unadorned platform, you feel as if you've touched the roots of Hokkaido's vibrant lifestyle.

Kiyosato town. This station, which was once called Kami-Shari, is one of the most beautiful places to look up at Mt. Shari, a magnificent peak. The mountain that rises above the neat cityscape changes its appearance depending on the viewing angle, but the view from this station is particularly sublime and leaves a deep impression on travelers. This town is known for its clear flowing water and the special shochu made from it, and the air around the station also gives off a refreshing impression. As you look out the train window, you can see the scenery change from wilderness to rich cultivated land after this station. This station reminds us of the preciousness of connecting the blessings of nature and the lives of people through a single line called a railway.

Nakashari. The silhouette of a huge factory that suddenly appears in the path of the train is Hokuren's Nakashari Sugar Factory. It is no exaggeration to say that this station is truly a ``sugar station'' that has grown together with beets. In the past, dedicated lines were extended, freight trains came and went frequently, and loading work was carried out in a lively manner amidst the sweet smells in the air. Although the hustle and bustle of the area is now far away, the scenery of the overwhelming scale of industrial architecture and railroads still conveys the strength of the backbone that supported Hokkaido's modernization. The contrast between the inorganic concrete structures and the endless plains quietly reminds us travelers of the importance of industry in the northern land.

Shiretoko Shari. This station, which was once simply called "Shari," is now known throughout the country as the gateway to world heritage sites. The station building has been given a modern look, but when you stand on the platform, the majestic sight of Shari-dake towering in the background and the roar of the Okhotsk waves as you head towards the station will quietly make your heart pound. In the past, the Nehoku Line branched off from here, and there is a history of people harboring dreams of crossing the Koshigawa River, which ended up being an unfinished line. I can't help but feel that behind the glamor of the city as a tourist hub, the tenacity of the northern reaches that the railway was trying to open up is still very much alive today. From this point on, the train leaves inland and finally enters a difficult area along the coast. There is a dignified atmosphere at this station that seems to encourage this determination.

Stop breaking up. After passing through a vast agricultural area, this station stands quietly at a point where the Sea of ​​Okhotsk finally approaches. Inside the old wooden station building, a ramen shop now known throughout the country hangs its curtains and satisfies travelers' hunger. The unique atmosphere created by the scent of soup stock wafting through the station building, mixed with the exhaust smoke of the trains, is one of the best parts of traveling by train. The remains of the former freight sidings bear the weight of the role this area played as a distribution center for agricultural products. In the winter, the cold air brought in by the drift ice envelopes the platform, making the loneliness of the remotest place even more profound. Although it is not a flashy tourist destination, it is rare to find a station that blends lifestyle and travel so well.

Hama Koshimizu. Here we can see the modern station, where the station building has become integrated with the roadside station and has been forced to coexist with the motorized society. However, if you turn your attention to the scenery on the platform side, you will see a long, narrow sandbar separating the calm waters of Lake Tofutsu from the rough waves of Okhotsk. This area, once called ``Furutoi,'' is still a paradise for wild birds, where the harshness and gentleness of nature coexist. As you step away from the hustle and bustle of tourists and gaze at the straight road leading to the end of the railroad tracks, you will feel that the history of development carried by the railway and the landscape that has been preserved by nature are in perfect harmony here. In contrast to the flow of cars on national highways, the constant rhythm unique to railways seems to somehow echo proudly.

Primeval flower garden. This temporary station, which only appears from May to October, is truly a ``flower platform'' set in the middle of nature. Immediately beyond the platform, there are sand dunes covered with blooming Japanese lilies and lilies, and the colors can be seen through the train windows. Since the Showa era, many travelers have disembarked at this station in the summer and enjoyed strolling through the short northern summer. Although the station's facilities are minimal, the view of Okhotsk from here is exceptionally blue, and the train, a tool of civilization, blends into the most primitive landscape, giving a strange sense of satisfaction. Surrounded by the sound of the ocean and the scent of flowers, you will forget about time for a while. The reason why such luxury is allowed is because of the special magical power that this station has.

Kitahama. As the station closest to the Sea of ​​Okhotsk, it is one of the most famous stations, etching its name on the map. The business cards and notes of travelers that fill the walls of the old station building tell how many people this place has become their ``spiritual final stop.'' In winter, when drift ice fills the horizon, if you stand on the platform, you can almost hear the sound of the ice rustling on the wind. The light shining from the coffee shop inside the station building is like a lighthouse for lonely travelers, giving them courage to face the harsh northern seas. It is also known as the setting for a movie, but even after stripping away the decorations, the rusted handrails and wooden walls that withstood the sea breeze are what convey the true image of this station. This gives us a vivid sense of the weight of the word travel passion.

Mokoto. Exposed to the sea breeze of Okhotsk, the wooden station building still stands majestically and retains the vestiges of the late Taisho era. In the past, it was the starting point of the Higashi-Mokoto Village Railway that led to Higashi-Mokoto Village (now Ozora Town), and there was a time when it was vibrant with the collection and distribution of agricultural products. Inside the station building is a coffee shop with a strong Showa-era atmosphere, and the aroma of coffee wafting from the former office gently soothes the chilled bodies and minds of travelers. Behind the station, faint traces of a former starch factory and warehouses remain, reminding us of the time when this area played a part in industry in the northern land. The sea outside the window is endlessly blue, but I can't help but feel that the indomitable spirit of the people who have overcome the harsh winter is etched in its stillness.

Masuura. The station is located one level lower than the national highway that runs parallel to the railroad tracks, and it literally feels like you're huddled on the shore of Okhotsk's waves. This area, which was once bustling with trout fishing, now has the atmosphere of a quiet fishing village, and the white waves surging through the train window remind us once again that this is the end of our journey. When you arrive at the platform, the unobstructed sound of the ocean waves vibrates your eardrums, and the scent of the ocean fills your whole body. The section from here to Abashiri has a ruggedness that shows that the railway was constructed while fighting against the sea, but the tranquility of the unmanned station contrasts with the roughness, making the journey even more memorable. Isolated from the hustle and bustle of civilization, you can just listen to the waves and wait for the next train. That's what luxury time is all about.

Katsuradai. As the final destination, Abashiri, approaches, the line turns away from the coastline and runs up to higher ground. This station is located behind Abashiri Prison, and although it is located in a residential area, it has a unique quietness that makes it feel isolated. The structure of the station, which is sandwiched between tunnels at both ends, gives off a sense of urgency, as if you are waiting on the sidelines of a stage, and it gives you a feeling that once you pass through this tunnel, you are finally at the end of your journey. The platform offers a panoramic view of the city of Abashiri and the Sea of ​​Okhotsk, offering a quiet bird's-eye view of the contrast between modern city life and unchanging nature. I can't help but feel that the atmosphere of the days when steam locomotives would pant up this steep slope and slide into the city of Abashiri is still ingrained in the slopes of Kiridoshi. It is a station that makes you feel the power of railways that lies behind the scenes of everyday life.

Abashiri. This station, which is the terminus of the Senmo Main Line and the starting point of the Sekihoku Main Line, has long reigned as a railway crossroads in eastern Hokkaido. The vertically written station name sign posted at the entrance of the station building, which is rare even in Japan, is said to contain a wish for those released from Abashiri Prison not to go sideways, and it silently speaks to the weight of history that this city has carried. Standing on the dead-end platform, you can feel the glory of the days when the express trains Taisetsu and Niseko took a break after long journeys, and you can feel the rusted edges of the tracks. The unique smell of the sea breeze wafting in front of the station and the exhaust smoke of diesel cars is the very memory of Abashiri for travelers. The ultimate terminal station has a somewhat lonely yet powerful embrace. Surrendering yourself to it is the perfect way to end your trip to the north.

Minoota. It is a strategic railway hub located at the northern end of the Nobi Plain, where the Takayama Main Line, the Taita Line, and the Nagaragawa Railway, which inherited the former Japanese National Railways Etsuminami Line, intersect. Looking around the spacious grounds, you can still feel the soot emitted by the steam locomotives and the reverberations of the heavy diesel sounds of the Kiha 58s still lingering in every corner of the platform. Even though we are being swayed by modern, neat cars, when we get off at this station, we feel the formality of the station as the starting point of our journey, and the unique sense of exhilaration that makes us feel like we are being rushed to some destination, and that is the real pleasure of traveling by train.

Maehira Park. It is a relatively new station, established after management was transferred from the Japanese National Railways to the third sector. However, the greenery of the trees outside the train window and the calm atmosphere surrounding the station do nothing to diminish the good old lyricism of this line. The quietness of the road leading to the park seems to retain a faint memory of a time when this area was once a wilderness, and the sound of trains accelerating and decelerating strangely echoes around. Although it is a newly built station, it has quietly blended into the line's history, and I can't help but think that it symbolizes the survival of local lines in modern times.

Kamono. With a single platform sitting alone in the middle of fields as far as the eye can see, it gives you the feel of a local Japanese station. This station still has the atmosphere of an idyllic time when people who took a break from farming would look at the clock at the sound of a distant train whistle. You could call it luxury without anything. For travelers escaping the hustle and bustle of the city, the ``scenery of tranquility'' that surrounds this station may be the best reward. The wind in Kamono is so clear that it makes you think of this.

Fuka. This station, which used to be called ``Itadori,'' has settled on its current name after going through a turbulent history with the merger of towns and villages in the Showa era. This neighborhood is dotted with rows of old houses, and you can feel the vestiges of an ancient highway, and you can feel the rich history of the area even through the train window. The appearance of the station building gives the impression of a silent guardian who has seen off countless commuters and students. Even as times change, we continue to support the same daily traffic. This solid role is what makes us feel proud of this station.

Seki Tomioka. This station is like a boundary between Seki City, known as the city of cutlery, and where the sounds of trains gradually begin to mix with the sounds of daily life. There are also industrial parks in the surrounding area, and the vitality of the area, which has transformed from a once purely rural area into a hub of modern industry, can be seen from the train window. However, when you stand on the platform at dusk, the wind blowing from the shadows of the mountains reminds you that you are still in the countryside of Mino. The hidden charm of this station lies in the mysterious harmony in which industry, nature, and history overlap like layers.

Sekiguchi. When you step off the platform of this station, your eyes will be drawn to the sight of a modern convenience store integrated into the station building. In the days of the Japanese National Railways, travelers would have been greeted by a rustic wooden station building, but as the times changed, the appearance of the station also evolved to become more closely connected to daily life. However, the lively voices of local students coming in and out of the store, and the quiet moments waiting for the train to arrive, give us a sense of the timeless railway landscape. If you peel back the layer of convenience, you will see that the deep love for the region that Nagaragawa Railway has cultivated over the years is pulsing through it.

Before the cough terrace. This new station, which was born in the Reiwa era, has the mission of serving as a new gateway to Seki, the cutlery town. While it provides access to modern tourist facilities, there is a unique sense of tension in the air, as you can hear the breathing of ancient craftsmen from the train windows. Part of the charm of traveling is the moment of confusion at a new station name, and the fact that the number of stations continues to increase in line with the trends of the times is proof that this line is still alive. At this point where traditional blacksmith techniques and modern tourism intersect, the train quietly runs through a continuation of history.

Seki. This station, which is the headquarters of the Nagaragawa Railway and also has a depot attached to it, has a personality that makes it worthy of being called the heart of the line. As I listen to the somewhat proud sound of the engines of the diesel cars standing at the back of the platform, I feel that the passion for the ``Zento'' that was once a dream of the National Railways Etsumi Minami Line is still alive in this area. Looking out over the rooftops of knife factories surrounding the station, the weight of industry that this town has built up closes in on travelers. The presence of Seki Station, which is not just a transit point but also the spiritual pillar of this line, gives a special feeling to those who love railways.

name_en: In front of Seki City Hall
text_en: In front of Seki City Hall. As its name suggests, this station is an important administrative center, and it looks as if it is a slice of the quiet daily life of the city. This station, which was newly built at the end of the Showa era, has now completely blended into the cityscape and plays an indispensable role as a means of transportation for people going to government offices and nearby residents. Although there are no flashy tourist attractions, the true nature of the area may be hidden in these stations that are rooted in daily life. This is an honest station where the vibrations caused by the acceleration and deceleration of trains teach us about the ``breathing of the railway,'' which is different from the texture of the paved road.
name_fr: Devant l'hôtel de ville de Seki

text_en: Yuchi Sekishita. This place name, also known as a difficult-to-read station name, makes us feel the pride of this area with a long history. As you pass the station, the greenery outside the train window becomes darker again, giving you the feeling that you are entering the deep heart of Mino. The fact that this former rural area has been slowly transforming into a residential area, yet still maintains a dignified tranquility, is probably a result of the dignity of this area. When you step off the platform and think about the murmuring of the Nagara River in the distance, you are reminded once again of the fact that railways transported not only goods and people, but also the culture of the land itself.

Matsumori. This station is located on the run-up section of the train as it passes through the city of Seki and finally heads toward the Okumino mountains. A tranquil rural landscape spreads out from the train window, and the train retains a strong vestige of the rustic local railway that the National Railways Etsumi Minami Line once served. In contrast to the hustle and bustle of the nearby expressways, time passes by at this station at a slow pace, and the sound of the rails tapping against the joints is strangely haunting. Even though it has been washed away by the waves of modernization, it subtly conveys to travelers the ``emotion of transportation'' that railways originally possessed.This kind of unassuming appearance is truly desirable.

Mino City. This station, which was once called Minomachi Station and was a busy station connecting with the Meitetsu Minomachi Line, is still an important node on the journey to Kitano. As soon as you step out of the station building, you can feel the lingering scent of Edo, known as the ``Udatsu-no-Rising Townscape,'' and the pride of being a Japanese paper village is felt in every corner of the city. The harmonious combination of historic townscapes and railways makes it a perfect subject for travelogues. When you sit on an old wooden bench and wait for the next train, you will feel as if you have turned back the clock to a beautiful day in the Showa era.

Umeyama. It is a station that is close to the center of Mino City and has a refreshing atmosphere where you can see the bustle of students commuting to their school. From this point onwards, the scenery of the city passing through the train window gradually begins to take on the color of a mountainous area, and I can feel my love for traveling deepening even further. Although they do not have particularly large facilities, each of these small stations has a history of supporting local life and at the same time turning the railway, a tool of civilization, into a part of the landscape. It's also fun to admire the appearance of the passing station while surrendering to the rhythm of the sound of the wheels.

Yunodo hot spring mouth. This station, which used to be called Minoshita Cave, came to be named after its role as the entrance to the hot springs. The greenery of the mountains that loom behind the station becomes even darker, and the clear stream of the Nagara River occasionally makes an appearance. If we think back to the days when hot spring bathers would descend upon this platform with their hearts full of anticipation, even the cold rails seem to have a certain warmth to them. The path that leads to the remote hot spring area seems to be asking us what kind of "relaxation" is that has nothing to do with today's fast-paced society.
name_fr: Bouche de la source chaude de Yunodo

text_en: Suhara. This station is at a dramatic turning point, where the main character of the train window changes from residential buildings to the majestic flow of the Nagara River. The surface of the river that flows right next to the station reflects the changing faces of the four seasons, allowing you to truly enjoy the thrill of riding a train along the ``Water and Green Corridor.'' Suhara Shrine is located nearby, and has a long history of watching over the safety of water transportation, making the atmosphere of this area even more solemn. While feeling the wonders and blessings of nature up close, the carelessness and dependability of traveling along a narrow railway intersect. This is what makes me feel that this is the essence of the Nagaragawa Railway.

Mother field. This station, located along the meandering path of the Nagara River, is a reminder of the river's once prosperous transport of timber. There is something warm about the name of the station, and the platform, which is placed alone in the countryside, gives the impression of a mother-like embrace that gently welcomes travelers. Although we cannot deny the harsh reality of depopulation in modern times, looking at the seasonal flowers blooming in front of the station and the carefully maintained waiting room, you can clearly feel the love the people who live there have for the railway. In an age where only efficiency is pursued, the existence of stations like this is a kind of relief.

Kio. This station stands quietly in a section where the mountains loom over the river and the railroad runs through the small gap between them. You can hear the murmuring of the Nagara River just below the platform, and if you happen to open the window while the train is stopped, the cool mountain air and the smell of the river will flow into the train. In the days of the Japanese National Railways, how much trouble did it take to get the tracks through this rugged terrain? It is strange that when we think about the hardships of our predecessors, the railway, which is simply a means of transportation, begins to look like a kind of monument. It is a quiet station where you can get a glimpse of the abyss of nature.

Yasaka. The area around this station, which is said to be close to Japan's population center, can truly be called the highlight of a trip to the ``middle of Japan.'' However, without flaunting such an exaggerated title, the station itself maintains an extremely simple and unadorned beauty, which is truly disgusting. The bridge that takes you to the other side of the Nagara River can be seen nearby, and the sound of trains crossing the bridge reverberating off the mountains is so beautiful that it seems like the scenery from a railroad model has been made into reality. Yasaka Station has an atmosphere that tells travelers about the richness of the area by just being there without saying anything.

Minamikotakara Onsen. This is an unusual station that was born from the wisdom of modern railway management, with a direct connection from the station platform to the hot spring facility. The luxury of soaking in hot water immediately after getting off the train would have been unimaginable in the days of steam locomotives, but this is the new form of "railway travel for the Reiwa era." The combination of the rising smoke from the hot springs and the latest light diesel trains is a testament to the hard work that has gone into ensuring the survival of the railway. Soothe the fatigue of your journey with a bath and wait for the sound of the next train to arrive. There is no other more luxurious way to spend your time.

Oya. This station, where trains are waiting to be exchanged, is a key point in the operation of the Nagaragawa Railway, and has the appearance of a ``key point.'' The good old railway system still pulsates through the station building, which has been built since the days of the Japanese National Railways, and inside the premises, where you can still feel the feel of well-used switches. Waiting for the opposite train to arrive, I listen closely to the sound of the tablet being replaced (now computerized, but I can almost hear it) echoing in the silence. For modern people who are in too much of a hurry, fleeting stops provide a valuable reprieve to regain peace of mind.

Fukuno. As the train runs along the meandering Nagara River, this station gives you the feeling that you are finally entering the heart of Gujo. The surrounding area is dotted with private houses, and the color of the soil in the plowed fields reminds us of the strength of our ancestors who cultivated this land. The silence of the unmanned station deepens as the sound of the train engine recedes, and the murmur of the river takes center stage. It's not a flashy tourist destination, but the true face of Gifu.

Kariyasu Minami. Located in the center of what used to be Minami Village, it is a station that somehow proudly carries the memory of the glory where express trains stopped. The plaza and buildings in front of the station have faint traces of the bustle of the Showa era, reminding us of a happy time when railways were closely connected to local life. Nowadays, the train only quietly picks up passengers at each station, but its calm demeanor is what supports the backbone of this line.

Akaike. The area around this station is a section where the Nagara River carves into the steep rock surface, and the dynamic scenery becomes the highlight of the train window. The station itself is simple, but the blue water you can see from the platform is refreshing enough to wash away the souls of travelers who have become dirty from the hustle and bustle of the city. Alongside lines of cars passing by on the national highway, the railway weaves through mountains and crosses rivers at its own tempo. It is a perfect observation point where you can enjoy the original richness of railways, unrelated to modern speed.

Deep door. This station is quietly rooted in a place where mountains approach from both sides and the sky feels even smaller. The steep terrain, where Japanese National Railways steam locomotives would have once climbed this hill panting and their view obscured by smoke, has not lost its power even today. The sound of a railroad crossing echoes in the silence, and the creak of the rails as the train accelerates and decelerates. All of these things give us a sense of the tenacity of the people who have continued to protect the railways in the face of harsh nature.

Aioi. The station serves as a transportation hub where roads cross rivers before the final approach to Gujo Hachiman. There is an old bridge built nearby, and its geometric beauty creates an atmosphere that can be said to be the fruit of Showa era civil engineering technology, something that is not found in inorganic concrete construction. The importance of the role this station has played as a lifeline connecting mountain villages. It is a place where you can take a break and prepare your mind for your next big destination.

Gujo Hachiman. It is one of the most famous stations on this line, and the wooden station building, which retains a strong vestige of the early Showa era, is truly a registered tangible cultural property. If you stand on the platform, the former freight sidings and vast premises will eloquently tell you about the vibrancy of the past. The elegance of a water town and castle town gently envelops the entire station, immediately inviting travelers who disembark to the ``world of Gujo''. I can't help but feel happy that the cultural heritage of railways is still alive and well today.

In front of the nature garden. This station was established at the end of the Showa era as a base for young people's outdoor activities, and in contrast to the rugged nature surrounding it, it has a bright and open atmosphere. With the clear waters of the Nagara River in the background, the platform is a special place where you can feel the seasonal breeze directly on your skin, living up to its name as a ``natural garden.'' Although it is a new station, it blends into the surrounding landscape and quietly watches over the changing seasons, giving the impression that it is an ideal example of a railway coexisting with nature.

Yamada. This station is at the entrance of the train as it leaves the hustle and bustle of Gujo Hachiman and returns to the rustic landscape of mountains and fields. In the past, farmers who disembarked here would have hurried home, swinging their baskets on their backs, and even now you can still see it, and it feels as if time has stopped. Although there are no flashy tourist attractions, you can get off at this station and just look at the clouds passing by. Such casual luxuries are exactly the moments of bliss that railway travelogue writers seek.

Tokunaga. This station, which was once the political and economic hub of Yamato Village, is still lined with houses and shops, allowing you to feel the breath of the area up close. The scenery around the station has been slowly repainted from the pastoral past to a modern lifestyle, but even so, the sunlight streaming into the platform is filled with the calmness of this land. Trains continue to run quietly, supporting people's lives. It makes me feel that it is the accumulation of these activities that forms the annual rings known as history.

Gujo Yamato. The station used to be called Mino Yamato and was an important station connecting with Japanese National Railways buses. Today, as the gateway to the roadside station ``Kokindenju no Sato Yamato'', it is crowded with many vacationers, and the station building has also been reborn, but the pride that flows through its roots as ``the village of poets'' remains intact. Amid modern facilities, the travel spirit of the Showa era suddenly appears. Enjoying the mix of old and new, the train finally heads into the depths of Okumino.

text_en: Manba. This station is quietly located in a section where the clear waters of the Nagara River are becoming increasingly blue, and the railway line closely follows the meandering of the river. It is located near the northern end of what was once Gujo Yamato Village, and is surrounded by rustic farmhouse roofs, making it look like a slice of Japan's original landscape. When you step onto the platform of an unmanned station, all you can hear is the murmur of the river and the sound of the wind. This tranquil space, separated from the modern society that demands efficiency, is the best medicine to soothe the troubled souls of travelers.

Kamimanba. This station, located a short distance from Manba Station, is the successor to the so-called ``Petition Station,'' which was established in the 1950s. Although it is a simple structure with only one short platform, its small size still conveys the warmth that the local people have cherished and cherished as their means of transportation. The scenery seen from the train window changes the color of the mountains with each season, and in winter they are covered in deep snow. In this harsh natural environment, we still retain the memories of a time when railways were the only window to the outside world.
name_fr: Des dizaines de milliers de jeux

text_en: Onaka. This station, located near the border between the former Gujo Yamato Village and Shiratori Town, is in a place that gives you a sense of the harshness of the uphill slope towards the watershed. A dense forest looms behind the platform, and you get the illusion that you can hear the breathing of the steam locomotives that once passed by, exhaling smoke in their desperation. The silence around the station is not just a feeling of desolation, but also a sense of respect for the history of maintaining railway lines over a long period of time. The fact that the huge railway system is made up of a series of small stations like this makes me want to correct myself once again.

Oshima. This station is located just before entering Shiratori's urban area, where the plains spread out slightly. In this area surrounded by mountains, the spacious countryside provides a momentary sense of freedom that pleases the eyes of travelers. When we think back to the past, when agricultural products were transported from here on freight cars to markets far away in Nagoya, we realize that this humble home was also an important stage that supported Japan's rapid economic growth. It is the kind of station where you can feel the layers of history and raise your expectations for the next big station.

Mino swan. In the past, it was an important station that was bustling with activity day and night, serving as a connection point with the Meikan Line of the Japanese National Railways bus service and as a base for mountain climbing in Okumino. Looking around the spacious grounds and stately station building, you can vividly recall the vibrancy of the past, when many skiers and mountain climbers would spend the night here, or take a bus ride to the Fukui area. A place where the railway completes its role as a "road". Even now that it has become part of the third sector, this heavy atmosphere has not faded, and it seems to be quietly asserting Okumino's pride.

text_en: Shiratori Plateau. This station, which was once called ``Futukamachi,'' was given its current name after being given a new look as an access station to a ski resort. As we passed the station, the slope became even more severe, and the diesel engine roared as we gained altitude. The scenery of the plateau that stretches out from the train window is completely different from the atmosphere of traditional satoyama, and it makes you feel close to the sky. Although station names and appearances have changed in response to the demands of the times, railways continue to transport people. I feel that this unchanging activity has a thread running through the ever-changing landscape of tourism.

Hakusan Nagataki. It is located in front of the gates of Nagataki Hakusan Shrine, which flourished as a base for the Hakusan faith since ancient times, and the station's deep history can be felt from the name of the station. When you step onto the platform, the dignified air unique to the sacred area stings your skin, giving you the illusion that the power of faith that has remained unchanged since ancient times is swallowing up even the modern equipment of railways. The former Etomi Minami Line may have left its footprints in this area, or it may have been an act of admiration for the sacred mountain, Mt. Hakusan. Even the sound of a railroad crossing alarm, which echoes in the sacred silence, seems to have a somewhat ritualistic ring to it.

Kitano. This is the terminal station where the 72 km long railway that continued from Mino-Ota finally comes to an end. If you look at the broken rail beyond the platform, you will see the painful yet beautiful remains of the dream of the ``Etsubi Line'' that was once supposed to cross this area and connect with the Etsubi North Line on the Fukui side. The manually operated turntable that remains on the premises is a witness to a time when steam locomotives once changed direction and prepared to head south again. This point, where the loneliness of a dead end and the sense of accomplishment of having completed a journey intertwine, is the sacred place that a travel writer should reach at the end.

Tateno. After all, this station is well-known among railway fans as a key point on the three-stage switchback. This spot, where the Hohi Main Line and the Minami Aso Railway part, is marked by the history of the struggles of our predecessors as they tried to overcome the steep terrain of Aso's somma. Standing on the platform, the sound of the Shirakawa River flowing through the deep valley floor intersects with the sound of the engines of diesel cars tackling steep slopes, gently reminding us of the days when D51s would climb up hills panting and smoking soot. As the gateway to Aso, this station bears the weight of the fact that the railway has made steady progress without going against the terrain.

Changyo. The old wooden station building welcomes you with an indescribable warmth. This station building, which still retains much of its appearance from when it first opened in 1938, is now being used as a cafe by local volunteers, and has become a place for travelers to quench their thirst and relax. The mountains of Aso that can be seen from the edge of the platform change color with each season, and the clear air of the highland makes you forget the hustle and bustle of the city. Even in every pillar of the building, you can feel the vestiges of a time when trains were not just a means of transportation, but a part of people's lives and memories. The relaxing time that flows through this station is truly a treasure of Minamiaso.

Join us. It's a truly rustic station that stands alone in the middle of a rural landscape. Surrounded by fields that stretch as far as the eye can see, the activities of the people working hard at farming add a lively color to the scenery seen from the train window. An unmanned station can sometimes give a sense of desolation, but here I feel a sense of peace as I blend into the local life. The wind blowing through the simple concrete platform carries the scent of the season, silently telling us that this area is a rich agricultural area. This small station certainly has the luxury of nothing.

text_en: Aso Shimoda Castle. In the Heisei era, the former Aso Shimoda Station was transformed into a unique station building modeled after a castle. The station has the word ``castle'' in its name, and there was once a hot spring facility inside the station building, giving a sense of its ambition as a tourist hub. The joy of seeing trains return to this area after overcoming the great hardship of the earthquake must have been indescribable for the local people. In contrast to the imposing appearance of the station building, the gentle mountain view of Minamiaso that can be seen from there still gently soothes the hearts of visitors. It is a station with a mysterious charm that combines novelty and nostalgia.

name_ja: 南阿蘇水の生まれる里白水高原
name_en: Birthplace of Minamiaso water, Hakusui Plateau
text_en: Hakusui Plateau, the birthplace of Minamiaso water. This station once boasted the longest station name in Japan, and as its name suggests, it stands behind the rich springs of Aso. The long name, which consists of 22 hiragana characters, expresses pride in the land and gratitude for the water. When you stand on the platform, you can feel the refreshing wind blowing through the bottom of the caldera, bringing with it the presence of clear water. Just following the letters on the station name signs from the edge can be a challenge, but that can also be said to be one of the small pleasures of traveling on this railway. The rich land nurtured by the famous water continues on forever beyond the railroad tracks, giving you a sense of its expanse.
name_fr: Lieu de naissance de l'eau de Minamiaso, plateau de Hakusui

text_en: Nakamatsu. When you get off at this station, you can feel the depth of Minamiaso's heart. It's a piece of history where even express trains once stopped here, and it's somehow proudly floating around here. The station building's features also have a style that is rooted in this area, and conveys the warmth that the local people have continued to cherish. In spring, the area is crowded with tourists visiting the nearby Isshingyo Daizakura, but there is something hard to give up on the luxury of standing alone on a quiet platform in a season when there is no such hustle and bustle. Its appearance, carrying the Five Mountains of Aso on its back and calmly supporting the railway, shows us the true pleasure of railway travel.

Aso Shirakawa. As the name of the station suggests, it is a place where you can feel the stirrings of life as Aso's underground waters begin to moisten the surface of the earth. The simple yet dignified wooden station building quietly speaks of the bygone Showa era. When you get off the platform, you can hear the sound of running water coming from everywhere, and you are once again convinced that this is the richness of Aso. The time spent waiting for the train while listening to the creaking sound of the rails on a quiet afternoon during the agricultural off-season helps modern people regain the peace of mind that they had almost forgotten. This station shows us how the railway, a tool of civilization, is in perfect harmony with the workings of nature.

Minamiaso Shirakawa water source. This new station, which was built in 2012, serves as the main entrance to the famous Shirakawa water source. Although it is a relatively new station, the way it blends into the surrounding scenery gives a sense of respect for the ancient railroads. There is a water source right next door that boasts a spring water capacity of 60 tons per minute, and its refreshing air surrounds the entire station. It promises a refreshing moment, like getting off the train midway through your journey and immersing yourself in a clear stream of water. The history and pride of this area is condensed in the new station name.

Viewing platform. As the name suggests, you can enjoy an unobstructed panoramic view of the five Aso mountains. The station itself is a very simple structure with just one platform, but it is this stripped-down appearance that brings out the greatest treat of all: the scenery. This place, which was once the setting for a soft drink commercial, now has the feel of a holy place that many young people visit, but for railway fans, it is just a measuring stick for measuring the majesty of Aso. As I sit on a hill with nothing to block the wind and gaze at the vast expanse of grassland and the sky, I am reminded that the train I rode on is just one point in this great natural world.

Takamori. It is the terminal station of the Minamiaso Railway, and at the same time, it is also the site of a grand dream that once included extending the line to the Miyazaki Prefecture side. The newly rebuilt station building serves as a symbol of recovery from the earthquake and gives us a sense of the strong progress we have made. However, if you look at the end of the dead-end line, you can see the sadness of the unfinished railway that led to Takachiho, which was the goal of the former Takamori Line. The fragrant smell of grilling the famous dengaku food floating around this station and the atmosphere of the historic brewery will leave you with a deep feeling that is perfect for the end of your trip. Takamori Station teaches us that a terminal station is not just the end of a line, but a place where one begins to think about a new journey.

Kagoshima central. When you get off at this station, which was once called "Nishikagoshima," you can still feel the pride of being the southernmost terminal in Kyushu mixed in with the particles in the air. In the past, the limited express train ``Tsubame'' and sleeper express ``Hayabusa'' arrived at the end of their long journeys with sooty faces. With the arrival of the Shinkansen, the station building has been completely renovated into a modern look, with a large Ferris wheel sitting on the roof, but am I the only one who feels uneasy about it? Still, if you stand at the edge of the platform and look at the purple smoke spewing out from the diesel cars on the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line, you can feel the unmistakable feeling of being at the edge of the south. Starting from this station, the long railway that continues to Makurazaki begins. That feeling of exhilaration is the real pleasure of traveling by train.

Gunmoto. This small station, the first station after leaving Kagoshima Chuo, is buried in the hustle and bustle of the city, yet it maintains the elegance of a single-track train. Surrounded by residential areas and schools, this station is bustling with students in the morning and evening, and while its location suggests that it was once connected to a streetcar, it still has the simple appearance of a temporary residence as a JR station. In today's world of elevated railways, seeing off a train from the platform with your feet on the ground seems like a truly luxurious way to spend your time. The feeling of life in the houses along the railroad tracks is within reach from the train window. It is this intimacy that makes us feel that this is the true nature of railways in local cities.

Minami Kagoshima. This is the junction with the Kagoshima City Tram, and is a place where you can see the unique sight of railways and tracks running side by side. As if to confirm the history that the station was once used for cargo handling, the area around the station has the lingering scent of rugged industry. The old stone walls and the texture of the concrete, which has darkened over time, evoke memories of this neighborhood that supported the heavy industrial era of the Showa era. The moment the light motor sound of the city tram intersects with the heavy engine sound of the diesel cars inherited from the JNR era, I feel a sense of pride in this station as a transportation hub. I am humbled by the fact that even though their appearance has changed due to modernization, they continue to play an honest role as people's transportation.

Usuku. This station, which once called itself ``Ujuku Town,'' has now transformed into a modern townscape lined with large commercial facilities. However, if you stand on the platform and look at where the tracks are going, you will notice that there is a laid-back atmosphere that is unique to the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line. I heard that during the Showa era, this area was still a quiet landscape with fields spreading out, but now it is a bustling commuter town. Despite being washed away by the waves of rapid urbanization, the structure of the station itself is extremely simple, and this gap is what piques the interest of travelers. Although it wears a cloak of convenience, underneath it hides the bones of a good old local station. It gives me that impression.

Taniyama. It was once the gateway to Taniyama City and one of the main stations on the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line. In recent years, its appearance has changed completely due to the elevation, and it has become a bit of a pain to find remnants of the Showa era, but the importance of the station name has not changed. This area once had a prosperous history as ``Taniyama-juku,'' and was full of vitality as merchants and travelers came and went. The view of the city from the elevated platform is orderly, but if you close your eyes, you will remember the scent of tea and the warmth of the people that wafted through the old wooden station building. The layers of history are clearly piled up inside the modern concrete structure. I believe that it is the duty of a travel writer to sense that invisible depth.

Jigenji Temple. As the station name suggests, this station is located near the former famous temple, Jigen-ji Temple, and has an air of purity. With the lush greenery of Jigenji Park in the background, you can almost hear the whispers of the trees in the wind. This place has also been baptized by the era of elevated railways, but it is gratifying to see the intention to harmonize with the surrounding natural environment. In early summer, the park is crowded with people admiring the nemophila and cosmos, and the railway conveys the changing seasons. A land with a religious background continues to function as a modern railway station. I cannot help but think that there is a gentle coexistence of the sacred and the profane, which the Japanese have cherished since ancient times.

Sakanoue. As the name suggests, this station is located on the way up from the Kagoshima Plain to the Shirasu Plateau, and is a testament to the harshness of the terrain. There are many universities and high schools in the area, and this station is always filled with the excitement of young people, and boasts one of the busiest numbers of passengers on the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line. The diesel car pantly climbs the hill, and from the platform we finally arrive at, we can see the wave-like roof tiles of a residential area stretching out into the distance. This plateau, which was once an empty field, has grown into a town of this size through post-war residential development. I am deeply moved by the fact that it was undoubtedly this single, narrow railway that supported that history.

Goino. Once you pass this point, the train finally leaves the hustle and bustle of the city and enters a scenic landscape rich with travel sensations. This station is also known as the gateway to Hirakawa Zoological Park, and on holidays, the sound of laughter from families echoing through the platform. I feel that the somewhat nostalgic and warm atmosphere that the old wooden station building exuded has not been completely lost even though it has become a modern, simple station building. The trees surrounding the station are getting greener, and the nameless flowers blooming next to the railway lines are a feast for the eyes of travelers. This is the entrance to the ``original scenery of local railways'' that I love so much.
