text_en: Hirakawa. The moment you step onto the platform of this station, you notice the scent of the ocean tickling your nostrils. This is a station that can be called a turning point, as Kinko Bay finally appears and the main focus of the train window changes from residential buildings to the sea. The area around the station retains the atmosphere of an old fishing town, and the scenery of narrow alleys is clearly engraved with the Showa era lifestyle. The moment you wait for the next train while looking out at the calm ocean waves allows you to enjoy the luxury of ``tranquility'' that modern society has forgotten. I can't help but look forward to the journey ahead, where the railway and the sea will continue side by side. It is a station that deeply shakes the traveler's spirit.

Sezekushi. This station is located right on the edge of the waves of Kinko Bay, and has a style that is worthy of being called a ``sea station.'' The blue sea stretches out right in front of the platform, and the majestic Sakurajima Island proudly shows off its ridgeline on the opposite shore. In the past, we would listen to the sound of the sea from the window of a diesel car that had stopped for a long time while waiting to cross an oncoming train. The sea breeze you feel as you cross the old overpass is a bit sticky, but it pleasantly soothes the fatigue of your journey. Although the colors of the building have faded with the passage of time, the beauty of the view from here remains timeless. This is a truly splendid stop that confirms this.

Middle name. When you get off at this small station, the first thing that catches your eye are the silver tanks of the huge oil storage base that sits behind it. In contrast to the huge infrastructure that supports Japan's rapid economic growth and controls the nation's energy, the appearance of an unmanned train station stands out in stark contrast. I can't help but think that this extreme contrast symbolizes the path that modern Japan has taken. There was once a time when it was bustling with people involved in base construction, but now the silence is broken only by the sea breeze caressing the skin of the tank and the occasional sound of a passing train engine. This landscape, where the dynamism of industry and the tranquility of the countryside coexist in a strange way, gives us the feeling that it is a cross-section of society that a train journey can teach us.

Kiiri. This area is home to one of the world's largest oil transfer stations, and is also an important base station on the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line. There was a time when people lined up to get commemorative tickets because the name of the station had the auspicious meaning of ``containing joy.'' When you stand on the platform where the limited express train ``Ibusuki no Tamatebako'' stops, you can feel that the city's former vitality as the center of Kiiremachi is still alive and well. In front of the station, there are shops that retain the nostalgic atmosphere of the Showa era, and you can almost hear the hustle and bustle of the base workers who once supported this area, like a hallucination. Although it is a modern energy supply base, the area around the station has a relaxing atmosphere typical of a southern country. This duality is the true depth of the town of Kiiri.

Maenohama. The station is sandwiched between National Route 226 and the waves of Kinko Bay, and although it looks cramped, it is located in an open location. The view of the ocean from the platform is unobstructed, and the hazy view of the mountains of the Osumi Peninsula in the distance is reminiscent of a painting. I have heard that in the past, the sandy beach was close to this station, and people could be seen fishing with seine nets. Nowadays, a breakwater has been built and the scenery has changed somewhat, but the scent of the sea and the soothing sound of waves still conveys the ``journey to the southernmost tip'' that was loved by travelers in the Showa era. Just stare at the sea while feeling the wind pressure of the passing high-speed train. This is a luxurious way to spend your time.

Ikimi. When I add the word ``nukumi'' to the name of this difficult-to-read station, I feel the warm sound soothing away the fatigue of my travels. Although it is now known as a beach where young people gather to enjoy surfing, the station itself is surprisingly quiet, hidden in the shadow of a pine forest. This place, near the border between Kagoshima City and Ibusuki City, must have once been nothing more than a remote fishing village, but the joy of connecting the world with the opening of the railway must have been immeasurable to the people of the time. Sitting down on a bench in the old waiting room, the sound of the sea and the sounds of cicadas mix together, creating the illusion that the hands of a clock have stopped somewhere in the Showa era. This is the station that gives you that mysterious floating feeling.

Satsuma Imaizumi. The station's name, ``Imaizumi,'' comes from the Imazumi Shimazu family, the birthplace of Atsuhime, which vividly colored the turbulent period at the end of the Edo period. As soon as you step out of the station, you'll be greeted by old stone walls and a streetscape with traces of samurai residences, inviting you into the depths of history. If you think about whether the young Atsuhime once felt the wind of this land and gazed at the waves of Kinko Bay, this mere railway stop begins to feel like a gate that transcends time and space. Looking out the window of a train waiting for single-track replacement, I look at the roofs of a village that gives a sense of its layered history. There, you can experience a mellow time that you can never experience in modern travel where speed is the only pursuit. It is a truly interesting station where history and railways intersect.

Miyagahama. This small station is located just before the train passes Satsuma Imaizumi and finally enters the heart of Ibusuki, where the view suddenly opens and the sea approaches. The waves of Kinko Bay are crashing just behind the platform, and the sound of the sea resonates pleasantly with the idling sound of the diesel engine. There must have been a time when the cheers of beachgoers gathered in this area in search of the summer sunshine could be heard. Nowadays, it has the feel of a quiet, unmanned station, but the way the leaves of the cycads planted next to the tracks sway in the breeze, it truly evokes the feeling of traveling in a tropical country. The view of the Osumi Peninsula on the opposite shore from here changes its appearance from moment to moment depending on the weather, pleasing the eyes of travelers. Just before entering the city of Ibusuki, which has been developed as a modern tourist destination, it is one of the secret joys of traveling by train that you come across a station like this, which is rustic and gives you a sense of the vestiges of a time when people's lives were directly connected to the sea.

Nigatsuden. As you look out the peaceful window of the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line, the name of this station suddenly appears, and it has a somewhat old-fashioned, yet warm sound to it.

This station, which was founded in 1933 as the terminal station of the Ibusuki Line, has now completely blended into the scenery of Kagoshima, a tropical country. When you arrive at the platform, you are greeted by the soft light of the southern country, along with the lingering scent of exhaust smoke from diesel cars. The area around the station retains strong traces of the hot spring inns of the past, and the very existence of this station gives the illusion of digging up the strata of history.

Of particular note is the presence of Nigatsuta Onsen, also known as ``Tono-no-Yu'', which is located a few minutes walk from the station. This famous hot spring, which is said to have been visited by the former lord of the Satsuma domain, Nariaki Shimazu, for its hot spring treatments, continues to be a part of the lives of the local people today. Although the station building itself has been transformed into a modern, simple structure, the time that has passed behind it is unmistakable, giving us the feeling that it is a continuation of the Showa period and even the early modern period.

While approaching Ibusuki, a major tourist destination, I dared to get off at this small station. There, the scent of indigenous life and the quiet spirit of travel that are not mentioned in tourist guides are certainly alive and well.

Ibusuki. When you get off the train at this station, the sea breeze and the refreshing, tropical air tickle your nose. Kagoshima Central -- The journey of the diesel train south from the former Nishi-Kagoshima Station reaches its climax here. Once known as the "Hawaii of the East," many young people descended on this platform as a honeymoon mecca, filled with hope for the future...I can't help but feel that the echoes of the hustle and bustle of the Showa era still lurk in the shadows of the platform's roof.

The palm trees decorating the front of the station and the route leading to the sand bath hot springs give it the appearance of a resort area, but at its core is Satsuma's rustic and sincere hospitality. If you spend your time waiting for your train while soaking in the footbath, you will realize that in today's fast-paced world, the hands of the clock are ticking a little more slowly here. The sight of the limited express train ``Ibusuki Tamatebako'' spewing out a mist that resembles black and white smoke also blends into the station's somewhat theatrical, yet endearing, travel spirit.

Yamakawa. If you expand the map, it becomes obvious that Yamakawa Bay is a good natural port formed by volcanic activity, and this station is located at the entrance to it. The train leaves Ibusuki and has the atmosphere of taking a breather before finally entering the southernmost unexplored region of the mainland. There is a history that this station was once the terminal station of the Ibusuki Line, and even now it is a key operational point where many trains are forced to turn back at this station.

A steep mountain looms behind the platform, and the deep blue ocean spreads out below. At this station, you can't help but feel that the scent of the sea and the weight of daily life coexist in contrast to the glamor of Ibusuki. As you exit the station building, the smell of smoky bonito flakes wafts on the wind, quietly telling you that this is a land that has been known as a bonito town since ancient times and has lived in harmony with the blessings of the sea. The sight of the railway stretching further south from here to Mt. Nishioyama and Makurazaki gives a sense of an endless journey, and mysteriously tightens the hearts of travelers.

Oyama. As you travel further south on the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line, the majestic sight of Mt. Kaimondake, also known as ``Satsuma Fuji'', approaches you with an even larger and overwhelming presence. Oyama Station is a truly beautiful small station that stands quietly at the foot of such a famous mountain. There is no fancy station building, just a simple platform that runs through the line. However, there remains the true serenity of a railway, without excessive production.

As you get to this point, the number of trains visibly decreases, and only the sound of the joints on the tracks punctuates the surrounding silence. In spring, the bright yellow of the rape blossoms that decorate the sides of the railroad tracks, the deep green of Mt. Kaimondake, and the blue of the tropical sky create a stunning three-color combination, creating a paradise for those who love railways. Not that there is anything. Just looking up at the famous peak and waiting for the train to arrive. That luxurious idle time is what is most lost and most precious in modern railway travel.

Nishioyama. As the southernmost station in JR Japan, when you get off at this station, which is famous all over the country, you are overwhelmed by the perfect conical shape of Mt. Kaimondake towering in front of you. Who could have predicted that so many tourists would visit when it opened in 1965? In the past, it had the appearance of a station at the far end, just sitting alone in a field.

Nowadays, there are things like ``yellow mailboxes that bring happiness'' placed there, making it look a little more like a tourist destination, but when you stand at the edge of the platform and feel the wind blowing at you, you get a quiet feeling that you are at the end of the mainland, in the remotest part of the country. The strong tropical sunlight mercilessly illuminates the single-track platform, and beyond that lies Mt. Kaimondake. This pure composition is what makes this station so special.

In the past, there were many travelers who thought of the thousands of kilometers of railway that stretched between Wakkanai Station and Wakkanai Station, the farthest point in the north. Even if the Shinkansen runs and the shape of the trains changes, this station's significance as the ``pole'' will never fade in the slightest.

Satsuma Kawajiri. This small station is the next stop on the train that runs from Nishioyama to the base of Mt. Kaimondake. This is a place on the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line that is especially close to Mt. Kaimondake, where you can feel the strength of the mountain's surface up close. Although the station building is simple, the village of Kawajiri, a port town, spreads out just beyond the platform, and the life of the people, the mountains, and the sea exist as a trinity.

The scent of the ocean and the wind blowing down from the mountains. When I think of the many young people who once used this station to commute to work or school, looking up at this overwhelming mountain every day, I can't help but feel a sense of envy at the luxury of their daily lives. Occasionally, the scent of boiling fish from nearby waters wafts from the back alleys of the village. Although it tends to be hidden behind famous tourist spots, this station has a rich atmosphere that embodies the culture of Satsuma.

Just quietly listen and compare the sound of the waves and the idling sound of a diesel engine. That kind of luxurious time is still left here.

East Kaimon. This unmanned station, literally located due east of Mt. Kaimondake, appears to travelers as simple and unsettling. Surrounded by vast fields, a single rail stretches straight under an unobstructed sky. I feel that the origin of the act of ``travel'' brought about by railways remains here.

The area in front of the station has a somewhat earthy smell that reminds you of the hardships of our predecessors who pioneered this land. There was a deep silence after the train left, and the only sound that reached my ears was the sound of the wind rustling the grass. It is in these ordinary stations that the virtue of ``enjoying solitude'' that was associated with train travel in the Showa era is quietly alive and well.

As I huddle in the shadow of the waiting room, which is too small to be called a station building, I get the feeling that I am standing at a single point on the map, a very delicate point. This angle of viewing Mt. Kaimondake diagonally from behind is also really interesting as it gives us a different look at the mountain.

Open hearing. As a climbing base for Satsuma Fuji, this station was once bustling with climbers and tourists. Shops line the area around the station, and you can still feel the pride it has as a regional hub. However, the main attraction is Mt. Kaimondake itself, which sits behind this station.

Standing on the platform of this station, looking up at the height of the mountain is truly divine. In the past, many hikers must have put their heavy backpacks back on their backs at this station and headed for the summit. As times have changed, the hustle and bustle of the station has subsided, but the mountain is still there, welcoming visitors with kindness and sometimes harshness. We travelers feel a moment of peace in its unchanging appearance.

The seasonal flowers blooming next to the railroad tracks inside the station are a heart-warming reminder of the thoughtfulness of the railway workers. This is not just a passing point, but a solemn gateway where the mountains and people meet.

Irino. After passing Kaimon, the train gradually leaves the mountains and enters a plateau filled with tea plantations. Irino Station stands at the entrance. As the station name suggests, this station is located at the entrance to a field, giving you a sense of the dry atmosphere brought about by Kagoshima's unique whitebait plateau.

Although there are no great scenic spots in the surrounding area, this fact highlights the sincere way in which the railway functions as a means of transportation for people's lives. An old bench on the platform, a rusty station name sign. Each one of them silently speaks of the stars that the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line has accumulated. This is a station that strongly reminds us that the true travelogue is hidden within the ordinary scenery.

The green tea plantations visible from the train window are dazzling. If you get off at this station and walk aimlessly along the farm roads, you will be able to feel for yourself the powerful vitality that Satsuma's rich soil nurtures.

Ei. Every time I come into contact with this noble name, which can be read as ``Ei'' with just one letter, I am reminded of the depth of the deep bosom of the land of Satsuma. The station is located on a hill slightly above the coastline, and from the platform you can see the faint sparkle of the East China Sea. In the past, a wooden station building welcomed travelers, but now it is mainly a simple waiting room. However, it is the texture of the concrete exposed to the sea breeze that gives us a sense of the reality of this farthest route. The difficult-to-read place names unique to this area still convey the pride of this former samurai village. Every time the train door opens, a humid tropical breeze flows into the train, a quiet reminder that we are near the edge of the mainland.

Nishikyuan. As the center of the Eiwa region, this station is the heartbeat of life. There are many government offices and schools in the area, and in the evening, the cheerful voices of local students echo through the platform. This is where you can see the true nature of a station, which is more than just a transit point and is rooted in the community. I feel an indescribable sense of relief when I see the same scenery of going to and from school that has remained unchanged since the Showa era. It is easy to imagine that the station used to be a commissioned station, with station staff standing at the ticket gate and interacting with passengers. Even in today's deserted silence, the warmth of a land where people have lived side by side remains on the worn benches in the waiting room.

Goryo. This station, where the train slides in while drawing a gentle curve, is surrounded by vast fields, giving it a truly refreshing appearance. In the past, many agricultural products were transported from this area on freight cars. When you arrive at the platform, the smell of earth and grass mix, and you are enveloped in a somewhat nostalgic, original Japanese landscape. There are no special facilities, just a single rail and a wide open sky, leaving you with the luxury of being here. The view of Mt. Kaimondake from here is also exceptional, and as the mountain recedes, it makes you realize that you are traveling deeper into the interior of Nansatsu.

Stone wall. Although the name is reminiscent of Ishigaki Island in Okinawa, this is the stone wall in Satsuma. The platform, located quietly behind a small village, gives the illusion that time has stopped. The stone wall around the station tells the story of the origin of its name, quietly conveying the wisdom of the way of life that our ancestors built in this harsh natural environment. The scenery seen through the train window is like a plain but tasteful painting. A landscape of masonry that has remained unchanged since the Showa era and the latest diesel trains. In this contrast, I can't help but feel the accumulation of time that has been brought to us by railways.

Mizunari River. Contrary to its name, which suggests that you can hear the sound of a river, the station is located on the border of a quiet forest and fields. In the past, people carrying baskets on their backs may have walked back and forth along the path that led from here to the sea. I can't help but feel the strong vitality of railways, as this narrow path carved out by the Showa era railways continues to exist, albeit slowly but powerfully, even today. The silence in front of the station is broken only by the sound of the engines of the diesel cars, which run several times a day. However, travelers feel a kind of sacredness in the fact that this sound is the only bond between this land and the outside world.

Ei Okawa. From near this station, the train will once again have a close view of the sea. The blue ocean that passes through the train window is the biggest treat for travelers. The station itself is quiet, but the scent of the area that once served as the gateway to Okawa's village, where many travelers came and went, still lingers in the air. The way the rusted rails shine in the setting sun seems to symbolize the history of this line itself. The sound of the ocean waves reaches the platform, and the scent of the ocean hits your nose. If you get off at this station and walk aimlessly down the road that leads to the coast, you will be able to experience the essence of travel, where solitude and freedom coexist, as sought after by the great writers of the Showa era.

Matsugaura. Beyond the pine trees lined up like a windbreak, the East China Sea stretches out. If you sit down on the bench on the platform, you can hear the sound of waves in the distance. It is a station filled with a poetic atmosphere that would make a Showa era poet want to stop by and take a quick stroke. Although the number of trains is limited, it is this inconvenience that makes the journey even more profound. In the past, people would have descended from this station to the sea, waiting for boats to return from fishing. Although it is now a quiet, unmanned station, the pleasant breeze blowing through it makes me feel that it will never change, no matter how many decades pass.

Satsuma salt shop. The station name reminds us of the fact that salt was once produced in this area. The area around the station today is a mix of quiet residential areas and fields, but I am moved by the fact that the memories of the industry of the past are still engraved in the place names of the area. The simple platform without a station building actually enhances the sense of unity with the surrounding scenery, making you feel as if you are part of the scenery. While waiting for the train to arrive, I suddenly looked down at my feet and saw a nameless flower plant firmly spreading its roots. Precisely because it is not a glamorous tourist destination, these casual moments at the station become deeply embedded in the memories of the trip.

Shirasawa. It is a station with a calm appearance that gives you the feeling that Makurazaki is finally approaching. In a terrain where mountains loom out into the sea, the railway skillfully threads its way through the gaps. As you stand on the platform, you can feel the sea breeze even stronger, as if to tell you that your journey is nearing its end. The footprints of the Showa era railroad workers are engraved on them, showing how they worked hard to protect the tracks in this harsh terrain. As I look at the quiet villages around the station, I can't help but think that here, too, there are many layers of quiet lives that have been lived alongside the railway. It's a short but intense moment of rest just before the final station.

Satsuma board. One station before Makurazaki, it is a station that can be said to be a prologue to the actual final destination. There is Kagoshima Fisheries High School nearby, and young people who aspired to become ``sea men'' probably roamed this station in the past. Perhaps it's because of its history that you can feel a youthful vigor mixed with the scent of the ocean. Once you pass this point, the line finally comes to a dead end, and you slip into the farthest corner of Makurazaki. The chimneys of seafood processing plants begin to appear from the train window, and the smell of bonito flakes begins to waft in the air, foreshadowing the end of the trip. As an introduction to this, this station plays a truly somber role.

Makurazaki. It is the terminal station of the Ibusuki Makurazaki Line, which runs from north to south of Japan. The bustle of its former location as a connecting point with the Nansatsu Railway is now a thing of the past, but there is a catharsis that is hard to put into words at that point where the line ends. The sound of the sea, the smell of bonito flakes, and the sense of accomplishment of having reached the end. The scene of the "end" that Showa travelers sought still exists here today. A new station building was built in the Heisei era, but the sense of travel that lingers behind it is reminiscent of the obsession with railways that has continued since the Taisho and Showa eras. The railway ends here, but the memories of the journey continue to expand endlessly from here. That is the true magic of the terminal station.

Goryokaku. This strategic point, where the Southern Hokkaido Isaribi Railway branches off from the Hakodate Main Line, is a vast site where freight trains connected to the Seikan Ferry once rested. Although it is a little far from Goryokaku, the historical site that the station name suggests, the heavy smell of iron from the locomotives standing within the station strongly reminds us that we are at the throat of the northern railroad. There was once a time when the area was lined with brick engine sheds and the soot from steam locomotives covered the sky, but now modern electric locomotives are quietly waiting for their turn. Standing on the passenger platform, the rhythm of the long freight trains slowly passing by feels like the pulse of logistics that has continued since the Showa era. This station is not just a transit point, but a microcosm of the transportation history that the city of Hakodate has carried, engraved on the rails.

Nanaehama. This station is the first station that greets you as you pass through the city of Hakodate and the train begins to run, echoing the sound of the Tsugaru Strait. When you step onto the platform, your nose is mixed with the sea breeze and the dry smell typical of an industrial area tickles your nose, which can be said to be proof that a cement factory and lumber-related facilities were once rooted in this area. Hakodate Bay stretches out right next to the station, and you can see the gentle silhouette of Mt. Hakodate in the distance. The sight of a large ferry still gliding slowly through the sea, tracing the wake of the old Seikan ferry that disappeared into the waves, evokes a quiet emotion in the hearts of travelers. Even now, with the development of residential land and the scenery of people commuting to work and school on a daily basis, this station, which is close to the water's edge, still retains the atmosphere of a northern town that has lived alongside the sea.

Higashikunebetsu. This station, which seems to be placed alone in a vast plain, has a waiting room that is converted into a freight car and is known as the so-called ``Daruma Station.'' It is a great accent that invites the traveler's feelings. This place, which has a history of once being a signal station and later upgraded to a passenger station, gives you a sense of the original simplicity of a railway without excessive decorations. The surrounding area is a mix of idyllic countryside and residential areas, with railroad tracks running straight through the land to the north. Every time the train door opens, only the sound of the railroad crossing alarm echoes in the silent air. The inorganic yet warm landscape seems to retain traces of the period of high economic growth. The sight of a diesel car driving away with the roar of its engine, carrying fragments of everyday life, is a sight that epitomizes the real pleasure of local private railways.

Kunebetsu. This station is home to an ancient village, and its two-sided, two-track platform plays the role of train exchange, giving it a sense of stability that is closely connected to local life. The area around the station was once plagued by flooding from the Ono River, but thanks to the efforts of our predecessors, it has a history of being transformed into a prosperous living area. Although the wooden station building has long since disappeared and been replaced with a concrete station building, standing at the edge of the platform and looking out at the mountains in the distance, you will be reminded of the same harsh nature and living side by side ever since the city was first developed. The momentary encounter between an outbound train and an upbound train is not just a process on the timetable, but also a moment when the flow of time intersects for the people living in this area. This station quietly offers the luxury of being away from the hustle and bustle of the city and just listening to the sound of the railway.

Kiyokawa mouth. This station, which is the entrance to the center of Hokuto City, is also the closest station to the city hall, so it has a somewhat neat and calm appearance. As the name of the station suggests, the area was once moistened by the flow of pure water, and from the platform you can feel the crisp air of the northern country. Although it is located in a residential area, the scenery behind the station still has plenty of space, and the deep view typical of Hokkaido pleases the eyes of travelers. When we think of the dream traces of the Kamiiso Express Electric Railway Project, we can't help but feel the changes of the times when we see the leisurely arrival and departure of single trains today, but it can also be said to be part of the honest history of railways. The sight of local students walking down the platform with familiar steps confirms that this station is still beating steadily as the heart of the region.

Kamiiso. When talking about this station, it is impossible to avoid passing by the huge factory complex of Nippon Cement, now Taiheiyo Cement, which has an overwhelming presence from the train window. In the past, there were many dedicated lines leading to factories, and freight cars carrying limestone were constantly coming and going at this station, making it a symbol of the industrial town of Kamiiso. The long conveyor belt pier that juts out into the sea boasts a majestic appearance that gives it an exotic feel, and can be said to be a valuable heritage that conveys the enthusiasm of the Showa era, which was filled with industrialization. Once you get off at the passenger platform, the wind from the sea blows through the huge factory buildings, and the texture of the steel and concrete deepens the atmosphere of your trip. Even though the former boom has changed, the unique atmosphere where the strength of heavy industry coexists with the tranquility of the northern sea still leaves a deep impression on visitors.

Moheji. Located at the western end of Hakodate Bay, at the mouth of the Moheji River, this station has been watching over a quiet village with a hidden history of the Ainu Kotan for many years. When you stand on the platform, the scent of the ocean and the sound of the murmuring of the river mix together, making you realize once again the richness of the northern land. In the past, you could see the Seikan ferry crossing the sea in the distance, and the railway played an important role in logistics, but now it is also known as the place where the blue passenger train ``Hokutosei'' quietly spends the rest of its life. The sight of these sleeper passenger cars, which still convey the glory of the past, deeply moves the hearts of not only railway fans but also those who know about the journeys of the Showa era. The windbreaks surrounding the station block the wind and give the station a warm, sunny feel, giving you a sense of the accumulation of time that you would never miss on a hurried journey.

Oshima Tobetsu. The first thing that catches your eye when you get off the train is a beautiful tree-lined avenue that leads up a gentle slope to a Trappist monastery. A time of quiet prayer has been flowing in this area since long before the railway opened, and the station itself seems to be part of that sacred atmosphere. The unique scenery that combines the Western atmosphere of the red-brick monastery with the northern fishing village, which can be called the original landscape of Japan, gently and deeply stimulates the eyes of travelers. In the past, many dairy products were shipped from this station, and the railway has a history of supporting local life and industry. I'm sure I'm not the only one who gets the illusion that the wind blowing through the platform carries the scent of a distant, exotic land. This place, where faith, life, and railways harmonize in exquisite balance, is a precious sanctuary where you can forget the hustle and bustle of the Reiwa era.

Kamaya. This station is nestled in a narrow area where the sea and mountains meet, giving it an atmosphere that can be described as a ``fishing village station.'' The Tsugaru Strait stretches out right in front of the platform, and in winter, it feels so realistic that you can almost feel the spray of the rough waves reaching you. There was probably a time when the area around the station was filled with the scent of dried herring and kelp, but now only the sound of crashing waves and the roar of diesel engines resonate quietly. The station building, which maintains its dignified appearance even when exposed to the sea breeze, seems to symbolize the strength of the people who live here. Even if you are not a railway photographer, the beautiful curves of the railway line that draw a large arc along the sea will take your breath away. The luxury of not having anything is certainly alive at this small station.

Izumisawa. This station is located where trains traveling along the southern Hokkaido coastline take a short break inland. There was a time when water was supplied to steam locomotives, and it was an important transportation hub that literally served as a ``spring''. Nowadays, that bustle is a thing of the distant past, and it functions as a calm station surrounded by quiet residential areas and lush greenery, but the ruins of its spacious grounds are still a reminder of the prosperity of the past. The structure of the station building and the layout of the platforms retain the simplicity and robustness that has remained unchanged since the Showa era Japanese National Railways era, giving visitors a strange sense of security. As a railway travel writer, the moment when a train's headlights approach from afar and illuminate the quiet platform at dusk is one of the most exciting scenes. This station, which has a humble yet solid history, is home to a northern drama that should be passed down.

Fudakarari. The sound of ``sak-kari'' in the station's name reminds us of the expanse of wetlands and grasslands of the past, but today's train windows offer a rich landscape of alternating views of the calm ocean and mountains. With a rich forest looming behind the station and the Tsugaru Strait spreading out in front of it, it is in a luxurious location where you can enjoy both the mountains and the sea at the same time. In the spring, flowers blooming along the railroad tracks delight the eyes of travelers, and in the winter, a blanket of silver covers everything. This small station has been silently watching over the changing seasons for many years. The liveliness of this area, which once flourished as a fishing hub and a lumber shipping port, has now been sublimated into a quiet daily life. If you stand on the platform and look out into the distance at the Shimokita Peninsula on the other side, you will be reminded of just how far away you are in the far north.This is a station suitable for contemplation.

Kikonai. This station, which was once a branch of the Matsumae Line and has now been renovated as a stop for the Hokkaido Shinkansen, is truly a ``door'' in the history of southern Hokkaido's railways. The vestiges of the once lively wooden station building have been hidden beneath the modern elevated station building, but the remains of the old railway lines that still remain in every corner of the station and the many intricate points that tell the story of this once being a railway town. Along with the ``Kanchu Misogi'' festival held every year, this station has received the enthusiasm of people overcoming the harsh winter. The way the sharp acceleration sound of the Shinkansen intersects with the peaceful engine sound of the Isaribi Railway is really interesting, as if we are looking at the fault lines of the times. Standing at this station in Kikonai, where the sadness of a terminal station and the vibrancy of a transit point coexist in a strange way, one can feel that the wishes of the people who have been connected by the railway are still flowing.

Tsugaru Goshogawara. Although it is a connection point with the JR Gono Line, as soon as you cross the overpass, you are transported to the unmistakable Tsugaru Railway. This place used to be full of life and was filled with timber from the Tsugaru Forest Railway, one of Japan's three major forest railways, but now it has the feel of a quiet starting station where the sooty scent of the stove trains heralds the arrival of winter. The texture of old buildings and well-worn wood at ticket gates conveys the forgotten weight of railways in today's era of rushing for efficiency. As travelers wait for the train to depart, the faint smell of heavy oil mixed with the blowing wind drives travelers north.

Togawa. It is at this stop that the train passes through the city of Goshogawara and stops to take a deep breath. The former Togawa Station has a history of changing its location due to river improvements, but the current simple single platform gives off a sense of desolation that makes the vastness of the Tsugaru Plain stand out. Although it is surrounded by residential buildings, the summer grass that grows along the railroad tracks and the blizzard of snow in winter tell us that this area is unmistakably part of the original landscape of Tsugaru. It is a station with a mysterious appearance that makes you feel like you are being taken somewhere far away, even though it is in your daily life.

In front of the five agricultural schools. As the name suggests, this station is located at the edge of the vast campus of Aomori Prefectural Goshogawara Agriculture and Forestry High School, and is a place where the vibrancy of young people and the tranquility of the northern country coexist. The windbreak line of pine trees that crosses the train window is like a shield that protects the school building and fields from the harsh nature of Tsugaru, and the laughter of students echoing on the platforms after school also blends in with the sounds of the season on this railway. This small station, where young people who will be responsible for the future of agriculture get on and off, is more than just a route to school; it feels like it embodies the pride of people who live with the soil.

Tsugaru rice cake. It is reminiscent of the bygone days when freight sidings were spread out and it flourished as a hub for transporting lumber from the Iizume Forest Railway. Although it is now an unmanned station, the station building, which has been maintained by local volunteers, and the exhibits in the museum attached to it, convey the enthusiasm of the days when the railway was the pride of the region. If you look at the remains of the old rails and switches that remain in the spacious grounds, you can see the afterimage of the days when steam locomotives were panting and replacing freight cars. When you get off at this station, which seems to be placed alone in the middle of a plain, the accumulation of Tsugaru's history quietly approaches your heart.

Bishamon. Surrounded by windbreaks of deep pine trees, this station is one of the most isolated and beautiful stations on the Tsugaru Railway. There are very few houses around, and all you can hear is the sound of the wind rustling through the trees and the voices of birds chirping in the distance, but this feeling of solitude is what makes traveling so rewarding. There is a history in which firewood and other materials cut from the nearby mountains were once loaded onto the platform, and even in the now quiet corner of the platform, it feels as if memories of the past labor have been deposited there. The comfort of the moment of silence after the train leaves is a luxury that cannot be replaced by anything else.

Kase. The old wooden station building gives us a sense of its strength, having withstood Tsugaru's harsh winters. The tranquil atmosphere that the station itself gives off is so unwavering that the memories of painted trains that were once all the rage are now just one chapter in the station's long history. When you stand on the platform and look out at the horizon, the wind that shakes the rice ears and the snow that whitens everything in winter speak volumes about the unchanging life of this place. I can't help but think that the way they are firmly rooted in the earth, even though they are at the mercy of the changes of the times, truly symbolizes the way of life of the people of Tsugaru.

Kaneki. This town, where Dazai Osamu's birthplace ``Shayokan'' is located, is a key operational hub for the Tsugaru Railway, and still exudes pride as a ``town of writers.'' The stately townscape that tells of the prosperity of wealthy farmers and merchants of the past has the power to transport travelers who step off the station back to the Showa era or even older times. When you get off the platform waiting to change trains, the tension of the time when tablets were handed over mixes with the peaceful atmosphere that envelops you, creating a unique sense of travel. After passing this station, the train finally enters the depths of the Tsugaru Peninsula. It is a station that exudes a dignified dignity that encourages this kind of determination.

Ashino Park. The rows of cherry blossom trees that extend their branches to cover the railroad tracks give the area the appearance of a ``railway tunnel'' in spring. In a corner of this park, where the young Osamu Dazai would have walked with friends or lost in thought, stands a coffee shop in an old station building, and the memories of thousands of travelers are etched into each of its sooty walls and well-worn pillars. The scenery loved by the writers of the Showa era is still alive today, either through the train windows or in the snowflakes falling on the platforms. This is a miraculous ``stagnation'' in today's era of rushing towards efficiency, and it provides travelers with a sense of supreme comfort.

Kawakura. This small station, which seems to be tucked away in the middle of a vast countryside, also serves as a gateway for visitors to the nearby Kawakura Jizo statue. The tranquil atmosphere of the Jizo statue, which is reminiscent of Sai no Kawahara, gives off a sense of solitude, as if the wind carries it all the way to this platform. I can't help but think that the sight of the windbreak pine trees that surround it, watching over the railroad tracks while blocking the harsh Tsugaru snowstorms, embodies the spirit of patience unique to northern Japan. Because it's an empty station, you can listen to the faint sounds of the changing seasons. Such a luxurious time is flowing at this station.

Inside Osawa. This station, located on the banks of a reservoir, has a particularly simple appearance among the Tsugaru Railway. In the past, timber and agricultural products were shipped from this area, and freight cars would have frequently come and gone, but traces of history can be felt in the slight ups and downs on the side of the tracks and in the now quiet space around the station. The humble yet powerful life of the village that spreads out in front of the station is connected to the outside world through a single thread: the railway. This fact makes us realize once again the importance of the historical role that local railways have played. This station tells us about the fundamental tranquility of the land, which you cannot understand just by passing by.

Fukagoda. Surrounded by copses and gentle hills, this station is filled with tranquility and is worthy of being called ``the northernmost stop.'' While the national highway passes nearby and modern logistics are moving rapidly, this station is the only station that quietly continues to protect the railway, as if time has stopped moving. Standing on a simple concrete platform and listening to the sound of a train's engine moving away, you become acutely aware of how far away the hustle and bustle of everyday life is. The simple questions of why the station is here disappear in front of this overwhelming feeling of loneliness. However, just the fact that the railway is there makes me feel like it's enough.

Tsugaru Nakazato. The title of Japan's northernmost private railway terminal has a somewhat lonely yet proud ring to it. When you look at the stop at the dead end, you realize that this is the end of the railway, and at the same time, the beginning of a journey on foot that will take you deeper into the Tsugaru Peninsula. The human-powered turntable and the spacious grounds create a sense of fatigue and relief that is typical of a "terminal station." It can be said that this is a time of rest that both the train and the travelers can equally enjoy after a long journey. The smell of boiled food wafting through the station building and the quiet conversations of local people. All of these things make the end of the journey sweet and a little sad. Beyond this point, there are no more rails. This purity is deeply engraved in the hearts of travelers.

Takasu. When a traveler crosses the overpass from the platform of the Ou Main Line and heads towards the small ticket gate of the Akita Nairiku Jukan Railway, he or she feels as if he or she is crossing a certain border. This station was once the starting point of the Aniai Line and was a busy distribution center for Akita cedars cut from the mountains, and even today it still has a sense of pride as the gateway to northern Akita. The juxtaposition of JR's heavy rails and the Nairiku Line's slender rails quietly tells of the changes of the times. The nostalgic smell of the city floating around the station building and the idling sound of diesel trains waiting for departure. Mixing these together, it feels like a prelude to the rugged yet beautiful mountain route that is about to begin. When you look at the large timetable, this station gives you the illusion that the memory of the smoke that steam locomotives once spewed out lingers in your mind.

West Takasu. Just a few minutes from Takasu, the starting point, this station stands quietly on the edge of the city, and has the feel of being the first gateway to a hidden village, escaping the hustle and bustle of the city. Although it has a simple structure with a single platform, the way the railway line blends closely with the surrounding residential area reminds us that railways are the bloodline of our lives. From the train window, you can see the peaceful houses of Kita-Akita, and the everyday scenery of students commuting to school and people returning from shopping appears to the traveler as an extremely luxurious and ``extraordinary'' experience. Although there are no flashy tourist facilities, it is precisely in these ordinary small stations that the weight of the railroad's history is felt. As the train slowly picks up speed and passes between houses on its way to the next station, I gradually feel the realization that the real inland journey is about to begin.

Jomon Ogada. The reason why this station, which was once called ``Ogada,'' has been given a new look and a long history is because of the existence of the Isedotai Ruins lying nearby. When you land on the platform, you will feel that the sky that the Jomon people looked up at 10,000 years ago is still as high and expansive as ever. Vast fields spread out around the station, and during the season, beautiful rice field art delights the eyes of travelers, but at the root of this is the work of people who have lived in harmony with the soil. The contrasting existence of the modern railway system and ancient ruins maintains a strange harmony here. It's a space that gives you a sense of the accumulation of history, and it's a shame to overlook it as just a transit point, and it's strange because the regular joint sounds made by the rails sound vaguely like an ancient heartbeat.

Ohnodai. As its name suggests, this station is located on a spacious plateau and has a somewhat proud vantage point overlooking the surrounding industrial parks and vast farmlands. The area around the station is neatly divided, and you can feel the history of development and industry, but once you step onto the platform, you will find that the silence of the original Tohoku landscape reigns. The pride of the railway, which has quietly watched over the development of this region since the days of the Anigo Line, shows us the luxury of nothing. In the afternoon, the only sounds are the wind blowing across the plateau and the rustling of grass. When I'm waiting for a train, I feel like I'm being reminded of the pointlessness of rushing to my destination. In today's world where efficiency is so important, a few minutes spent at a station like this is an irreplaceable mental respite.

Aikawa. This station, located in the center of the former Aikawa town, has a dignified appearance that conveys the memories of a town that once flourished in the plywood industry. The structure of the station building and the size of the platform retain the vestiges of the vibrancy of the past, reminding us of the history of the station, where many workers and daily necessities once passed through it. Although it now has a calm appearance, the pride that it has had with the railway is still alive in the townscape that spreads out in front of the station. When trains on the up and down lines exchange trains, there is a brief signal exchanged with the driver of the oncoming train, and a calm atmosphere on the platform. All of these are proof that this station has functioned as the core of the local community for many years. Even though the smell of wood has disappeared and times have changed, the dignity of this station as the ``face of the town'' does not seem to have wavered in the slightest.

Uesugi. Some travelers may see this station name and think that it is a place related to Uesugi Kenshin, but this place is actually located in the heart of Akita's mountains, in a quiet village in what was once Aikawa-cho. The platform is surrounded by rural scenery as far as the eye can see, and the only sound that can be heard is the sound of ears of rice swaying in the wind, making it a true example of the original scenery of northern Akita. The waiting room, located on a single platform, has a sturdy structure that is a testament to the harshness of winter, and gives you a sense of the harshness and strength of the railway that runs through the north. In today's world, where many things are being lost due to the wave of efficiency, getting off at this station provides a luxurious moment that feels like turning back the clock a little bit. As the train moves away, silence once again envelopes the area, with only the wind blowing through. I can't help but think that the essence of train travel lies in its pure simplicity.

Yoneuchizawa. This station was once the gateway to Moriyoshi Town, and has served as a key logistics and transportation hub for the area since the days of the Anigo Line. In the past, wood was cut from here along the Anigawa River and loaded into freight cars and transported all over the country...I feel that the hustle and bustle of those days is still ingrained in every corner of the station building. As you walk in front of the station, you'll find buildings that still retain the character of a former post town and timber distribution area, quietly telling you about the rise and fall of this area. Nowadays, its role has changed, and it now resembles a quiet small station in a rural area, but the stately appearance of the station building clearly shows the vestiges of a time when railways were the "pride" of the region. The view of the mountain ridgeline from the platform is as beautiful as ever, and travelers who visit this area are welcomed into the deep embrace of northern Akita.

Katsurase. As the train heads deep into the mountains along the meandering Ani River, this station quietly appears. Surrounded by steep mountains, the murmur of the Anigawa River can be heard right next to the platform, giving you the real thrill of riding a mountain route. There was once a mine nearby, and the lights of daily life were much brighter than they are now, but it's strange that the current tranquility seems to be the most appropriate décor for this station. When you stand on a simple platform and take a deep breath of the cool air, you feel a sense of comfort as if your spirit, worn out by the city, is purified. Railways and stations just continue to exist silently, as if refusing to become flashy tourist destinations. His brutal sincerity deeply penetrates the hearts of the travelers, and when the train starts moving again, they feel a sense of regret.

Animaeda Onsen. It is truly a beloved ``Yunoyado Station,'' with the word hot spring in the station name and a hot spring facility attached to the station building itself. The reason why this station, which was once called Animaeda, was reborn with a hot spring facility was due to the passionate desire to revitalize the region with the railway at its core. When you arrive at the platform, you will feel the faint scent of hot spring water, and you will be tempted to relieve the fatigue of your journey. The way stations are not just ``passing points'' but ``destinations'' where people gather and talk seems to be an ideal example of what modern railways should be. If you look out the window after taking a bath, you will see Mt. Moriyoshi bathed in the sunset light, and evening smoke rising from the chimneys of the houses...such a casual, but extremely valuable scene of Japan still exists at this station.

Maeda Minami. This station, located in the middle of a gentle curve, is known for being the model for an animated movie in recent years. However, unrelated to such temporary trends, this station has been integrated into the local culture since ancient times. A simple wooden waiting room, a platform that slopes along a curve, and surrounding areas are dense forests and fields. The composition they create has a somewhat sad, yet warm feeling of nostalgia in the traveler's mind. The sight of young people visiting the area as a sacred place for movies is one aspect of modern times, but in essence, it is a pure place where people can just quietly wait for the train and greet their loved ones. When the rails glow dimly and we hear the sound of diesel engine engines in the distance, we are overwhelmed by the indescribable lyricism of this small station.

Obuchi. Just as we passed Maeda Minami and the flow of the Anigawa River began to reflect the colors of the mountains, this station appeared, modestly nestled next to the railroad tracks. Surrounded by mountains, at first glance it appears to be just a small station in the mountains, but once you get off the platform and listen closely, you realize that you are surrounded by pure silence, dominated only by the sound of the murmur of the river and the sound of the wind. How did our ancestors, who pioneered this land in the past, long for a railway in this harsh natural environment? If we think about the lines of history, even platforms that are just concrete slabs begin to take on an indescribable weight. To ears accustomed to the hustle and bustle of the city, even the occasional chirping of birds echoes like a fragment of the eternity of time that this station has carved out. After the train leaves, all that is left on the platform is a refreshing atmosphere and a quiet sense of anticipation for the next journey.

Aniai. When you get off at this station, which can be called the heart of the Akita Nairiku Jukan Railway, the smell of oil and the creaking of iron eloquently tell you that this is not just a transit point. This region has always been filled with the excitement of industry, ever since the days when it flourished with the Ani Copper Mine and boasted the highest output in the East. Even today, the train depot is located there, and the sight of diesel cars waiting in the inspection and repair depot gives a sense of the pride of this line. The triangular roof of the station building soars as if to pierce the sky, giving the illusion that memories of the soot emitted by steam locomotives are still lurking somewhere in the shadows of the building. In the rows of houses surrounding the station, there is a hint of the pride of the past as a prosperous mining town, and here travelers will experience the ``middle end'' of the long story of traversing the inland. It is an important base station, where you can't help but feel a deep respect for the lives of the people this railway has connected, while being drawn in by the scent of horsemeat stew.

Arase. When the train starts running again with the bustle of Aniai in the background, it soon arrives at this simple station. As the name of the station suggests, the Ani River that flows right next to the station has rough rapids that chew through the rocks, and the harshness of the terrain is what gives the station its character. In the past, a lot of wood was shipped from this area, but now there is a railway line that protects the village in the mountains. The mountain surface that looms behind the platform changes its color dramatically with each season, and from the budding of spring to the harsh white of winter, travelers are mercilessly exposed to the changing seasons of the northern country. When we step off at a station like this and watch the taillights of the train depart, we simultaneously feel the smallness of our own existence and the depth of the earth's embrace of accepting it. Although there aren't any flashy tourist attractions, the rhythm of the rail joints is the only thing that controls time in this area... There's no better place to experience such luxurious solitude.

text_en: Kayakusa. For those whose hobby is railway photography, the name of this station has a special resonance. The sight of the train crossing the Omata River Bridge immediately after leaving the station has become an essential ``face'' on posters and postcards for this line. However, the station itself has an extremely tranquil appearance, and this contrast evokes a sense of travel. The beauty of the valley seen from the bridge feels like the handiwork of God, but the foundation that supports this gigantic structure lies in the everyday life that this small station protects. When the leaves turn red, the surrounding mountains turn a fiery vermilion, and when combined with the red of the iron bridge, it creates a world of rich colors that is out of this world. A heavy yet somehow light metallic sound when a train crosses a railway bridge. The moment we hear it echoing through the valley and being sucked into the mountains, we are convinced that this railway is completely integrated into nature.

lol inside. The name of this mysterious station, which you will never forget once you hear it, is said to be derived from the Ainu word for ``nai'' (river), which literally means ``laughing inside,'' which makes travelers' jaws drop. However, when you actually get off at the station, what you find there is not so much laughter, but a solemn silence nestled in the deep forest. In the past, there may have been more lights of people's lives in this area, but now there is a silent confrontation between the life force of nature trying to return to the mountains and the single railway that holds it back. The Nemagari bamboo grown around this station must have been the joy of spring for the people of northern Japan, who had survived the harsh winter. The brightness of the station name and the harsh surrounding scenery. When we place ourselves in this exquisite balance, a calm calm comes to our hearts. It is a station with a mysterious magnetic field that makes you feel like you don't care about the trivial things in life when you just stare blankly at the trees on the opposite bank while waiting for your train.

Iwanome. This station appears quietly as the train passes the base station of Aniai and sinks deeper into the mountains and rivers. Surrounded by steep mountains, cedar trees are planted neatly on the slopes, perhaps a remnant of a former lumber export hub, and the pride of forestry, which was Kitaakita's core industry, can still be seen today. When you stand on the platform, all you can hear is the sound of the wind rustling the branches and leaves, and the sound of the Anigawa River chewing on the rocks in the distance. The single platforms with no special decorations are proof that the railway is not a luxury item, but rather serves as a means of transportation for the people living in this area. For someone who is used to the over-the-top services of the city, this stripped-down simplicity can be refreshing. When you listen to the sound of the track joints cooling in the silence after the diesel cars leave, it is a station that makes you feel as if the weight of the years that this railway has carved out is slowly approaching your heart.

Hitachiuchi. For those who know about the era when it was the last terminus of the former Japanese National Railways Aniai Line, this station holds a special feeling. In the 1950s, when the railroad suddenly ended here, there was an unexplored virgin forest that continued from here. Around the station, there are remains of a former lumberyard and a townscape that tells of the vibrant forestry industry of yesteryear, which tells us of the heavy mission that the mountain railway had. The magnificent view of the Hitachi Uchikawa Bridge that can be seen as soon as you exit the station is a silent reminder of just how difficult the construction of this line was. Although it is now one of the transit stations, it still retains its character as a ``terminal station'' and has a somewhat desolate feel, which may be due to the pride that this area has had in maintaining its ``end of the world'' status for a long time. If you look up at the sky from the platform, the soot and smoke spewed out by the steam locomotives of the past can still be seen floating in the air, giving you the illusion of a multilayered history.

Okuani. When you land in this sparsely populated area, there is a deep silence that seems to have rejected the sounds of civilization. As the name of the station suggests, it has a sense of secluded area worthy of being called Ani's ``inner parlor'', and the branches and leaves of the trees that approach right next to the platform invite travelers into the abyss of deep greenery. Immediately ahead, the Junisho Tunnel, the longest in Akita Prefecture, awaits with its pitch-black mouth open, and this station is filled with the tension of being the ``starting point of a mountain pass,'' so to speak. How much sweat did it take to climb this steep mountain? When we think about the hardships of our predecessors, the sound of a modern diesel car gently climbing up a hill somehow sounds like a prayer. There are no vending machines or fancy signs here. However, there is a luxurious space where you can confront the rails, the mountains, and yourself. The few minutes we spend at this station quietly teaches us the richness of the act of "waiting," which busy modern people have forgotten.

Ani Matagi. Just hearing the name brings to mind a train traveler's mind the solitary image of the ``hunters'' living in the steep, snowy mountains. This station, which was created when the entire line was opened to traffic between Hitachinai and Matsuba, is located in a place that can be called the highlight of the Inland Railway. The station building is a warm wooden structure reminiscent of a mountain hut, and has an atmosphere that gently conveys the ancient spirit of Matagi to modern travelers. There are also spas such as Uchito Onsen in the surrounding area, and you can feel that the culture of this area, which is tied to mountain worship, is still alive in the lives of the people. What spreads out outside the window is no longer the scenery of a village, but the wild beauty of nature itself, and it is easy to see how the railway is being modestly routed through the bosom of nature. The sound of the train passing over the mountains and through the deep valleys echoes the prayers that the Matagi once offered to the mountain gods, and it enhances the feeling of traveling.

Tozawa. When we finally reach the place where the light shines through the long darkness of the Twelve Tunnels, which is more than five kilometers long, there is a tranquil atmosphere that is somehow different from the Ani Valley we had seen earlier. This is truly the ``watershed'' of the Akita Nairiku Jukan Railway, and it is a place that makes you feel a major turning point in the journey from north to south. The platform, which is quietly placed in the mountains, has a warm atmosphere that kindly accepts the diesel cars that come over the mountain pass and gives them a moment of respite. The rustic appearance of the mining railways of the past has faded, and in its place, travelers are now greeted by the gentle expression of a mountain village that coexists with the harsh nature. Nameless flowers blooming next to the railroad tracks and the sound of deer singing in the distance. All of them seem to be enjoying the joy of being connected to each other by overcoming the barrier of this railway. Even as I feel the elegant atmosphere of Kakunodate, my destination, slowly approaching, I am convinced that the cool air I can enjoy at this mountain pass station is the real thrill of the trip.

Kamihinokiuchi. When many people hear the name of this station, they may think of giant paper balloons flying up into the winter night sky. However, when there is no hustle and bustle of festivals, this station is simply enveloped in the silence of the deep mountains, facing the harsh nature of northern Akita. In the past, when the JNR Kakunodate Line used to terminate here, the railway was stopped because a steep mountain pass blocked its path. If you look around from the platform, you will see that steep mountains approach from all sides, and that the railway line is nestled in a small area of ​​flat land carved out by humans. When you step off at this station, you can feel that the earnest desire that the pioneers of the past had, to cross the mountains and connect with the outside world, is still alive in the light of the rails. Although it doesn't have flashy tourist facilities, it is a truly dignified station where you can feel the faith rooted in the land and the pride of the people who protect it, along with the cool air.

Left street. It is a station that has the feel of a hidden village, where even if you unfold the map, it will take some time to confirm its location. The simple structure of a single platform eliminates unnecessary decorations and simply emphasizes the fact that the railway is there. From time to time, the dense forest that surrounds the area gives off the feeling of a mountain spirit appearing, which pleasantly stimulates the traveler's sense of solitude. There are few people living here, and the only background music at this station is the chirping of birds and the sound of treetops swaying in the wind. I can't help but feel that the memories of the forest iron that once passed through this area and the lives of the people who lived with the mountains still linger in the air, along with the smell of the soil. Although it is a place without modern facilities, it is these small stations that teach us the luxury of ``nothing'' and allow us to experience the essence of the intellectual game that is train travel. The time you spend alone on the platform, listening to the sound of the train receding away, is a spiritual purification that nothing can replace.

Nakazato Ugo. This simple station appears as the train crosses mountains and passes through valleys, finally approaching the entrance to the Senboku Plain. The two characters ``Ugo'' in the station's name tell travelers that this is a signpost that leads to the heart of what was once Dewa Province. The waiting room, which is set in a rural setting, gives you a sense of the sincerity of waiting for passengers, whether it's a snowstorm or a blistering summer day. The gently sloping land surrounding the station and the private houses lined up neatly on it. All of these are the result of a life that has been based on the solid bloodline of railways. This station is located at a time when the scenery seen from the train window is changing from the steep mountainous terrain to the soft countryside. It is a station filled with a sense of relief, as the regular rhythm of the rail joints harmonizes with the color of the expanse of the sky, gently relieving the tension of the journey.

Pine needles. It was once the terminal station of the Japanese National Railways Kakunodate Line, and for a long time its name has been etched into timetables as the dead end of the ``Cecum Line.'' It also served as the western gateway to Lake Tazawa, and the bustle of the past, when tourists and local residents mixed together, can still be felt in one corner of the spacious grounds. Although it is now an intermediate station, the length of the platform and the space in front of the station convey the pride of a time when this place was the ``end of the world'' and the vestiges of the tenacity to aim beyond that point. Even now that the entire line has been opened and it has become a transit station, it is still a mysterious station that somehow retains the desolation characteristic of a "terminal station" and the weight of the history pioneered by the railway. Immediately after leaving the station, you can see the mountains that embrace Lake Tazawa across the countryside below, and you will be reminded once again of the great role that railways have played in this area. The joy of connecting at the end of a rail and the emotion of a lost terminal station. This station, which combines both of these aspects, is a microcosm of railway history.

text_en: Ugo Nagatoro. Although it is just a short distance from Kakunodate, the last stop, the area around this station is truly spectacular and stretches out into endless countryside. The rich blessings brought by the clear waters of the Hinokiuchi River have fertilized the soil of this area, and the railway has played a vital role in transporting these blessings. If you stand on the platform and look around, you will be able to see the wide unobstructed sky and the sea of ​​golden rice ears that will delight your eyes. Even though the smoke from the steam locomotives that once ran through this area has been replaced by the exhaust sound of today's diesel trains, it feels like the peaceful time that passes through this area has not wavered in the slightest. The combination of the horizontal horizon seen from the train window and the mountains in the distance suggests that this long inland journey is coming to an end, and gives us a sense of loneliness.
