text_en: 八津。 This small station appears just as the rugged mountains of Senboku finally recede into the background and you begin to see a calm expanse outside the train window. In spring, the cluster of Katakuri flowers spread out behind the station is covered with a purple carpet, and the sight of enjoying the late spring in the northern country is like a painting. This land, which was once opened as part of the National Railways Kakunodate Line, is still alive with the smell of earth and the lives of people who are sensitive to the changing seasons. Standing on the platform and feeling the wind caressing your cheeks, you will be reminded that the railway is not just a means of transportation, but a messenger of the seasons. As the sound of the train engine fades away and the silence returns, the ephemerality of a flower's life intersects with the eternity of the railway...One of the things unique to Yatsu Station is that you can indulge in such luxurious contemplation. Even if there is no flashy station building, the beauty of nature, which changes its appearance with each season, is the ultimate luxury.

Saimyoji Temple. Located in the center of the former Nishiki Village, this station, which, as its name suggests, gives you a sense of the history of the ancient temple, is also famous as the home of the local specialty, the Saimyoji Chestnut. The rich soil that nurtures these chestnuts, which are said to be the size of babies, extends far and wide around the station. The appearance of the station building has a sense of authenticity as a regional hub, and is reminiscent of the days when freight cars full of agricultural products used to travel through this area. When you step off the platform, the rich sunlight of the Senboku plains shines down on you, relaxing the hearts of travelers who have crossed the mountains. There is an aesthetics of down-to-earth life here that stands out from modern tourism, and through the device of railways, it quietly stirs the sensibilities of us travelers. The brilliance of the rails blends into the cityscape, and the atmosphere at this station is filled with proof that it has continued to support people's daily lives.

Ugoota. It is at this station that the train, which has passed through the steep mountainous region, finally reaches the heart of the Senboku Plain. It is surrounded by vast, unobstructed rice fields, and the mountains of Dewa can be seen through the haze in the distance, making it a truly original Japanese landscape. Although it has a simple structure with only one single platform, the spaciousness of the sky and the clear scenery set it apart from previous mountain stations. If you imagine steam locomotives in the past powerfully moving along tracks that ran straight through the plains, you can clearly see that railroads were the main artery that watered this rich land. When you stand on the platform during the season when the ears of rice shine golden, the breath of the earth and the coolness of the rails create a mysterious harmony that quietly tells you that the end of your journey is near. In today's world, where efficiency is paramount, the very fact that a station like this exists that allows you to monopolize the vastness of the sky feels like a miracle.

Kakunodate. The long journey of the 100km long Akita Nairiku Railway is finally reaching its grand conclusion. Once you arrive at the entrance to this town, known as ``Michinoku's Little Kyoto,'' the black walls of samurai residences and the elegant appearance of weeping cherry blossoms will transport you back to the Edo era. The modern platforms of the Shinkansen lined up with the somewhat modest platforms of the Nairiku line give a sense of the layers of the times. Once the starting point of the Kakunodate Line, this station is now the final stop for all lines, and there is a mixture of relief at the end of a journey and regret at leaving behind something that is hard to leave behind. Once you pass through the ticket gate and walk into the city, you will feel the dignity of history, and with the memories of the mountains connected by railways in your heart, you will take a new step. This station makes me feel that it is the perfect link between the harsh nature of northern Akita and the sophisticated culture of Senboku.

Nishiwakamatsu. It is a place where the Tadami Line and the Aizu Railway part, so to speak, a turning point of fate. The size of the premises, which was once bustling with the traffic of lumber and cargo, is a faint testimony to its former glory. Currently, it is located in a calm residential area on the west side of the castle town of Wakamatsu, but the beautiful curves of the two lines as they approach each other and then move away from each other encapsulate the travel spirit inherent in railways. Even though it has been reborn as a modern Hashigami station building, when you step onto the platform, you get the illusion that the memory of smoke that was once emitted by steam locomotives is wafting out from somewhere.

Minamiwakamatsu. This is a relatively new station, having opened in 1985, just before the Japanese National Railways was about to close its history. Industrial parks spread out in an orderly manner around the area, creating a landscape that symbolizes the modernization of the Aizu Basin. The simple structure with only one platform can be said to be a product of an era that pushed forward with rationalization, but the contrast with the single-track trains that run on it gives a sense of modern sadness. Even within the station's appearance, which emphasizes functionality, there is a sense of core strength that is unique to Tohoku stations that can withstand Aizu's harsh winters.

Kadota. The large site where trains were once exchanged is now stripped of the railroad tracks on one side, giving it a spacious and desolate feel. If we unravel the history of Kadota Village, from which the station's name originates, we will discover the rich climate that has supported rice cultivation in this area since ancient times. The rural scenery that stretches out from the train window changes its appearance with each season, delighting the eyes of travelers passing by. Although it now stands quietly as an unmanned station, the smell of the soil that once filled the area with the energy of loading agricultural products still seems to permeate every corner of the platform.

Amaya. As its origin, which began as a temporary boarding station, shows, it has a humble appearance, as if it had been forgotten in the middle of a rice field. The appearance of a single waiting room, too simple to be called a station building, is proof that railways are deeply ingrained in every detail of life. The silence that comes after the sound of the train engine fades away provides a luxurious time that you can never experience in the city. This station, where you can directly enjoy the breath of nature such as the sound of the wind rustling the rice ears and the chirping of birds in the distance, is the scenery that makes you feel the real pleasure of traveling on a railway.

Ashinomaki hot spring. In the past, it was called ``Kamimiyori'', a name typical of a small station in the mountains. Today, it is known throughout the country as the gateway to hot springs and as the station where the cat stationmaster works. Former railway equipment is carefully stored inside the station building, making it look like a small museum, which is a distasteful performance for railway fans. Although it is a little far from the hot spring town, I can't help but think that the ``frustration'' is what conveys the original emotion of hot spring travel in the Showa era to the present day. It is a station that at the same time brings the tension and anticipation of the journey into Oku-Aizu, with the mountains approaching.

Okawa Dam Park. The station's name was once called ``Funoko,'' but it has a history of being renamed with the appearance of a gigantic artifact. When you arrive at the platform, you can see the blue water of Lake Wakasato and the majesty of the dam that blocks it, bringing a modern tension to the quiet mountain setting. Its location, sandwiched between tunnels, shows how the railway struggled to overcome the rugged terrain. Although it has now been developed as a park and is a place of relaxation, it gives off a mysterious melancholy feeling, as if the memory of the old train line that once ran through the valley is quietly settling in the shadow of the concrete fortress-like structure.

Ashinomaki Onsen South. This station also had the strange fate of being moved to its current location, losing its former name of ``Kuwabara'' to the bottom of the lake due to the construction of the Okawa Dam. Occasionally, a breeze blows through from the platform set up high, as if it awakens memories of the village that lies beneath the surface of the lake. There are few people living in the surrounding area, and the silence between the mountains and the water reigns supreme, but its solitary appearance reveals the profile of a railway that has been washed away by the waves of modernization. At first glance, it appears to be a functionally oriented structure, but for travelers looking out at the changing windows of the train, it is a valuable stop that allows them to experience the abyss of Aizu's nature.

Yunokami Onsen. This station building, said to be the only one in Japan with a thatched roof, serves as a time machine that transports visitors back to the Edo period. As soon as you step into the waiting room, the smoke rising from the hearth lingers on the sooty ceiling, and a nostalgic scent tickles your nostrils. There is also a footbath next to the station building, and while waiting for the train, people are constantly chatting and relieving themselves from the fatigue of their journey, which is a sight unique to this station. Cherry blossoms in the spring, autumn leaves in the fall, and thatched roofs covered in snow in the winter perfectly embody the seasonal charm of Aizu. More than just a transportation hub, the station itself feels like a complete cultural heritage.

Tower of Hetsuri. The station takes its name from the scenic spot of strangely shaped rocks that have been carved out over a million years, and is a key tourist hub. Just as the word ``hetsuri'' means ``cliff'' in the Aizu dialect, you will be overwhelmed by the power of seeing the beauty of nature up close. The station itself is a simple single-sided platform tucked away in the woods, but the path that leads from there to the scenic spot is filled with a sense of anticipation as you head towards an unknown, spectacular view. It is crowded with people during the tourist season, but in the silence between the arrival and departure of trains, you can feel the eternal flow of the river carving into the rocks. It is a scene where the mystery of nature and the railway are in perfect harmony.

Yagoto. It's a station that gives you a sense of security, as if it's quietly protecting the daily life of Aizu, even though it's in between gorgeous tourist spots. It has a history of being a busy place for shipping stone and lumber produced in the area, and the surrounding villages are dotted with substantial houses. The scenery seen from the train window is that of a peaceful mountain village, and it makes us realize once again that the railway still functions as the artery of life in this region. There is no flashy production, but if you stand on the platform, the wind blowing down from the mountains behind will sway the plants and trees, giving travelers a moment of peace. I can't help but think that this is exactly what a local private railway station should be like.

Aizu Shimogo. It used to be called ``Narahara,'' an old-fashioned name with a somewhat earthy smell. It bears a heavy responsibility as the gateway to Shimogo Town, and the appearance of the station building has a corresponding dignity. When you get off the platform, you can see the deep mountain range of Aizu looming over the roofs of the houses surrounding the station. For railway enthusiasts, it's easy to imagine the bustle of the Showa era, when lumber and agricultural products were loaded onto freight cars and transported to the city. Although it now has the feel of a quiet local station, the clean air within the station building still strongly asserts that it is a nexus of Aizu's history and life. Even though it is equipped with modern facilities, time seems to move slowly at this station because it has not lost its essence as a ``stop''.

Hometown Park. This station was born during the turbulent era when the name of the era changed from Showa to Heisei, and in the midst of a new journey as a third sector railway. As the name suggests, there is a vast park right behind the station, and it is a popular place for residents to relax. Although the station structure itself is quite simple, the seasonal colors of the park that can be seen from the train window add color to the otherwise inorganic railway. This is a departure from the simple and sturdy station construction of the Japanese National Railways era, and is presenting a new type of station that is closely connected to the community. However, the tranquility of the surrounding area and the sound of the horn announcing the arrival of the train echoing through the mountains give you a sense of the travel experience that is unique to Aizu's railways. It is a masterpiece of a modern small station that is new, yet has a modesty that blends into the scenery.

Trout farm park. This station was also called ``Aizu Ochiai,'' which is a somewhat melancholy name during the JNR era. As the name of the station suggests, there is a rainbow trout farm nearby, and it is a reminder that the laughter of tourists could once be heard all the way to the platform. The area around the station is surrounded by dense forests, creating a different world from the hustle and bustle of the city. The luxurious time of sitting on a bench on the platform and simply waiting for the next train is the most relaxing thing for modern people. As the old name ``Ochiai'' suggests, it feels like the memories of the area as a place where roads and people intersect have melted into the quiet breeze. It is a truly atmospheric stop that combines the splendor of a sightseeing base with the solitude of a small station in the mountains.

Aizu Nagano. Travelers are slightly surprised to discover that there is another Nagano, not Nagano in Shinshu, but here in Aizu. The remains of the spacious compound are still visible, proving that it was once a prosperous place for loading and unloading cargo. Its vastness makes the current quiet situation stand out, and silently tells us the history of the rise and fall of railways. A calm village spreads out around the station, and you can feel the strong vitality of Aizu's farming villages. When you stand on the platform and look out over the railroad tracks, you can see the gentle curves of the railway, giving you hope for an endless journey. The simple, unadorned appearance of a station building can be said to be the true scenery that draws the pen of a railway travel writer.

name_en: In front of Tajima High School
text_en: In front of Tajima High School. As the name suggests, this station is used by young people on their way to school and is filled with lively voices in the mornings and evenings. This station, which opened at the end of the Showa era with the high expectations of the local people, continues to quietly watch over the students commuting to the school. Although the station structure is simple in pursuit of functionality, it still represents the original scenery of railways, which are closely connected to our daily lives. When I watch young people getting off the train, I feel like I'm suddenly reliving memories of the Showa era after school. For these people who spent their youth with railways, this small platform will become a stage that will remain in their memories for the rest of their lives. They are a valuable presence that continues to infuse the railway with the vitality of youth amidst the changing times.

Aizutajima. It is the political and economic center of Minamiaizu, and it is also the border between electrified and non-electrified sections, making it a key point for railway operations. From here to the north you can hear the sound of diesel engines, and to the south you can hear the sound of trains running smoothly. It is this contrast that makes this station such a special place. The station building has been reborn in a modern style, but once you step out into the city, you will find the tradition of the Aizu Tajima Gion Festival, one of the three major Gion festivals in Japan, still alive. I can't help but feel that the vestiges of those days, when steam locomotives would have refilled water and the engineers could take a breather, are still lurking somewhere in the hustle and bustle of the platform. It is the end of a journey and the starting point of a new journey. It is a perfect blend of the unique excitement of a terminal station and the calmness of a regional city.

Nakaarai. As the station next to Aizu Tajima, it is quietly located in a quiet countryside. The platform, located at the bottom of a basin surrounded by mountains, nestled in a sea of ​​golden rice ears, exudes the modesty of a small local private railway station. The contrast between the wide sky and the single railroad track is impressive, making you imagine that it was once more vibrant. The way the wind generated by the passing express train sways the flowers on the roadside is a perfect luxury for travelers away from the hustle and bustle of the city. Although there are no flashy tourist attractions, this is why the ``inherent tranquility of railways'', undisturbed by anything, continues to exist here.

Aizu Araumi. In the past, it was known as ``Araumi'', and as the name suggests, it was full of charm as a base for crossing the rough mountain. The memory of steam locomotives panting over steep mountain passes during the JNR era is still alive in the silence of the station. Although the structure of the station building has changed over time, the ridgeline of the surrounding mountains remains as majestic as ever since the days when our predecessors struggled to build the railway. In winter, the railways are covered with deep snow, making the harsh conditions even more obvious, but this is the true nature of Tohoku's and Aizu's railways. Although it has a rough name, it is a station that somehow feels inclusive and kindly accepts travelers.

Aizu Yamamura Dojo. This station was newly built at the end of the Showa era with the hope of revitalizing the region, and as its name suggests, it is a gateway to learning about mountain village life. Although the name of the station has an educational sound, the surrounding area is surrounded by an air of purity that makes you feel like your spine is stretching. When you arrive at the platform, the rustle of the trees and the chirping of birds will encourage you to have a dialogue with nature, something that modern people have almost forgotten. It embodies a new type of station that is closely connected to the local area, something that would have been unimaginable during the JNR era, and it has now become a familiar part of the landscape. Although it is not flashy, it is literally a ``dojo''-like station that provides visitors with a place for quiet contemplation.

Shichigatake trailhead. This station has long been familiar to mountain climbing enthusiasts as the starting point for climbing Mt. Shichigatake, a famous peak that boasts an altitude of 1,635 meters. It was once called "Itozawa" and has a history of watching over a quiet mountain village. Although the station's name has been changed, it now has a more touristy feel, but the atmosphere is still that of a small station surrounded by steep mountains. The sight of mountaineers carrying heavy backpacks landing on the platform reminds us that trains are not just a means of transportation, but a gateway to adventure. It is a unique station where a sense of exhilaration and solitude coexist, as the mountain breeze blows through the platform, inviting you to even greater heights beyond the tracks.

Aizu Plateau Ozeguchi. In the past, it was called ``Aizu Takinohara'' and was the terminal station of the Japanese National Railways Aizu Line, where the dead-end railway line attracted travelers. At that time, this was the end of the railroad, and from there the only way to go was by bus to further unexplored areas. Currently, it has an imposing presence as a contact point with the Noiwa Railway and a vast gateway to Oze. Limited express trains come and go frequently, and its former image as a terminal station in the middle of nowhere has faded, but the deep mountains that surround it still quietly tell us that this is Aizu's inner quarters. From the appearance of the station building, you can feel the weight of its history, which has evolved from what was once a dead-end line into a major artery connecting north and south.

Mito. It is a strategic point on the Joban Line, and is a station that still conveys its pride as a former castle town of the Mito Tokugawa family. Although there are only a few traces of the steam locomotives that used to hang out on the vast grounds, the moment the Kashima Rinkai Railway's diesel cars start rolling onto the modern elevated tracks, you can feel the hustle and bustle of the city suddenly receding. In contrast to the bustle of the north exit, the scene of the platform where the Mito Line, Suigun Line, and this Oarai-Kashima Line intersect has a heavy history of many layers of railways. The sound of the diesel car's engine, which heralds the start of a journey, echoes off the steel beams, giving it a special atmosphere.

East Mito. With the hustle and bustle of Mito in the background, it is a quiet station where the train waits at the top of a high elevated track. The surrounding area has long since changed its appearance from a rural area to a residential area, but as you stand on the concrete platform, you can feel the humid wind blowing through, which is typical of the area's proximity to the Naka River. The appearance of an unmanned station actually highlights the ``everyday life'' of this line and encourages travelers to take a moment to reflect. This casual stop, located in a place slightly removed from the logic of the city, plays the role of ``between the lines'' in a railway travelogue.

Tsunezumi. It is an elevated station that suddenly appears in the middle of a vast rural landscape as far as the eye can see. This location, close to the former center of Tsunezumi Village, makes you realize once again the vastness of the Kanto Plain. In the spring, the paddy fields reflect the sky like a mirror, and in the autumn, the golden rice ears ripple, providing the luxurious contradiction of viewing Japan's original landscape from a modern civil engineering structure. When you see people working in the fields in the distance, you are reminded that this railway functions as a blood vessel for the local community. Even the time spent waiting for the train on the windswept platform feels like becoming part of this vast landscape.

Oarai. It is the heart of this line, and is a lively station where the scent of saltwater and fish tickles travelers' nostrils. In the train depot next to the station building, vermilion diesel cars are resting, and even non-railway fans are captivated by their functional beauty. As a town in front of the ancient Oarai Isosaki Shrine, and as a port town with a modern ferry terminal, this station is a nexus where diverse cultures come together. When you suddenly come across an old woman returning from local shopping amidst the hustle and bustle of tourists, the ``smell of life'' that this station has gives you a deeper sense of travel.

Hinuma. This station, which suddenly appears as the train passes through a cut-through and a forest, is a place that symbolizes the tranquility of the waterside. The brackish water lake and swamp that spreads out below is a treasure trove of rich nature where small boats for fishing for redworm float and migratory birds can rest their wings. From the concrete platform, you can enjoy a picturesque view of the sparkling water and surrounding greenery. For travelers tired of the hustle and bustle of the city, getting off at this station and letting the breeze blow across the lake may be the ultimate luxury. Nature and man-made objects are in quiet harmony, creating the illusion that time has slowed down.

Asahi Kashima. This station, which was once the center of Asahi Village, stands like an isolated island in the sea of ​​vast melon fields that surround it. The view from the elevated platform gives you a sense of the strong agricultural life of Ibaraki, with the smell of earth wafting through the air. The station's somewhat rustic and straightforward structure, reminiscent of the days of freight trains pulled by steam locomotives, gives travelers a strange sense of security. This is a stop that makes you feel like you can't help but think about the history of pioneering as you gaze out the window at the flat land that stretches out while being swayed by modern diesel trains.

Tokujuku. This station, which suddenly appears after passing through a deep green cut-through, has the feel of a secret stop hidden in the forest. The surrounding area is dotted with old villages, and you can even get a glimpse of the storehouses and hedges from the train window that give you a sense of the accumulation of history. Even at the moment when a modern stainless steel car slides into the station, time passes by at this station, and it is enveloped in a mysterious silence, as if it is still a tranquil afternoon in the Showa era. Although there are signs of human habitation, the station itself gives a gentle feeling, as if it were being embraced by nature.

Shinhokota. It is an important base on this line, reminding us of the history of its connection with Kashima Railway, which once led to Hokota Station. When you get off the train in front of the station, you can feel the mixture of the commercial prosperity of the past and the vibrancy of an agricultural city that continues to this day. Although it is a modern concrete elevated station, the atmosphere in the waiting room seems to be steeped in the warmth of the words exchanged between travelers and locals. I can't help but think that its appearance still conveys the pride of the days when trains were not just a means of transportation, but functioned as the backbone of the city.

text_en: Lake Kitaura. As the name suggests, it is one of the most scenic stations on the line, with the calm waters of Kitaura spreading out across the train windows. When you stand on the elevated platform, the wind blows across the lake unobstructed, and you are enveloped in a tranquil atmosphere where you can even hear the flapping of waterfowl's wings. As I gaze at the lake's deep red surface at dusk, I am reminded that the real pleasure of traveling by train lies in quietly enjoying the subtle changes in scenery. The waterside scenery has the power to make people feel sentimental, which makes this simple station even more appealing.

Ocean. Although this station, named after the former Ocean Village, cannot directly see the rough waves of the Pacific Ocean, it has a sense of openness that befits the majestic sound of its name. The sight of a haze rising at the end of a straight line of track symbolizes that the railway is a path of hope that leads to an unknown land. The windbreak forest of pine trees dotted around the area carries the slightest hint of the sea breeze, giving you a renewed sense of exhilaration towards the end of your trip. The vast sky and the straight tracks that rival it - the scenery that can be said to be the origin of railways remains here.

Kashima Sea. Contrary to its grand name, the station itself is quite simple, but it is an elevated elevated station with a somewhat majestic presence. If you open the map, you should see the rough waves of the Pacific Ocean spreading out to the east, but the pine trees that serve as windbreaks block that view, and the area around the station is surrounded by a quiet rural landscape. It is also fun to stand on the platform and look for the smell of the sea breeze while feeling the presence of this ``invisible sea.'' The dry sound of diesel exhaust now shakes this plain in place of the smoke spewed out by steam locomotives, but this station teaches us that the essence of the ``solitude of travel'' carried by trains has not changed in the slightest since the Showa era.

Kashima Ohno. The well-organized station building and grounds testify to its pride as the center of Ono Village in the past. Surrounded by houses that make you feel the breath of daily life, you can once again realize that this railway is not just a sightseeing route, but is deeply rooted as a ``transit'' for the local people. The view from the elevated bridge symbolizes the richness of this land near the easternmost tip of the Kanto Plain, and the depth of the forest seen in the distance gives a sense of approaching Kashima, an ancient place of worship. Although it may not be particularly glamorous, the atmosphere at this station is filled with the sincerity of the railways that support our daily lives.

name_ja: 長者ヶ浜潮騒はまなす公園前
name_en: In front of Chojagahama Shiosai Hamanasu Park
text_en: In front of Chojagahama Shiosai Hamanasu Park. Station names that are so long that they cannot be read in one breath stand out in the timetable. However, when you actually get off the train, you will find yourself at a surprisingly quiet stop nestled in the lap of nature. The gap between the long modern name and the rustic appearance of the home creates a strange sense of humor in the hearts of travelers. The observation tower of the park from which the station takes its name rises in the distance, and beyond that you can probably hear the sound of the waves of the Kashima Sea. The luxury of a railway journey, where one can simply listen to the sound of the wind without being bound by formality, is hidden in this station with a long name.

name_tw: 長者濱潮騷濱名洲公園前

text_en: Wilderness stand. The sound of that name somehow feels like the harshness of the pioneering era and the breath of a new era. The residential area that spreads out around the station tells of the history of how a once-wilderness turned into a place of human activity, but the wide blue skies unique to this area still give travelers a sense of freedom. Once you pass this point, the feeling that you are finally approaching Kashima's industrial area and the Jingu forest begins to drift inside the car. A moment of tranquility before the end of a journey, or the anticipation of new encounters - such a half-hearted yet endearing feeling emanates from this simple station.

name_ja: 鹿島サッカースタジアム
text_en: Kashima Soccer Stadium. It is a truly interesting place, once a freight station called ``Kita Kashima'' that has changed its appearance in response to the demands of the times. A group of railway lines spread out on the site of a vast freight yard, which is usually sparsely populated, is a reminder of the vitality of this once coastal industrial area. However, on match day, the silence completely changes and is replaced by the excitement of tens of thousands of people. This extreme contrast between "motion" and "stillness" can be said to be the unique charm of this station. As the point of contact between the Kashima Rinkai Railway and the JR Line, the scenery where rusted railroad tracks and modern stadiums coexist makes you feel like you are looking at a microcosm of modern times, where the industrial heritage of the Showa era intersects with the culture of the Heisei era.

Shibukawa. It is truly a nodal point for travel, where the Joetsu Line separates from the Azuma Line. In the past, a streetcar called the Ikaho Orbital Line ran from in front of this station, transporting visitors to the hot springs, but now the modern Hashigami station building welcomes travelers. However, once you arrive at the platform, the majestic sight of Mt. Akagi and Mt. Haruna rising in the background makes you realize once again that this is a key location in Bando. The sight of the limited express ``Kusatsu Shima'' sliding into the mountains of Azuma after a short stop really gives you the feel of a regional trunk line. From here on, the train increases in altitude along the Azuma River. The atmosphere at this home is filled with anticipation for the journey.

Gold Island. This is the first stop after leaving Shibukawa. A tranquil rural landscape spreads out around the station, and you can feel the hustle and bustle of the city seem to be fading away. This station once had a busy history of shipping gravel, but now it has the feel of a quiet, unmanned station. There are old houses lined up in front of the station, giving it the feel of being the entrance to a nostalgic Showa era village. From here, the train begins preparations to head towards the mountainous region in earnest, feeling the presence of the Azuma River on the right. As a relay point, a peaceful time passes through this platform.

Grandmother Island. It is one of the best small stations on the Azuma Line with a tranquil atmosphere. There is only one platform on one side, and just beyond that you can see the clear stream of the Azuma River and deep greenery, letting you know that it is a place far away from the hustle and bustle of the city. There is something nostalgic about the sound of the station's name, and if you listen carefully to this place, where few people even get off the train, all you can hear is the sound of the wind, the voices of birds, and the murmuring of a distant river. Railway photography enthusiasts are drawn to the simple beauty of the area around this station, and are no doubt interested in tracking down trains crossing the railway bridges in this area. It is a station that makes you feel the luxury of having nothing.

Onogami. For railway enthusiasts, this is an inseparable ``ballast'' station. There is a vast quarry near the station, and andesite was once mined from there and loaded onto freight cars as gravel to support the Japanese National Railways' tracks. Even today, the traces of the side tracks and the traces carved into the mountain surface retain strong memories of the industry. The station itself has a simple appearance, but it gives off a unique sense of strength, as if the heavy stone culture forms the backbone of this area. The atmosphere at this station is filled with pride in having supported the railway infrastructure from the ground up.

Onogami Onsen. As the station name suggests, it is a luxurious station with a hot spring facility located just a stone's throw from the platform. Although it is a relatively new name, having been renamed in the Heisei era, the appearance of the station is well-suited to the local steam. When the train door opens, you can even feel the faint scent of a hot spring wafting through the air, and you are tempted to get off the train and take a bath. Unlike hot spring towns decorated as tourist destinations, this is the gateway to a simple hot spring town loved by locals. Its unpretentious warmth melts the hearts of travelers.

City castle. It is a station that stands quietly on a small flat area of ​​river terraces created by the Azuma River. Although the station building is simple, the surrounding mountains and the river flowing below show that this station is located in a harsh natural environment. After passing this point, the Azuma Line finally enters the rugged terrain that leads to Azuma Gorge. You could say that the station is filled with the calm before the storm, like the eve of a festival. The surrounding area is dotted with fine tiled-roofed houses, perhaps a remnant of the area's long history as a sericulture area, giving us a glimpse of the rural landscape of Joshu. When I happened to look out the train window on a journey, I noticed its quiet presence. That's what this station is like.

Nakanojo. It is the administrative and commercial center of Azuma County, and has been a bustling station since ancient times as the gateway to Shima Onsen and Sawatari Onsen. When you step off the platform, you can feel the atmosphere of a dignified local city, and you can hear the hustle and bustle of travelers who used to transfer to buses and head to hot springs deep in the mountains. Although the station building has been given a new look over time, the appearance of the plaza and shopping street in front of the station still retains strong traces of the Showa era. It continues to quietly fulfill its role as a starting point for journeys from here over the mountains and further into the hinterland. It gives us such a feeling of reliability. The sight of a limited express train proudly stopping here also adds to the prestige of this town.

Gunma Haramachi. When you hear the name of this station, even if you're not a history buff, you can't help but look up at the steep rock face of Mt. It has a prosperous history as a castle town connected to the Sanada clan, and the area around the station is still dotted with substantial merchant houses. Even before the railroad was opened, this area is remembered as a key point along the Azuma River where people and horses came and went. It's hard to imagine from the current quiet station entrance, but the old stone walls and alleys quietly remind us of the days when the area was booming due to the cocoon trade and timber exports. It is a station that makes you feel the layers of history. The steep mountains visible from the train window give us a sense of the rough journey that is about to begin.

Gohara. This area is well-known among archeology fans as it is where a heart-shaped clay figure, a nationally designated historical site, was excavated just after getting off the station. A steep cliff looms behind the platform, and it is clear that the railway was built by finding a small piece of flat land in the harsh terrain created by the erosion of the Azuma River. When I find myself in the silence of an unmanned station, I can't help but think back to the eternity of time, wondering if the people of the Jomon period also felt this wind and watched the same river flow. Even in this day and age where modern trains run by, this station is the only one that retains a mysterious tranquility, as if it has continued to breathe since ancient times. The fact that an ordinary small station is actually the gateway to thousands of years of history makes you feel the depth of your journey.

Yagura. It is one of the most modest stations on the Azuma Line, with one stop on one platform. Right next to the station, there are ``Yakura Birdhead Flowers'' and large cherry blossom trees that bloom beautifully in spring, making you feel the change of seasons most closely. It continues to play its role as the entrance to the village, and although it is not glamorous, it does exude the scent of a down-to-earth lifestyle. This small station, which is easy to overlook when you see the scenery passing by through the train window, may actually be the purest preservation of Japan's original scenery. It makes me feel that kind of emotion. The platform, which stands quietly and withstands the wind pressure of passing express trains, gives a lovely feeling.

Iwashima. This is an important turning point in the history of railways, as the old line once branched off from here and entered deep into the scenic beauty of Azuma Gorge. Nowadays, the scenery around the station has changed completely due to the replacement of a new line with the construction of the Yamba Dam, but even so, the memories of the railway etched in this area will never disappear. The surrounding area's history as a hemp production center and the rough rock formations carved out by the Azuma River continue to delight travelers today. While we miss the train windows that have been lost, we quietly watch over the new history of the railway. This station has such a calm and independent attitude. From here on, the train enters a modern section with continuous tunnels and bridges.

Kawaraya hot spring. It is a station with a turbulent history that has changed from an old station that sank to the bottom of a dam to a new town on high ground. When you get off the train at the new, modern station building, you'll be overwhelmed by the sight of the dam lake spreading out below you and the huge bridge that spans it. The old wooden station building and narrow alleys smelling of sulfur are now a memory, but the enthusiasm of the people who continue to protect the hot springs in this new location can be felt from this new platform. A place where nostalgia for what has been lost and hope for the future intersect. There is definitely a ``new travel atmosphere'' unique to this station that symbolizes the current Azuma Line. It is part of the nature of travelers to look down on the surface of the lake and look for the remains of old railway lines.

Naganohara Kusatsuguchi. This station, which was once simply called ``Naganohara,'' now serves as the literal gateway to the famous hot springs of Kusatsu Onsen, and serves as the terminal station for the limited express ``Kusatsu Shima.'' When you arrive at the platform, the sound of the engine of the express bus heading for Kusatsu echoes, and the loud voices of tourists dominate the area. However, if you turn your attention, you will find that the ruins of the Taishi Branch Line, which once ran from this area to the mines of Shirane Volcano, are faint reminders of an industry that has disappeared into the depths of history. The area in front of the station has become unmistakably modern due to the construction of the dam, but the cool mountain air still gives you a strong sense that this is a high-altitude backcountry area of ​​Joshu. The bright lights of tourism and the shadows of the industrial railway of the past. This station stands at the intersection of both.

Gunma Otsu. After passing the gorgeous Naganohara Kusatsuguchi, the train finally enters the heart of the Azuma Line, Tsumagoi Village. This station has a strong sense of being a quiet station, separated from the hustle and bustle of tourist areas. If you look around from the platform, you'll see fields bathed in the soft light of the highlands, giving you a sense of openness reminiscent of a small train station in the north. With the village of Otsu in the background, which once prospered as a post town on the road leading to Shinshu, the track slowly gains altitude. Once you pass this point, the patchwork of cabbage fields begins to decorate the train windows, and the journey begins to take on the character of a highland train. Although it is an ordinary stop on the way, you can see the true image of rural Joshu without any excess.

Feather tail. In the past, freight cars used to transport sulfur produced from nearby mines frequently came and went from this station, and it has a history of playing a major role as a logistics hub for the Azuma Line. Now that its role has ended, it is a quiet, unmanned station, but the spacious station interior and the remains of the side tracks silently tell us of its former glory. The murmur of the Azuma River flowing right next to the station and the voices of birds echoing in the mountains. When you place yourself in the silence, you can almost hear the echoes of a time when railroads supported local industry and supported Japan's modernization. The former ``Sulfur Road'' has now transformed into a ``tourist road,'' but the simple and sturdy appearance of this station still resonates with travelers today.

Fukurokura. This station, which is quietly located at the bottom of a deep valley created by the Azuma River, has an atmosphere that befits its name as an unexplored station. The platform is made of simple wooden boards, with a steep slope looming behind it, completely blocking out the hustle and bustle of the city. There are only a limited number of trains that stop here, and getting off here feels like an adventure in itself. However, this silence is the real pleasure of traveling by train, and when you stand still in the silence after the train has left, you feel as if you are one with nature. In the winter, it is covered in deep snow, and in the spring, it is covered in fresh greenery. It is a hidden station on the Azuma Line that embraces the changing seasons in its purest form.

Manza/Kazawa Exit. It is the de facto terminal station for many trains, and the elevated platform where the highland breeze blows through makes you feel like the climax of your journey. As the station name suggests, it is a base for wide-area tourism that connects to Manza Onsen, Kazawa Onsen, and even Karuizawa, and has a history of being filled with many skiers and summer visitors. The altitude is over 700 meters, and the air is so clear that it can feel chilly even in summer, which tells you that this is a special place. From here on, the line continues for just one stop, as if enjoying the afterglow of the journey, all the way to the last stop, Omae. While many travelers get off here and transfer to buses, this quiet station maintains its pride as the ``terminus of the plateau'' of the Azuma Line.

Omae. This is the true final station of the Azuma Line, the end of a long journey. The platform is a straight line, and the dead-end roadblocks are cruelly but quietly telling us that we can't go any further. There are only a few private houses, cabbage fields, and a clear stream near the source of the Azuma River around the station, so there is not the slightest bit of glamor as a tourist destination. However, it is precisely at this ``end of nothing'' that lies the true lyricism that railroad travel writers seek. As I stare at the end of the tracks in silence while waiting for the train to return, I am deeply moved by the fact that Japan's railway network is spread out like a web, but it ends in a small place like this. The end of a journey is always the beginning of new thoughts. This is what Omae Station will teach you.

Kiryu. This station is the gateway to the textile capital, which was once hailed as ``Nishijin of the west, Kiryu of the east.'' This place, which shares the platform with the JR Ryomo Line and Towatetsu, has been transformed into a modern elevated station, but it retains something of the elegance fostered by the city's history. Once you get off the platform and go out to the north exit, you will see a plaza where trucks used to transport silk thread, and in the distance the mountains of Akagi greet you. When you feel that the saw-roofed factories and brick buildings dotted around the city are still alive and well, starting from this station, it reaffirms the importance of the history of railways transporting culture. Even though we have moved from the era of express trains to the era of leisurely rolling trolley trains, Kiryu remains a key transportation hub.

Shimoshinden. It is a station with a history of originally being a signal station and being promoted to a passenger station at the end of the Showa era. The true value of this station lies in the existence of the adjacent Takasaki Vehicle Center Kiryu Branch. From the train window, you can see old soldiers who have finished their duty quietly waiting to be dismantled, and elite soldiers lined up waiting for their turn, creating a kind of sacred place for railway enthusiasts. The simple home, which stands quietly in a residential area, is not glamorous, but it is a truly simple and sturdy place where you can feel the breathing of the vehicles and the enthusiasm of the mechanics. The charm of Shimoshinden lies in its exquisite sense of distance, where the behind-the-scenes scenes of railways blend into the everyday scenery.

Old man. As a connection point with the Tobu Railway Kiryu Line, this station can be said to be a key point in the operation of this line. It used to be called Aioi Station, but in order to avoid confusion with a station of the same name in Hyogo Prefecture, the name was changed to the rather quaint name ``Growing Old Together.'' The sight of passengers passing over the narrow overpass gives us a sense of its vitality as a transportation hub that has remained unchanged since the Showa era. Watching the Tobu Line limited express ``Ryomo'' slide in, it makes you realize that this is an important place to pass the baton between Tokyo and the Ashio Mountains. The quiet atmosphere created by the old wooden station building, combined with the busyness of passengers transferring, creates a unique atmosphere that greatly enhances the atmosphere of the journey.

Sports park. While there are many historic stations that look old, this station has a relatively new and cheerful look. As its name suggests, it was established as a station to provide access to Kiryu City Sports Park, and its location, surrounded by lush greenery, gives a momentary sense of refreshingness to the scenery from the train window. Just a short walk away is the Jomo Electric Railway's Kiryu-kyujo-mae Station, and this area, where these two lines run side by side, is an interesting point where the local foot traffic is intricately intertwined. The bustle on days when there are games or events is one thing, but listening to the sound of the wind on a quiet platform in the afternoon is also a luxurious way to spend time. It is a station with a mysterious harmony, where modern facilities and old-fashioned countryside scenery intersect.

Omama. Carrying a history dating back to the Ashio Line era, this station currently reigns as the center of the Watarase Keikoku Railway. When you get off the train at this station, you will see the vast grounds of the station, which are quiet reminders of its former glory. The station building's features are also stately, giving it both a splendor as the starting point for the Watarase Keikoku tourist train and a sense of pride as the gateway to the historic city. The area around the station is lined with soy sauce breweries, giving the illusion of a nostalgic, mellow aroma wafting through the entire city. The appearance of this station evokes a moment of peace and anticipation before entering the steep valley of the Watarase River, making it feel like a major turning point in your journey.

Kamishinbai. Anyone who sees this station building will feel as if time has stopped. The wooden station building, which still retains much of its original appearance when it opened in 1919, has been designated as a nationally registered tangible cultural property, and it is no exaggeration to call it a living architectural museum. The well-used wooden ticket gates and the texture of the roof tiles layered to prevent rain leaks give the impression of a work of art created by a master craftsman named Togetsu. It can be said that there is a place that is extremely rare in modern times that teaches us how enriching the time spent simply sitting on a bench on the platform and waiting for the train is. Even the sound of a railroad crossing alarm echoing in the silence reaches travelers' ears like soothing music at this station.

Main inn. It is a truly modest station, overlooking the rapids of the Watarase River, nestled in a small gap between National Route 122 and the river. Once you arrive at the platform, you will be reminded once again of the ruggedness of the Ashio Mountains by the sheer mountain surface on the opposite shore and the roaring force of the water. Around the station, there are several old houses lined up close to each other, giving us a sense of the lives of the people who lived alongside the railway in this harsh terrain. When I think back to the days when freight trains bound for the Ashio Copper Mine struggled up this steep slope, I feel a quiet emotion at the weight of the role this small station played. Its simple and sturdy appearance, devoid of any ornate decorations, symbolizes the true nature of Watetsu.

Water marsh. The station is known for having a hot spring facility inside the station platform, which is rare even in Japan. It is said that in the past, it was used as a wood collection and distribution area, with many logs piled up on the freight sidings, but now the ``Mizunuma Station Center'' signboard serves as a lighthouse to soothe the fatigue of travelers. Listening to the sound of the clatter announcing the arrival of the train while enjoying the breeze of Watarase in an open-air bath is a moment that encapsulates the real pleasure of traveling by train. There is also a legend of kappa around the station, and the strange harmony between such folklore and modern hot spring facilities makes you feel the deep bosom of this area. The moment you sit on the bench on the platform after taking a bath and wait for the next train is a luxurious moment that cannot be replaced by anything else.

wreath. It is a station with a strong history that once prospered as a post town on the Copper Road, which transported copper from Ashio. A short walk from the station will bring you to the beautiful wooden school building of the former Hanawa Elementary School, which is a registered tangible cultural property of the country and is a testament to the high aspirations for education in this area. The station itself is a quiet, unmanned station, but the old storehouses and stone walls dotted around it silently speak of its pride as a former logistics hub. It is also the hometown of Wasaburo Ishihara, the father of nursery rhymes, and the sight of the melody playing on the platform blending into the clear mountain air is truly full of emotion. It is a calming station where past and present coexist quietly, giving visitors a moment of reflection.

Nakano. Even on the Watetsu line, it is a place that is especially quiet and has the feel of a small station in the mountains. Although it is surrounded by gently sloping land and has only one simple platform without a station building, I feel that this actually highlights the purity of the railway system. Cherry blossoms in the spring and autumn leaves in the fall decorate the platform, making it one of the places where you can most closely experience the changing seasons. There aren't any particularly famous or historic sites, but as a travel writer, I find it irresistible to get off at this station and wait for the next train while listening to the sound of the wind passing by. Although it is not flashy, it quietly but powerfully presents the true richness of everyday railway scenery.

Elementary and junior high school. When you get off at this station, which is nestled in the deep mountains, the air feels even cooler, and you get the feeling that you have finally stepped deep into the heart of Ashio. The remains of the large grounds tell us that in the past, much wood was exported from this area, and that there was a time when forestry resources supported Japan's modernization. If you climb a few kilometers up the mountain from the station, the mighty ``Konaka no Otaki'' will be waiting for you, but the station itself is so peaceful that it gives you the illusion of being swallowed up by the deep greenery. As I look at the wildflowers blooming along the railroad tracks and listen to the sounds of birds echoing in the mountains, I begin to feel that the railway is a piece of equipment that is integrated into the larger workings of nature. It is a station that gives you a mysterious sense of elation, as if it were standing on the border between civilization and nature.

Kobe. The pronunciation is different from that in Hyogo Prefecture, and the local custom is to call it ``goudo.'' In the past, the area beyond this station was not open to traffic, and it has a long history of serving as a terminal station. Perhaps for this reason, the premises are spacious and have a stately atmosphere that still conveys the glory of the past. The highlight of this station is, of course, that Tobu Railway's classic 1720 series ``Deluxe Romance Car'' has been preserved for the rest of its life as a dining car. Even if you are not a railway fan, the sight of the jukebox-like car body that adorned the golden age of railways in the Showa era, standing against the backdrop of the Watarase mountains, is something that touches your heart. In spring, the station is filled with peach blossoms that fill the entire station, giving the area a peach-like beauty. There is no other station where a love of history and railways has come to fruition so beautifully.

Sawairi. It is the last station in Gunma Prefecture, and once you pass it you will finally step into Tochigi Prefecture, giving it the feel of a border station. On the side of the platform, the famous stone ``Sawairi Mikage'' produced in this area is proudly placed, preserving the memory of the days when stone transportation was booming. The murmuring of the Watarase River becomes even more rugged as you reach this area, and the vibrations of the train as it weaves through the huge boulders give you a sense of tension as you venture deep into the mountains. Although the station building was rebuilt to a simpler one, the clear air emitted by the surrounding cedar forest and the occasional chirping of birds create a tranquil atmosphere that makes you forget the hustle and bustle of the city. Railways crossed mountains, carrying people and carrying stones. The traces of these activities make us feel that they are quietly but firmly rooted in this land.

Original direction. This is the first station in Tochigi Prefecture, and it is hidden at the bottom of a deep valley. There is only one platform on a small piece of flat land between the national highway and the river. The purity of the scenery makes travelers realize once again how rugged the Ashio Mountains are. It has a history of once when the copper mine was at its peak of prosperity, and a cableway ran here, connecting the blessings of the mountain with the people's lives. Nowadays, only the sound of the river echoes through the premises, and the occasional breeze carries the scent of the season, but it is this silence that brings back even more vivid memories of the hustle and bustle of the past. The mountainside on the opposite shore, which can be seen from the train window, has deepened its greenery to heal the scars of past smoke pollution, quietly telling the story of the railway's history of hardship and rebirth.

A tunnel. It is the gateway to the center of the Ashio Copper Mine, and its name itself refers to the entrance to the mine shaft, making it a truly outstanding station. It is closer to the city center and sightseeing at the Ashio Copper Mine than Ashio Station, and can be said to be the place that retains the most traces of its former bustling mining town. The structure of the station building is also dignified, and the pride that once supported ``the largest copper mine in the East'' oozes out from its appearance. Once you get to the platform, you'll find a path where miners would have walked shoulder to shoulder in the past, and beyond that, you'll see the remains of a huge ore processing factory towering over you with the majesty of an ancient ruin. Industrial heritage has become part of the landscape and continues to be part of local life. The time that this station has marked is more than just a record of transportation, it makes us feel that it is a microcosm of Japan's modernization itself.

Ashio. This station, which bears the name of the line, has many side tracks running through its spacious premises, and is an eloquent reminder of the days when it was once a key hub for freight transportation. This place, where silence reigns today, was once crowded with freight cars shipping copper, and the smoke from steam locomotives scorched the sky. The sight of the preserved old freight cars spending their remaining lives quietly on the rusted rails makes not only railway fans but also visitors think deeply about the changing times. The stately wooden station building has been designated as a nationally registered tangible cultural property, and the memories of countless travelers and workers are engraved in each of its solid beams and pillars. Enjoy the weight of the place name Ashio in its vast grounds and tranquil atmosphere. This is what we can say is the blissful time spent at this station.

Mato. It is the terminal station for passenger operations on this railway that started from Kiryu. The line used to continue on as a freight line to the former Ashio-Motoyama Station, but now the dead-end car stop quietly signals the end of the journey. The mountains that tower behind the station have a history of being devastated by smoke from a former smelter, but now they are gradually regaining their greenery through the planting of trees, and seem to symbolize human mistakes and the will to rebuild. If you're lucky, you may even see a Japanese serow that has descended close to the platform, making you realize that this is literally the final stop deep in the mountains. Mato is filled with the sense of desolation that is typical of a terminal station, but also with the refreshing feeling of having completed a journey. The railroad hits a mountain, and you have no choice but to walk on your own. It is a place that teaches us the essence of such a journey.

Shimodate. Mito Line, Kanto Railway, and Moka Railway. This station, where three railroad tracks line up against each other, is the gateway to the city of Shimodate, which once flourished as a ``commercial capital.'' When you cross the overpass, you feel like you can hear the nostalgic bustle of the city mixed with the smell of diesel. It used to be a busy area for cargo handling, and there is a history of many goods being transported to the entire Kanto region via this area. Especially if you stand on the Moka Railway platform, on weekends you can still look for the remnants of the powerful smoke emitted by the C11 in the shadow of the old overpass. You can feel that the pride of being not just a transfer station but a key hub for railway transportation still emanates within its premises.

name_en: In front of Shimodate Second High School
text_en: In front of Shimodate Second High School. This station was newly built in 1963, near the end of the Showa era, and as its name suggests, it is a base for commuting to the school. Although it is a simple structure with only one platform, the hustle and bustle of young people in the mornings and evenings is so lively that it overwhelms the sound of diesel engine engines. It can be said that this station embodies the lightness of everyday transportation that was not present in the days of the JNR Moka Line. Looking at the station, which is surrounded by houses and filled with the scent of everyday life, makes me realize once again that the railway is not just a means of transportation, but the very lifeblood of the city. The role played by this relatively new station on this line, which has a long history, is no small one.

Folded book. This station, where upper and lower trains exchange trains, is a place where you can feel the real thrill of traveling on a single track. This area was once a thriving area for tobacco cultivation, but now you can see a peaceful rural landscape stretching out from the train window. Although the wooden station building has changed in appearance, I get off at the platform to wait for the oncoming train and enjoy the quiet time. This seems like a luxury in today's world, where efficiency is prioritized. When I look at the old equipment that remains inside the station and the beauty of the neatly lined railroad tracks, I feel as if memories of a time when time flowed more slowly come back vividly. This station carefully preserves the vestiges of an era when railways were closely connected to local industry.

Higuchi. Located at the northern tip of Ibaraki Prefecture, this station gives off the feeling of being on the border, as it will soon enter Tochigi Prefecture. The station, which was renamed from ``Higuchi'' in 1988, is surrounded by the unpretentious scenery of the foothills of Mt. Tsukuba. You could call it luxury without anything. Just looking at the rails stretching straight and blending with the greenery in the distance makes me feel like I'm experiencing the essence of railway travel. Contrary to the hustle and bustle of National Route 294 that passes in front of the station, the time passing on the platform is endlessly tranquil, and this is what makes this station so appealing. It feels like the perfect place for a traveler to stop off mid-way and indulge in some solitary contemplation.

Kugeta. This is the station that announces that we have finally crossed the prefectural border and entered Moka City, Tochigi Prefecture. Located in the center of what was once Ninomiya Town, there are still rows of old houses around the station, giving it the calm appearance of a local city. There is a history that a lot of agricultural products were once loaded into freight cars from this station and sent to various places, so you can't help but feel the bustle of the past by looking at the length of the platform. The station building was later renovated into a retro Western-style building, which seems to symbolize the line's character as a tourist railway, which makes me smile. In early summer, the sweet aroma of the surrounding strawberry fields can be felt, and the very appearance of the station expresses the richness of this fertile land.

Terauchi. As the name suggests, this area has had deep connections with temples and shrines since ancient times, and the area around the station has a calm atmosphere. A momentary silence in front of the city of Moka. The fields that spread out next to the railway change color with the seasons, pleasing the eyes of travelers. Did visitors to nearby temples also use this station in the past? We feel relieved that there is a landscape that remains unchanged even though it has been washed by the waves of history. In this way, the train stops at each station and breathes in the local air. The peace of mind that traveling through trains that stop at each station has always fascinated me as a railway travel writer. The few minutes you spend at this small station before reaching the next station, Moka Station, will deepen the flavor of your trip.

Moka. When you get off the train at the central station that bears its name, the first thing that catches your eye is the majesty of the station building, modeled after a giant steam locomotive. This town, which once flourished as a distribution center for Moka Momen and the heart of the Moka Line, has not lost its deep love for railways. The sound of the train whistle echoing from the adjacent Kyuroku Hall evokes a heart-wrenching feeling of nostalgia for those who know the sooty smoke of the Showa era. Looking at the quiet yet eloquent appearance of the old rolling stock preserved inside the station, you will realize that the railway is more than just a means of transportation, it is an integral part of the local culture itself. I have a bad habit of looking for traces of the old engine shed and signs of the railroad workers who worked there in the shadows of modern station buildings.

Kita Moka. This station is located at the entrance where the train passes through the city center of Moka and once again enters the countryside. In spring, the cherry blossoms and rape blossoms blooming along the railroad tracks create a beautiful scene that looks like something out of a movie. From the days when the Moka Line silently played a role as a means of transportation for people's daily lives and as a route for transporting soldiers and supplies, to its current quiet appearance, how many travelers has this landscape seen off? Houses are lined up right next to the station, and the sounds of daily life are just around the corner, but once the train doors close, the train journey begins again in silence. Even though we are aware of the gorgeous colors of the seasons, it is also a treat to sit on this platform at dusk on an ordinary day and feel the gust of wind blowing at us.

Nishitai. This station, where upper and lower trains exchange trains, is a place that gives you that pleasant tension of a ``meeting'' that is unique to single-track railways. I feel an indescribable sense of peace in the old wooden waiting room and the neat layout of the platform, reminiscent of the era of tablet exchange. There was once a time when agriculture was flourishing in this area, and the area was full of energy and energy. Although the number of people waiting for trains is now sparse, the windbreaks surrounding the station and the appearance of old farms still convey the richness of Shimotsuke. The diesel cars slowly braked and passed each other as if looking at the oncoming train. In those short stops, we can discover the ``punctuation points of travel'' that are being lost.

Kitayama. It is a simple station with a one-sided platform that looks like it is placed in the middle of a gentle curve. Surrounding you is an endless rural landscape and the misty peaks of the Nikko Mountain Range in the distance. Here, there are no noisy information announcements or waves of busy people that you would find at a metropolitan station. However, the regular sound of the railroad ties tapping and the sounds of insects coming from the grass will quietly deepen your sense of travel. Considering its original purpose when it was established in 1933, I feel that the pride of the railway that supported the development and development of this area can be felt from this small platform. When I look at the richness of nothing and how the railway is completely integrated into the landscape, I can't help but feel my spine grow as it teaches me the futility of hasty travel.

text_en: Mashiko. It goes without saying that it is the gateway to the famous pottery village. This area was loved and nurtured by Shoji Hamada, the father of the Mingei movement, and even the station building itself has a certain artistic flavor. The elaborately designed station building with its large roof symbolizes the cultural weight that this city has developed over the years. In the past, Mashiko ware was shipped from this station all over the country and around the world, so just standing on the platform gives you the illusion that you can smell the earth and feel the heat of the fire. This station, which is crowded with people during the pottery market, usually has the atmosphere of a calm local city. When travelers step outside the station, they are greeted by an unchanging landscape of handicrafts dotted with climbing kiln chimneys, making them keenly aware of the achievements of railways in transporting and preserving culture.

Nanai. This is a place where your journey on the Moka Railway will become even more profound. There was a time when this station was the last stop on the Moka Line, and its long history is reflected in the spacious interior of the station. Although the surrounding area retains the vestiges of an old farming village, there is a sense of a dignified and refreshing atmosphere. Although it is sad that the former wooden station building has been lost, its functional beauty, with which up and down trains are still being replaced, seems to symbolize the robustness of the railway system. The view of the village of Nanai from the train window gives us a sense of pride in the fact that we have lived together with the railway, even though it has overcome the turbulent waves of history. Instead of regretting the days gone by, we should admire the peaceful scenery that is here now. That is the privilege granted to travelers who get off at this station.

Tatara. The sound of the name makes you want to look for the embers of the old ``Tatara Iron Works.'' It is a quiet station in the countryside. There is no need to trace the footsteps of the powerful families that once ruled this area, and the harmony of the rolling hills and countryside surrounding the station truly embodies the original landscape of Japan. At first glance, it is an unmanned station with an unremarkable single platform, but the refreshing breeze that blows through it makes you feel that it is the greatest gift to those traveling on the railway. In the nameless flowers blooming by the roadside, we find remnants of a time when the JNR Moka Line was not just a means of transportation, but also brought a breath of civilization to these remote areas. This is a luxurious way to spend time that modern people, who prioritize efficiency, have forgotten.

Ichihana. This is an exchange station where trains that have run through Haganono pass each other to take a breather. Located in the center of Ichigai Town, it has a proud history of supporting the region's economy as a distribution center for agricultural products. Although the station building has been renovated, the platform waiting for an oncoming train still seems to have the unique solidity of the days when steam locomotives stopped, panting heavily. The area around the station is home to offices and schools, and it still functions as the heart of the town, making it a great example of how the good times of the Showa era, when railways were the foundation of life, have been carried over into the present day. I suddenly find memories of the days when tablets were exchanged in the shadow of an old overpass. It is a station that invites that kind of wanderlust.

Sasahara field. It is a truly modest, unmanned station nestled in the heart of the mountains of Mogi. This station, which opened its doors in 1985 when the Moka Railway changed to the Moka Railway, is enveloped in a mysterious silence, as if the spirits of the forest had chosen it to wait for trains. Surrounded by deep greenery, the appearance of the building, where you can hear the chirping of birds more closely than the presence of people, is truly interesting, as it seems to be witnessing the process of assimilating the railway into nature. Over time, the once brave word ``pioneer'' has sublimated into the gentle scenery of ``coexistence.'' Standing in this small home, you can feel the changes in history. Forgetting about the hurried journey, I watched the lone diesel car disappear into the forest. That is the correct way to spend your time at this station.

Amayaba. This station is located halfway up the railway as it tackles its final uphill climb before its final destination in Mogi. On the day the steam locomotive is put into service, the sound of the locomotive's life-killing roar echoing through the surrounding mountains as it tackles the steep slope of 25 percent. The station itself faces the national highway and has a modern appearance, but as soon as you step onto the platform, you can still feel the tension of crossing the mountain pass, faintly but surely. After passing this point, the train descends the hill at a familiar pace and heads for the terminal station. In other words, it is a place where you can take a deep breath before the climax of your journey. A railway, a mass of iron, resisting the natural law of gravity. This station continues to quietly watch over its health.

Mogi. This is the final station where the long journey of the Moka Line comes to an abrupt end. It is the nature of travel writers to discover in the vacant land beyond this station the remains of the dream of the Nagakura Line, which was once supposed to be a major trunk line connecting Ibaraki and Tochigi. It is said that this town once prospered due to the cultivation of tobacco, and the scent of tobacco can be found even in the station premises, and it still retains a somewhat lonely, yet warm atmosphere that is typical of a dead-end station. On weekends, many people gather to watch the steam locomotives proudly changing direction on the turntable, but once the hustle and bustle has passed, the tranquility that can only be found at a terminal station, similar to the ``resignation'' that has come to accept everything, returns to the platform. Beyond the end of the rail, a new story begins. With such a premonition, I pick myself up and start walking into town.
