text_en:
Isumi Railway. This railway, which runs from Ohara, where the sea breeze of Sotobo is fragrant, to Kazusa-Nakano, deep in the Boso Peninsula, was once called the Japanese National Railways' Kihara Line. Its name was a nod to the grand dream of the Boso Cross Railway, which would connect Kisarazu and Ohara, but the dream of a full line did not come true, and now it quietly supports the lives of the area as a third sector.

As the train leaves the Ohara campus and begins running alongside the gentle flow of the Isumi River, a peaceful rural woodland scene unfolds that is worthy of being called ``Japan's original landscape.'' In the spring, rapeseed flowers line the tracks in yellow, and in the fall, the rice ears shine in golden yellow. This gives the impression that time flows slowly in this space, which is a clear departure from modern railways that strive for efficiency. There was a time when the Kiha 52 and Kiha 28 from the JNR era served as the "face" of this line, but even if the trains change, the "Showa era" that hangs over the unmanned station's wooden benches and cut-throughs surrounded by greenery will never fade. Seeing them joining hands with the Kominato Railway at Kazusa Nakano, we travelers are reminded of the warmth of railways that is disappearing.

Ohara. This is the connection point with the Sotobo Line on the east coast of Boso, and is the starting point for the Isumi Railway to turn inland. This line, which was once called the Japanese National Railways Kihara Line, runs from here towards Kazusa Nakano. When you land on the platform, instead of the sound of the sea, you can hear the powerful heartbeat of the diesel engine. The area around the station is also known as the town of spiny lobster, and has a unique atmosphere that combines the vibrancy of a fishing town with the feeling of traveling by train. This station still plays a role as a node connecting the sea to the mountains, a role that has not changed since the days of the Japanese National Railways. Travelers can't help but feel a sense of anticipation as they finally get to shake off the hustle and bustle of the city and delve into the depths of Boso.

West Ohara. After leaving the hustle and bustle of Ohara, the train quickly slips into the quiet countryside. Although it is a simple station with just one short platform, it retains the richness of ``waiting time'' that urban stations have forgotten. There was nothing to obstruct the view, just the vast breadbasket of Chiba. I feel that this emptiness actually highlights the strength of the single iron band that is the railway. The gazes of people who would once have watched the trains pass by while they were doing their farm work are still reflected in this landscape. It is a place that can be called the original scenery of railways, a truly peaceful place that gives you an illusion.

Kazusa East. In the past, many agricultural products were probably loaded onto freight cars from this area and transported to the city. Nowadays, it has the feel of a quiet, unmanned station, but the calm, village-like appearance of the area around the station conveys the weight of its history, which has been shared with the local people. The structure of the station also retains the vestiges of the old crossing facilities, conveying the pride of the days when railways were the main means of logistics. The sound of the train engine echoes through the mountains, and the surrounding greenery becomes even darker. It makes you realize that your journey is gradually approaching the mountainous region of Boso. Although it is not flashy, it is a truly desirable station that gives off a sense of down-to-earth lifestyle.

Nittano. In the spring, both sides of the railroad tracks are covered with rape blossoms, creating a sight that resembles running on a yellow carpet, which is why many people are familiar with the track. The sight of photographers setting up tripods can now be considered a seasonal feature of this station. However, on a quiet afternoon outside of the flowering season, just looking at the rice ears and fields swaying in the wind, the tranquil beauty inherent in railways and rooted in daily life emerges. An unobstructed expanse of sky and rows of evenly spaced telephone poles. The geometric landscapes they create remind us of the real thrill of train travel, which has remained unchanged since the Showa era.

Kuniyoshi. Even within the Isumi Railway, it is a station with an especially dignified and stately character. Once upon a time, even express trains stopped here, and its history as a key transportation hub for the region is obvious when you take a look at the spacious grounds and impressive station building. In recent years, the area has become more and more popular with various initiatives, but essentially it has not lost its pride as a place of refuge for the people living in this area. The old diesel trains preserved on the sidings are not just exhibits, but rather ``living proof'' that preserve the memories of the golden age of railways. If you stay at this station for a while, you can feel the remnants of a time when trains were not just a means of transportation, but a culture itself.

Kazusa Nakagawa. After passing Kuniyoshi, the train is about to enter the heart of Boso, and this is the station located at the entrance. Surrounded by vast rice fields, the building's appearance is reminiscent of the original scenery of a Japanese farming village, giving it the feel of a resting place in a rice field rather than a station. There must have been a time in the past when people working in the fields used the sound of trains as a clock. The station is now quiet and unmanned, but when you stand on the platform, the only sounds you hear are the sound of the wind rustling the rice ears and the chirping of birds in the distance. We are once again taught that this ``luxury of nothing'' is the true treat of traveling on local trains. Rather than being left behind by the waves of modernization, it is a station that gives off a sense of strength and remains as it should be.

Shiromigaoka. Although it is a relatively new station in the history of Isumi Railway, its name comes from the hill overlooking Otaki Castle. Surrounded by newly emerging residential areas and commercial facilities, the station offers a breath of modernity that sets it apart from other stations that still retain the vestiges of the good old Kihara Line. However, as the train slides onto the platform, if you suddenly look out the window, you can see the white walls of Otaki Castle on the edge of a mountain in the distance. At that moment, I am convinced that there is a certain thread of history still alive in the modern landscape. Although it is a new station, its name is imprinted with the history of the area, and it plays a role in conveying to the present the extent of the former castle town. It can be said that it is a truly interesting point where old and new Boso intersect.

Otaki. It is the center of the castle town built by Honda Tadakatsu, one of the Four Heavenly Kings of Tokugawa, and is a key station that supports the operation of the Isumi Railway. The station building's dignified appearance is truly worthy of being the gateway to Boso's Little Edo. There is a train depot attached to the premises, and the sight of diesel cars lining up to relax gives us a sense of the pride of the days when railroads were the backbone of the city's industry and culture. In the past, Japanese National Railways employees worked hard to create this tradition, and now people who love railways are preserving this tradition. The old hand-painted signs and well-used equipment seem to be ingrained with a deep love and trust in the railway system. It is a famous station with a dignified atmosphere that will help you straighten your spine for the second half of your journey.

Kotani Matsu. This station stands quietly on its way, leaving the bustle of Otaki and returning to the quietness of the mountains. Located one step down from the national highway, the platform is surrounded by a bamboo grove and lush trees, giving it the feel of a secret place hidden from the rest of the world. In spring, the cherry blossoms next to the railroad tracks bloom beautifully, pleasing the eyes of many travelers, but the tranquility of the time when there are no flowers is also something special. When you get off at this station, you can clearly see that the railway does not force its way into nature, but rather follows the terrain and progresses in coexistence with the trees. In today's hectic society, the time spent sitting in a simple waiting room chair and waiting for the next train may be the most luxurious way to spend your time.

East Somoto. It looks like it's nestled in the middle of a rural area, and it has the typical atmosphere of an unmanned station on a local line. Although it is a bit small for a station building, the well-maintained waiting room is filled with memories of words that locals and travelers may have exchanged. Of particular note is the ``fortune'' device attached to the station name sign, and this playfulness adds a ray of joy to the otherwise inorganic journey. When you look around you, you can only see the sky spreading out and rows of telephone poles lined up at equal intervals. There is a landscape here that evokes a sense of nostalgia that makes you want to look for the remains of the smoke spewed out by the steam locomotives of the past. This station silently tells us that the essence of train travel is hidden within the ordinary scenery.

Kugahara. A platform made of a single board suddenly appears in the deep forest of Boso. It has an extremely tranquil appearance, which is worthy of the name ``Secret Area Station.'' There are no houses in the area, and the dense trees that threaten to cover the railroad tracks seem to be rejecting the wave of modernization. What were the people who once used this station thinking as they stood in this deep green silence? When the sound of the train engine moves away, all that is left is the sound of the wind, the chirping of birds, and the faint sound of the railway cooling. In today's world, where we are all about convenience, the fact that these ``empty'' places have been preserved feels like a miracle in itself. It is a rare place that reminds us that the civilization of railways is deeply embraced by nature.

Total source. This station, located close to the gentle flow of the Isumi River, has been overseeing the logistics and people's traffic in this area since ancient times. In spring, the cherry blossoms and rape blossoms along the railway line bloom profusely, providing travelers with a beautiful landscape that looks like a painting. However, after such a colorful season, it may be said that the calm and calm atmosphere is the true value of this station. The way the diesel car carefully passes through the large curves near the station, twisting its body, creates the illusion that you are looking at a model railroad diorama. The memory of the days when steam locomotives would wheedle up hills in the days of the Japanese National Railways still remains strong in the atmosphere of this quiet village.

Nishihata. As the terminal station approaches, the train finally enters the mountainous backbone of Boso. The area around the station is dotted with private houses clinging to the slope, showing that people's lives are closely connected to the railway. When you get off at these small mountain stations, you can't help but think of the hardships faced by our predecessors on the Kihara Line, how they overcame this rugged terrain and extended their tracks into the hinterland. The ridgeline of the mountains seen from the platform changes color with the seasons, pleasing the eyes of travelers, but at the same time, there is also a hint of the quiet determination of the people who live with the harsh nature. This place is filled with a strange emotional atmosphere that is a mixture of the unique sense of exhilaration that comes from a station one stop before the final stop, and a sense of desolation.

Kazusa Nakano. It is the terminus of the Isumi Railway, and at the same time it is the connection point with the Kominato Railway, making it a key location for the Boso Cross Railway. In the past, when the Japanese National Railways Kihara Line was extended to this area, the villagers welcomed the train with great joy, and the weight of that history is engraved in this station building. The appearance of the station building, which resembles a thatched roof, is filled with a poetic atmosphere befitting a ``terminal station,'' creating a unique atmosphere where the end and beginning of a journey intersect. In a place where two different railways are connected by a single line, you can't help but feel the mysterious connection that the culture of railways has, which goes beyond mere transportation convenience. I got off the train here and transferred to an old diesel car that stopped on the opposite platform. At that moment, we realize that we are immersed in the most beautiful legacy left by the Showa era.

Goi. Once you cross the overpass from the Uchibo Line platform, you will find yourself in the world of Kominato Railway, where time seems to have stopped. The vermilion and cream paint colors of the Kiha 200 class resting in the engine room are reminiscent of the JNR diesel trains of the past, preserving memories of the Showa era. With the hustle and bustle of the Keiyo industrial area in the background, as the diesel engine begins to make a deep roar, you can feel the emotion of the journey as you finally venture into the interior of Boso gradually but surely increase.

Kazusa Murakami. This is the first station after leaving Goi, and although it is located in a residential area, it somehow has the scent of an ancient capital. Nearby is the ruins of Kazusa Kokubunji Temple, and the weight of the history of this area, which was once the center of politics, is quietly deposited in this simple platform. As the sound of the train engine fades away, silence returns and only the sound of the wind can be heard. This station makes you feel like it continues to protect this ``forgotten time'' right next to the city.

Ama Ariki. It's a very poetic station name, and once you hear it, you'll never forget it. It is said that there was once a plan to extend the railway from here to the Chiba city area, but now the platform is just quietly illuminated by the soft light of Boso. The appearance of the old wooden station building looks like a small resistance from the railways to the modern society, which is all about efficiency, and it brings great peace of mind to us travelers. Getting off at this station is literally nothing but a journey through time.

Kazusa three-pronged. Surrounding the station are pipelines leading to an oil complex, creating a mysterious landscape that resembles a combination of an industrial area and a rural village. However, the station building itself is small and somewhat modest. In this place, where the arteries of civilization intersect with the quiet lives of people, the original scenery of railways as a ``carrier'' is still alive. The contrast between the silver pipes and the golden ears of rice seen from the train window makes you feel like it tells the story of this line's unique history.

Kazusa Yamada. As you approach the murmuring of the Yoro River, you will arrive at this station. The area in front of the station, which would once have been bustling with people carrying gravel for the Yoro River, is now shrouded in silence, as if time has stopped, which also highlights the character of this line. The warmth that the wooden station building exudes combines the strength that has withstood the wind and snow for many years, and the kindness that does not turn away visitors. Every time the train door opens, a nostalgic smell of earth flows into the train.

Light wind tower. It is the gateway to a residential area that was developed in the middle of the Showa era with dreams of a new lifestyle. Compared to the older stations around it, it has a modern appearance made of concrete, but because of that, the ``hope for the future'' of the time has now been sublimated into a somewhat nostalgic feeling. When you look up at the cityscape that stretches out on the slopes, you can feel the years that the railway has nurtured the region and the people who have put down roots here. This station, with its mix of old and new scenery, can be said to be one of the multifaceted charms of the Kominato Railway.

Umatate. The name retains the vestiges of the old highway where horses once roamed. The greenery surrounding the station has deepened even further, making you realize that the depths of the Boso Peninsula are finally increasing. The time spent sitting on a bench in a wooden station building, simply waiting for the train to arrive, reminds us of the virtue of "waiting" that modern people have forgotten. The sound of the train's horn echoing through the mountains and the sight of it slowly approaching the train line makes you feel like you're looking at a painting.

text_en: Kazusa Ushiku. This is the operational base for this route, and was once a busy core station with bus connections. There are old shops lined up in front of the station, and the unique vibrancy of a local city in the Showa era can still be felt. The sight of many trains turning back here and preparing to cross the mountain reminds us of the concept of ``rest'' that railways originally had. The quiet breathing of the city that spreads out beyond the ticket gate gives travelers a momentary sense of security and prepares them to head deep into the mountains ahead.

Kazusa Kawama. A single home stands alone in the middle of a rural landscape. Why is this scenery so moving? There is nothing to block the surrounding area, just the seasonal winds that cross the rice fields and blow through the platform. There is a kind of ultimate functional beauty in which the railway is completely integrated into the landscape. When the train doors close and silence returns, you can feel the richness of this station's ``emptiness'' deeply penetrating your heart.

Kazusa Tsurumai. This station building, which was selected as one of the top 100 stations in the Kanto region, is a true example of the Showa era railway heritage. Adjacent to the ruins of a former power plant, it still retains the atmosphere of a heavy industrial structure, yet it is awe-inspiring to see it still in operation. It is often used as the setting for movies and dramas, and this is simply because the ``universal nostalgia'' that this place has resonates with people's hearts. The years carved into each wooden pillar silently tell us the story of history.

Kazusa Kubo. A large kosun tree stands watching over the station, and its overwhelming presence clearly depicts the changing seasons. In autumn, the home is covered with a golden carpet, creating a fantastic scene that looks like a scene from a movie. As you huddle in the small waiting room, you can feel the preciousness of how railways have played a part in the lives of local people, and how time has passed together with them. It is rare to find a space where nature and man-made things are in such harmony.

Takataki. Lake Takataki spreads out near the station, and the air is moist with the presence of water. This artificial lake, which was once built to prevent the Yoro River from overflowing, has now become a familiar part of the landscape, creating a new sense of travel. The station building that welcomes worshipers to Takataki Shrine, located on the shore of the lake, has both the glamor of a tourist destination and the tranquility of a remote area. When the wind crosses the surface of the water and blows through the platform, you can feel the fatigue of your journey being gently relieved.

Satomi. In the past, this station, where tablets were exchanged and the quick movements of railway workers could be seen, still has a sense of pride as a railway ``workplace''. On weekends, locals open direct sales stands, turning the time spent waiting for the train into a warm place for socializing. The site where steam locomotives once refilled water silently proves the long history of this station, and it tickles the intellectual curiosity of travelers. It makes you feel like the body heat of the people supporting the railway is permeating every corner of the station.

Meal allowance. The old history of Kazusa is engraved in this difficult-to-read station name. It is said that the name came from the legend that a local person offered food to Emperor Kobun who fled the Jinshin War, and it gives you a sense of the depths of history. Nowadays, it is known as an art station with what is said to be the world's largest toilet, but its true charm lies in the tranquility of the Satoyama surrounding the station. In spring, cherry blossoms and rape blossoms decorate the platform, and at night, the illuminated rice fields reflect the train like a mirror. This scene shows us how railways can harmonize beautifully with nature as part of nature.

Tsukisaki. From here on out, the feeling of going deep into the mountains of Boso becomes even more intense. The forest radio station, which has been renovated from a former station, and the appearance of an old moss-covered platform give you the illusion that you have wandered into a fairy tale world. Around this station, there is also a road that leads to the "Chibanian" stratum that tells the story of the history of the earth, giving us a sense of a grand flow of time that goes beyond being a mere railway station. As I watch the exhaust smoke from diesel cars dissolving into the dark green air, I am convinced that this place has not been left behind by the wave of modernization, but was deliberately chosen to remain here.

Kazusa Okubo. When you get off at this station, which is quietly located in the deep forest, you will see a picture of Totoro on the wall of the station building, which will melt your heart. It is said to have been drawn by children from Okubo Elementary School, which used to be here, and there is something touching about the way it continues to watch over the station even now that the school is closed. The mountains loom behind the platform and the small village spread out below. The thin rail that connects them all shows how closely connected they were to people's lives. There aren't many stations that can be described as luxurious.

Yoro Valley. It stands out in a dignified manner and can be called the highlight of Kominato Railway's tourism. There is a footbath in front of the station, and travelers who have finished hiking are surrounded by steam as they wait for the train to arrive, a sight that is a daily sight at this station. This station, which used to be called ``Asaohara,'' was changed to its current name in order to serve as a tourist route, and has quietly watched over the changes of the times. The hint of the deep valley behind the station building and the smell of sulfur wafting in from somewhere give you a strong impression that this is the back seat of Boso.

Kazusa Nakano. It is the junction of the Boso crossing, where the vermilion diesel cars of the Kominato Railway meet the yellow cars of the Isumi Railway. In the past, this station has always played the role of a ``boundary'', serving as a connection point with the Japanese National Railways Kihara Line, and even more anciently as a terminal station that dreamed of extending to the Chiba city area. Today, the thatched roof that adorns the roof of the station building quietly welcomes those who have completed a long journey or those who are about to begin a new journey. The sight of two private railways lining up hand-in-hand seems like a sign of solidarity for the survival of local railways, and I can't help but feel deeply moved.

Tsurumi. It is a strategic point between Keihin and the starting point of the Tsurumi Line, so it retains some dignity. As you cross the long platform of the Tokaido Main Line, cross the overpass, and head towards the elevated Tsurumi Line platform, even though there is a modern device called an automatic ticket gate, there is a unique sense of tension as you enter the coastal industrial area. In the past, many freight trains departed from and arrived at this station, and it has a history of being part of the main artery that supported Japan's rapid economic growth. It is a sight unique to this station that among the passengers transferring, there are many ``industrial warriors'' dressed in work clothes, a clear contrast from the suits heading for the city center. Standing at the edge of the platform, one gets a sense of the inorganic yet powerful iron town that lies ahead of the intricate railway tracks. The contrast between the modernized station building and the branch line platform, which still retains traces of the Showa era, gives travelers a strange sense of relief.

National highway. When you step into this station, you feel as if time has stopped at the time it opened in 1945. The Daiichi Keihin National Highway passes overhead, and the station building built under its heavy guard has the exposed concrete surface and even the bullet holes from machine gun fire that survived the war. The light that shines into the dimly lit premises has a dampness that bounces off modern LED lighting, giving it a dull glow reminiscent of incandescent lights at twilight. In the arch-shaped space under the viaduct, the remains of the shops that once stood there lie silent, and even the sound of the wind passing through them can be heard like a whisper telling of the bustle of the past. In the world of Reiwa, it must be said that there are very few places in the suburbs of Tokyo that have maintained such a rich ``Showa era'' tranquility. Every time the trains on the up and down lines roar overhead, it makes me realize that this old building is still very much alive and well.

Tsurumi Ono. This station, which used to be called ``Kogyo Gakko-mae,'' served as a dividing line between the simple and sturdy residential area that surrounds it and the large factories that lie ahead. Once you get off the station, you will see a quiet streetscape that retains the atmosphere of a downtown area, and you can hear the lively voices of students attending a nearby high school, but on the other hand, the deep bass sounds of factories carried on the sea breeze remind you that this area is deep in the Keihin Industrial Area. The station building itself is a simple structure, but I feel that its modesty embodies the idea of ​​the railway as a place of unpretentious living. It gives the impression that the footprints of the many people who once used this station to commute to the factory are carved into the concrete of the platform. Although it is not a flashy tourist destination, the certainty that daily life is connected by the iron thread of railways quietly permeates the hearts of travelers.

Bentenbashi. Once you cross the bridge from which the station takes its name, you will find yourself on a vast site that supports Japan's heavy industry. This station is adjacent to the Tsurumi Line train depot, so railway enthusiasts can't help but feel the beauty of its functionality as a base for train operations. When you get off the platform, you can see a herd of trains parked right in front of you, quietly standing there like racehorses waiting for their turn. During the morning and evening commuting hours, people heading to nearby major electronics manufacturers and shipyards are expelled and sucked in again. This regular flow of people gives you the feeling that it is the heartbeat of this line. The air, where the scent of the ocean and the smell of oil mix slightly, seems to contain a sense of pride as a working town, which is different from Tsurumi's port town. The nameless flowers blooming next to the railroad tracks, adding the only color to the inorganic steel landscape, somehow evoke a sense of the poetic sentiment of the Showa era.

Asano. The station is located at the heart of the fan, where the main line of the Tsurumi Line and the branch line heading towards Umi-Shibaura split into a fan. The station is named after Mr. Soichiro Asano, who can be said to be the father of the Keihin Industrial Area, and it quietly tells the history of the development of this land, which was opened up through reclaimed land. Standing on the triangular platform, one can see the rails leading to the sea on one side and a deeper industrial area on the other, emitting a dull glow, inviting the traveler's mind into the industrial labyrinth. When I think about the history of the many freight trains that used to pass through this junction in a hurry, I feel that the current silence actually emphasizes the importance of this station. The moment you sit on an old bench exposed to the sea breeze and wait for the next train gives you a taste of the luxurious ``blankness of the Showa era'', cut off from today's speedy society.

Shinshibaura. This station, located one step before the end of the branch line and facing the canal, has a heavy responsibility as the gateway to Toshiba's huge office. As you look at the ripples of the Keihin Canal right next to the platform and the silhouettes of cranes and gas tanks on the opposite shore, you realize that this place is as quiet as an ``isolated island.'' The number of general passengers getting on and off the station is extremely limited, and the unique rhythm of this station is created by the activities of people who move in time with the start and end signals of factories. Standing on the borderline where sea and land, industry and daily life intersect, you can feel the breath of steel and concrete that supported Japan's modernization, along with the scent of the ocean. At dusk, the way the factory lights sway on the canal's surface reminds us once again that even inorganic landscapes can have a certain emotion.

Umishibaura. It goes without saying that it is a unique terminal station that always makes its name in railway travelogues all over the country as the famous ``station where you cannot go out of the ticket gate.'' Just beyond the platform fence is the ocean of Keihin Canal, and the moment you step off the train, you are enveloped in an overwhelming sense of openness with an unobstructed view. The unique structure of the station itself, which is located on Toshiba's premises, is proof that the railway is deeply entrenched in the forefront of industry, and its strict boundaries further enhance the desire to travel. When you look at the boats passing by on the opposite shore and the Tsurumi Tsubasa Bridge at Umishiba Park, which is open to the general public, you will forget that you are only a few minutes from the center of Tokyo. This station, where the solitude of a dead-end car park and the majesty of the sea that stretches out in front of you coexist, is both the final destination of a journey and the perfect starting point for new thoughts.

Peace of mind. This station, named after Mr. Zenjiro Yasuda of the Yasuda Zaibatsu, is still an important hub for freight transportation and retains a strong atmosphere. When you look at the huge oil tanks surrounding the station and the side tracks leading to the US military's oil storage facility, you can clearly sense the pride that this area has in supporting the backbone of Japan's energy supply. In the past, tank cars full of oil were sent across the country from this station, and it gives the illusion that the roar of the steel still lingers in your ears. When you walk in front of the station, you can see the few remaining wooden buildings and old shops from the Showa era, giving you a sense of the quiet but certain traces of life after the frenzy of the period of high economic growth had passed. The scenery of a train yard, where inorganic freight cars sit quietly, presents us with a kind of art that is the result of the pursuit of functional beauty.

Musashi Shiraishi. Named after Motojiro Shiraishi, the founder of Nippon Kokan, this station is deeply etched in the memories of railway fans because it once had a platform with a sharp curve that branched off to the Okawa branch line. Nowadays, the platform has been removed and the station stands quietly on the main line, but if you get off the station and walk around the area, you can still see the intricate alleyways and old railroad crossings that remind you of the bustling times of the past. When you think about the history of how Mr. Shiraishi's ideal of an industrialized nation took root in this area and eventually developed into a huge industrial complex, the simple station building becomes even more dignified. The sound of distant factory operations and the vibrations of large trucks that can be heard through the gaps between the trains makes us realize that this station is still an active ``industrial port.'' The atmosphere, where the smell of iron and the old townscape mix together, gives travelers a sense of nostalgia and an irreplaceable sense of security.

Okawa. As the terminus of a branch line that slightly branches off from Musashi Shiroishi, there is a quietness here that will make you forget the hustle and bustle of the city. The station's name comes from paper manufacturing magnate Heizaburo Okawa, and its appearance, surrounded by high walls and huge factories, gives the impression of an industrial dead end. There are long periods during the day when no trains come by, and the sea breeze blowing across the rusted rails is a quiet reminder of the glory of freight transportation in the past. If you stand at the edge of the platform, you can see the remains of the former dedicated line, which is buried in weeds but still retains its outline, and you can clearly see the traces of the railways that have carried the heavy burden of Japan's modernization. When the sound of the motor of a single-row train returning home with only a handful of passengers echoes off the concrete walls and disappears, travelers can't help but feel a deep attachment to the unique solitude of this place.

Hamakawasaki. This station, where the Tsurumi Line and the Nambu Branch Line intersect, has a truly strange and interesting structure, with two station buildings separated by a public road. The entire station area is adjacent to the vast grounds of JFE Steel, and the constant sound of freight train shunting work and the heavy roar of locomotives make you keenly aware that this is the heart of logistics. The complex wiring that can be seen from the overpass can be called a labyrinth of iron, and it is a testament to the strength of the railways that supported industrialization in the Showa era. Even the hassle of passing through an automatic ticket gate and walking along a public road to transfer trains, which is a little outside of modern efficiency, adds spice to the station's unique history and atmosphere. Rusty steel, the smell of oil, and chimney smoke in the distance. All of these things come together to form this station's unique ``working railway'' aesthetic.

Showa era. This station, which is named after the era name itself, has continued to watch over turbulent times since its opening in 1930. The station's name comes from the adjacent Showa Fertilizer, now Resonac, factory, and as soon as you exit the station building, you can see the silver pipes of a gigantic chemical plant writhing in front of you. At dusk, the long shadow of the inorganic steel tower stretches over the platform, as if to quietly convey the pride that this place has had in supporting the dawn of Japan's chemical industry. When we imagine the scene in which many factory workers would have disembarked at this station and proudly looked up at the smoke billowing in the sky, the sight of it as a quiet, unmanned station today evokes deep emotion. Sitting on the simple platform and being blown by the wind blowing in from the canal, you can feel that although the visible scenery has changed, the strength of the ``Showa'' era, which flows like a basso continuo, still has roots in this area.

Ogimachi. The final destination of the main line of the Tsurumi Line is a mysterious space where dead-end tracks and somewhat leisurely cats coexist. The station's name comes from the Asano family's crest, which means "fan," indicating that this is the end of Soichiro Asano's dream of reclaimed land. The sight of the tracks continuing uninterrupted past the platform and being sucked deeper into the factory proves that railways are still functioning as an active logistics device. The moment you wait for your return train in the air where the scent of the ocean and the smell of coal mix together gives you a strange sense of accomplishment of having arrived at the edge of the city, and a somewhat lonely sense of travel. Behind a long line of freight trains moving slowly, the canal leading to the Pacific Ocean gently reflects the light. A solemn yet somewhat humane landscape befitting a terminal station in an industrial area remains here.

Takaoka. As a key point on the Hokuriku Route, this station was once the site of the express trains ``Raichou'' and ``Shiratori'' that left their majestic footprints. With the opening of the Hokuriku Shinkansen, the parallel conventional line was transformed into the ``Ainokaze Toyama Railway,'' but even now, even though the area has been elevated, the heavy atmosphere of the foundry industry that this town is proud of has not been lost. The Johana Line and Himi Line start here and extend their tentacles north and south, and the sound of diesel car engines echoing through the concrete premises evokes the nostalgic scenery of railroads. If you look around the station, you will see the approach to Zuiryu-ji Temple, the family temple of the Maeda family of the Kaga Domain, and you will feel the multi-layered nature of history. Even though the former station building has been replaced with modern facilities, the station's pride as a transportation hub has not wavered in the slightest.

Etchu Nakagawa. This is the station where the Himi Line train that leaves Takaoka stops for the first time. Schools such as Takaoka Polytechnic High School and Takaoka High School are located right next to the station building, and the platform is filled with the energy of young people during rush hours. The city hall and art museums are within walking distance, and it is in a position that is close to the cultural center of the city of Takaoka, but its appearance is extremely simple and somehow exudes the intellectual tranquility of a regional city. The castle park of Maeda Toshinaga, who once ruled this area, is also nearby, and along the railway line, you can enjoy the atmosphere of each season. As I stood on the single-track platform, a short diesel train slowly approached. It is this sight that teaches us the preciousness of time in today's hectic world.

Noh town. This was once a railroad crossroads dominated by the hustle and bustle of freight transportation. The Shinminato Line branched off from the Himi Line, and freight cars bound for the huge factory complex were constantly passing through this station, using this station as a relay point. Today, the passenger platform is quiet, but when you look at the remains of the vast grounds and side tracks, you get the illusion that the pulse of the chemical and metal industries that supported this country's rapid economic growth is still echoing from underground. The area around the station is lined with lumber factories and warehouses, and the smell of salt and oil mixed together creates a travel atmosphere unique to port cities. On this flat horizon, where steam locomotives once pulled heavy freight cars, there is still a strong ``iron will'' that continues to support the backbone of industry.

Fushiki. This station has been the gateway to the port town, where Otomo Ieyamochi admired the scenery since the Manyo period. It once prospered as a port of call for Kitamaebune ships, and since the Meiji era, it has been responsible for the logistics of Hokuriku through the cooperation of railways and ships. The stately structure of the station building and the remnants of a freight branch line that once extended to the wharf tell us that this station was not just a transit point, but had a role as a large ``terminal point.'' When I landed on the platform, the wind blowing from the mouth of the Oyabe River shook the old shed. Historic sites such as Nyoi no Watari and Shokoji Temple tell us about the depth of history that lies behind the station. It is this sense of calm and stagnation before the Himi Line rushes out onto the coastline that invites travelers to take a moment to rest and ponder history.

Etchu region. This station stands quietly at the place where the train passes through the city of Fushiki and finally reaches the coastline. The station is close to the ruins of Etchubu-bunji Temple, which is where the station's name comes from, and it still conveys the depths of history that have continued since the Manyo era. A steep mountain looms directly behind the platform, and the blue expanse of Toyama Bay awaits you below. I can't help but wonder if the sound of the waves crashing against the rock surface was the same as it is now when Otomo Ieyamochi ruled this land. Although it is a small unmanned station, it is no exaggeration to say that the ``sea window'' that begins here is one of the highlights of railway travel. Standing in this place where the multi-layered history and the harshness of nature coexist, you will be reminded that railways are not just a means of transportation, but a bridge that connects time and space.

Rainy day. Just hearing the name of this station makes the heart of anyone who loves railways swell. The legendary ``Yoshitsune Rock,'' where Minamoto no Yoshitsune sheltered from the rain, sits right next to the railroad tracks, and the snow-capped Tateyama Mountain Range can be seen across the Sea of ​​Japan from the train window. Stations with such dramatic scenery are rare even across the country. In the past, many photographers would line up with tripods to capture that fleeting scene, and even today, you can still see pure amazement at the beauty of nature in the expressions of people landing on the platforms. The sea breeze blows across the platform, and the sound of the waves coming and going in harmony with the sound of the diesel car's engine is a scene that seems straight out of a travelogue. It is a station with such magical power that everyone can't help but stare out the window as they pass by.

Shimao. This station appears as the train passes through a dramatic rocky area on a rainy day and winds once again through a peaceful pine forest. Right next to the station is a beautiful sandy beach with white sand and green pine trees, giving off a nostalgic yet quiet atmosphere that symbolizes the summer vacation of the Showa era, which was once filled with beachgoers. The rows of pine trees that act as windbreaks, and the calm sea that stretches out beyond them, offer a gentle contrast to the rough coastline we saw earlier. Inns and old houses still remain around the station, and the scent of the sea can even be felt in the station's waiting room. The atmosphere of this ``casual seaside station'' that has remained because it was spared from becoming a flashy tourist destination is a quiet prelude to the end of the journey. As you stand on the single-track platform, the sound of waves coming from the sandy beach evokes memories of seasons gone by.

Himi. The dead-end track quietly tells us that this is the end of the railway. As the terminus of the Himi Line, the area's vast grounds are a reminder of the glory days when large quantities of seafood were once loaded into freight cars and shipped from here to all over the country. As soon as you step out of the station building, you will find yourself in a thriving fishing port town located at the base of the Noto Peninsula, and the aroma of seafood such as yellowtail can be felt everywhere. Along the route leading to the port, the old spirit of fish wholesalers and craftsmen is still alive and well, giving you a sense of the strength of the people who have overcome the harsh Hokuriku winters. The train quietly awaits its next departure at this place, where the sense of relief at the end of a journey, which is unique to a terminal station, is mixed with the time to return to daily life. It is this unwavering pulse of life, located in a place where railways run out, that provides the perfect emotional ending to your journey.

Unazuki. This station is the gateway to the rugged nature of Kurobe Gorge, and is the site of the passion that was once devoted to power development. Once you get off at the station building, the cool breeze of the Kurobe River caresses your cheeks. I can't help but feel a certain sense of emotion at the fact that this railway, which was originally built in the Taisho era as a track for transporting materials for the construction of a power plant, continues to spin its small wheels as one of Japan's leading mountain sightseeing railways.
The narrow-gauge freight cars and passenger cars that line the platform are small and adorable, but their features have a rugged, functional beauty that allows them to survive the steep slopes. In contrast to the hustle and bustle of the hot spring town in the background, the entire station is filled with a quiet sense of tension, as if from here we are entering an unexplored region. When Shunzo Miyawaki visited this place in the past, he may have sensed this unique ``sign of departure.'' It's also fun to look beyond the railway while imagining things like this.

Kuronagi. This is the first stop after leaving Unazuki, and it is literally a ``treacherous place'' as it clings to a sheer cliff. Right next to the station, a 60-meter-tall rear bridge shows off its red steel frame, and the dry rumbling sound of train wheels is sucked into the deep valley floor. The lingering sound can be said to symbolize the depth of Kurobe Gorge.
The important role of this station is to serve as a ``hot water route'' that delivers the source of Unazuki Onsen. If you look at the mountainside, you will see hot water pipes running along the mountain like blood vessels, making you realize that this is not just a scenic spot, but an active industrial heritage site that supports human life. Only a few people are disembarking from the platform, but in that silence, you can still feel the strong presence of men facing the harshness of nature, which has remained unchanged since the early days of power development.

text_en:
Bell fishing. This area, which has the character ``bell'' in its name, is said to have been named because its unique topography resembles the shape of a bell. It is no exaggeration to say that the main features of this station are the natural open-air bath that gushes out on the banks of the Kurobe River, and the presence of perpetual snow that does not melt even in summer.
It is a peaceful landscape where mountaineers and tourists can relax, but if you look at it from the perspective of a railway fan, the real pleasure of this line is the way trains come and go and the switchbacks that take place here. The wisdom of our ancestors who tried to make the most of the limited flat land and overcome the steep terrain comes back to us with the dull sound of the switchgear. The whiteness of the eternal snow seen from the train window provides a refreshing feeling that makes you forget the hustle and bustle of the city, but at the same time, it also quietly speaks to the weight of history, showing how many harsh winters this valley has endured.

Keyakidaira. It is a terminal station that is accessible to the general public, and from here it leads to the forbidden area of ​​the Kansai Electric Power Kurobe Exclusive Railway, which continues to the Kurobe Daiichi Dam and is only accessible to select people. Standing at this point, which is about 600 meters above sea level, the mountains you can look up to are even higher, the valley below is even deeper, and you will be overwhelmed by the enormity of the natural formations.
The area around the station is dotted with rough rock walls called Hitokuiwa Rocks and steep roads leading to Meiken Onsen, and you can't help but think of the fierce human drama that went into the construction of the ``Black Four'' in the past. Even though it functions as a terminal, there is a sense of desolation at the very end, probably because this is the border between civilization and virgin forest. As we watch the small trolley train that has been bouncing all this way, waiting for its turn to depart, and think about the sweat and tears that were shed to build this railway, and the source of the electricity that supported Japan's modernization, the end of the journey becomes the beginning of new reflections.

Minamitoyama. It is a truly interesting sight to see the city's tram line and the Fujikoshi/Kamidaki Line railway line connected here. This area was once the starting point for the Tominan Railway, and there is still a train depot there, and the smell of iron and oil wafts through the air. The inorganic concrete appearance of the station building, which also serves as a station building, is like a relic that still conveys the energy of modernization during the Showa era, and the sight of passengers quickly changing from the streetcar gives us a sense of its pride as the artery of the city. I feel like I get a glimpse of the simple and sturdy side of the Toyama Local Railway organization.

text_en: Asana town. When I get off at this station, which has only one single platform and has no frills, I feel like I have come into contact with the essence of daily life on a local private railway. Although it has a long history, having opened in the Taisho era, its appearance that quietly blends into the surrounding residential area shows how the railway has taken root in people's lives. This area must have once been a rural area, but now trains run between the rows of houses. In the short time you spend standing on the platform waiting for the breeze, you can feel the vestiges of the rural landscape of the past intersecting with the quiet breath of modern life.

Kamihori. The idyllic atmosphere of the Kamidaki Line becomes even more intense when you arrive at this station. The wide structure of the building, which may have once housed a freight siding, somehow reminds us of the bustle of the past. This area has a long history of prospering as a gathering and distributing area for agricultural products, and the scenery that stretches out through the train window seems to have a strong earthy smell. Although it doesn't have particularly flashy equipment, the rusted fences and well-worn wooden benches testify to the integrity of the railway, which has remained unchanged over the years.

Kosugi. As an important station on the former Hokuriku Main Line and the current Ainokaze Toyama Railway, this station has a special character. As the center of Imizu City, the memory of the area flourishing as a post town on the Hokuriku Kaido in ancient times is reflected in the calm townscape around the station. The long platform remembers the long formations of limited express trains ``Raicho'' and ``Shirasagi'' that once ran through it, and now serves as a regional transportation hub, receiving the hustle and bustle of students and commuters. The wide Hokuriku sky that can be seen from the overpass, and the history of the solid station building withstanding the wind and snow, give travelers a deep sense of relief.

Cloth city. When I hear the name of this station, I feel like it evokes memories of a distant time when there were markets along the highway and people who sold cloth gathered there. This station, which has been rooted in the southern part of the Toyama Plains since its opening in 1919, has now completely blended into a calm residential area. With its short platform and simple waiting room, it has an appearance that befits a small local private railway station, giving off a sense of purity without excessive decoration. In the past, the sky may have been more spacious, but even now, the sound of the railroad crossing announcing the arrival of a train still echoes as the heartbeat of the city's reliable life.

development. The name of the station is very straightforward and conveys a desire for the future, but in reality, the area surrounding the platform is a mixture of peaceful countryside and new housing. The aspirations of our ancestors who cultivated the land and expanded the lives of the people are condensed in these two letters. Around the station, the remains of a former rural area coexist with a modern appearance that has accepted the expansion of the city, and it seems to quietly tell the story of the changes of the times. This unmanned station, which has no special structure, continues to function casually but reliably as a means of transportation for the region, and it shows us the original landscape of the existence of railways.

Tsukioka. When you get off at this elegantly named station, you can feel the clean air that leads to the end of the Toyama Plain and the foothills of the Tateyama Mountain Range. The spacious premises, which would have once been bustling with freight transport and trains passing by, is a reminder of the importance of the Kamidaki Line in the past. The warm appearance of an old wooden station building, as if its corners have been worn down over the years, melts the hearts of travelers. The view of the well-maintained rice fields visible from the train window and the rows of old farmhouses that stand watching over them convinces us that Japan's original landscape is still alive here.

Daisho. The name of the station has a profound sound, hinting at the existence of a village headman who once ruled this area. This station is located on an alluvial fan created by the Joganji River, and is in a truly scenic location with a close view of the Tateyama Mountain Range. The surrounding area is dotted with ancient villages, and the appearance of the houses that make you feel the weight of history conveys the strength of the rural culture of the past. Standing on the platform and waiting for the train while feeling the wind blowing down from the distant peaks can be called a blissful moment that makes you forget the hustle and bustle of modern life. Toyama's simple and sturdy culture is firmly rooted in this small station.

Upper waterfall. When you get off at this station, you can feel the pride of the town, which once prospered as the center before the merger of towns and villages, quietly coming through from the spaciousness in front of the station and the appearance of the old houses. The weight of its history, which was founded in 1912 as the terminal station of the Tominan Railway, is not just for show, and even today it still exudes the dignity of being the core station that bears the line's name. The wooden station building gives off a somewhat sooty yet warm atmosphere that makes you feel the warmth of people, presenting us with a typical scene of local private railways in the Showa era. When you look at the spacious grounds where a lot of agricultural products were once loaded onto freight cars and transported to the city, you can once again get a sense of the long history of this area and the great role that railroads have played.

Okawa temple. In the past, along with the bustle of the amusement park, many families would arrive at this station on holidays with cheers, but the current silence has brought those memories into sharp relief. The cliff-like location overlooking the clear waters of the Joganji River is proof of how railways have connected people to their destinations while facing the harshness of nature. Even after the hustle and bustle of leisure has passed, the same pure breeze still blows through this area, where the approach to Osen-dera Temple, the ancient temple from which the station takes its name, continues. The deepening shadow of the mountain seen from the edge of the platform gives the traveler a feeling of tension as the train finally leaves the plains and enters the deep heart of Tateyama.

Iwatoji Temple. This strategic location, where two railway lines, the Fujikoshi-Kamitaki line and the Tateyama line, converge, is full of majesty as the ``gateway to the mountains.'' The stately wooden station building, which retains a strong vestige of the Taisho period, is so famous that it has even been chosen as the setting for a movie, and the moment you pass through the ticket gate, you feel as if the hands of the clock have been rewound several decades at once. As the entrance to Oyama Shrine, this station has welcomed many worshipers and travelers since ancient times, and has a unique atmosphere where the culture of prayer and modern railways are inextricably linked. The complex intertwining of two railway lines within the premises gives us a strong sense of the functional beauty of the railway system and that it is the juncture of the long journey that Toyama Regional Railway has taken.

The old residential area around the station has been carved out over many years with the sound of trains arriving and departing, and the breath of life that has passed through them over the years is quietly ingrained in the hearts of travelers.

Although it has a simple structure that would have been unimaginable in the heyday of railways, it creates an intimacy similar to that of a streetcar. The Tateyama Mountain Range suddenly peeks out over the roof of the house flowing outside the window. It is the station that provides the most familiar and clear picture of Toyama's daily scenery.

Nowadays, the hustle and bustle of the past has calmed down, but the presence of heavy factories and the appearance of old shops surrounding them still conveys the unique melancholy of the industrial city of the Showa era. The smell of iron and the nostalgic remnants of wooden buildings mix together to create a somewhat rustic yet warm atmosphere unique to this station.

At dusk, watching students line up on the platform on their way home from school, you can feel the essence of a place called a station, which remains unchanged despite the changing times. This peaceful tranquility that makes you feel a little removed from the hustle and bustle of the city is the secret ingredient to your travel spirit.

text_en: Minamitoyama. This station is the junction of the Fujikoshi Line and the Kamidaki Line, and is also a connection point with the city train, making it a station with a lot to see. A streetcar depot is also attached to the spacious premises, and the mixture of old and new vehicles once again reminds us that Toyama is a ``railway kingdom.'' When you think about the fact that the Sasatsu Line once ran from here, you can't help but be impressed by how thick the history of the railway is. The footsteps of passengers transferring trains, the sound of train horns, and the lively atmosphere that continues to give this station its unique character.

text_en: Electric Railway Toyama. This terminal, which is located under the elevated Hokuriku Shinkansen, maintains its dignity as the gateway to the Tateyama Mountain Range. It used to be a large station building above ground, but its appearance has changed with the demands of the times, and now it has a modern look. However, once you pass through the ticket gate and stand on the platform, you'll find a heavy-duty train, typical of local trains, waiting to depart, and it will lift your spirits. People passing by are carrying backpacks and buying ekiben. All of these things eloquently demonstrate that this is not just a transportation hub, but a ``starting station'' where dreams and aspirations intersect.

Inari town. This corner of the fan, where the main line and the Fujikoshi line split into left and right, gives you a sense of the original railroad scenery whenever you visit. In the vast garage behind the platform, famous cars that once ran through the hustle and bustle of the city are quietly spending the rest of their lives blowing in the Hokuriku wind. When I look at the overlapping railroad tracks and the appearance of the old overhead wire poles, I feel like I can hear the ``breathing of railroads'' that has been forgotten in this modern era where efficiency is the only focus. The regular vibrations that occur when a train crosses a turnout connects past prosperity with present peace. This is the station that gives you a mysterious sense of security.

Shinjo Tanaka. It is located in such a place that you can feel that you are about to start your real journey by train after passing through the city of Toyama. Although it is a relatively new station, having been built in the Heisei era, the surrounding landscape, where houses and fields intermingle, creates a calm atmosphere typical of Toyama. As the station name suggests, this place is a combination of the former names of ``Shinjo'' and ``Tanaka,'' where old and new ways of life coexist. The line of trees flowing outside the window and the ridgeline of Mt. Tateyama in the distance make this station not just a passing point, but an important bookmark where you can feel the breath of the area.

Higashishinjo. When you step into the old wooden waiting room of this station, you feel as if you have traveled back in time to the Showa era. There are traces of the old highway in front of the station, and you can't help but think of the days when people's lives revolved around this station. A solid tiled roof and well-used benches. They are also evidence of the history of seeing off and welcoming countless commuters and students. The sound of a railroad crossing as a train approaches echoes through a quiet residential area. Even that tone reaches my ears with a somehow nostalgic and compassionate feeling. That kind of warm atmosphere still lingers in the air at this station.

Ecchu Ebara. This station, which is close to the majestic flow of the Joganji River, is located at the intersection of development as a residential area and the traditional rural landscape. When you stand on the platform, you can feel the breeze blowing across the river and feel the breath of nature overlap with the rhythm of the railway. Considering the history of this area, which once prospered as a farming area blessed with abundant water, it becomes clear that the orderly townscape of today was also built on the efforts of our predecessors. Although it is not overly decorative, it is no exaggeration to say that its simple and sturdy appearance, which silently supports daily life, is the true essence of the local railway line.

Etchu Misato. This is a station that makes you realize that you have finally crossed the Joganji River and stepped deep into the vast Toyama plains. The surrounding green rice fields and the mountains of the Northern Alps tower beyond them. The view from this station is full of tranquility, worthy of being called an original Japanese landscape. The remains of the campus, which was once bustling with rice shipments, evoke a faint melancholy. However, even today, when you see local children running energetically on the platform, you can see that the railway is cherished as a local treasure, and it makes you smile.

Etchu Funabashi. The entrance to Funahashi Village, known as the smallest municipality in Japan, has a truly stylish design, with a library attached to the station building. Books and railways. At first glance, the two seem unrelated, but they harmonize perfectly at this station, creating an intellectual tranquility. While waiting for the train, I turn the page and suddenly look up and see the railway. It makes me think that there is no such thing as luxury time. The big aspirations of a small village have come to fruition in the form of this station building. Travelers cannot help but feel deep respect for this spirit.

Terada. The structure of this station, where the Main Line and Tateyama Line are intricately intertwined and the platforms are arranged in a V-shape, gives it the feel of a sacred place for railway fans. Walking along the passages that extend from the station building to each platform, you will feel a strange sense of exhilaration, as if you were walking inside a gigantic mechanical device. In the past, many mountaineers and tourists would transfer here and depart for their respective destinations. The echoes of that bustle can be felt in every corner of the wooden handrails of the old overpass and rusted signboards. This place is filled with the unique sense of tension and anticipation that comes with being at a crossroads.

Etchu Izumi. This small station, which blends into the surrounding quiet countryside, gently embraces the ``solitude'' that is the real pleasure of train travel. A home placed alone in a sparsely populated area. However, there is certainly a solid work being done by people who need this station. The sound of the wind shaking the rice ears and the distant sound of trains running. A space where all other sounds are excluded is the best medicine for a mind tired of the hustle and bustle of modern society. The luxury of nothing exists in this station. It's worth visiting here just to enjoy the tranquility.

Ainoki. It is located in the center of Kamiichi town, giving it a somewhat nostalgic ``entrance to the town'' feel. The area around the station is lined with old private houses, giving it an intimate atmosphere where you can hear the greetings of people passing by. The unique culture and lifestyle that once existed in a small regional city is still preserved around this station. It gives me such a sense of relief. Sitting on a bench on the platform and looking at the city lights at dusk, I get a keen sense of how railways are more than just a means of transportation, they have played a role like a bond that binds the hearts of local people together.

New Ainoki. This station, which was born as a new lifestyle base not far from Ainoki Station, is simple yet pursues modern convenience. The existence of these new stations in the subway, which has many old stations with a long history, is proof that the railway is still evolving and continues to exist. New housing has sprung up around the station, infusing the station with the vitality of the younger generation. Here you will find a light and airy ``Reiwa railway landscape'' that is completely different from the stately station buildings of the past. While cherishing the past, we extend the track toward the future. It is also a great experience to stand on this fresh platform and feel the strong will of Chitetsu.

Launched on the market. This station, which forces you to switchback, a kind of railway ritual, makes you feel like it's a major turning point on the subway main line. At this point, the train changes direction and begins running again, looking up at the Tateyama Mountain Range. This area was once bustling with visitors to Oiwasan Nissekiji Temple, and even today, it is still home to pride as a temple town and the industry that supports Toyama's medicinal capital. The stately appearance of the station building conveys its dignity as not just a transit point, but as the ``face'' of the town. The sight of the driver and conductor rushing back and forth across the platform. It is in this repetition of daily life that the beauty of style that local railways have continued to preserve resides.

Shingu River. After passing through the switchbacks at Kamiichi, the train begins to slip out onto the plains again, and this is the first quiet stop where the train can catch its breath. Surrounded by lush countryside as far as the eye can see. The memories of those idyllic times, when villagers used the sound of trains as a clock during breaks from farm work, are still vivid in the village. If you sit in the simple waiting room and look out the window, you will see a sea of ​​ears of rice that changes color with each season. Its graceful appearance, devoid of ornate decorations, quietly tells us how the railway blends into nature, as part of the earth.

Middle summation. It is deeply connected to the Toyama plains and has the feel of a rural station. The old-fashioned atmosphere that the wooden station building exudes is full of irresistible charm that would make any Showa era travel writer want to stop writing. In the past, many agricultural products were shipped from this station, and the smoke from the steam locomotives would have wafted into the sky. Although it is now a quiet, unmanned station, the contrast between the neatly divided fields and the mountains towering in the distance speaks louder than anything to the rich history that this area has nurtured.

Nishikazumi. This station, located on the edge of a local city where houses and fields coexist, makes us realize how deeply railways penetrate into the details of people's lives. In the morning and evening, students commuting to school decorate the platform, and in the afternoon, a quiet time passes by in the sun. It is this accumulation of casual scenery that is the greatest driving force for maintaining railways. There are no special sights. However, each frame of people's lives seen from the train window becomes the best landscape painting for travelers. This is the station that makes you feel that way.
