text_en: Nishinamegawa. As you approach the entrance to Namekawa's urban area, the unique sense of tension as the houses approach the railroad tracks further enhances the emotion of the journey. There are schools and hospitals nearby, and you can clearly see how people's lives circulate through the station. Paths that retain traces of the old highways intersect with railroad tracks, and the sound of railroad crossing alarms echoes as the rhythm of life. The somewhat nostalgic and lively atmosphere of this neighborhood seems to symbolize the health of a local city that has remained unchanged since the Showa era, and makes it feel truly reliable.

Nakaname River. It is located in the former central city of Namekawa, and the area around the station is lined with historic buildings and shops. The pride of this area, which once prospered as a post town on the Hokuriku Kaido, seems to be reflected in the appearance of the station. The concrete station building still retains the vestiges of the period of high economic growth, and has a somewhat urban feel to it. However, once you step into the alley, you will find an old townscape with the sea breeze of Toyama Bay blowing through. The old and new eras are intricately intertwined, creating a unique and profound atmosphere. This gives us a sense of the ``core'' of the town of Namekawa.

Namegawa. It is a connecting point with Ainokaze and Yama Railway, and is a station that enjoys the reputation of being the home of the firefly squid, a mystery of Toyama Bay. Although they share a spacious campus, the subway platform has a somewhat modest, yet unique atmosphere that gives a sense of self-respect. It feels like the excitement of the days when black freight cars were lined up to transfer cargo to and from the Japanese National Railways still lurks in the rusty color of the rails. Sea and mountains, main lines and branch lines. This station, where these intersect, shows us how multi-layered the travel network is.

Hamakazumi. As the name of the station includes the word ``hama'', it is a station full of lyricism, with the faint smell of sea breeze wafting through the air. The green pine trees in the windbreak forest planted along the railroad tracks have continued to watch over the harsh winters and mild summers of Hokuriku. The scenery is as beautiful as a painting. You can't help but feel nostalgic for the simpler times when people used to walk along the path leading to the seaside, carrying their burdens on their backs. The sound of the waves echoing in the distance overlaps with the sound of the train running. This pleasant silence is the greatest luxury at this station.

Early month addition. This station is close to the clear flow of the Hayatsuki River, which carries water from the melted snow from the Tateyama Mountain Range, and is a place where you can feel the power of nature firsthand. There are also industrial parks in the surrounding area, creating a scene that is like a microcosm of Toyama where nature and industry coexist. When a railroad was built by overcoming the Hayatsuki River, which was once feared as a torrent, what great hopes must our ancestors have had? The roaring sound of people crossing the railway bridge gives this station a unique sense of dynamism. In its echoes, I can't help but feel the footsteps of modernization and an unchanging reverence for nature.

Etchu Nakamura. The extremely simple wooden waiting room, as if the flow of time had stopped just at this station, deeply soothes the hearts of travelers. There is no need for a fancy station building. This station proves that as long as it has two rails and a small roof to protect it from the wind, it can become a fine stop. The sounds of birds can be heard from the surrounding forest, and the shadows of people working hard in the distance. The tranquil moments created by these events help modern people regain the ``mental peace'' that they had almost forgotten. Because there is nothing, there is everything. It gives me a sense of that kind of philosophical flavor.

Nishiozu. Once upon a time, this station was the gateway to Mirageland, and the station still retains the vestiges of gorgeous memories, when the platform would be filled with the cheers of children on holidays. Even now, I can see the Ferris wheel in the distance from the train window, and it evokes a faint melancholy, as if I were following in the footsteps of a dream. This section, which continued to run with the expectations of people visiting aquariums and parks, must have had the atmosphere of a special day on the subway. Sitting down on an old bench and looking out towards the sea, the bustle of the past mixed with the calm sound of the sea today gives a deep aftertaste that is perfect for the end of your trip.

Electric Railway Uozu. The majesty of the Station Department Store, which once gained fame as ``Japan's first elevated shopping street,'' is now fading into memory, but if you stand on the platform, you can feel the unique ``height'' that Uozu's once prosperous city left behind. If you look below, you can see a network of alleys that were once crowded with people visiting department stores, and you can still see the traces of the dreams of Showa era urban planning. Nowadays, the hustle and bustle has calmed down, and the texture of the concrete, washed by the sea breeze, gives this station a rather bland feel. The pride of Uozu, which has proudly lived as a port town and a commercial capital, still lives on quietly in this slightly elevated platform.

Shin Uozu. This place, which was once called ``Uozucho Station'', is a connection point with the Ainokaze Toyama Railway, and is full of vitality, with the lines of travel intersecting at all times. When passing through the underground passages between the platforms of both lines, the cool air smells like the familiar smell of coal and oil. Is it just a traveler's sentiment? In the past, many tourists who descended on this area in search of the mirage were welcomed by heavy railway vehicles and transported to Unazuki's inner parlor. The weight of that history is quietly hidden behind modern information signs. Every time the wind from the sea blows through, I am once again reminded of the important role this station has played as a "node".

Keida. This station is like a boundary line, where the train passes through the city of Uozu and finally enters the heart of Kurobe. The sea looms right next to the station, and the pine trees that form the windbreak show off their strength, having withstood the harsh winds and snows of the Hokuriku region. This platform, which was once the gateway to a fishing town and bustling with people transporting freshly caught fish, has now become a quiet place where only the sound of the sea and the sound of trains can be heard. As I sit in an old wooden waiting room and watch the color of the sky change every moment, I get a keen sense of how railways have continued to run in close contact with the workings of nature. Elegance within simplicity is the essence of Keida Station.

Electric Railway Ishida. In the past, special trains carrying beachgoers must have dropped off many cheering children at this station. Nowadays, such a lively summer seems like a distant past, and the area around the station is so calm and peaceful. A well-organized residential area and fields appearing in between. There is a landscape that can be called ``everyday beauty'' that is free from excess decoration. A well-used bench in the corner of the station building and a slightly faded timetable. Each one of them serves as a clock and a walking stick for the people living in this area, and is proof that they have lived together for many years. Even if a traveler decides to get off the train mid-way, the station welcomes them with the same tranquility. It makes me feel that kind of deep pockets.

Electric Railway Kurobe. This station, which used to be called ``Nishimikkaichi'' and then ``Sakuraicho'' before settling on its current name, is the heart of the northern subway, carrying a history dating back to the Kurobe Railway. In the past, materials and personnel needed to support the national project of constructing the Kurobegawa No. 4 Power Plant used this station as a starting point to venture into the mountains. I can't help but feel that that strong sense of mission still lingers in the style of the station building and the spacious grounds. Although it is now the core station of a quiet town, the neatly lined side tracks and the space reminiscent of the past for freight transport silently convey the pride of Kurobe as an industrial city. Divergence and convergence of railroads. It is such a stately station that just looking at the dramatic scenery makes your journey even more intense.

Higashi Mikkaichi. Located in the old town of Kurobe, you can feel the liveliness of the shopping street that stretches all the way to the railroad tracks from the train window. Once a center of commerce along the highway, where the voices of people could be heard constantly, this place still retains the intimate atmosphere that is typical of a ``town''. Every time the train door opens, the fragrant smell of soy sauce wafts in from somewhere, and the sounds of dinner preparations. These things give a warm blood to the inorganic existence of railways. The stately structure of a former merchant's house adds depth to the scenery around the station, reminding us of its importance as a base for daily life, not just a transit point.

Ogyo. It is located at a pleasant turning point, where the scenery outside the train window changes from that of the city to the rich countryside. The area around this station is dotted with old farmhouses, and their appearance, protected by a forest of mansions, symbolizes the typical beauty of the Toyama plains. There is a tranquility here that harkens back to a simpler time when people carrying heavy agricultural equipment would head to town from this platform. The sound of a railroad crossing announcing the approach of a train is absorbed by the mountains in the distance. In the lingering sound of that sound, you can feel the eternity of time that this land has been nurtured. It's not flashy, but it's a station that you'll never get tired of, and it's a station that gives you a real taste of the place.

tenement house The sight of a simple, one-track platform standing alone in an endless field of fields gives us a sense of the ``wabi-sabi'' of railways. Although the waiting area is too simple to be called a station building, it actually exudes a sense of purity that allows it to stand against the overwhelming nature that surrounds it. In the past, when this area was cleared and a railway was laid, the local people must have welcomed this station with great joy. This station seems so rooted in the earth that you can't help but imagine such things. At dusk, when the Tateyama Mountain Range turns red, travelers standing on this platform can experience a strange sense of unity, as if they are part of the vast landscape.

New Kurobe. This new station, which was born with the opening of the Hokuriku Shinkansen, is the very ``wind of Reiwa'' that has been blown into the long history of local railways. Modern facilities and a Shinkansen viaduct towering right next to it. They are giving new vitality to this line with a long history. However, even though it is a new station, the view of the mountain ridges and the cool wind blowing from there are no different from those of Kurobe, which was once loved by our predecessors. The old and new eras join hands, connecting the journey into the next century. Scenes that give you a sense of hope are spreading here. The traditional local railway has powerfully knocked on the door of a new era. The proof of that determination can be felt in this fresh home.

Tongue mountain. With the arrival of its modern neighbor, Shin-Kurobe Station, its historical tranquility has become even more prominent, making it a truly interesting station to visit. The station's appearance against the rolling hills, which is probably the origin of the station's name, gives it the feel of a ``satoyama station.'' You can almost hear the powerful footprints of people who once used this place as their base for mountain work. I sit on an old wooden bench and wait for the train to arrive. However, that alone is a luxurious time that cannot be replaced by anything in modern times. In a world that keeps changing, it teaches us the value of things that don't change. That kind of philosophical flavor resides in this small station.

Young chestnut. As the station name suggests, it is a truly refreshing stop surrounded by clear water and greenery. The rice fields seen from the platform reflect the sky like a mirror each season, or become a golden sea swaying in the wind. It is no exaggeration to say that the sight is a reflection of the richness that railways have brought to Japan. In the past, the rice transported from here kept many people alive. That sense of gratitude can still be felt in the calm atmosphere around the station. The sound of trains, the sound of the wind, and the sound of water in the distance. The symphony at Wakaguri Station, where these things are mixed together, gently and powerfully revives the tired souls of travelers.

Tochiya. This station is like a prelude to the end of the expansion of the Kurobe Plain and the railroad's entry into the increasingly steep mountain gorge. As the area begins to be surrounded by mountains, the sound of the train's motor becomes even more powerful, heightening travelers' expectations even further. In the past, the blessings of wood cut from the mountains and the abundant water of the Kurobe River must have been transported to this area through the main artery of railways. Although it is now an unmanned station in a quiet mountainous area, the deep greenery that looms behind the platform and the occasional sound of the river make you forget the hustle and bustle of the city. It is filled with a refreshing air that is suitable for the ``entrance to the canyon''.

Urayama. It is a station where you can feel up close how the railway overcomes the steep slopes as it weaves through the rugged terrain carved by the rapids of the Kurobe River. How much sweat was shed here to support the once grand national project of power development? The rustic masonry slopes and old telephone poles give you a sense of the layers of history, and the atmosphere of Showa era train travel remains strong. The villages around the station are nestled close to each other as if carrying the mountains on their backs, conveying the strong living strength of the people who have lived alongside the harsh nature. The moment when the train slowly climbs up the hill and slides into this station, the ``gasp of the railway'' is what tells us the real pleasure of traveling.

Lower exit. This station, located close to a small village in the mountains, gives the illusion that it has been there for decades, as part of the landscape. A simple platform and a small waiting room that has withstood the elements. The fact that they maintain only the bare minimum of functionality is a quiet testament to the fact that the railways were not a luxury, but a ``line of life'' for the people living in this area. When the train doors open, a rich mountain scent flows in. Once upon a time, people who finished their mountain work would take a breather at this station and think about the lights of the town. This simple scene still exists quietly next to the railway.

Get down. This station is at a dramatic turning point, as the railway makes a sharp turn along the right bank of the Kurobe River, and the gorge begins to reveal its true form. Just look at the sheer cliffs and the rough rocky bottom of the river from the train window and you'll see just how difficult it was to build a railway through this rugged terrain. The station itself is tranquil, but beneath that tranquility is the tenacity of our ancestors who tried to overcome nature, and the deep trust in the civilization of railways. The sound of the train's horn reverberates through the mountains, disappearing in layers. While savoring the afterglow of that sound, the journey continues deeper into the abyss.

Love book. This area, which bears the legend of Aimoto Bridge, which was once considered one of Japan's three most unusual bridges, is a geographically interesting place where the Kurobe River flows into an alluvial fan. The station itself stands quietly in the village, but the view of the rushing Kurobe River from here is an eloquent testimony to the fact that the history of power development has been with this river. In the past, personnel and supplies for dam construction were constantly transported from this station, and it must have been a hotbed of excitement as a front-line base for modernization. Although times are calmer now, there is still an irresistible energy in the air at this station, where the forces of earth and water intersect.

Uchiyama. Surrounded by deep mountains, the station offers a mysterious sense of isolation, as if it were isolated from the outside world, making it a favorite station for travel writers. Why is there such a fine railway running through this sparsely populated area? The answer lies in the hidden resources of the land of Kurobe and the wisdom of the people who tried to utilize them. When you're left alone on the platform after the train leaves, all you can hear is the sound of the wind and the roar of the river. By immersing ourselves in this absolute silence, we may be able to touch the essence of the act of ``travel'' for the first time. The air at this station is so clear that it makes you think so.

Otozawa. As the name of the station suggests, the sound of the rushing water of the Kurobe River constantly surrounds the platform. This place, which was finally reached by carving a steep cliff and repeatedly building tunnels and bridges, has a solemn atmosphere that makes you feel as if you are pushing the limits of railways. I can't help but think of the days when people who worked on dam construction in this area once listened to the sound of this torrent and held on to hope for the future. The water of Kurobe, peeking out from the edge of the platform, is filled with a deep blue color that draws you in, and confronts the traveler with the unfathomable majesty of nature. There are very few stations in Japan where you can listen to the ``voice of the living earth'' so closely.

Unazuki Onsen. The terminal point of the main line and the starting point for the unexplored Kurobe Gorge Railway. This is truly the place where the dreams of Toyama Regional Railway have come to fruition. Once you get off the platform, you'll be greeted by the smell of sulfur from the square in front of the station and the steam rising from the fountain. Although its appearance has changed from the former wooden station building, the sound of the Peace Bell echoing in the mountains and the atmosphere of the town lined with old inns still have a strong Showa era hot spring atmosphere. This feeling of exhilaration, unique to terminal stations, is a mixture of the sense of relief that the journey has come to an end and the sense of adventure as you head further into the countryside. While looking at the lights that decorate the Unazuki night, we can deeply appreciate the weight of the history and culture that railways have carried.

Terada. This station, where the main line and Tateyama line split into a V-shape, still conveys a unique sense of tension as a turning point in a journey. In the past, many mountaineers would carry large backpacks and change trains from here, aiming for the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route. You can feel the remnants of that lively atmosphere filled with anticipation in the historic wooden pillars and the well-worn texture of the overpass. Standing on the platform and looking at the rails splitting into two directions, I am reminded once again that railways are not just a means of transportation, but a bridge that connects our hearts to our destinations. The original functional beauty of railways and the somewhat nostalgic "Showa era transfer scenery" still exist at this station.

Chikozuka. This station, whose name suggests an ancient legend, stands quietly in a vast countryside. The legend of Chiko-no-zuka, from which the station's name originates, is evidence of the area's ancient history, and when combined with the idyllic scenery outside the window, it quietly stimulates the imagination of travelers. The simple platform is dotted with houses reminiscent of Toyama's famous ``sansei-mura,'' which harmonize with the backdrop of the Tateyama Mountain Range. The appearance of this station, which is free from excessive decoration, shows us how railways have naturally and sincerely integrated into people's lives as part of the earth. The time you spend waiting for the train to arrive while listening to the sound of the wind rustling the rice ears is truly the best part of traveling.

Tazoe. This station is located in a place where the rural scenery that adorns the windows of the Tateyama Line has become even more profound. If you look around the station, you'll see Toyama's traditional east-facing houses with heavy tiled roofs, giving you a sense of the rich agricultural culture that this area has fostered. In the past, the sound of trains was the rhythm of life for people working in the fields, and it appears that this happy symbiotic relationship continues even today. When I sit on a bench on the platform and watch the figures moving agricultural equipment in the distance, I get a strange feeling as if time is slowly flowing backwards. In fact, the deepest sense of travel is hidden in the ordinary scenery of everyday life. This small, unmanned station is silently telling us this.

500 koku. This station, which derives its name from the fact that the harvest in this area was once 500 koku, is the center of Tateyama town and still conveys the pride and vitality of the area. Although the station building itself has been renovated in a modern manner, the old townscape and shops surrounding the station retain the dignified dignity of a former regional city. In the past, how many people passed through this ticket gate, whether it was the base of the mountain railway or the center of local government? The sight of people passing by the station as trains arrive and depart proves that the railway is still beating as the heart of the town. Harmony between traditional place names and new station buildings. There, you can feel the layers of history that the town of Tateyama has walked through.

Enoki town. As the name of the station suggests, the large Enoki tree was once a landmark for travelers. With a school nearby, this station is filled with the lively voices of young people in the mornings and evenings, giving it one of the freshest atmospheres among subway stations. However, if you find yourself in the silence of the afternoon, you will realize that there is a calm time that is unique to Hokuriku's private railways. The smell of daily life suddenly wafts from the eaves of the houses lining the railroad tracks. This intimacy is what makes the Tateyama Line so interesting, as it has both the lightness of a streetcar and the prelude to a full-fledged mountain railway. It is truly a wonderful experience to listen to the sound of trains slowly approaching while feeling the remnants of the old highway.

Lower tier. This station, located on a vast terrace area formed by the Joganji River, has a unique atmosphere that makes you feel the strangeness of the topography. As the station's name suggests, it is located on the ``lower step'' of a terrace, making travelers aware of the dynamic formations created by Toyama's nature. It is surrounded by tall windbreaks and a solidly built farmhouse. The landscapes woven by these stories testify to the wisdom and efforts of our predecessors, who faced the harsh natural environment and turned it into abundance. Looking up at the Tateyama Mountain Range from the platform, the mountain range becomes even more rugged, giving off a solemn atmosphere as if the railway is finally determined to penetrate into the heart of the mountains.

Kamagafuchi. The name of the station is reminiscent of the legend that the Joganji River once raged and created a deep abyss, giving us a sense of the ruggedness of the terrain and the power of water. The area around the station is now a peaceful rural landscape, but the powerful sound of the place name shows that the area has not forgotten its history with the wonders of nature. The old wooden waiting room exudes a melancholy atmosphere that still retains the atmosphere of the ``stops'' described in travelogues from the Showa era. The sound of the train's motor echoes in the distant mountains, and at that moment when silence returns, travelers feel a deep sense of satisfaction. The glow of the railway passing through the village with its dark tiled roofs quietly illuminates the unchanging activities of this area.

text_en: Sawanakayama. This station is located at the entrance where the calm plains that extend from Gohyakukoku begin to change into the rolling hills that serve as the vanguard of Tateyama. The simple, one-line platform is dotted with rice paddies filled with abundant water and farmhouses protected by mansion forests, preserving the beautiful original scenery of the Toyama plains. In the past, firewood and charcoal and agricultural products were actively transported from this area, making us think of the railway as the only artery that supported the local life. The train headed for the Tateyama Mountain Range is still running smoothly here without panting. The sound of the light joints being absorbed into the silence of the mountains brings an indescribable sense of freshness to the hearts of travelers.

Iwatoji Temple. This station, which joins the Fujikoshi and Kamitaki Lines, is the gateway to Oyama Shrine Mae Hoheiden, a base of Tateyama worship, and is filled with dignity that has attracted many worshipers since ancient times. When you step into the solid wooden station building, which still retains a strong vestige of the early Showa era, you will see the pride of being a terminal that supported the mountain climbing boom in the past, etched into every scratch on the pillars. Multiple railroad tracks cross the vast premises, and the intricate branching of passing vehicles gives the impression of a strategic railway hub. In this place, where the enthusiasm of visiting shrines and temples in the past intersects with the expectations of modern mountaineers, the timeless ``prayers'' and ``traveling sentiments'' hang in the air like mist.

Yokoe. Once you pass Iwakuraji Temple, the sight of the plains disappears from the train window, and the steep gorge carved out by the Joganji River approaches. The area around this station was once known as a base for climbing Mt. Tsubasa, and as a place surrounded by primeval forest that had the feel of a secluded area. When you stand on the platform, the sound of the river's murmur echoes even higher, and the cool wind blows through, making you realize how much altitude you've gained. I feel like there are remnants of a time before the development of electric power, when the wild nature remained as it was, hidden in the huge stones next to the railroad tracks and the thick trees. It is a station that gives you a pleasant and tense feeling of stepping far away from the hustle and bustle of the city and into the abyss of nature.

Chigaki. The biggest attraction of this station is not the station itself, but the Chigaki Railway Bridge that you cross immediately after the train departs. The sight of the train straddling the deep valley of the Joganji River is the biggest highlight of the Tateyama Line, and the view from the train window is truly breathtaking. The solid, rusted truss structure eloquently tells us how fierce the challenges faced by our predecessors who built this iron bridge were against the ravages of nature. The villages around the station are also lined up against the slopes overlooking the river, giving us a sense of the strength of the people who have lived with the harsh natural environment. The deep vibration that resonates in your stomach when you cross a railway bridge is the true travel feeling that this station has.

Arimineguchi. As the station name suggests, it used to be the base for the construction of the Arimine Dam and the entrance to the Arimine Forest Road, and has a history of heavy traffic between people and goods. The reason why the station was renamed from the former ``Omi'' reveals the passion for the national project of power source development hidden deep in the mountains. Nowadays, that hustle and bustle is a distant memory, and the station building has regained its calm as a quiet mountain stop. However, the large station plaza and old warehouses give a faint hint of its former glory as a transportation hub. It's a truly luxurious experience to be immersed in the feeling of standing at the entrance to a remote, unexplored region while feeling the wind blowing down from the depths of the forest.

Main shrine. As we approach the final destination, Mt. Tateyama, the surrounding area begins to take on the atmosphere of a deep mountain valley. It is said that there was once a lively village near this area where people working on the construction of the power plant lived, but now it has the atmosphere of a railway ``hidden village'' where silence reigns. A shrine standing quietly in front of the station and moss-covered stone steps. They quietly assert that this area has been a sacred area for mountain worship since ancient times. Only the sound of the train's motor keeps the rhythm of modern times etched in this seemingly eternal still time. A confrontation between bare nature and railways, without any over-embellishment. It is this solemn scenery that gives us a deep aftertaste that is suitable for the final stage of a journey.

Tateyama. The train journey that started from Dentetsu Toyama has finally reached its final destination. This is no longer just a railway station, but serves as a majestic ``gate'' to the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route, the home of the gods. Once you get off the platform, the station is filled with the hustle and bustle of people heading to the cable car and the unique energy of the mountain men. This exhilarating feeling has remained unchanged since the golden age of mountain climbing. The contrast between the majesty of the snow-capped mountains that Showa era travelers would have seen and the modern station facilities makes us realize that we are truly standing at the intersection of civilization and nature. The railway ends here, but the traveler's thoughts continue higher and higher into the sky. It is a famous station among famous stations, where a refreshing sense of loss and new expectations intersect, which is unique to a terminal station.

In front of Minamitoyama Station. This is a major junction in the southern part of the city, where Toyama Local Railway's railway line and track line work hand in hand. When you get off at the bus stop, the tram depot is right next to you, and the colorful cars waiting for their turn create an intimate atmosphere that makes you feel like a small bird resting its wings. The spacious grounds are reminiscent of the heyday of railways, when the Sasatsu Line branched off from here, and it still retains its pride as a ``transport hub.'' The sound of the bell announcing the departure of the train and the heavy sound of the hanging motor. This mixes with the vibrancy of the city of Minamitoyama, inviting travelers to the heart of the ``Water City.''

Omachi. When you get off the bus stop, you will find yourself in a calm cityscape where old houses and new lifestyles coexist. The way the tracks run through the center of the road and the crowds of people on either side clearly shows how integrated the streetcars are into the city's landscape. Although there are no special tourist attractions, it is the place where you can experience the simple daily life of Toyama most closely. It gives us the illusion that the smell of dinner preparations is wafting through the window of a train passing by the eaves. In today's era of efficiency, it is this sense of leisurely speed that gives us peace of mind.

Horikawa Koizumi. This area, where major roads intersect, has a constant flow of people and cars, giving you a strong sense of the pulse of the city. In the past, this area was lined with shops and was probably filled with shoppers and students. The traces of that bustle can still be felt everywhere, and the faces of the people waiting for the train at the bus stop reflect the steady footsteps of the people who live in this town. The glow of the trajectory as it glides on the asphalt continues into the city center, weaving between buildings. The sight is like seeing a microcosm of the modernization that a local city has undergone, and it evokes a sense of pride and a little bit of sadness.

Koizumi town. It is a place that symbolizes the "frequent consideration" of the city tram, which has stops just a few hundred meters apart. There is no large station building, the platform is just one step higher than the sidewalk. However, there is an ideal form of public transportation where the elderly and children can easily use trains. If you look into the back alleys lined with what were once small factories and old wooden houses, you'll still find a sense of life that hasn't changed since the Showa era. Every time a train passes by, the entire city seems to take a deep breath, and there is a quietness here that is filled with vitality. I am once again impressed by how streetcars function as the capillaries of the city.

Nishinakano. Dotted with science museums, libraries, and lush parks, this area is full of the intellectual flavor of Toyama. The tree-lined avenues seen from the train window change color with the seasons, giving people a sense of peace as they pass through the city. In the past, young people eager to learn would get off at this bus stop and row out into the sea of ​​knowledge... imagining such a scene is one of the pleasures of being a travel writer. Modern cultural facilities and traditional trams that connect them. This exquisite contrast speaks to the deep bosom of the city of Toyama. This is a truly quaint stop where the tranquility of academic life and the hustle and bustle of everyday life blend comfortably.

In front of Kokando. When you hear the name of this station, there is no one who does not think about the history of Toyama's ``medicine''. The stately factory and museum towering in front of the bus stop are the very symbol of Toyama, the pharmaceutical capital. In the past, drug dealers carrying willow medicine boxes on their backs traveled all over the country, making Toyama famous. Its wealth and tradition shaped the cityscape of this area and became the driving force behind the construction of railroads. When you get off at the bus stop, you can feel the smell of herbal medicine coming from everywhere, probably because of the weight of the history of this place, which has been carved out for more than 300 years. While preserving tradition, we continue to support modern health. That sense of pride reverberates through this city with the sound of trains arriving and departing.

Uehonmachi. As you climb up the gentle slope from Kokando-mae, you will find yourself in the calm atmosphere of a commercial area. In the past, the area from here to Nishimachi was lined with long-established shops that supported Toyama's economy, and was filled with the energy of people passing by. Nowadays, that hustle and bustle has been replaced by an elegant calm, but you can still feel the pride of the city as a merchant town in every detail of the cityscape that you can see from the train window. If you take a quick look down the alley, you'll see old storehouses and lattice houses, and the contrast with the modern streetcars is truly beautiful. It is a stop that condenses the ``elegance'' of the city, so it would be a waste to just pass by.

Nishimachi. For the citizens of Toyama, this place occupies an absolute position as the ``center of the city.'' In the past, many people may remember a scene where a ``handling tower'' stood in the center of an intersection, and signal staff would deftly handle trains. In front of the bus stop is TOYAMA Kirari, which boasts a modern architectural beauty, but the full-length arcade that spreads out at its feet still has a strong Showa era feel to it. Shopping at a department store, spending time at a movie theater. The tram continues to carry the memories of those special days. This square, where people's expectations and vitality intersect, continues to beat strongly as the heart of Toyama.

Nakamachi (Nishimachi Kita). Just a stone's throw away from Nishimachi, where trains from the north converge, the frequency of trains coming and going is increasing, creating an irresistible vibrancy for train enthusiasts. The former "Nishimachi" bus stop was a little far away before it was renovated into its current form, and it can be said that the convenience of the town has improved dramatically. If you look around you, you'll see banks and office buildings, and you'll see the footprints of Toyama's modernization. While waiting for the train while being blown by the wind from the building, I watch the competition between new and old cars passing in front of me. Just by doing that, you can realize just how diverse and rich Toyama's public transportation system is.

text_en: Aramachi. This point, where the former Hokuriku Highway intersects, has a long history of flourishing as a transportation hub. When you get off the bus stop, you will still see the stately buildings of old drug dealers and merchant houses, proof that the city of Toyama has strongly recovered from the bombings of the air raids. If you think of the road that once ran east from here to Edo and Kyoto, you can see that the tram rails also play a role as a modern-day "highway." There is something nostalgic about the sight of a train passing through the streets at dusk, when the street lights are just beginning to come on, and it is full of dignity as a ``Japanese urban landscape'' that should be preserved.

Sakurabashi. This stop, located at the foot of the bridge that crosses the Matsu River, is one of the most scenic spots in Toyama. Matsukawa, which was once the outer moat of Toyama Castle, is now a beautiful tree-lined avenue, with cherry blossoms in full bloom in the spring and autumn leaves coloring the water surface in the fall. When a train crosses a bridge, your field of vision opens up for a moment, and you feel as if the wind blowing across the river reaches inside the train. The harmony between the design of the bridge built in the early Showa period and the trains that glide over it is truly a painting. Along with the few civil engineering heritage sites that survived war damage, the ``emotion'' that this town has cherished is gently blended into the name Sakurabashi. This is a stop that makes you feel that way.

name_en: In front of the electricity building
text_en: In front of the electricity building. The ``Toyama Electric Building'' towering in front of the bus stop boasts a majestic appearance that can be said to be the hallmark of Hokuriku's modern architecture. Its stately exterior, designed in the Art Deco style, is a symbol of the prosperity of Toyama, the power kingdom. Once upon a time, the gentlemen responsible for Toyama's future gathered in this building and drew a blueprint for the city. As a witness to that history, the tram has continued to run in front of this building without change. The train lights reflecting off the building and the view of the elegant lobby through the windows silently tell us that this is not just an office district, but a place where Toyama's intelligence and pride come together.

name_en: In front of the subway building
text_en: In front of the subway building. This station, which is located behind the Chitetsu Building, which is the headquarters of the Toyama Regional Railway, has a dignified atmosphere that befits the entrance to a ``railway castle town.'' Once upon a time, many timetables were drawn up in this building, and the fate of the line was decided...I feel that the excitement of the site can still be felt from the building's appearance. A calm moment passes here, as if the train is catching its breath a little before the huge terminal called Toyama Station. People heading to the station or out on the town. The window lights of the head office building that continue to watch over them are the very will of the subway, which continues to support the movement of this city. It is a truly interesting stop that foreshadows the end or beginning of a journey.

name_ja: 電鉄富山駅・エスタ前
name_en: In front of Dentetsu Toyama Station/ESTA
text_en: In front of Dentetsu Toyama Station/ESTA. This stop, nestled in the heart of the huge terminal building ``Esta'' on the subway main line, is the point of contact where long-distance trains and city trains shake hands. In the past, travelers returning from Tateyama or Unazuki, carrying large luggage, would transfer to the tram here. The gorgeous display windows of department stores that we see on those occasions have served as a sort of dividing line, marking the end of our journey and the beginning of our daily lives. Although the appearance of the buildings has changed over time, the cheerful footsteps of people heading out into the city from here have not changed at all since the Showa era. It is like a bookmark that turns the pages from the big story of railways to the small story of walking around town.

Toyama station. This is a utopia that modern Japanese railway technology has reached, where streetcars slide directly under the elevated Hokuriku Shinkansen. The railway that once separated the north and south sides of the station has been removed, and watching the streetcars leisurely passing by makes you realize that the blood flow of the city has become truly connected. At first glance, the sight of state-of-the-art LRT trains quietly arriving and departing may seem like a futuristic city, but it is also a pleasure for travelers to recall memories of the solid brick station buildings and sooty overpasses of the past on the other side of the elevated tracks. An unchanging sense of mission as a transportation hub is alive in new things. They are condensed under this open dome.

Shintomi town. This is the stop where the train departs from the huge Toyama Station and first immerses itself in the hustle and bustle of the city. There are business hotels and restaurants in the area, and you can clearly see people in business suits returning from business trips, and the liveliness of people heading out into the night through the train windows. In the past, this area must have had its own unique bustle as a downtown area located in a prime location in front of the station. Nowadays, it gives an impression of being orderly, but if you take a step down the alley, you can hear the breathing of Toyama's past through the gaps between the old buildings. The track leading to the city center is surrounded by buildings and feels slightly narrow. That feeling of oppression is the prelude to the city journey that is about to begin.

name_en: In front of the prefectural office
text_en: In front of the prefectural office. When you get off the bus at the stop, you will see the grand and magnificent Toyama Prefectural Government Building, which was completed in 1930, in front of you. Looking at the beautiful exterior of the building in the early modern revival style, I am once again reminded that this is the political center of Toyama Prefecture. The calm water surface of Matsukawa flowing in front of the station and the fountain in Kencho-mae Park. The orderly scenery they create has a mysterious power that transforms even the sound of busy trains into something like elegant music. The disciplined atmosphere that once existed in the government district still lingers around this bus stop. Streetcars are a perfect match for this place, which is a symbol of stability and trust that is timeless.

Marunouchi. This stop, which is close to the inner moat of the former Toyama Castle, has the dignity of being a strategic point where the loop line diverges. The time you spend waiting for the train while looking at the stone walls that retain the remnants of the past and the water in the moat is a time when you can feel a piece of history. From here, the loop line that curves southward and the line that continues straight ahead diverge, giving a sense of an ``intellectual divergence'' in railways. The name reflects the pride of being a castle town, and the latest low-floor vehicles smoothly cut curves. It is this contrast between old and new that speaks louder than anything else about the harmony between tradition and innovation that the city of Toyama has enjoyed. The way the greenery of the castle ruins is reflected in the silver body of the train is worth seeing.

Suwakawara. This stop is located in a peaceful residential area where the train passes through the bustling government district and castle ruins, allowing you to take a breather. Its name reflects its history as the riverbed of the Jinzu River, and the area is surrounded by quiet temples and old private houses. This neighborhood, one step away from the hustle and bustle of the city center, is filled with the simple warmth that trams have as ``community transportation''. As I surrender to the peaceful scenery of everyday life flowing outside the window, I feel the tension of the train journey gradually melting away. There are no special sights. However, there is a certain life there and the sound of the railway that supports it. This is the true face of the city, worthy of being featured in a travelogue.

Annoya. After passing this stop, the train finally approaches Yasunoya Ohashi Bridge, which spans the Jinzu River. The Jinzu River, which was once feared as a raging river in the Hokuriku region, has changed to its current flow after the Meiji period when the river was abandoned, but in the Yasunoya area, you can still feel the echoes of the history that the river once created. Toyama Prefecture Gokoku Shrine is located right next to the stop, and the deep greenery of the forest is quietly reflected in the aluminum body of the train. The journey from here to Gofuku on the opposite bank after crossing the bridge is the only open section of the track line that weaves through the city, where the sky is wide open. The sound of the joints carving on the iron bridge echoes through the wind blowing across the river. At that moment, travelers can experience for themselves the flow of water that forms the backbone of the city of Toyama.

name_ja: トヨタモビリティ富山Gスクエア五福前（五福末広町）
name_en: In front of Toyota Mobility Toyama G Square Gofuku (Gofuku Suehirocho)
text_en: In front of Toyota Mobility Toyama G Square Gofuku. The long and modern name of the station may be confusing, but this is a historical place that was once called ``Gofuku Suehirocho'' and was also known as ``Shin-Toyama Station'', which served as a connection to the Imizu Line. This spot, where the train takes a sharp curve to the left after crossing the Jinzu River, must have once had a unique atmosphere, as it was the starting station for a railway that extended to the suburbs. Nowadays, the area is lined with commercial facilities and has been completely repainted into a sophisticated modern landscape, but one of the secret pleasures of railway travel is finding the remnants of the terminals of yesteryear in the curves of the tracks and the division of land. Even if a bus stop bears the name of a modern company, the unchanging memories that have continued to support the movement of people rest quietly at its foundation. The difference between old and new is what makes Reiwa's railway landscape so interesting.
name_fr: Devant Toyota Mobility Toyama G Square Gofuku (Gofuku Suehirocho)
name_tw: 豐田汽車富山 G Square 五福（五福末廣町）前

text_en:
In front of Toyama University. This stop, which is the final stop for one line, is also the end of a single-track section, so it has the quiet, lonely feeling that is typical of a terminal station. The sight of the rails cutting off just beyond the platform is always a sad sight, giving the feeling of the end of a journey, but the fresh energy of the students that emanates from this scene cancels out that desolation. If you think of the fact that the Imizu Line used to extend a railway line from here towards Toyama Bay, you might think that the entrance to a lost landscape is hidden on the other side of this parking lot. The backs of young people disappearing into Gofuku Campus and the train returning to the city center. It is this repeated rhythm of daily life that gives this dead-end railroad a never-ending vitality.
[Station name] International Conference Center Station

name_en: In front of the International Conference Center
text_en: In front of the International Conference Center. It is a stop on the ``Centram'' loop line, which was born in the Heisei era, and surrounded by modern hotels and conference halls, it is a place that symbolizes the ``public'' face of Toyama. The track, which traces the ruins of the former inner moat of Toyama Castle, allows us to see the contrasting beauties of old and new at the same time: the glass-enclosed modern architecture and the stone walls of the historic castle ruins. When you get off at this station, you get the illusion that the tranquility of the old samurai residences is rising slightly from the concrete floor of today. Although it is not a flashy tourist destination, the atmosphere of this area, with its well-organized urban functions, is very intelligent, and gives a sense of pride as the hub city of Hokuriku. The way the silver vehicle appears with its smooth curves and blends into the scenery as if it were sent from the future is truly spectacular.
name_fr: Devant le Centre International de Conférences

text_en: Major mall. The road is paved in the style of cobblestones and the sky is wide with no telephone poles. This is one of the most stylish spaces where Toyama's urban planning came to fruition. Once you get off the bus stop, you will find yourself surrounded by a cultural atmosphere centered around the Civic Plaza, and the steps of the people who are enjoying walking around the city seem to be light and airy. This area is said to have once been home to the Otemon Gate of Toyama Castle, and it still retains its status as the city's ``main gate.'' The intimacy of the tram passing slowly, as if joining a line of pedestrians, seems to offer a happy answer to the question of how public transportation and humans should coexist. At dusk, when the track glows golden yellow under the soft streetlights, this street takes on a fantastical beauty that makes you forget that you are in Japan.

In front of Grand Plaza. Adjacent to the center of Nishimachi and directly connected to a huge all-weather plaza, this stop is Toyama's ``bustling crossroads.'' While holding the memories of the time when the long-established department store "Yamato" once stood across the street, it now invites people to the newly reborn plaza. When you get off at the bus stop, you can hear the lively voices coming from the arcade and the music from the event, making you realize that this city is still alive and well. People carrying shopping bags and young people waiting to meet each other. Amidst the bustle that engulfs all of them, the tram stands proudly and naturally. This place, where Toyama's commercial history and modern lifestyle intersect, is the perfect stop to recharge your energy.

Kogoda. This station, where the Tohoku Main Line, Ishinomaki Line, and Rikuu Higashi Line are divided into four directions, has a personality worthy of being called a ``crossroads of railways.'' This place was once home to a steam locomotive depot and the sky was scorched by smoke, but now it has the charm of a quiet junction. As you cross the overpass that spans the vast campus, you will once again realize that this is a crossroads for those traveling north and those traveling east. You can no longer hear the voices selling the station's famous ``Yama no Kami Manju,'' but when you stand on the platform, you can feel the lingering scent of the railway's once prosperous days wafting in from somewhere. The weight of the history of the railway system that has supported and moved this town is engraved with as many tracks as there are tracks.

Kitaura. With the bustle of Kogoda in the background, this quiet station is the first stop for diesel cars on the Rikuu East Line. Beyond the platform, the countryside stretches out as far as the eye can see, and here you can see the life of the earth, which changes color with each season. There aren't any flashy tourist facilities, just a straight railroad track and an old waiting room watching over it. However, the time that passes as trains arrive and depart has a weight and leeway that is clearly different from that in the city. When the sound of the wind rustling the rice ears and the distant sound of farm work mix with the sound of a diesel engine, the traveler finally sheds his or her everyday life and begins to open his/her heart to the journey of Michinoku. Because of its simple structure, the atmosphere of the land is conveyed directly.

Rikuzenyachi. As the name suggests, this area has a topography that gives you a sense of the remnants of what was once a rich wetland and valley. The rice fields on both sides of the railway line are lush in early summer and golden in autumn, making them a perfect symbol of Miyagi's fertility. The station itself has a simple appearance with a platform on one side, but it seems that this simplicity actually emphasizes the smell of the earth and the freshness of the water. As you sit on a bench in the waiting room and listen to the chirping of birds and the sounds of insects while waiting for the next train, you are reminded of how the railroad has naturally integrated into the life of this region over the years. You could call it luxury without anything. This small station is certainly alive with the tranquility of Tohoku's original scenery, which you wouldn't notice just by passing by.

Furukawa. This station, which has transformed into a modern elevated station as a connection point with the Tohoku Shinkansen, can be traced back to a time when it was once called Rikuzen Furukawa. This town has prospered as the center of Osaki Kodo and as a transportation hub, and despite the modern hustle and bustle of the Shinkansen, it still maintains its pride as a post town. If you step off the platform of a conventional line and look at the light shining through the gaps in the elevated tracks, you will notice that the waves of modernization and the atmosphere of local lines strangely coexist. When you transfer from the Shinkansen to the Rikuu Higashi Line, and while you wait for a short while you feel the breeze blowing on the platform, you suddenly feel like you can feel the breath of this city's history of commerce and agricultural administration. It is a shame that it cannot be used as a mere transit point, but it gives a sense of the maturity of a regional city.

Tsukame. The station is located at the entrance where the train passes through the urban area of ​​Furukawa and gradually enters the depths of the Osaki Plain. There are residential buildings scattered around the area, and people commuting to work and school can be seen in the morning and evening, giving the area a strong sense of life. However, while the national highway runs right next to the station and offers a modern landscape, standing on the platform you can see the shadows of the Ou Mountains in the distance, giving you a sense of the depth of your journey ahead. You could say that this place is on the borderline where the hustle and bustle of the city and the tranquility of the mountains meet. As the train accelerates and the Tsukame platform recedes, the scenery outside the train window becomes even more green. It makes you feel as if you are at a turning point, where the beginning of your journey is over and you are invited to embark on a full-fledged ``Oku no Hosomichi'' journey.

Nishifurukawa. This area, which used to have the station name ``Nakashinden,'' has flourished as a strategic point on Ugo Kaido, a side road of Oshu Kaido, since ancient times. In the Taisho era, a light railway called Sendai Railway branched from here to Kami District, and if you trace its remains, you can remember the days when the railway was the artery of the region. Nowadays, only a single platform and an orderly station building greet travelers, but the expansive space in front of the station quietly preserves memories of the past, when the station was bustling with cargo handling and transit passengers. The scenery of Osaki Koudo that spreads out from the train window also shows signs that we are finally approaching the mountains from this point on, which further heightens the anticipation of the railway journey. The pride of the land and the evolution of the railway are etched in this quiet station.

Higashi Osaki. This station is located in a place where the window of the train heading towards Naruko changes from the residential area to the expanse of lush rice fields. This place is right in the middle of Miyagi's proud breadbasket. As the seasons change, the scenery unfolds, with the blue rice rippling in the wind or the golden ears bowing their heads, which can be called the original landscape of the Japanese spirit. Although it is a small station with only a simple waiting room, it is completely unrelated to the hustle and bustle of the city and is filled with a quietness that feels like the breathing of the earth. Every time the train door opens, the air that flows in brings with it a sweet, earthy scent. It shows us how the railway, a tool of civilization, coexists humbly with the workings of nature, and the beauty of that harmony.

Nishiosaki. After leaving Higashiosaki, the train travels deeper into the plains and arrives at this station. The area around the station is dotted with ancient villages, making you feel that people's lives are closely connected to the railway. When you stand on the platform of this station, which was once called ``Kamiiwadeyama,'' the outlines of the mountains in the distance gradually become clearer, giving you a sense that you are nearing the end of the Osaki Plain and the entrance to the mountainous region. Although there are no flashy tourist elements, the daily scenes of local students and people returning from shopping getting on and off the train remind us once again that the essence of local lines is what they are. What railways connect is not just points, but the steady journey of the people who live there.

Iwadeyama. When you get off at this station, you can feel the atmosphere of the castle town of Iwadeyama Castle, which was once the residence of the Date clan, floating throughout the city. The weight of the history of this area being the political center of Oshu for over ten years until Date Masamune moved to Sendai is reflected in the appearance of the station building. Around the station, old storehouses and a charming townscape remain, demonstrating a perfect harmony between the modern era brought by the railway and the tradition nurtured by the castle town. This station, where steam locomotives once refilled water and prepared to cross the mountain pass, now serves as a quiet storyteller of history, gently welcoming visitors. When we step onto the platform and look up at Shiroyama, we are all moved by the fact that the One-Eyed Dragon's ambition lies beneath this sky.

Yukikan. Located right in front of the station is Yubikan, one of Japan's oldest academic institutions, making it a rare station in Japan that bears the name of a cultural heritage site. An academic school built on the site of the former samurai residence of Iwadeyama Castle and its beautiful garden. The fact that modern railways are directly connected to this historical space makes me feel the deep sense of this line. It used to be a temporary boarding area, but now it also serves as a cultural hub for the area. Admire the seasonal colors reflected in the garden's pond and feel the breath of history in the silence. You are guaranteed such a luxurious time just a few minutes walk from the station. For those who travel with a spirit of intellectual exploration, there are not many stations that are as appealing as this one.

Uenome. This station is located at the point where the train finally begins to follow the flow of the Eai River, with the lingering traces of Iwadeyama's history behind it. Although it is a simple structure with a single-sided platform, the surrounding greenery becomes even thicker, and the wind blowing through the train window has a coolness to it. The charm of this station can be said to lie in the richness of its ``emptiness.'' If you walk down the narrow road in front of the station, you will find the peaceful life of a farming village right there, with deep mountains in the background. The sight of the railway quietly blending into this area as a part of the land has a strangely calming effect on the hearts of travelers. In today's world where efficiency and speed are all that is required, I would like to reaffirm the luxury called "time" that these small stations continue to protect.

Ikezuki. Legend has it that this is the birthplace of the famous horse ``Ikezuki,'' which gained fame in the fight for the lead in the Ujigawa River during the Genpei War, and it has an elegance that befits its name. A roadside station has been built in front of the station, and today it is a busy place with many cars stopping by, but if you go back to the railway line, you will find that it still maintains a quiet space that is unique to railways and is somewhat removed from the world. It has a history of being used by people working in the mountains and hot springs as the entrance to the Onikobe area in ancient times. The remains of the former freight siding give us a faint glimpse of the bustle of the past. The pride of being a horse-producing area and the strength of the people who have lived with the harsh nature are still alive in the landscape that surrounds this station.

Kawatari Onsen. The moment you step off the platform of this station, the faint scent of sulfur tickles your nostrils, letting you know that you are at the gateway to Naruko Onsen Village. It was once opened as ``Kawatari'' and has a history of continuing to bring in many hot spring bathers for a long time. When you step out of the station building, the clear stream of the Eai River flows, and beyond that, a good old hot spring town awaits travelers. Kawatari no Yu is also known as ``Beriberi Kawatari'' and is a famous hot spring that has been used to soothe the fatigue of common people. The benefits that the railway brought to this hot spring area are immeasurable, and even today, when people step off the train and head to the hot spring inn, there is a lightness filled with anticipation. It's not flashy, but the hot spring atmosphere of Tohoku that deeply permeates your mind and body begins here.

Naruko Gotenyu. As its elegant name suggests, the station's name comes from ``Gotenyu,'' where the Sendai feudal lord once visited for a hot spring bath. As the nearest station to Higashi Naruko Onsen, although it is small, it has an appearance that is full of the atmosphere of a hot spring area. This station, which used to be called ``Higashi Naruko,'' has been renamed to make the historical background of the area clearer. There are hot spring inns with self-catering facilities right next to the station, creating a unique atmosphere where long-term guests can relax and enjoy the atmosphere of the hot springs. The view of the chimneys of the hot spring town and the murmur of the Eai River from the station's overpass. I am deeply impressed by how all of this is completed as a single landscape through the setting of the journey, the railway.

Naruko hot spring. This station on the Rikuu Higashi Line is one of the best tourist hubs in the Tohoku region, combining railways, hot springs, and the traditional craft of kokeshi dolls. Steam billowing high into the air and giant kokeshi dolls decorating the station building. The way they greet travelers is nothing short of spectacular. This station, which was once extremely busy with frequent express trains arriving and departing, now has the atmosphere of a calm tourist destination. There is a footbath on the premises, where travelers can surrender to its warmth for a while while waiting for the next train. The steepness of Naruko Gorge that approaches behind the station and the warmth of the people's activities. This contrast is deeply engraved in the hearts of those who visit this station. It is a sacred place that you cannot avoid on your journey through Michinoku.

Nakayamadaira Onsen. After passing through the steep gorge of Naruko, the train climbs higher to reach this station, which is surrounded by the tranquility of the highlands, close to the prefectural border between Miyagi and Yamagata. In the past, it was known as ``Nakayamadaira'' and was a difficult place for steam locomotives to make their final push over the Ou Mountains. In front of the station, the C58 steam locomotive that once ran through this area is quietly spending the rest of its life, conveying memories of the golden age of railways. Among Naruko Onsenkyo, it boasts an especially abundant amount of hot water, and is proud of its ``Shitodoke no Yu,'' which has a uniquely slimy texture. The surrounding area is surrounded by deep forests, and in the fall, you can even get the illusion that the station is buried in a sea of ​​autumn leaves. It makes us want to quietly reflect on the hardships of our ancestors who connected railways while facing the harsh nature.

Sakaida. As soon as you set foot in Yamagata Prefecture from Miyagi Prefecture, the train arrives at this ``watershed'' station. In front of the station, there is a small ditch where the rain separates and flows into the Pacific Ocean and the Sea of ​​Japan, a quiet reminder that this is the backbone of the Ou Mountains. This place, where Matsuo Basho once resided in a ``honin's house'' and reflected on the steepness of the country's borders, is now dominated by the silence of an unmanned station. Standing on the platform, the clear air unique to the highlands fills your lungs, reminding you once again of the amazement that a train can take over such a high place. Although it may not have flashy decorations, the appearance of this station, born of geographical necessity, is an irreplaceable source of travel inspiration for travel writers.

Akakura Onsen. This station, which used to be called "Tomizawa," is one of the key points on the Rikuu East Line on the Yamagata side. Although it is a little far from the station to the hot spring town, the area around the station retains a quiet rural landscape. In winter, this area becomes one of the heaviest snowfall areas in Japan, and there is a history of Russell cars desperately clearing the snow to clear the way. When you arrive at the platform, the deep view of the mountains in the distance gives you a sense of the ruggedness and richness of the journey ahead. How much did people in snowy regions rely on this railroad? It feels like the weight of that lifestyle is ingrained in even the pillars of the old waiting room.

Tachikoji. As the train passes Akakura Onsen and approaches a gentle downhill slope, this small station appears. Although it is a simple building with just one platform, the surrounding countryside has a refreshing quality that makes it worthy of being called the original scenery of Yamagata. I have heard that there was once a forest railway in this area, but now the only sound is the sound of diesel car engines echoing through the mountains. There are no notable tourist attractions. However, the existence of this station, which quietly watches the changing seasons passing through the train window, makes me feel that it plays a role like a ``punctuation mark'' on a local train journey.

Mogami. In the past, this station was known as ``Uzenmukai-cho'' and was a bustling center of the area. It is an important operational base on the Yamagata Prefecture side of the Rikuu Higashi Line, and the atmosphere that once stopped even express trains still remains within its spacious grounds. Now that the station is named after the town, the station building has been updated, but even so, the pride that this area was at the center of logistics and exchange in the Mogami region is clearly felt by the travelers standing on the platform. As soon as you step out of the station, you can hear the murmuring of the Oguni River, a tributary of the Mogami River, and the old shopping street gives you a sense of the rich history. It's also fun to look for the remnants of the railroad's once prosperous days in its modern, functional beauty.

Ohori. This station stands quietly as the train leaves Mogami and heads toward the Mogami River. The landscape, surrounded by mountains and dotted with several farmhouses, gives the illusion that time has stopped. The time you spend standing on the platform of this station, waiting for the next train, can be truly a luxurious moment to have a conversation with yourself. In the winter, it is buried in a world of silver, and in the spring, it is enveloped in a burst of greenery that sprouts all at once. From this small station, you can feel the miracle that the railway has been able to connect to this day, while enjoying the power and blessings of nature. Here you can see the original, simple appearance of railways, without any flashy presentation.

Usugi. The train runs along the Ogunigawa River, a tributary of the Mogami River, and it's a station that has an atmosphere that makes you stop by. The area surrounding the station is lined with giant cedar trees, giving the station a strong sense of being a ``cedar village,'' as the name suggests. The main characters here are not the railway or people, but the trees with deep roots in this land and the flowing river. The view from the platform is beautiful, like a landscape painting, and calms the hearts of visitors. When the horn that announces the arrival of a train shakes the quiet air of the forest, the traveler is convinced that he or she is in the deep embrace of nature. Because it is a simple home, it feels like the spirits of the land are speaking to you.

Semi hot spring. When you hear the name of this station, everyone thinks of the legend of Minamoto no Yoshitsune and Benkei. In the past, it was called ``Uzensemi'' and welcomed many travelers as the entrance to the famous hot springs along the Oguni River valley. A steep mountain looms just behind the station building, and a clear stream flows in front of it. I am humbled by the tenacity of our predecessors when it comes to building railroads through this narrow terrain. The hot spring town is just a short walk away, and the sound of the river that can be heard when crossing the bridge tells the story of the distant past when Yoshitsune and his servants lived in this area. I am excited by the feeling that the smell of steam, which soothes the fatigue of a journey, will waft all the way to the platform.

Higashi Nagasawa. This station is located where the view is gradually opening up after passing through the deep valley of Semi. This is the place that can be called the entrance to the Shinjo Basin, and it is also the point where the train, freed from the pressure of the mountains, begins to run with ease. The station itself is an unmanned station with one platform on one side, but the surrounding area is surrounded by well-organized farmland, which conveys the hard-working lifestyle of the people who have survived the harsh winters of the Mogami region. If you pass by this station at dusk, when the lights are on in the windows of the houses, you will feel as if the warm scent of people's daily lives can reach the inside of the train as they head home. This is the kind of station that gives you a sense of nostalgia, with its feet on the ground, rather than flashy travel vibes.

Nagasawa. Although it is only one station further from Higashi-Nagasawa, you can feel a different depth of history here. There was once a time when the area was bustling with activities such as transporting lumber, and the spacious grounds and some of the old equipment secretly convey the vibrancy of the past. The appearance of the station building embodies the rugged yet warm functional beauty of Showa era railway architecture. The forest that spreads out behind the platform seems to symbolize the richness of the forestry industry that once supported this area. Nowadays, there are fewer passengers getting on and off the train, but that doesn't change the fact that this station has always served as the "gate" to this area. When you sit down on an old bench, you feel like you can hear the sounds of a bygone era.

Minamishinjo. One stop before the final stop, Shinjo. Although parallel to the Ou Main Line, this station intentionally has an independent platform, and it is a place where you can feel the ``beginning of the end'' of your journey on the Rikuu East Line. The railway lines come together from the left and right, giving the impression of a double track, but each line has a different origin, creating a scene that symbolizes the fun of railways. As the city of Shinjo approaches, the hustle and bustle begins to mix in, giving the impression that the trip is coming to an end, but the Rikuu Higashi Line platform seems to be somehow still holding on to the echoes of the journey deep in the mountains. It's the perfect place to quietly look back on the long journey that brought you here while feeling the slightly humid wind that is typical of the basin.

Shinjo. The journey on the Rikuu East Line that started from Kogota will finally come to an end at this large terminal. This station, which was once the site of a locomotive depot and the crossroads of Tohoku where steam locomotives spewed smoke, has now been reborn into a sophisticated appearance as the terminal station for the Yamagata Shinkansen. However, if you look at the brick engine shed that still remains in the corner of the station and the sturdy structure unique to the snowy country, you will be convinced that this is a sacred place that has continued to protect the northern railways. During the festival season, majestic floats parade through the city, showing how much the people and wealth brought by the railway have enriched this city. This is a place where the modern symbol of the Shinkansen and the travel spirit of local trains intertwine, and travelers are excited about their next destination.

text_en: Maego. This station can be said to be the centerpiece of Yuri Kogen Railway's operation. Even non-railway enthusiasts can't help but feel deeply moved by the fact that ``tablet exchange'', which is now rare in Japan, is still being carried out in this Reiwa era. At that moment when the up and down trains quietly meet each other and the ticket is passed from one driver to the other, we witness the sure form of ``trust'' that the Showa era railways had. I feel an indescribable sense of relief in knowing that the concept of a blockage in the past is no longer just a record, but is now pulsating as a living, breathing railway.

Symbolizing Akita's pride as a rice producer in the past, the train windows are filled with ears of rice that shine green in early summer and golden in autumn. The simple appearance of the waiting room silently tells the story of its history of enduring many harsh winter snows and winds, and travelers find its solitude rather comforting. The vibrations caused by the acceleration and deceleration of the train resonate with the calm flow of time in this area, and you can feel the hustle and bustle of everyday life far away.

There used to be a stately wooden station building here, which soothed the hearts of travelers, but the dignified atmosphere that surrounds the station has not wavered in the slightest, no matter how much time has changed. The murmuring of the river mixes with the sound of the train running, deepening the emotion of traveling inland. It can be said to be a truly blissful moment to entrust yourself to a diesel car that starts running again, while searching every corner of the landscape for the remnants of a time when forestry flourished and water transport was the norm.

The moment when the low sound of a diesel engine approaches, breaking the silence, breathes life into this lonely station, it reaffirms the robustness of railway culture.

During the short stop, you can see the village from the train window and get a sense of the peaceful daily life of this area, making you feel sad that the journey is coming to an end.

Beyond the dead-end car stop, you can see the magnificent foot of Mt. Chokai and the cityscape that has seen many frosts over the years. The appearance of the station building conveys how the local people have carefully protected the railway and cherished it as a part of their lives. The quiet atmosphere of this station quietly teaches us the truth that the end of a journey is the beginning of a new one.
