text_en: Choshi. This station, which is the terminus of the Sobu Main Line and the starting point of the Choshi Electric Railway, can truly be called the gateway to a place where land runs out. A small ticket gate stands apologetically but resolutely at the end of a long JR platform. From there, it feels like you are continuing into another world where another time passes. As you exit the station building, the faint scent of soy sauce wafts through the air, telling you of the town's long history of flourishing as a brewer. This place, which was once bustling with freight cars and water transport along the Tone River, now has a quiet travel atmosphere. Although the station building has been rebuilt into a modern one, the look in the eyes of the people waiting for the train to arrive and depart still shows the same ``attachment to the terminal station'' that has remained unchanged since then. What kind of scenery will the short journey of a few kilometers that starts from here show us? I boarded the small train with anticipation and a little emotion.

Nakano Town. This station, which has a garage attached to it, is a place that can be called the heart of Choshi Electric Railway. As soon as you arrive at the platform, you'll see a row of aging cars huddled together in front of you, and the dry sound of metal hitting metal echoing from the back of the inspection and repair shed. The fragrant smell of soybeans is carried on the wind from the huge adjacent Yamasa soy sauce factory, and this mixes with the smell of railroad oil, giving us an indescribable sense of the strength of industry. The small station building, which also serves as the headquarters, is simple but proud, and gives off a sense of the tenacity of the people who are trying to maintain the railway. If you look around, you'll see old soldiers who once ran on the Eidan Subway and Keio Electric Railway going about their second and third lives. Those of us in the middle-aged generation are reminded of our own circumstances and can't help but get excited when we see this. It is no exaggeration to say that it is truly a living museum of railways.

Kannon. The station building has an impressive design reminiscent of a Swiss mountain hut, and its name comes from the nearby Iinuma Kannon (Enpukuji Temple). In the past, many people would gather at this station in search of the famous ``Taiyaki.'' Nowadays, that fragrant smell has disappeared, but the atmosphere of the temple town that spreads around the station is still alive and well. The way the train winds its way through the densely packed old shops and residences gives you a sense of warmth and connection to daily life, something you don't find on trains near the city. The weight of its history as the 27th temple of the Bando Thirty-Three Kannon temples may have given the station a somewhat solemn atmosphere. Every time the train doors open, religious worshipers and local shoppers board and alight, reaffirming that this short line is not just a tourist attraction, but the lifeblood of the region.

Honchoshi. This station, which stands quietly at the bottom of a deep cut, gives the illusion of being swallowed up by a green tunnel. A dense forest looms behind the platform, and in summer, powerful cicada showers pour down from the old bridge that spans the railroad tracks. As the name suggests, this region, once called "Shimizu," is blessed with high-quality water, and has a history of supporting the production of soy sauce in Choshi. Choshi City Shimizu Elementary School is located right next to the station, and when it's time for school to go, the lively voices of children bring the quiet forest station to life. In recent years, the station building has been renovated and has attracted attention due to TV programs, but the underlying ``quiet and humid atmosphere'' feels like it has not changed at all since the Showa era. There is no better place to escape the hustle and bustle of the city and just listen to the quiet sound of the creaking rails.

Kuroo Kasagami. This station, which has Choshi Electric Railway's only exchange facility, is a sacred place for railway fans. The scene of ``tablet exchange'', which is now rare in Japan, is a daily occurrence here. The weight of the ticket passed from the station staff's hand to the driver is the weight of a heavy responsibility in the name of safety, and its ceremonial gesture is imbued with a human warmth and trust that modern ATS (automatic train stopping systems) lack. The moment when two trains line up on the platform and pass each other as if praying for each other's safety can be said to be the real thrill of railway travel. Cabbage fields spread out around the station, and the smell of earth wafts in with the sea breeze. When we think back to the days when fish caught on the coast of Kurohae were transported from this station to all over the country, we are reminded of the great historical role this station played, not just as a relay point.

Nishikai Kashima. This station, which was established relatively late in 1970, is characterized by its simple structure, nestled in a vast cabbage field. There is only a small waiting room above the platform, and the unobstructed view of the sky opens the minds of travelers. When Choshi's specialty, ``lighthouse cabbage,'' is in season, it becomes a green carpet as far as the eye can see, and an old orange and blue train passes slowly through it. The scenery is as beautiful as a painting. It may not be as glamorous as a tourist destination, but here you can find an unadorned daily life that could be called the ``original scenery of life''. The smell of dinner coming from nearby houses and the barking of dogs. As I watch the railway blend into these casual activities, I feel the fatigue of my travels quietly receding.

Umikajima. This place, which has the proud title of being the easternmost station in the Kanto region, retains its memories as a resort that was once visited by many literary figures and artists. The story of Yumeji Takehisa's love affair with his beloved Hikono and his inspiration for ``Yoimachigusa'' is very famous. Although the station building is simple, it has the refreshing feel of a beachside villa, and you can hear the faint sound of the ocean waves. It is said that the area got its name from the sea lions that used to flock to this area, but now it is just a quiet residential area and fields. However, the height of the sky and the strength of the light clearly convince us that the sea is nearby. I can't help but feel that the eternal time that Yumeji must have seen, like the waves coming and going, is still flowing through this station. For those seeking the romance of days gone by, this is an essential stop.

Kimigahama. Once you step off the train and feel the sea breeze, you will be greeted with a spectacular view of Kimigahama Shiosai Park, which has been selected as one of Japan's top 50 lighthouses. The station itself is unmanned, with just one platform lying desolate, but its simplicity actually seems to enhance the grandeur of nature. For a time, the station was known as the ``Cat Station,'' where the cats that lived there would welcome travelers, and the reason for such a peaceful time is probably due to the tolerant nature of this area. As you walk toward the shore, the sound of the crashing waves of the Pacific Ocean becomes louder, and the view soon opens up to reveal a coastline of white sand and green pine trees. When you want to enjoy solitude, or when you're at a crossroads in life, getting off at this station and looking out at the ocean is an irreplaceable luxury.

Dog barking. The luxurious station building, modeled after a Portuguese palace, gives the line a sense of pride as a central tourist hub. The terracotta-style tiles stand out against the white walls, and the fragrant smell of baking ``Nure Senbei'' wafts through the premises. Here, the remnants of the era when railways were at their most glamorous coexist beautifully with the vibrancy of a modern tourist destination. Just a short walk from the station, the white-walled Inubosaki Lighthouse stands out with its stark appearance, and the sheer cliffs covered by the rough waves will heighten your travel spirit to its peak. In the past, there was a history of special trains carried by Japanese National Railways carrying many tourists, and the bustle of this station has been a major pillar supporting the continued existence of Choshi Electric Railway. The smiles of people choosing souvenirs and the steps of young people heading towards the lighthouse. Looking at such scenes makes us realize that the railways transport not just people, but also intangible assets called ``memories.''

Togawa. This is the place where the railroad tracks run out. The wooden station building, which has welcomed travelers in its unchanged appearance since its opening in 1920, has the deep wrinkles of many years. As you sit down on the well-worn bench in the waiting room, you will feel as if you have traveled back in time to the Showa era. Beside the station building, old train cars that were once active are quietly spending their remaining lives, and the weight of history that their rusted bodies convey is overwhelming. Once you leave the station and go down the gentle slope, you will find yourself in the middle of a traditional fishing town that has been around since the Edo period. Houses with lattice doors, narrow alleys, and the smell of salt water. The dead-end railway line shows that this is not just a passing point, but a complete world. At the end of our journey, we waited for sunset at this station. For a railway travel writer, this can be said to be a moment of bliss.

Takasaki. It goes without saying that it is a key transportation hub, and it is also the historical starting point that once supported the export of silk. When you step off the Joshin Electric Railway platform, you can feel the atmosphere of a quiet and proud local private railway, which is completely different from the hustle and bustle of JR. The colorful train cars lined up on the head-end platform look like they are enjoying a second life here, while still retaining traces of the former Seibu Railway. The feeling of exhilaration that comes from knowing that the train journey to Shimonita begins from here will never fade, even if the times change.

Minami Takasaki. This is the first stop after leaving Takasaki, and there are residential buildings right next to the station, giving it the feel of passing through the backstreets of the city. There was once an industrial park and a flour mill nearby, and the remnants of the days when freight transportation was popular can be felt from every corner of the narrow platform. At the end of the sharply curving railway line, the city of Takasaki recedes into the distance, giving you the feeling that you are finally stepping out into the plains of Joshu. Sitting in the simple waiting room reaffirms the close connection between daily life and railways.

Me in Sano. This station, whose name comes from the old ferry that was mentioned in the Manyoshu poem, is a new station built in the Heisei era. However, the murmuring of the Karasugawa River flowing right next to it, and the scenery overlooking it, still convey the feeling of travel from ancient times. It is a mysterious place where modern convenience and deep history intersect as you hear the roar of trains crossing the bridge. It's also fun to feel the river breeze on your skin and think about the people who once crossed here by boat.

Nekoya. As we approached this station, the view from the train window suddenly changed to mountainous terrain, and the roar of the train became even more powerful. It stands quietly at the foot of the mountain near the ruins of Kanai Castle, giving it the feel of a ``hidden village station.'' The simple home with only one side blends into nature, and the sound of rustling leaves on the trees soothes the dry soul of the city. If we remember the history of this place as a strategic base, this seemingly ordinary scene takes on a different weight.

name_en: In front of Takasaki University of Commerce
text_en: In front of Takasaki University of Commerce. This station, which is filled with the lively voices of young people, is relatively new to Joshin Electric Railway. The texture of the concrete is refreshing, and the sound of the footsteps of the students is clearly heard. The contrast between the school building in front of the station and the mountains of Joshu in the background gives us a sense of hope for the future and the unwavering harmony of nature. It is truly reassuring to see railways as a device supporting educational settings while blending into students' daily lives.
name_fr: Devant l'Université de Commerce de Takasaki

text_en: Mountain name. This station has a definite presence as the station in front of Yamana Hachimangu Shrine, which respects its ancient history. When trains pass each other on the island platform, the silence of waiting for the train to be replaced is the real pleasure of traveling by train. The area around the station is dotted with ancient tombs, and one of the three monuments of Ueno, the Yamana Monument, is also nearby, giving the area a sense of ancient romance. When you look at the stone station building and old overpass, you get the illusion that time has stopped, and you can feel the layers of history firsthand.

Nishiyama name. After leaving Yamana and gliding through the countryside for a while, this station appears, and the word tranquility fits well with it. The lush greenery that surrounds it vividly shows off the changes of the four seasons and is a feast for the eyes of visitors. This place, which once would have been dominated by agricultural activities that took advantage of the vast land, now functions as a peaceful place to live. It may be an exaggeration to say that it's a luxurious experience, but it's rare to find a place where waiting for a train can feel so luxurious.

Horse garden. This area is known for the ``Baniwa Nen-ryu'' school of swordsmanship, and even the name of the station gives off a sense of dignity and strength. When you stand on the platform, you get the feeling that you are stepping on the same ground that martial artists of the past would have walked on. Old private houses remain around the station, and the large roofs from the days when sericulture was popular testify to the area's former prosperity. The scent of plants and trees carried on the wind makes one feel the strength of the vitality of this land, and it seems to stretch the spine of the traveler just a little.

Yoshii. This station, which is one of the main stations of Joshin Electric Railway and the core of the town, has a somewhat nostalgic and dignified appearance. The structure of the station building and the size of the platform are reminiscent of the days when freight handling was popular. As you walk in front of the station, you will see a shopping street that retains the atmosphere of the Showa era, and you will feel the warmth of the people's lives. Many travelers use this place as a base to visit the Tago Monument, which shows us that railways are firmly rooted in this culturally rich town.

Nishiyoshii. This station, located quietly in a residential area, is located in a landscape that looks like a casual slice of everyday life. It may not have any major characteristics, but I feel that its ``ordinaryness'' is what gives this line its depth. At dusk, when the lights of the houses begin to light up one by one, the lights of the train slipping onto the platform bring peace of mind to people on their way home. Although it is not flashy, it makes us realize once again the importance of railways that support our daily lives.

Joshu Araya. The two characters "Joshu" in the station name give a sense of pride in this area. The farmland that surrounds the station and the mountain range beyond it are the very original scenery of Japan. When you step off at this station and breathe in the dry wind, you will feel a sense of freedom, as if the fatigue from your journey will just disappear. In the silence of an unmanned station, the occasional sound of a railroad crossing bell becomes a pleasant accent to the ears. The ``new mansion,'' as the name of the place suggests, has been polished by history and has developed a deep flavor.

Joshu Fukushima. This station once flourished as a center where agricultural products and silk fabrics from the surrounding area were gathered. The vibrancy of the past seems to have calmed down in the wooden ticket gates and waiting room lined with old benches. If you take a short walk in front of the station, you will see old warehouse-style buildings here and there, which tell the story of the rich history that this area has had. If you stand on the platform and look into the distance, you can almost hear the murmuring of the Kaburagawa River, and the dry Joshu wind blows comfortably.

Higashi Tomioka. As the eastern gateway to the city of Tomioka, this station has an orderly appearance. Although it is a relatively new station, having been built around the end of the Showa era, it has become a familiar part of the area as a means of transportation for people commuting to the surrounding residential areas and schools. The townscape of Tomioka that can be seen from here feels like time is passing peacefully, even though it is experiencing the waves of modernization. It has now become a part of our daily lives to see travelers walking lightly with their hopes of visiting the World Heritage Sites in their hearts.

Joshu Tomioka. It goes without saying that it is the closest station to the well-known Tomioka Silk Mill, and can be said to be the most important station on this line. Although the station building has been given a modern look, the pride that supported the Meiji Industrial Revolution still remains in the atmosphere. The design, which is inspired by brick construction, seems to be an attempt to convey the glory of the ``silk road'' of the past. Once the train leaves, the platform, which is crowded with tourists, becomes quiet again, and you can feel the weight of its rich history.

Nishitomioka. Located in a calm residential area, a little away from the hustle and bustle of Tomioka, this station is a no-nonsense station that is close to the lives of local people. There is a high school nearby, and in the mornings and evenings the area is filled with the energy of young people, but there is something special about the quietness in the afternoon. As you wait for your train in the small waiting room, the flowers beside the tracks sway in the breeze, making you feel the transition of Joshu's short summers and long winters. It makes us realize that the true value of railways lies in the simple everyday life.

Joshu Nanukaichi. This station, which is close to the former castle town of the Nanokaichi clan, exudes a dignified elegance. Schools and public facilities are gathered around the station, and the sight of students coming and going is a symbol of the intellectual and calm atmosphere of this area. Considering the historic cityscape in the background, it feels like it's not just a transit point, but a scent of culture floating around here. Standing on the quiet platform, you can almost see the route that the feudal samurai walked in the past, which overlaps with the modern railroad.

Joshu Ichinomiya. This station has been revered since ancient times as the gateway to Nukisaki Shrine, the Ichinomiya Shrine in Ueno Province. There is something sacred about the atmosphere in front of the station that leads to the approach, and it makes you feel like your spine is stretching. If you think about the unusual structure of the shrine's unique ``kudari shrine'', you will begin to think of the station itself as an entrance to a sacred space. The atmosphere is solemn, and the sight of the railway coexisting with the gods who have continued to protect the land is truly Japanese and atmospheric.

Shennonghara. This station is located in a place where the mountains gradually approach and the scenery becomes more powerful. As befits the name, which seems to enshrine the god of agriculture, the area is surrounded by rich arable land, and the smell of Joshu soil is strong in the air. The simple wooden waiting area has the dignity of having withstood the wind and snow, and offers a gentle welcome to visitors. It is the kind of place where you can feel the breeze of passing trains and pay respect to the people who live together with the land.

Minamijai. Because of its unusual name, even if you are not a railway fan, you may have heard of this station at least once. However, despite its strange name, the station itself has a very calm appearance, blending in with the quiet mountain village. There are traces of the time when cargo was transported from this station, and the spacious premises give a sense of pride as a former transportation hub. It is easy to get distracted by the interesting name, but what is actually there is a reliable and honest railway scenery.

Chihira. The end of the line, Shimonita, is finally approaching, and the line cuts into a valley deep in the mountains. This station is surrounded by deep greenery, and only the sound of the trains echoes through the valley, giving it the feel of an unexplored station. In this sparsely populated area, the secluded home feels like a hideaway where you can forget the hustle and bustle of the city. Looking out the window at the clear stream of the Kabura River, you can feel the end of a journey that takes you deep into the bosom of nature.

Shimonita. It is the last stop on the Joshin Electric Railway, and is a proud town that has prospered as a distribution center for konnyaku and green onions since ancient times. When you look at the parking lot at a dead end, you realize that this is the end of the railroad, and you feel a mixture of desolation and a sense of accomplishment at the end of your journey. The remains of the stately wooden station building and the freight cars parked within the vast grounds clearly demonstrate that this place was once the heart of logistics. As soon as you step out of the station, the unique heat of the basin surrounded by mountains will give you the perfect ending to your trip.

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_2
text_en: Katsuta. A Minato Line diesel train is waiting quietly, but with a certain presence, in a cutout-like corner of the Joban Line's vast platform. This area once flourished as a business castle town for Hitachi, Ltd., and as a transportation hub since the days when steam locomotives were belching black smoke. When you step into a single-car diesel car with the hustle and bustle of JR express trains rushing in and out, you feel as though time begins to flow in its own way, separate from the main line. This platform has been transporting commuters and students since the days when it was called Ibaraki Kotsu, and there is a quiet sense of pride in the fact that the railway is still deeply rooted in local life. The departure bell that signals the start of a journey somehow rings nostalgic in my ears.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_3
text_en: In front of the machine. This station, which was once called ``Nikko-mae'', is a true example of the ``factory gates'' that supported Japan's rapid economic growth. The fence that leads to the factory from which the station's name comes from stretches out along the railroad tracks, and in the morning and evening you can see people dressed in work clothes filling this small platform. When you find yourself in the silence of the day, the hum of machinery that can be heard leaking from the huge building reminds you of the passion of Japanese manufacturing in the past. I can't help but feel that this area goes beyond simply functioning as a stop, and is presenting us with a fragment of the history of an industry that has taken root in this area, and that has lived together with the railway. Even though the station name has changed to a modern one, the atmosphere is unmistakably reminiscent of the Showa era.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_4
text_en: Kanegami. As the train weaves through residential areas, it arrives at this station, which has exchange equipment. The Katsuta Garrison of the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force is located right next to the station, and the regular sounds of footsteps and engines can be heard from time to time, testifying to the special historical background of this area. However, if you look around the station, you will find a mix of old houses and new houses, and the fields that spread between them create a somewhat tranquil atmosphere. This land, which may have once had a military aspect, is now integrated into the scenery of the railway that supports the peaceful lives of the people. During the short time it takes to wait for an oncoming train, the sound of dry rails echoing throughout the area gives you a sense of calmness that is typical of a key regional private railway station.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_5
text_en: Nakane. Of all the stations on the Hitachinaka Seaside Railway, this is the station that most strongly appeals to its lyricism. There are only a few houses in the surrounding area, just a few homes placed here and there in the vast rural landscape. This place has long been known as a sacred place for railway photographers, and the sight of diesel cars running through the area against the backdrop of seasonal changes in the land is reminiscent of a painting. The landscape filled with the smell of earth and grass that was once common in rural areas of Japan has miraculously been preserved here. When you step off the platform and immerse yourself in the silence, unable to hear the sounds of cars passing in the distance, you feel as if the flow of time has completely stopped. I feel that this is the original scenery of railway travel that we are losing.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_6
text_en: Takada iron bridge. Although it is a new station built in the Heisei era, as the name suggests, the Nakagawa iron bridge that stands right next to it is a symbol of this line. In the past, the sight of trains crossing this iron bridge must have been like a clock for local people, reminding them of the changing seasons. Although the station itself has a modern and simple structure, the view of the majestic river flowing from there and the rhythmic vibrations of the iron bridge convey a sense of travel that has remained unchanged since ancient times. The fact that the new station is named after a historic iron bridge shows the local people's deep attachment to and pride in this landscape. The time you spend waiting for your train to arrive while enjoying the breeze across the river is a precious moment that helps you forget about the hectic pace of modern life.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_7
text_en: Nakaminato. It is no exaggeration to say that it is the heart of this line, and the place where the soul of the Minato Line resides. The appearance of the imposing wooden station building is a reminder of the bustle of the past, when it was the center of a fishing town and welcomed many travelers. Inside the station, old diesel trains that have finished their service are quietly spending their remaining lives, and the smell of oil and iron in the air creates the atmosphere of a Showa rail yard. Although you can no longer hear the sound of the scissors clicking when passing through the ticket gate, this space, still protected by the hands of station staff, retains the warmth of the railway that cannot be explained by efficiency alone. When travelers disembark at this station, where the liveliness of the port and good old railway culture intersect, they can truly experience the history of this land.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_8
text_en: Tonoyama. A train leaving Nakaminato climbs a gentle slope and slides onto this small platform set up between cuts. The surrounding area is a quiet residential area, but the banks and lush trees on both sides of the railway are a reminder of the hardships of civil engineering in the past. Although there are no flashy decorations, this modest appearance tells us that a station is not just a place to get on and off the train, but a punctuation mark of life that is closely related to the community. As you immerse yourself in the silence of the day, the sound of the ocean waves from a distance will subtly remind you that this is definitely a seaside town. The sight of trains naturally blending into everyday scenery has a strangely calming effect on travelers.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_9

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_10
text_en: Minohama Gakuen. This station name, newly carved in the Reiwa era, gives a sense of new life to the historic Minato Line. The contrast between the brand new school building and the vast sweet potato fields surrounding it presents a new way for regional railways to exist in the modern era. As a writer who loves the Showa era, it is true that I am a little confused by the freshness of the show, but the vibrancy of the students who fill the platform every morning and evening is the very essence of the unchanging vitality of railways through the ages. I want to quietly watch and see what kind of stories this station, which has been newly grafted onto the great tree of railways with a long history, will tell in the future. In this place where old and new intersect, you can't help but feel the changing times.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_11
text_en: Isozaki. Along with the large arc of the railroad tracks, the scent of dried potatoes, a specialty of Ibaraki, wafts around this station as the season approaches. The sight of potatoes lined up in neat rows exposed to the cold winter wind is a winter tradition in this area, and an indispensable color to the railway scenery. Old shops and houses remain in front of the station, and the remains of a freight platform that was once a busy place for shipping agricultural products remain, even though they are buried under soil. Although it is not flashy, it gives off a warm feeling, as if the memories of a time when the blessings of the earth and railways were closely connected are still being carefully preserved. I feel that there is definitely a kind of luxury that exists at this station.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

ID: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線_12
text_en: Ajigaura. This final station at the end of a long journey has a unique atmosphere that is a mixture of desolation and fulfillment. This area, which was once touted as ``the best beach in the East,'' now seems to be living out a quiet life with a vast sandy beach in the background. In one corner of the campus sits an old diesel car that has finished its useful life, and its rusted body silently tells the story of the weight of the many lives it has carried over the years. Beyond the broken track, there is nothing but an endless ocean, and as the journey comes to an end, it gives us a feeling of a new journey. When we step off at this station and look out at the horizon while being blown by the sea breeze, we can experience the true sense of travel that the railway has to offer.
sheetName: ひたちなか海浜鉄道湊線

text_en: Yoshiwara. From the Tokaido Main Line platform, we cross a narrow-looking passageway and head to the Gakunan train platform. This station was once called "Suzukawa" and has prospered as the gateway to the paper manufacturing industry since ancient times. Standing in the corner of the narrow platform, you can see the remnants of the days when freight trains came and went frequently during the Japanese National Railways era, visible in the layout of the tracks here and there. Today, small stainless steel vehicles sit quietly waiting to depart, carrying memories of the heavy cargo transportation of the past. With the hustle and bustle of the Tokaido in the background, this is where the nostalgic atmosphere of a local private railway begins.

In front of JATCO. This station, formerly known as ``Nissan-mae,'' is located just a stone's throw from a huge auto parts factory, as its name suggests. When the station first opened in the 1940s, travelers at the time would never have imagined that katakana station names would become so integrated into everyday life. When you arrive at the platform, you can hear the soothing sounds of the factory operating regularly, making you keenly aware that this is a site that has supported Japan's rapid economic growth. The contrast between the inorganic concrete and the surrounding greenery seems to symbolize the dual nature of Fuji, an industrial city.

Yoshiwara Honmachi. This station is essentially located in the center of Yoshiwara, which flourished as the 14th post town on the 53rd station of the Tokaido. As soon as you exit the station building, a shopping street spreads out, and old buildings that remind you of the bustle of the past are peeking out. If we trace the history of the post town, which was relocated due to a large fire, we can clearly see that this railway was not just a means of transport for industry, but was deeply rooted as a way of life for local residents. The calm faces of the people waiting for the train to arrive make you feel that the spirit of hospitality that has continued since the days of the post town is still alive today.

Motoyoshiwara. When you get to the area around this station, the huge chimneys of the paper mill begin to loom over you with an almost intimidating force. This station, which used to be called "Yoshiwara," has adopted its current name as history has changed, and its appearance is very practical. The railroad tracks that weave through the factory buildings resemble capillary vessels, and can be said to be proof that this city has lived with paper. When the distinct smell of pulp wafts on the wind, I realize that I am now in the heart of an industrial city.

Gakunan Harada. This station is a sacred place not only for railway enthusiasts but also for photography enthusiasts. The huge group of pipes that cross right next to the station gives the illusion that you have wandered into a science fiction world. In the past, many dedicated lines branched off from this station, and freight cars loaded with paper products departed across the country. Although the station is quiet now, the contrast between the warmth of the wooden structure of the station building and the cold metal of the factory towering in the background creates an indescribable sense of travel.

Hina. In the past, when freight transportation was at its peak, this station functioned as the heart of the Gakunan Railway. Even now, the large premises still retains a strong vestige of the days when freight cars were replaced, and it is a moving experience for those who know the past. When you look at the decorations inside the station building that are related to the legend of bamboo harvesting, you can feel the people's desire to cherish the natural features of this area, even in an industrial area that tends to be desolate. It's also fun to see the hustle and bustle of the past superimposed on the quiet side tracks.

Gakunan Fujioka. It is no exaggeration to say that this station, which has a garage attached, is the place where the ``soul'' of Gakunan Railway rests. Beside the platform, you can see electric locomotives, which were once the mainstay of freight transport, spending their remaining lives. During the Showa era, the steel giants who worked hard pulling heavy freight cars are now quietly looking up at Mt. Fuji. This appearance not only signals the end of an era, but also appears to be quietly watching over the role of a new railway. It gives us the feeling that this is a station where both the strength and ephemerality of the railway system coexist.

Suzu. Gradually, the greenery of the fields begins to blend into the scenery seen from the train window, and I breathe a little sigh of relief. The charm of this station is undoubtedly the majesty of Mt. Fuji that can be seen from the platform. This is one of the most scenic spots on the Gakunan Railway, where you can enjoy the unobstructed expanse of the foothills rather than looking through a factory chimney. Although the modern elevated Shin-Tomei Expressway crosses in the distance, it gives the illusion that time passing at this station has not changed much since those days in the Showa era.

Kamiya. This simple platform with only one line stands quietly in a residential area. There are no fancy decorations or large station buildings. However, it is these ordinary small stations that represent the true value of local private railways. The sight of students returning home from school chatting and waiting for the train at dusk is the origin of a timeless railway scene. It doesn't suit exaggerated historical narratives, but daily life begins and ends on this small platform. I feel like it teaches us once again the preciousness of this work.

Gakunan Ebi. Finally, we arrived at the final station. The track ends at the end of the two-way platform, quietly announcing the end of the journey. What is surprising is that the Tokaido Shinkansen passes directly overhead with a tremendous roar. This small terminal station retains the atmosphere of the Showa era, and the super high-speed railway that is Japan's main artery. This extreme contrast is truly interesting, as it seems to symbolize the current position of the Gakunan Railway. As I surrendered to the silence in front of the station while waiting for the train to return, I began to feel as if the short journey up to this point had been a journey back in time for decades.

Ogaki. It is a strategic point along the Tokaido Road, and was once the terminus of the rapid train called the Night Express or ``Ogaki Yako,'' and has attracted many young travelers. When you walk to the Tarumi Railway platform, you will find a tranquil atmosphere that is reminiscent of the JNR era. As the city is known as the City of Water, clear water springs up around the station, and its moisture is a blessing at the beginning of your journey. The diesel train heading north from here marks the first step into the depths of the Nobi Plain.

Higashi Ogaki. This station is located just before passing through the city of Ogaki and crossing the vast Ibi River. The area around the station is lined with factories and residences, creating a somewhat functional landscape that may be a vestige of the days when freight trains frequently came and went. It feels like a mixture of the vibrancy of local cities that supported Japan during its period of high economic growth, and the calm daily life that followed. The sound of trains accelerating and decelerating echoes through residential areas, reminding us that railways are the lifeblood of our lives.

Yokoya. Once you cross the Ibi River iron bridge and the view opens up, you will arrive at this simple station. The surroundings suddenly changed to a peaceful rural landscape, and the seasonal scent of earth flowed into the car on the wind. Its unpretentious appearance, with just the station name sign standing out, makes you feel the real thrill of traveling on local lines. The quiet rural time that has not changed since the days of the former Japanese National Railways Tarumi Line is still flowing here.

Article 19. The name of the place, which reminds us of the remains of the Jori system, makes us think of the long history that this area has had. The station stands quietly, surrounded by residential buildings, and quietly fulfills its role as a means of transport for the local community. Although there are no fancy decorations, its simplicity allows the rhythm of the rails and sleepers to be heard more clearly. I feel a sense of travel in the mysterious continuity between ancient place names and modern railways.

Mieji Temple. This station is located near Mieji-juku, the former 55th post town on the Nakasendo Road. The elegant sound of the station name conveys the bustle of the past, when many travelers came and went. Although it is now a quiet, unmanned station, if you follow the narrow alley in front of the station, you can still see traces of the old highway. Railways, a modern product, run through a town steeped in Edo period history. It is truly a luxurious experience to be immersed in such multilayered time.

Northern makuwa. This area is known for its production of mulberry gourds, and the smell of a rich lifestyle can be felt around the station. In the past, the vitality of textile factories and other industries probably came from here, but now the voices of students commuting to school have taken center stage at the station. The wind blowing through the station building feels like it's mixed with some nostalgic, original scenery of Japan. This makes us realize that railways still play an important role as the gateway to historic northern towns.

Morella Gifu. Although the name is somewhat confusing for a Showa era writer, it is a modern name, but a huge commercial facility is located right in front of the station. This relatively new station on the Tarumi Railway can be said to breathe new life into the good old local line. However, the sight of a diesel engine sliding into this modern landscape depicts a strange contrast between old and new. This is also one of the robust aspects of railways living in the Reiwa era.

Itonuki. When you get to this point, persimmon trees will be visible from the train window, making you strongly aware that this is the area where Fuyu persimmons, a specialty product, are produced. In autumn, the orange fruits are abundant and are sure to please the eyes of travelers. When you step off the platform, which looks more like a waiting room than a station building, you can feel the richness of the land where nature and industry are closely connected. The activities of people who live with the soil are quietly unfolding alongside the rails.

Honsu. It is the operation base of the Tarumi Railway, and the heart of this line where the train depot is located. Freight trains heading to the Sumitomo Cement factory used to make frequent changes, and the lively whistles echoed throughout the premises. Nowadays, the transportation of cargo has ceased, and the vast grounds still quietly testify to its former glory. However, the pride of railway workers still resides in the sight of the diesel cars lined up in the inspection and repair shed. The unique sense of tension and relief that emanates from this station gives us a sense of the end and start of a train journey.

Oribe. This station, named after the birthplace of Furuta Oribe, a Sengoku warlord and tea master, has a modern appearance attached to a roadside station. However, from this point on, the trail finally enters the Neo River valley, acting as a sort of trailhead. The mountains approach the window of the train, making you feel the air becoming even more dense. A sense of the dignified mountains begins to drift in, similar to the tranquility of a tea ceremony.

Kichihara. The clear stream of the Neo River flows right next to it, and in spring, cherry blossom trees decorate the railroad tracks, making it a picturesque place. Perhaps it's a remnant of the area's once-bustling lumber-carrying days, but there's something calming about this village in the mountains. The creak of the rails as they weave through the steep terrain sounds like a prelude to the full-scale mountain crossing that is about to begin.

Taniguchiguchi. As the gateway to Kegon-ji Temple, the Mangan Sacred Site of the Saigoku Sanjusansho Pilgrimage, this station has welcomed many worshipers since ancient times. Although it is no longer connected to the former Meitetsu Tanikumi Line, the atmosphere of the station is created by the pious feelings of the people who ride the bus from here to the temple. The sight of old passenger cars quietly spending the rest of their lives by the platform reminds us of the golden age of railways.

God sea. Mino Kamikai Station was famous as the terminal station during the era of the Japanese National Railways Tarumi Line. At the end of the dead-end railway line, steep mountains stand in the way, giving the illusion that this was once the northern limit of civilization. Although it is now a transit station, its sturdy structure still exudes the pride and dignity of its former terminus.

High school. After passing through Kamikai, we finally enter unexplored territory from the section that opened in 1960 and was extended in the 1980s. The station is located on a high embankment, and the view of the mountain village below is as orderly as a model world. The sound of the diesel engine engine echoing through the silence makes you feel that this is the only bond that connects this deep mountain region with civilization.

Nabehara. Every time you pass through a tunnel and cross a railway bridge, the beauty of the Neo River valley changes its appearance to become more rugged. There are very few houses around the station, and the world of deep mountains and valleys is spread out, dominated only by the sound of the wind and the murmuring of the river. This harsh terrain silently tells us just how difficult railway construction was in the past. It truly has the feel of an unexplored region, nestled deep in the bosom of nature.

Daily allowance. As the name suggests, it is located on a bright slope where the sun shines brightly. This is also a famous spot for cherry blossoms, and during the blooming season, many photographers gather to capture the moment. It can be said that it exists like an oasis on this route, providing a warm and soothing feeling even though it is a harsh mountain route.

Takao. Unlike Mt. Takao in Tokyo, this place is located on a steep path that leads to the deepest part of the Neo River. The mountains that can be seen from the platform are so steep that they seem to be off limits to humans. However, even in such places, there are definitely people who live there, and the railways support their lives. The sight of a single diesel car reliably climbing a mountain reminds me of the tenacity of Japan's railway network.

waterfowl. This station is located very close to the Neodani Fault, which appeared in the Nobi Earthquake of 1898. In this land where the threat of nature that has torn apart the land is still felt today, the fact that the railway continues to run as if nothing has happened is a testament to the strength of human will. Even though it bears the scars of history, the air of this place, where clean water flows, is as pure as ever.

Look at the barrel. Finally, we arrived at the final station. Just a short walk after leaving the station, the ``Usuzumi-zakura'' tree, which is over 1,500 years old, greets travelers with a timeless feel. The track ends here, but it also suggests that this is the starting point for a new journey. As you watch the smoke emitted by diesel cars melt into the mountains, you can feel the satisfaction of traveling by train. This is the perfect scenery to end your trip.

Hokutetsu Kanazawa. This station, which once maintained its majesty above ground, has now gone underground at the east exit of Kanazawa Station, masquerading as an urban tranquility. However, once you pass through the automatic ticket gate and step onto the platform, you will see the Hokutetsu 8000 series, once known as the 3000 series, the old Keio Electric Railway, quietly waiting for passengers, and the cool atmosphere unique to underground stations will make you look forward to the Asaden journey that is about to begin. With the hustle and bustle of JR Kanazawa Station behind you, this moment when you transfer to a small private railway in Hokuriku is an irresistible travel experience for train lovers. For those who are familiar with the remains of the station building that was relocated from the area near Kitama Station in the above-ground era, this underground space can also be seen as a layer of history that tells the story of changes over time.

Nanatsuya. This station, where the train crawls out of the basement and first falls asleep in the bright sunlight, is overlooked by the gigantic elevated Hokuriku Shinkansen, and the contrast between them is truly symbolic. In the past, a railway line ran from here to the banks of the Asano River, and if you think about the history of the area, where it was a busy siding for transporting lumber and other goods, its current quiet appearance can be said to be a glimpse of the changing times. Standing on the short platform hidden in the shadows under the overpass, I can strongly feel the vitality of local private railways, which is completely unrelated to the roar of the super express trains passing overhead. Considering that this place was once the starting point for going underground and the landscape changed dramatically, this is the turning point between ``modernity'' and ``reminiscence.''

Kamimoroe. While the urban area of ​​Kanazawa is gradually turning into a residential area, this station still retains a strong scent of daily life. Although the station is surrounded by large commercial facilities and seems to be enjoying the convenience of the Reiwa era, the simple structure of the station itself retains a strong vestige of the suburban trains of the Showa era. Looking at the silver trains blending into everyday scenery, we are reminded that trains are more than just a means of transportation, they are the arteries of the city. This area used to be a vast countryside, but now there are rows of houses, giving the impression that the waves of the times have completely swallowed up this station as part of the city. However, there is certainly a sense of warmth that is unique to private railways, which are rooted in the local community, and that continues to be felt even today.

Isobe. The best part of the Asanogawa Line, which runs past the eaves of houses, is concentrated around this station. The sounds of daily life in the houses approaching behind the platform and the warning sounds of railroad crossings create a pleasant rhythm, inviting travelers to an extension of their daily lives. Even though the rural scenery of the past has disappeared and it is now surrounded by concrete, this station still has a somewhat tranquil atmosphere that makes you feel the compassion that is unique to Hokuriku's private railways. The gentle curve immediately after exiting the station makes you imagine a time when trains pulled by steam locomotives moved slowly along, and the afterimage of history is superimposed on the scenery passing through the train window. Although it is an ordinary small station, there is a sense of pride that has been preserved quietly as the ``foot'' of the local people.

Index. Although the name of the station may sound somewhat fancy, this is the heart of the Asanogawa Line, where the headquarters of Hokuriku Railway is located. It once served as a hub for freight transportation, and you can feel the lingering scent of that atmosphere in the calm atmosphere around the station. I can't help but think that the simple contrast between the office building and the platform symbolizes the integrity of the railway business, which has nothing to do with glamor. Perhaps it is because of the secluded nature of this route that it maintains a tranquility that feels like a hideout, even though the company's headquarters is attached to it. Seeing the people who support the operation of trains come and go here every day, I can feel the professionalism that lies behind the everyday ``railway'' that we casually enjoy.

Three mouths. If you look at the map, you can see that this is a place where three rivers converge, and it makes you think about the flow of water in ancient times. The station itself is unmanned and quiet, but after a short walk you can see the Asano River embankment, giving you a sense of the ``water journey'' that the line's name suggests. The moment you pass by this small station, surrendering to the sway of the train, the weight of time that this village has lived through suddenly rushes through the train window. Even in the middle of a row of modern houses, the narrow road leading to the station still retains the presence of an ancient village, and this can be visualized through the device of a railway. It is in these small stations that hidden true scenery is hidden, the kind of scenery that makes you want to write about it as a travel writer.

Mitsuya. As the only exchange station on the Asanogawa Line, the sight of the trains above and below breathing in unison is like a ritual on single-track railways. It was once a place where vehicles could rest as the ``Mitsuya Vehicle Inspection Area,'' and the remains of that time still live quietly on the side tracks. It shows us that the few minutes of silence while waiting for an oncoming train is an irreplaceable luxury in today's fast-paced society. The sight of passengers crossing the railroad crossing and the short exchange between drivers. Each of these scenes feels like a valuable heritage that conveys the railway scenery of the Showa era to the present Reiwa era. The waiting time here is not a stagnation, but a gentle "punctuation mark" to help you move on to your next destination.

Okawabata. This place, with the Asanogawa iron bridge just outside the station, has a particularly open feel compared to the scenery along the Asanogawa Line. In the past, farmland spread around this area, and the harvest season probably had a different flavor, but now urban planning is progressing and you can hear the heartbeat of a new town. However, the wind blowing across the river surface blows across the platform, making you feel that you are approaching the final station, Uchinada. As the name of this station suggests, this place, located right on the edge of the river, seems to act as a dividing line between the city of Kanazawa and the seaside. Am I the only one who feels that the sound of the train crossing the bridge gets louder and louder, like a drum roll announcing the end of the journey?

Kitama. In the scenery surrounding the station, traces of the Hokuriku rural areas of the past can be seen slightly overlapping. As the name Kitama suggests, this area has been a residential area for a long time, and the station itself stands close to the local lifestyle. When you stand on the platform, which has no large-scale decorations, you can feel the weight of the history of railways, which have quietly but surely played a role as transportation for local people. If you look back at the history of Asaden's history with land improvement in this area, it's not hard to imagine how much hope a single rail has brought. Even though it is surrounded by modern residential areas, the evening light that illuminates the home has a mysterious power that evokes memories of a distant day.

Mosquito claw. This station, located at the northern tip of Kanazawa City, has a somewhat rugged background, having once been a busy distribution center for charcoal and firewood. As a railway hobbyist, it is a joy to discover the remains of a former logistics hub in the intricate topography and layout of buildings around the station. Just before the Asano River heads to its mouth, the train strongly steps onto the roadbed in this area, which looks a little rugged. Once you pass this point, you'll be faced with a steep incline towards the Uchinada, and you'll feel the tension of a run-up section. Although the appearance of freight has disappeared with the passage of time, the somewhat rugged atmosphere of the station continues to silently tell the history of this area.

Awagasaki. This station, where the railway lines curve sharply in front of the Otetsu Bridge that crosses the Asano River, is filled with a sense of tranquility before the highlight of the line. As the gateway to Awagasaki Amusement Park, which was once hailed as the ``Takarazuka of Hokuriku,'' you will feel as if the colorful memories of the area, which was crowded with many vacationers, are wafting away with the sea breeze. During the Taisho and early Showa periods, theaters and amusement parks spread here, creating a dream-like atmosphere, but now it has turned into a quiet residential area. However, the magnificent view from the train window as you cross the bridge still lifts the spirits of those who ride the train. The greatest significance of visiting this station is to enjoy the view of the great river that stretches out from the train window while tracing the remnants of a lost amusement park.

text_en: Uchinada. The terminal station of the Asanogawa Line welcomes travelers by sitting on the edge of a sand dune. For those who know the turbulent history of the Uchinada Struggle, the current calm atmosphere must be deeply moving. When I look at the end sign of the track that suddenly ends at the end of the platform and think of the Sea of ​​Japan that stretches beyond that, I feel that the story that was woven by a short private railway line is quietly coming to an end. I hear that there was once a plan to extend the line deep into the sand dunes, and this dead-end scenery gives us both the solitude and relief that only a terminal station can provide. Waiting for the train to return while being blown by the sea breeze is a luxurious time that is perfect for the end of a travelogue.

Nomachi. Just a few minutes by bus from Kanazawa's downtown area, Korinbo, this terminal station, which suddenly appears across the Saigawa River, is aptly described as a ``solitary terminal''. Considering the history of the area, which was once bustling with connections to city trains and a vast plaza in front of the station, its current serenity, as if it had been left behind, also invites a sense of travel. When you step inside the station building, which has a distinct wooden structure, you will see the high ceilings and old benches that still convey the warmth of the Showa era travelers. The inconvenience of not being connected to JR Kanazawa Station gives us a sense of the independent spirit of this line, and the moment we pass through the ticket gate and see the train stop on the platform, we are invited to a ``private railway journey'' that is cut off from our daily lives.

Nishiizumi. This station, which is the first station a train arrives at after leaving Nomachi and weaving through the rows of houses in the city, has some traces of its former freight transportation days. The Kanazawa City Central Wholesale Market is located near the station, giving a sense of its vitality as a distribution hub, while standing on the platform gives off the laid-back atmosphere typical of local private railways. In the Showa era, many goods were transported from this area, and when you understand the history of how it supported the city's economy, you will want to pay respect to even just a small station. The current platform is very simple, but I can't help but think that the light that shines through the gaps between the warehouses and houses that line the tracks is a testament to the steady history this station has had over the years.

New Nishikanazawa. This station, which was once called "Shin-Nonoichi," is located back-to-back with Nishi-Kanazawa Station on the JR Hokuriku Main Line (currently IR Ishikawa Railway), and has a history of being very busy with connecting transportation with the Japanese National Railways. The premises, where once freight cars would have been busily delivered and the whistles of locomotives echoed, now serves as a quiet transfer station. However, I can't help but feel a sense of pride as a former mainstay of logistics when I see the vast ruins of the campus and the intricately intersecting railroad tracks. When you stand on the small platform of the Hokutetsu Railway on a lower level while looking sideways at the modern platforms of the Japanese National Railways, you can feel the strong vitality of the small and medium-sized private railways in contrast to the huge main line.

Oshino. This station, which makes you feel like you have left Kanazawa City and stepped into Nonoichi City, is hidden in a residential area. In the past, there was a vast countryside surrounding this area, and it probably had an idyllic scene as a small rural station, but now it is surrounded by houses and the smell of life is thick in the air. When you stand on the platform, even for a short while waiting for the train to arrive, there is a sense of calm that makes you forget the hustle and bustle of the city. As the name of the station suggests, this place is steeped in the memories of the land since ancient times, and quietly shows us how the railway supported the development of the city and eventually became part of the landscape.

Nonoichi. This station, which has a history of flourishing as a post town on the Hokkoku Kaido road, is full of charm as a point where railroads and ancient roads intersect. It is located far away from JR Nonoichi Station, and the fact that it is close to the ancient center of the city makes you feel the accumulation of history. In contrast to the bustle of the road that passes right by the platform, the station itself maintains a simple, as if time has stopped, and this contrast is truly interesting. Trains now run lightly along the roads that travelers once walked. Is it part of the nature of travel writers to seek out the afterimages of a time when inns and merchant houses were lined side by side in the scenery seen from the train window?

In front of Nonoichi Institute of Technology. This station, which was once called ``Uenonoichi'' and ``Kodai-mae,'' is, as its name suggests, a lively place where young students roam. The sight of old railway facilities intertwined with young people aspiring to pursue cutting-edge studies is somehow heartwarming and gives a sense of the rejuvenation of the line. In the mornings and evenings, many students fill this small platform, giving the illusion that a modern vehicle has been breathed into the Showa era. The area around the station is lined with restaurants and apartments for students, reminding us that local private railways are not just relics of the past, but are an indispensable device for our ongoing lives. When I stand alone on the platform in the afternoon, after the hustle and bustle has subsided, I can sense a certain sense of hope on the road leading to the school building.

Horse change. The name of this station, which has an old-fashioned sound, seems to hint at the history of this area as a transportation hub and a place where people could change horses. Currently, it is located in a quiet residential area as an unmanned station with just one platform, but you can still feel the remnants of an old village in the curves of the tracks and the way the surrounding alleys intertwine. One of the best parts of traveling by train is the moment when the train quietly slides in and the door opens, reminding you of the roaring horses of the highway era. The real thrill of the Ishikawa Line, which runs as if passing through the gardens of surrounding houses, remains very much in the area around this station, and it makes us realize once again how closely railways have continued to be a close part of people's lives.

In front of the frame house. Although the name of the station gives a strong impression of the period of high economic growth, this is one of the bases of operation on the Ishikawa Line, and has a magnificent station building. In the past, large-scale housing complexes were built around this area, and it played a symbolic role as a new commuter town for Kanazawa. When you look at the nostalgic office smell that wafts through the station building and the neatly lined benches, you are reminded of the splendor of the past, when it was crowded with families. Currently, it functions as a station in a quiet residential area, but the tension when trains pass each other and the footsteps of people passing through the ticket gates make you feel the pride that this station continues to beat as the heart of the city.

Otomaru. This station, located on the outer edge of Kanazawa's urban area, is surrounded by the tranquility of a residential area. This area, which was once dominated by a vast rural landscape, is now home to an orderly row of houses as a base for daily life, but the appearance of the station itself still retains some of the simplicity of a former rural station. When you step off the platform, the nostalgic scent of earth wafts through the breeze, reminding you that the railway is a ``road'' that supports people's daily lives. It doesn't have any flashy facilities, but as I watch the silver trains disappear into the dusk, I'm suddenly drawn to the simple, everyday beauty of this station.

400,000. The unique place name is said to reflect the number of samurai who once lived in this area, or the amount of harvest, preserving the memories of the past. Although the station itself is a simple single-sided platform, the calm residential area that surrounds it gives a sense of the character of Kanazawa's commuter town. Every time the train door opens, the heartbeat of the quiet city flows into the train, inviting travelers into a moment of peace. In the past, it was possible to see the majestic view of Mt. Hakusan unobstructed from around this station. Although the scenery changes with the passage of time, I can't help but feel that the weight of the years that this station has passed is ingrained in each sleeper.

Yohari. It is a new station name born in the Heisei era that stands out among the Ishikawa Line, and its sound is imbued with hope for a new town. New residential areas are expanding around it, adding a new page to the line's history since the Showa era. Although the station has the latest facilities, the train that arrives is a classic Tokyu Corporation train, a contrast that makes railway fans smile and gives them a sense of the crossroads of the times. The once rural area has been given a new lease of life and is filled with the vibrancy of the younger generation. This station, which symbolizes the ``rejuvenation'' of the line, is like a ray of sunlight shining brightly into the future of the Ishikawa Line.

Soya. As you approach this station, you can see greenery between the houses from the train window, giving you a feeling that you are finally nearing the entrance to the foothills of Mt. Hakusan. Its simple appearance, without a station building, is reminiscent of the original scenery of local private railways, and its cleanliness, without excessive decoration, is pleasant. At dusk, the sight of the lights illuminating the platform and gently welcoming those rushing home makes us feel the love and kindness of the railroad, which remains unchanged through the ages. While imagining the engine sound of the non-electrified diesel cars that once ran through this area, I watch the modern train quietly accelerate. It is here that the ``memory of railways'' that has been passed down through the ages is certainly alive.

Dohoji Temple. This station, named after an ancient temple, exudes a quiet dignity reminiscent of the strategic point on the highway that once connected Kaga and Echizen. There are still old houses with tiled roofs in the surrounding area, and the contrast with the modern trains is really interesting. The ridgeline of the mountains seen from the platform feels even closer, and you can experience the exhilaration of seeing the railway cut into the heart of nature. It can be said that the history of the land and the railway are integrated into a deep scenery, and the waiting for trains to pass here is a blissful rest for travelers. This is a truly interesting station where you can see the sincere spirit of local private railway operation in the casual scene of exchanges.

Iguchi. This station, with its small waiting room standing alone, retains the atmosphere of a ``village station.'' The surrounding fields, which would once have been bustling with activity during the busy farming season, are now intermingled with residential buildings, creating a unique landscape. Because it is not a flashy tourist destination, the simple daily life of Ishikawa is alive and well, and it shows us that the true travel spirit is hidden in the casual scenery passing through the train window. In the silence where the sound of train joints echoes even further, you can savor the history of the area. These small stations are the driving force behind my writing as a travel writer.

Koyanagi. The name, which makes you think of a willow tree swaying by the railroad tracks, has a truly lyrical sound. Although the structure of the station is extremely simple, it allows you to directly feel the surrounding nature and the changing seasons. Flowers bloom on the ridges in spring, and in winter they are covered in silver snow. The silver train has continued to silently watch over the changing faces of the four seasons. Although this station does have some luxury, the view of the greenhouses and houses seen from the train window shows the close relationship between the railway and the people's lives.

Himiko. This station, which has a divine name reminiscent of mythical times, is like a solemn prologue just before reaching the city of Tsurugi. Perhaps it's a relic from the days when people dreamed of connecting to the old Kinmei Railway, but the spaciousness makes one imagine the expanse of the railway network in the past. The hint of the Tedorigawa River visible from the train window and the greenery of the looming mountain surface tell us that this is not just a suburb, but the entrance to a sacred place. The train's speed seems to slow down, perhaps as a sign of respect as it approaches its final station. The railway journey through the land where ancient legends lie is finally reaching its final stage.

Tsurugi. When you finally arrive at the terminal station, the solid wooden station building overwhelms travelers, making it the most sacred place on the Ishikawa Line. Considering the history of a railway that once extended beyond this point to Kaga Ichinomiya and even down to Hakusan, you can't help but feel the echoes of impermanence in the track ruins that disappeared beyond the parking lot. Vehicles with a history carved into them are resting inside the station, and the vibrancy of the former vehicle inspection area can still be felt. This place, which blends the atmosphere of this town that prospered as a temple town in front of Hakusan Hime Shrine with the atmosphere of the good old railway, is the perfect ending point for a travelogue. When you step out of the ticket gate and step out into the quiet streets, you feel deeply the richness that train travel has etched into your heart.

Takaoka. It has long prospered as a strategic point on the Hokuriku Main Line, and although it has now been replaced by Shin-Takaoka Station on the Shinkansen, it still maintains its pride as the center of western Toyama Prefecture. The Manyo Line begins here, and since the days of the former Kaetsuno Railway, the city's streetcars have been deeply rooted as a means of transportation for citizens. While the area in front of the station is being redeveloped and modern buildings are lined up, as soon as you step into the alley, you can feel the scent of the old castle town. From here, travelers can ride the red tram and row into the good old town of Takaoka.

Suehiro Town. It is located just a stone's throw from Takaoka Station, at the entrance to a shopping street with an arcade. This street, which once housed a department store and would have been crowded with shoppers, now has a somewhat calm and quiet appearance. Still, the signboards of the shops lined up here seem to be engraved with the liveliness of the Showa era. The sight of a streetcar rumbling across the street exudes a gentle melancholy that is unique to regional cities.

Katahara town. From this point on, the city's former merchant town's character becomes even stronger. The rows of earthen storehouse-style houses and stately bank buildings that line the left and right sides remain as symbols of Takaoka's wealth. The train runs majestically on the roadway, sharing space with cars, and it shows a truly splendid coexistence. This area is a reminder of the once prosperous commercial capital of Hokuriku, and even just looking through the train window makes you feel the weight of history.

Sakashita town. It is known as the closest station to Takaoka Daibutsu, one of Japan's three great Buddha statues. If you get off the station and walk a short distance, you can see the gentle face of the Great Buddha. It was originally the location of Takaoka Castle's Ashitemon gate, and it is interesting that the station's name comes from the undulating topography. The Manyo Line tracks, which run between old private houses, are completely integrated into the life of this town, creating an extraordinary atmosphere in the ordinary.

name_en: In front of the emergency medical center
text_en: In front of the emergency medical center. This station, formerly known as ``Honmaru Kaikan-mae,'' is located at the entrance to Takaoka Castle Park. The remains of Takaoka Castle, built by Maeda Toshinaga, still remain with lush greenery. The sight of the latest low-floor vehicles and nostalgic old cars passing in front of modern medical facilities makes you feel like you are witnessing a crossroads of time. History and modernity intersect on the tram rails.
