text_en: Hirokoji. It was once an important administrative and economic center of Takaoka, and is where the city hall and police station were once located. Although it has become somewhat quieter now, the contrast between the waves of cars rushing through the intersection and the calm, serene train running in the middle is a sight that can only be seen in a city with streetcars. The area around this station is dotted with old concrete buildings, which seem to convey the stubbornness of the Showa era, and somehow seem reliable.

name_en: In front of Shikino Junior High School
text_en: In front of Shikino Junior High School. It is literally a station located in front of the gate of the school. In the morning and evening, this small platform is buzzing with the bustle of students carrying their bags. There are many schools along the Manyo Line, and it's great to see young people using this old transportation system on a daily basis. Seasonal flowers bloom at the edge of the tracks, and the sight of the train moving leisurely through the residential area symbolizes the peaceful timeline that this town has.

name_en: In front of the citizen hospital
text_en: In front of the citizen hospital. The functional and clean hospital building can be seen from the train window. The train stops quietly, picking up people going to the hospital or visiting people. Here, you can really feel that the railway is not just a means of transportation, but a part of social infrastructure, literally part of people's lifelines. When you get to this point in the city of Takaoka, which stretches out outside your window, the sky seems a little wider, and it makes you look forward to your next destination.

Ejiri. This station is located at the border of Takaoka, where the scenery gradually changes to an industrial area and hints of a port. Although there are few traces of the past when the factory line branched out, the silhouettes of the factories lining the line give a sense of pride in supporting industry in this area. From now on, the tram will enter a special track and speed up its pace towards the sea. This station has a unique atmosphere that makes you feel like it's a break in your journey.

Asahigaoka. As you pass through the city, the scenery at this station gradually begins to calm down, giving you the tranquility of a residential area. A place like a rest on the way to the former Shinminato City. The roofs of houses lined up at even intervals can be seen from the train window, which also tells us the certainty of a life rooted in this area. Although there are no flashy sightseeing spots, it is precisely in these ordinary stations that the life-size face of the local city is hidden.

Ogibu. A huge factory plant appears beyond the train window, reinforcing the character of this line as an ``industrial transport''. The group of chimneys, including Nippon Soda, look like proud remains that supported Japan's postwar reconstruction. There is a mysterious sense of travel here, where the smell of steel and the sea breeze mix. This platform, which would once have been buzzing with the footsteps of factory workers, now stands with the quiet heartbeat of heavy and chemical industry in the background.

Shinno town. Although it is located just a stone's throw away from Nomachi Station on the JR Himi Line, it maintains the atmosphere of a streetcar. The tram moves lightly across the railroad tracks that were once frequented by freight trains. It is a remnant of the days when the railway network was spread out like a web. This place, where two different railway lines come together, is a historical nexus that is truly interesting for railway enthusiasts.

name_ja: 米島口アルビス米島店前
name_en: In front of Yonejimaguchi Albis Yonejima store
text_en: Yonejima mouth. The depot, which can be said to be the heart of the Manyo Line, expands and you can see the red trains taking a rest. It is very lively as a base for operations, and the scenes of crew changes seem to be some sort of solemn ceremony, which is interesting. Although the station's name, Supermarket, gives it a modern feel, the unique smell of oil and the creaking sound of the railroad tracks at the train depot remind us of the breath of the railway that has remained unchanged since ancient times.
name_fr: Devant le magasin Yonejimaguchi Albis Yonejima

text_en: Nomachi Exit. The walls of the factory are closing in once again, and the railroad tracks are extending powerfully. In this area where heavy and chemical industry is flourishing, trains have continued to transport working people silently. Its rugged, practical appearance is the true essence of this line, and it evokes memories of the labor of the Showa era. The landscape of ``coexistence of industry and railways'', which is disappearing due to modernization, is still alive and well here.

Shinyoshihisa. From here on, the train heads into an old townscape that still retains a strong vestige of the past. While modern road construction is progressing, one step into the alleys reveals the vibrancy of merchants from the Edo to Meiji eras. This station, which is both new and old, feels like a gateway to time travel. The platform, which is placed in the middle of the road and looks like a small safety zone, gives off the stamina of a streetcar.

Yoshihisa. This station is a nationally designated Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, so you can feel the weight of its history. Earthen storehouse-style houses and factory chimneys rising just behind them. This strange and beautiful contrast is what makes this route between Takaoka and Shinminato so interesting. Good old Japan lives hand in hand with modern industry. The sight of a train threading its way through these lines seems to be connecting the fault lines of history.

Nakafushiki. The journey on the Manyo Line is finally reaching its climax, with signs of Fushiki Port approaching from the train window. A gateway to the sea that has existed since the days of Kitamaebune. The stately warehouses and somewhat sooty appearance of the buildings testify to the strength of the building, which has survived many harsh Hokuriku winters. I even get the illusion that the scent of the sea is sneaking in through the cracks of the train. This is a truly romantic place where land railways and sea routes intersect.

Rokutoji Temple. Before crossing the majestic flow of the Shogawa River, we finally entered the town of Shinminato. In the past, the section beyond this point was a dedicated track for the Kaetsuno Railway, and ran more like a railway. The train accelerates powerfully while catching the river breeze. This station, with its expansive waterside scenery, gives travelers a temporary sense of freedom. From here, the story of the sea begins in earnest as we head towards our final destination, Koshinogata.

Takaragaike. It is a turning point in fate, where the Eizan Main Line and the Kurama Line part ways. This area, which was founded as Yamabata Station by the Kyoto Electric Light Company in 1923, is a quiet place where passengers heading for Mt. Hiei and those headed for Kurama cross paths. What used to be an at-grade crossing where people would give way to each other has now been transformed into a well-organized platform, but the creaking sound of the branching rails still evokes the same sense of travel. The presence of the Takano River flowing right next to the station and the somewhat spacious atmosphere within the premises are quiet reminders that this is a key transportation hub for Rakuhoku.

In front of Yahata. As the name suggests, this station is located at the entrance to the approach to Miyake Hachimangu Shrine, which has been worshiped as the ``protector of children'' since ancient times. In the past, a tram-like vehicle carrying worshipers can be seen leisurely stopping here. Nowadays, a quiet residential area spreads around the area, and the scene of daily commutes to school and work takes center stage, but as soon as you step onto the platform, you can feel the dignified silence that seems to be the entrance to a sacred area. It may not be flashy, but the ruts of life that support the depth of Kyoto are engraved here.

Iwakura. It is known as the place where Tomomi Iwakura, a patriot at the end of the Edo period, lived in seclusion, and the area has a multilayered history. When you get off at this station, you can see what was once a idyllic countryside, but now it has been developed into a peaceful residential area in Rakuhoku. However, if you look around you, you will see a series of mountains, including Mt. Hiei, that look like a folding screen, giving you a sense of security that is unique to the basin and makes you feel protected. Listening to the sound of trains accelerating and decelerating quietly in this place, one step removed from the center stage of history, is one of the best parts of traveling by train.

Kino. In the past, when you came to this area, you would feel like you were really close to the mountains, and you would feel like you were leaving the city of Kyoto. It is not hard to imagine that when it first opened in the early Showa era, it was just a stand alone station in a field. Nowadays, there are more universities and residences in the neighborhood, and modern young people have become more prominent, but the greenery of the mountains behind the station remains the same as it always was, providing a rest for the eyes of travelers. It gives us the feeling that the boundaries between the everyday and the extraordinary are intertwined on this modest platform.

Kyoto Seika Daimae. This station, which was newly built in the Heisei era, seems somewhat new to the eyes of a travel writer who loves the Showa era, but it is also proof that railways, as living beings as they are, have adapted to the times. The road leading to the campus is full of youthful energy, breathing new life into what was once a quiet mountain road. However, once the train leaves the station, the tranquil forest of the ancient city begins to dominate the train window once again. This station seems to symbolize the inclusiveness of the city of Kyoto, where old and new sit side by side, but never deny each other.

Nikenjaya. The station's historic name comes from the fact that there were once two teahouses where travelers on their pilgrimage to Kurama could rest their feet. In the past, it served as the ``boundary'' where the line would become a single track from here onwards, and it would finally take on the appearance of a full-fledged mountain railway. Nowadays, the double-track section has been extended and the scenery has changed, but you can still feel the density of the air change and the mountain air suddenly increase as you pass this station. Even if teahouses, the tellers of history, disappear, as long as their place names remain, we can still see the hustle and bustle of travelers in the past.

Ichihara. From this station onwards, the sound of the train running becomes more powerful, making you feel the determination to finally enter the depths of Mt. Kurama. The area around the station retains the atmosphere of a mountain village, and my heart is pounding with anticipation for the ``Momiji Tunnel'' that begins here. It is no exaggeration to say that the unique oppressive feeling of trees approaching from both sides of the tracks, which has remained unchanged since the Showa era, is the true essence of Eizan Electric Railway. An iron ring quietly carves the thin line between nature and humans. That sense of tension is what gives this station its atmosphere.

Ninose. It is a station that gives off the atmosphere of an unexplored region, as if sunken to the depths of deep greenery. The mountains loom right behind the platform, and in the fall, fiery autumn leaves envelop the vehicle, making it a truly beautiful mountain scene. Even though its form has changed, the warmth that the old wooden station building conveyed still exists in the tranquility of this area. The time spent waiting for the next train in this place, isolated from the hustle and bustle of the city, may be the greatest luxury for modern people. It gives you a refreshing and comfortable feeling, like the mountain air stinging your skin.

Kibuneguchi. The murmur of the Kifune River flowing directly below the platform is so close that it can even be heard inside the train. As the gateway to Kifune Shrine, which enshrines the god of water, this station has welcomed many worshipers since ancient times, and there is a certain purity to it. How happy we were when the railroad was brought to this area, which used to be accessible only through narrow mountain roads. Standing on the platform built in a narrow valley, you can feel the harshness of nature and the pride of the railwaymen who took on the challenge. The sound of water cleanses your soul and invites you deep into the mountains.

Kurama. A stately temple-like station building, befitting a terminal station, welcomes travelers. The giant tengu mask sitting in front of the station is quietly watching over the memory of the days when famous cars such as the Dena 21 class lined up next to each other. From this point on, there is no railway, and all that remains is to climb the sacred mountain on your own, marking a graceful end to the journey. A special time passes in this place, which is the end of a journey but also the beginning of faith. Even the sound of the air exhaled by a train after climbing a long hill sounds somehow filled with relief.

Demachiyanagi. As the terminal station of the Keihan Railway and the starting point of the Eizan Railway, this place has an atmosphere that makes it worthy of being called the gateway to Rakuhoku. As you climb above ground from the hustle and bustle of the underground, you will find the ``Kamo River Delta'' where the Kamo River and the Takano River join, and you will feel the gentle breeze of the ancient capital blowing through you. This area, which was once a bustling starting point for the Sabakaido road that leads to Wakasa, has now been transformed into a terminal where students and vacationers mingle. However, as I stand on the small platform of the Eizan train, a quiet sense of elation for the journey to the mountains that is about to begin wells up in my heart. Beyond the steel rails stretching north, the mountain range of Hiei quietly stands out, creating a unique magnetic field that makes you forget the turmoil of the city.

Former Tanaka. The platform, which looks like an excuse, was placed next to a large railroad crossing across Higashioji-dori, and it is a reminder of the tram. The area around this station retains faint memories of the former Kyoto tram line and the University of Tokyo line, and even if you are not a railway fan, you can still find a nostalgic ``Showa era'' street corner. The surrounding area is lined with cheap set meals catering to students and second-hand bookstores, and the atmosphere is filled with the scent of daily life and the enthusiasm of academics. Every time a train passes a railroad crossing, the city pauses and starts moving again. This rhythm can be said to be the very heartbeat of the town of Mototanaka. This landscape, which has nothing to do with modern elevated railways, and where the ground and tracks are closely connected, tells us about the richness of the times when railways were a part of everyday life.

Chayama/Kyoto University of Arts. In the past, it was simply called ``Chayama,'' and as the name suggests, it is an elegant place that is said to have been home to mountain villas and tea plantations for court nobles during the Edo period. Although it now bears the name of a university and is a station where aspiring young artists get on and off, the atmosphere surrounding the platform is still calm and does not disrupt the tranquility of the residential area. What makes this station interesting is that it combines the scent of sophisticated art with the familiarity of a downtown back alley. Once you pass through the ticket gates of a small, unmanned station, you will find that the nameless activities of life continue there, making you realize that a new culture is sprouting on top of the accumulation of history. Even though the tea gardens of the past have disappeared, the tranquility that flows here still plays the role of a cup of tea that soothes the souls of visitors.

Ichijoji. When you hear the name of this station, it may be a bit of an old-fashioned traveler's nature to think of ``Ichijoji Kudarimatsu'', where Miyamoto Musashi and the Yoshioka clan fought a duel. Nowadays, it is a bustling area known for its ramen throughout the country, but the station itself maintains a surprisingly rustic appearance. Although it is the entrance to the approach to famous temples in Rakuhoku such as Shisen-do and Manshu-in, it has an unpretentious daily life. The tranquility of a thousand-year-old temple and the vibrancy of today's young people lining up. This small station functions quietly as a node connecting both ends. At dusk, the sight of the train tracks illuminated by the lights on the platform conveys the emotion of travel more eloquently than any masterpiece.

Shugakuin. The station houses the depot that can be called the heart of the Eizan train, and is a station where you can see up close the small cars taking a short break. When you stand on the platform, the Hiei mountain range rising to the north comes very close to you, giving you the strong feeling that you have stepped into the northern limits of Kyoto. Once upon a time, this station was the starting point for a quiet rural landscape that continued to Shugakuin Imperial Villa, but now the breath of the railway has blended perfectly into the residential area. The structure in which the platforms for both the up and down lines are arranged in a staggered manner across the railroad crossings gives a sense of the vestiges of streetcars, creating an irresistible atmosphere for railway fans. This station, where the sounds of mechanics' hammers can be heard from time to time, is not just a transit point, but a sanctuary where the machinery of railways comes to life.

Takaragaike. The main line heading to Yase and the Kurama Line heading towards Kurama are divided into a V-shape, making it a key operational point. Standing on the triangular platform where two lines diverge, you will feel a strange feeling, as if you were standing at a crossroads in your life. Surrounded by the deep greenery of Takaragaike Park, the scent of trees that change color with each season will tickle the nostrils of travelers. Even when the Kyoto International Conference Center was established and the area began to take on the appearance of an international city, the station itself remained as quiet as ever. Even a moment of contemplation over which line to transfer to will add color to your luxurious journey at this station. Although it is a railway junction, this place is isolated from the hustle and bustle of the city, and the tranquility of the ``meeting'' that the railway originally had is still alive today.

Miyake Hachiman. It is the entrance to Miyake Hachimangu Shrine, which is known as the god of babysitting, and the entire station is somehow enveloped in a benevolent silence. Motifs of ``pigeons'', which are said to be messengers of the gods, can be seen throughout the platforms, adding a soft color to the otherwise bare railway facilities. The rows of old houses surrounding the station, along with the murmuring of the Takano River, remind us of the original landscape of Kyoto from a long time ago. Its modest appearance, as if refusing to turn into a flashy tourist destination, actually provides a valuable ``place of rest'' in modern times. Seasonal flowers blooming next to the railroad tracks and the dry sound of the circuit breaker. When these ordinary fragments of everyday life pass through Miyake-Hachiman station, they begin to shine like a poem. In a place where parents gather to wish for the healthy growth of their children, the railways also feel like they are being watched over kindly.

Yase Hiei Yamaguchi. Since the days when it was known as ``Yase Yuen'', it has been an impressive station with a large wooden roof that has both the desolation and dignity characteristic of a terminal station. The high ceiling and heavy steel frame that spread out beyond the ticket gate give you the illusion of having wandered into a rural European station. As a gateway to the cable car that climbs Mt. Hiei, this station has welcomed many worshipers and vacationers since ancient times, and the weight of history is engrained in each and every wall. The cool breeze of the Koya River blows through the platform, and the shadow of the mountain changes its appearance every moment.Although it is the end of the railway, it also gives us a sense of the beginning of a new adventure. Beyond the end of the rail where the rail stops, endless nature and mountains of faith lie ahead. This station is a silent reminder that a terminal station is not just a dead end, but a place where one can deepen one's thoughts.

Shijo Omiya. As the starting point of the Keifuku Electric Railway Arashiyama Line, this station has a unique atmosphere. The platform, which is nestled in a quiet corner of the station building, retains a strong vestige of the tram of the past, allowing you to forget the hustle and bustle of the city for a moment. There was once a level crossing with the Kyoto City Tram, and it has a history of being a bustling transportation hub. Although it is a place that is connected to Hankyu Omiya Station, there is a constant flow of people, but when you see a single-car train quietly waiting to depart under the dome-shaped roof, you can't help but feel the calmness that the terminal had in the Showa era. There are few settings as suitable as this as a prelude to the journey that begins here.

Saiin. It is a crossing point with the Hankyu Railway, and is a lively station where you can hear the constant footsteps of passengers transferring. Randen's platform is above ground, and the train tracks are impressive as they weave through residential areas. There used to be a large depot near this area, and it has a history of being a sacred place for railway fans. Development has progressed around the station, and the shadow of modern buildings has begun to fall, but the sounds of railroad crossing alarms and train horns still add a pleasant rhythm to daily life in this ancient capital. The slight difference in the reading of the place name and the station name seems to indicate the complexity of the history of this area, and it is of great interest to me.

Nishioji Sanjo. This point, where Nishioji-dori and Sanjo-dori intersect, is a place where you can truly experience the true power of streetcars. In the past, it was called ``Sanjoguchi'' and literally symbolized the western entrance to Kyoto. The creaking sound of the wheels and the shaking of the car body when switching from the dual-use track to the dedicated track create a sense of travel that modern, smooth trains don't have. The old townscape still conveys the memory of large factories once standing in this area, and many trains transporting workers. The sight of it running majestically in the middle of the road despite the waves of cars is a strong reminder of the days when railways were the mainstay of the city.

Yamanouchi. Anyone who stands on the platform of this station is amazed at its "slenderness." The safety zone that has been established in the middle of the road can be said to be a rare presence in Japan's railway landscape. The sight of cars slowing down and passengers carefully climbing the steps each time a train approaches seems like a quiet resistance to modern efficiency. This area was once a rich land lined with vast mansions, but now it is a quiet residential area with a calm atmosphere. The mysterious feeling that a slight line carved in the asphalt separates the ordinary from the extraordinary is a valuable experience that can only be experienced at this station.

Randen Tenjingawa. Although it is a relatively new station that was created in the Heisei era, it is a symbol of modern Kyoto as a connecting point with the Tozai Subway Line. In the past, the road section of Sanjo-dori Street used to continue in this area, but now a modern rotary has been built and the area is crowded with passengers transferring. However, once you step off the train, you can hear the murmuring of the Tenjin River in the background, making you feel that the nature of the ancient capital is still alive and well. This point where new and old intersect is like a mirror that most clearly reflects the changing times.

Serikunosha. As the station name suggests, Kijimaza Amaterasu Mitama Shrine, commonly known as ``Silkworm Shrine,'' is located right next to it. When you get off at this station, the atmosphere suddenly changes and you feel a sense of tranquility. The mysterious ``Three-Pillared Torii'' in the shrine grounds is a valuable relic that conveys the footprints of people who came here today, and it gives the illusion that the railroad, a tool of modern civilization, is passing through an eternity of history. The memory of the sericulture that once flourished in this area is now preserved only in the name of the station, but the deep greenery visible from the train window still maintains the dignity of the sacred area.

Uzumasa Koryuji Temple. When the door of the train opens, the magnificent tower gate of Koryuji Temple looms in front of you, a truly spectacular view. It is rare to see a landscape where temples and railways coexist so closely and naturally. Located on the road section of Sanjo-dori Street, the sight of trains, cars, and worshipers intermingling at the perfect distance gives you a sense of the aesthetics of life that is unique to Kyoto. The sight of a purple train slowly passing in front of the gate of an ancient temple holding the national treasure Maitreya Bodhisattva condenses the weight of time from the Showa era, or even before that.

Tsuji no Tsuji. It is a strategic point where the Arashiyama Main Line and the Kitano Line diverge, and can be called the heart of this line. The underground ticket gates and slightly intricately intertwined platform structure convey the vibrancy of the city that once supported the flourishing film industry. The area around the station is dotted with remnants of film studios and old shops that would have been frequented by people involved in the film industry, and you can't help but imagine the days when stars of the silver screen would descend upon this station. The sound of the train branching off to different destinations can lift the spirits of travelers a little.

Arisugawa. It is a station with a long history, and was once called "Saga Station." Once you cross the clear stream of the Arisugawa River, from which the station takes its name, you will feel a sense of exhilaration as if you are finally entering Arashiyama, the final destination. The area around the station is a calm residential area, but the reason why it still retains a somewhat dignified appearance is because of its undercurrent of memories as a former vacation home area. From the window of the train, which runs past the eaves of houses, you can see daily life in Kyoto at close range, and this is another major attraction of this line.

Kurumaori Shrine. When you get off at this station, the bright vermillion Tamagaki wall catches your eye before you even see the station name sign. Known as the god of performing arts, just looking at the names of famous actors and singers lined up along Tamagaki gives you a sense of the depth of Kyoto's culture. There was a time when it was called ``Saga-mae,'' and its bustling status as a temple town can still be seen today. The sight of a single-car train gliding quietly into the shrine without disturbing the tranquility of the sanctuary is a microcosm of this city, where faith and life are one. The sight of locals walking through the temple grounds with their accustomed pace, mixed with tourists, gives you the feeling that this is not just a tourist spot, but a living place.

Rokuoin. Despite the hustle and bustle of Arashiyama, the area around this station is surprisingly quiet. Just a short walk from the station, you will find an ancient temple associated with Yoshimitsu Ashikaga with its gates quietly open, and you can hear the sound of the wind blowing through the stone-paved approach. Although the home has a very simple structure, it gives off a sense of cleanliness that befits the entrance to a place of training. It's fun to imagine that movie makers of the past would have taken walks in search of this tranquil place between shots. Even travelers in a hurry on their way to sightseeing spots may feel a momentary moment when they pass by this station.

Randen Saga. The station was once called ``Saga Station'' and played an important role as a point of contact with the JNR San'in Main Line. Nowadays, the JR station building has a magnificent appearance and is crowded with people waiting for sightseeing trolley trains, but the small atmosphere of the Randen station building somehow retains the good days of the Showa era. If you go through the shopping street in front of the station, you will be right next to the vast grounds of Tenryuji Temple. Even in the midst of the wave of modern tourism development, the nostalgic smell of life that hangs around this station loosens the hearts of travelers. This point where the railroads intersect is a symbol of the depth of the ancient city.

Arashiyama. It is rare to find a station that has the character of a terminal station to this extent. In the past, travelers were welcomed by the large vaulted roof, but now the gorgeous decorations known as ``Kimono Forest'' let us feel the breath of a new era. Having a footbath on the platform is a smart way to soothe the fatigue of a long journey. As you exit the station, the wind from across Togetsukyo Bridge hits your cheeks, giving you the feeling that you have finally stepped into the scenic beauty of Rakusai. This station, which has welcomed countless travelers since it opened in the Taisho era, teaches us that the end of a railway is the beginning of a new journey.

Kitano Hakubai Town. It has a history of being a connection point with the Kyoto City Tram, and that the tracks extended all the way to the base of Kitano Tenmangu Shrine. Although it was forced to move to its current location in 1966 due to the extension of the streetcar line, it still maintains its dignity as the imposing starting point of the Kitano Line. The sight of a single train waiting to turn around at a dead-end car stop creates a sense of travel that is unique to terminals. Although it is located right next to the heavy traffic of Nishioji-dori, as soon as you step onto the platform of this station, you can feel the daily life of Kitano, where time passes slowly. During exam season, the train is filled with the tension of young people heading to Tenjin, which is a seasonal feature unique to this station.

name_ja: 等持院・立命館大学衣笠キャンパス前
name_en: In front of Tojiin/Ritsumeikan University Kinugasa Campus
text_en: In front of Toji-in Temple/Ritsumeikan University Kinugasa Campus. This station, which used to be simply called ``Tojiin,'' acquired a much longer name in line with the demands of the times. The sight of young students rushing past while taking in the tranquil forest of Toji-in, the family temple of the Ashikaga shogunate, is a strange harmony of old and new time. As you wait for your train under a simple wooden shed, you can hear the occasional buzz of the campus, adding a pleasant accent to the tranquility of the ancient city. Along the way to the former Omuro Imperial Palace, the role played by this station is not just as a base for commuting to school, but as a crossroads of culture. Walking through this neighborhood, which is also associated with Shozo Makino, the father of Japanese cinema, you can almost feel the illusion that you can hear the footsteps of the people who supported the golden age of the silver screen.
name_fr: En face du campus Kinugasa de l'université Tojiin/Ritsumeikan
name_tw: 東人院/立命館大學衣笠校園前

text_en: Ryoanji Temple. Although it is the gateway to the world-famous ``Rock Garden,'' the station itself is surprisingly modest, giving off a sense of life. It was once called the Ryoanji Road, and has a history of quietly fulfilling its role as a guide for worshipers. Along the railroad tracks that run past the eaves of houses, old one-story houses that still retain the lingering scent of the Showa era are lined up, offering a glimpse of Kyoto's true side, apart from the glamorous tourist spots. The time spent climbing the gentle slope north from here is a luxurious moment that can be called ``the prelude to the approach'' as you prepare your mind to enter the tranquility of the rock garden. Although it bears the name of a famous temple, I cannot help but feel the true richness of this route, with its unpretentious atmosphere.

Myoshinji Temple. This station blends in with the quiet alley that leads to the north gate of the vast Zen temple. It was once called "Myoshinji Road" and has a history of being a popular path for monks in training and worshipers. When you step onto the platform, you can smell the scent of everyday life coming from the eaves of private houses on both sides of the tracks. However, once you step into the precincts, you will find yourself in a disciplined yet tranquil space that has been hailed as ``the pillars of Myoshinji.'' At this point where modern asphalt roads intersect with the ancient spirit of Zen, I can't help but think that Randen's single-car train plays the role of a ferry that connects this world with the Pure Land. The true value of this station is the silence that comes after the sound of the train's motor has faded away.

Omuro Ninnaji Temple. The sight of the gigantic Niomon Gate of Ninna-ji Temple rising serenely behind the station building is nothing short of spectacular. This station, which was once simply called "Omuro," was changed to its current name out of respect for its status as a Monzeki temple. The station building itself has a traditional design that takes into consideration the surrounding landscape, and it is a shame that care has been taken not to destroy the atmosphere of the ancient capital. In spring, many people descend on this station in search of the late-blooming Omuro cherry blossoms, but even within its normally quiet appearance, there is a sense of elegance as a place connected to the imperial family. The moment we look up at Niomon from the train window, we are made to realize once again that we are placed in the great flow of history.

Utano. In the past, the station was called ``Takaoguchi'' and was the starting point for travelers heading to see the autumn leaves of Sanbi. Currently, it stands quietly in a quiet residential area, but in the section from here to Narutaki Station next door, the ``Cherry Blossom Tunnel'', known as Randen's most spectacular view, awaits you. The sound of a train making its way along a slight incline, weaving its way between private houses, has an atmosphere reminiscent of a small train station in the mountains. Even though the former name of ``Takao-kou'' has disappeared, the rich nature and tranquility of this area continue to captivate the hearts of people. I can't help but feel that my desire to leave the hustle and bustle of Rakuchu and finally head to Okusaga deepens even more here in Utano.

Narutaki. The train passes through the cherry blossom tunnel from Utano and slides past the eaves of houses, giving this station a special atmosphere. In the past, even more trees covered the tracks, and the lightness of this line, which evolved from streetcars, blended well into the quietness of the area. As you walk through the narrow alleys around the station, you will see small windows and hedges reminiscent of the Showa era, making you feel that the good old suburban life of Kyoto is still alive and well. The moment when you listen to the distant sound of a train passing on a single track on a platform where the hustle and bustle of spring has gone silent is a quiet way to enjoy the real pleasure of traveling on a railway.

Tokiwa. Located at the intersection with Marutamachi Dori, this station has retained its old-fashioned appearance even though it is in the midst of modern urban traffic. There was a time when there was a large-scale hospital nearby, so the station was named after that, but the current name ``Tokiwa'' quietly asserts that this area is connected to Empress Danrin, the empress of Emperor Saga. The sound of a railroad crossing when crossing a major road temporarily interrupts the flow of modern cars and seems to be a return to the days when railroads were the mainstay of the city. The abyss of history suddenly peeks out from the train window, and that difference is what makes this line so interesting.

name_en: In front of the photo studio
text_en: In front of the photo studio. Although it is the newest station on this line, having been newly established in 2016, the weight of history that its name carries is immeasurable. The name is fitting for the entrance to the heart of Uzumasa, which was once hailed as the ``Hollywood of the East.'' Although the station itself is modern and simple in construction, the short section from here to Kajinotsuji is still steeped in memories of the city where the nameless people who supported the golden age of the silver screen and the big stars of yesteryear roamed. Seeing the hustle and bustle of the former photo studio and the enthusiasm of activists on the other side of the new station building is another joy of traveling to tell the story of the Showa era in the Reiwa era.

Tsuji no Tsuji. After completing our journey on the Kitano Line, we returned to the junction with the main line. Going up from the underground ticket gate to the ground level and watching the complex interchange of trains on two lines is a blissful moment for anyone who loves trains. Just standing on the platform warms your heart as you realize how much dream and enthusiasm this station was once filled with when the movie industry was the mainstay of this town. The dry ``clack'' sound of changing points sounds like a signal that signals the end of one journey and the beginning of another destination. From here, you can head back to Arashiyama or return to Shijo Omiya, and the railway is always open.

Kisarazu. This station still retains its pride as a port town facing Tokyo Bay and as the starting point of the Kururi Line that cuts into the mountains of Boso. The hustle and bustle of the Kisarazu ships that once departed from Kisarazu Port to Edo are a distant memory, but when you land on this platform, the scent of the ocean and the exhaust smoke of the diesel cars mix together, somehow reminding you of the travel atmosphere of the Showa era.

If you look at the structure of the station, the expanse of the tracks overlooking the bridge station building tells of the prosperity of freight transportation in the past. Standing on the platform where the Kururi Line departs, my expectations for the abyss of Uchibo that I am about to head to increase. The deep idling sound of a diesel engine makes us forget the hustle and bustle of the city and invites us back to the origins of ``rail travel.'' The old shopping streets around the station and the back alleys where you can feel the remnants of the old Red Line also quietly tell us about the richness of time that this city has accumulated.

Gion. Travelers may be momentarily confused by the name, which brings to mind the gaiety of Kyoto, but what you will find here is the extremely calm daily life of Boso. This station, where the train takes its first breath after passing through the city of Kisarazu, has quietly carved out a history as the gate of Gionji Temple, a temple with a long history.

As the diesel car slides onto the short platform, you can see a calm residential area and some greenery spreading out outside the window. There is no flashy station building, and its simple appearance with just a single platform is a perfect representation of the character of the Kururi Line. The steps of the passengers as they disembark are also somewhat leisurely, making us believe that time passes in this land on a different scale than in the city.

Kazusa Kiyokawa. The two characters "Kazusa" in the station's name take us back to the old Ritsuryo era and the deep bosom of the Boso Peninsula. Once you get to this point, the clear stream of the Obisu River will occasionally peek out from the train window, reminding you of the history of this river, which once served as a key point for water transport, transporting Kazusa's products.

Although the station itself has a simple structure with only one line, it blends beautifully with the surrounding countryside. The blue color of seedlings in the spring and the golden ears of rice in the fall decorate the platform, reminding us once again of the role that railways have, which is to ``transport the seasons.'' The smell of earth and grass that flows in each time the train door opens loosens the soul of the traveler and serves as a good prelude to the scenery that will deepen further down the line.

Higashikiyo River. When you get off the train at this station, which is completely surrounded by rice fields, you get a strong sense that Boso has been a rich granary region since ancient times. The appearance of the waiting room, which is too modest to be called a station building, stands alone, proving that the railway is a minimal but essential device that connects points and lines.

The charm of this station lies in its wide field of view. An unobstructed sky and a land that changes color with each season. The sight of a single railway running through it is full of beauty, like a landscape painting. Listening to the sound of the rice ears swaying in the wind in the silence after the train leaves, I feel the strength of this land, which has continued to preserve its unchanged landscape even though it has been washed away by the waves of modernization.

Yokota. This station is one of the few on the Kururi Line where trains can be exchanged, and is not only a key operational point, but also a post station where travelers can take a break. A few minutes of silence as we waited for the oncoming train. The appearance of the platform retains memories of the days when drivers and station staff exchanged words and exchanged tablets, and it can be said to be the true essence of local lines.

In the past, a lot of agricultural products were shipped from this station, and the warehouses of shipping companies were lined up in front of the station, but you can still see faint traces of it. As you sit down on the bench of the station building, which retains its wooden atmosphere, you will be able to see the interaction between people through the railway that has not changed since the Showa era. When the train starts moving again and we feel the unique vibrations across the points, we are determined to once again venture into the depths of Boso.

East Yokota. This station is located on the way from the train departing from Yokota to the tranquility of the inland. The area around the station is dotted with farmhouses with groves that serve as windbreaks, giving a typical view of Boso's rural landscape.

This station does not have any flashy tourist attractions, but that is what makes you feel the ``beauty of blank space'' during your journey. Waiting for the train and just enjoying the time passing by. There remains a place in Higashi-Yokota where such luxury is allowed. Nameless wildflowers blooming beside the railroad tracks and the sound of tractors echoing in the distance. All of these are proof that the Kururi Line is deeply rooted in the region, and it calmly satisfies the hearts of travelers.

Makuta. This station, which stands behind the ``Makuta no mine'' that has been written about in poems since the Manyo period, is a place on the Kururi Line that has a particularly rich history. The unique sound of the station name quietly asserts that this area has been an important transportation hub connecting the eastern country and the capital since ancient times.

Once you get off the station, you can feel the pride of being a place connected to the Takeda clan in every corner of the city. Old shops around the station and flowers tended by local people. These stories demonstrate that railways were not just a means of transportation, but were loved as the bloodline of life. This station, which still conveys the warmth of the old wooden station building, is deeply etched in our memories as the most scenic and scenic view before reaching the castle town of Kururi.

Shimogun. This quiet boarding and alighting area is located just as the train passes through Makuta and enters the valley formed by the Obisu River. Surrounded by the gentle mountains of Boso, the area is dotted with private houses that cling to the slopes, and fields spread out at its feet. The scenery they create can be called the original scenery of Japan, giving us a sense of nostalgia and precious peace.

There is no building that can be called a station building, and the structure, with just a single platform nestled against the tracks, exudes the original freshness of a railway without excessive decoration. After the diesel car drives away with its engine roaring, all that remains in my ears is the sound of the wind and the chirping of birds. When we place ourselves in such silence, Shimogori Station silently tells us just how noisy our daily lives are.

Small chest. This station, which bears the name of Obisu River, which is the origin of the line's name, has a sense of pride that it has prospered as the political and economic center of this region since ancient times. There are small shops around the station, and the remnants of the days when it was once a bustling distribution center for agricultural products remain as the backbone of the town.

When you step into the station building, you will see a long history of local people waiting for trains and exchanging words. The wooden benches and handwritten information boards pasted on the bulletin boards are evidence that this station was not just a transit point, but a base for daily life. This small chest has a heavy atmosphere that instantly brings to mind the black smoke spewed out by steam locomotives as the train slides onto the platform.

Tawarada. As its name suggests, this station symbolizes a rich rice-growing region, and it is filled with a quiet, expectant atmosphere just before reaching Kururi. The rice paddies that surround the train dramatically change their appearance depending on the season, and the scenery passing through the train window clearly conveys the strength of farming.

The station itself has a simple structure with no frills, but this creates a beauty that blends into the natural surroundings of Boso. The sight of the railway line drawing a gentle curve as it heads toward the castle town of Kururi is truly the highlight of local train travel. The breeze that comes in through the train window is a mixture of the scent of the earth and the changing seasons, and it soothes the dry souls of travelers.

Kururi. This station, which is the center of the Kururi Line and still retains the character of a former castle town, is worthy of being called the ``Little Edo of Boso.'' As soon as you step onto the station platform, the coolness of the ``famous water'' gushing out from everywhere will soothe the fatigue of your journey. It is this pure water that has nurtured the town of Kururi and its sake, and has colored this station.

If you look around the station, you will see equipment for exchanging trains and old overpasses that quietly testify to the heavy responsibility that railways once held. Many passengers board and alight here, and after a short rest, the train prepares to head further into the mountains. The old wooden buildings in front of the station and the castle-like decorations also show us the depth of history that this area has had. It is impossible to talk about the essence of this route without stopping by Kururi.

Hirayama. After passing Kururi, the train finally enters a full-fledged mountainous area. When you get to the area around this station, the flat rural scenery you had before fades away, and you can clearly see that the railroad tracks weave through the steep terrain.

In front of the station, there are shops where travelers of the past would have stopped, and the quiet scenery gives the illusion that time has stopped. The sound of a diesel engine echoing in the mountains is absorbed by the surrounding trees, creating a unique sense of solitude. However, that solitude can also be said to be the real thrill of traveling by train to the farthest reaches of civilization. The unpretentious yet dignified atmosphere of the Hirayama station building naturally straightens the spine of travelers.

Kazusa Matsuoka. As the word "Matsuoka" in the station name suggests, this area is dominated by the unique and complex topography of Boso, made up of pine forests and hills. Considering that this line was once part of a grand plan to cross the Boso Peninsula and connect to Ohara in Sotobo, the sense of ``loneliness on the way'' that this station has takes on a new meaning.

The surrounding houses become sparse, and the force of nature increases. Still, the light from the light bulbs on the platform and the neatly tended flowers beside the tracks remind us that this place is an extension of human activity. As the train passes through the tunnel and heads to its next destination, the quiet echo left by this station makes us reconsider the preciousness of the existence of railways.

Kazusa Kameyama. Terminal station on the Kururi Line. This dead-end train track marks the end of a story. The unfinished dream that was once supposed to extend the line beyond this point is now submerged on the calm surface of Lake Kameyama, and there is a somewhat melancholy yet contented silence that is unique to a terminal station.

The moment when the train stops its engine and silence returns to the platform. We keenly feel the thoughts of the people and the weight of time that this railway has carried. As soon as you leave the station building, the dam lake expands and you feel that you have reached the deepest part of Boso. Looking at the rusted bollards while waiting for the train to return, I am convinced that the end of a train journey is always the beginning of a new one.

Dosan Line. From Tadotsu, a ``important railway hub'' where ferry boats from Sanyo once arrived, through the rugged spine of Shikoku to Tosa in the southern part of Japan, this straight path can truly be called the epitome of crossing Shikoku. As the train leaves behind the idyllic countryside of the Sanuki Plains, passes Kotohira, the base of Kotohira Shrine, and begins to challenge the Asan Mountains, the atmosphere outside the train window changes completely, giving us a sense of the wildness inherent in railways and the awe of Mother Nature.

This line, where steam locomotives once roared, and later DF50 diesel locomotives echoed the unique sound of their engines throughout the valley, is now lightly traversed by pendulum-type express trains. However, the tenacity of our predecessors who continued to challenge difficult terrain is still alive in the sight of running through the steep canyons of Oboke and Koboke. Looking down on the rapids of the Yoshinogawa River, the remains of switchbacks such as Tsubojiri and Shinkai remind us of the hardships of the past. When we, as travelers, come into contact with the bright lights of Kochi that spread beyond the Shikoku Mountains, we once again realize the weight of the history that this railway has connected.

Tadotsu. It is no exaggeration to say that Shikoku Railway started from this station, and it is truly the ``birthplace of Shikoku Railway.'' If you look inside the premises of this important station where the Yosan Line and Dosan Line separate, you will see the brick water tower where steam locomotives roared in the past, still standing proudly. This area, where the Tadotsu factory is located and where many famous cars have been produced, is filled with the spirit of the craftsmen who support the railway. The smell of machine oil that wafts through the area as the limited express trains rush past tells us that this is not just a transit point, but a place where the soul of the railway resides. As I gaze at the rails branching out while being blown by the Seto Inland Sea wind, I am once again reminded of the Shikoku Route journey that begins here.

Kinzoji Temple. This station, nestled in the gentle sunlight of the Sanuki Plain, exudes tranquility as it is the gateway to Kinzoji Temple, the 76th temple of the Shikoku Sacred Site. It is well known that General Maresuke Nogi once used this temple as his quarters when he was commander of the Zentsuji Division, and the appearance of the station gives the impression that it has a faint atmosphere of harshness carried by the soldiers of the Meiji era. Surrounding it are golden rice fields and the graceful ridgeline of Sanuki Fuji (Mt. Iino) nestling beyond it. Escape from the hustle and bustle of the city and just listen to the sound of the wind rustling the rice ears, and you will realize that time here, carried by the railway, passes slowly. The moment when you stand on a simple platform and wait for the next train is the blissful blank moment in a railway travelogue.

Zentsuji Temple. It is a station that has two roles: it is the birthplace of Kobo Daishi, and it is also a military capital where the 11th Division of the former army was located. The wooden station building, built in 1892, is the oldest active station building in Shikoku and has been designated as a national registered tangible cultural property, and the time imprinted on its solid beams and pillars leaves a silent impression on visitors. The well-organized streetscape in front of the station and the group of brick warehouses are reminders of the former prosperity of the military capital. The scent of temple incense intersects with the reverberation of footsteps in military boots, and it is this station's unique multi-layered history that deepens the sense of travel. When you sit down on the bench of the old station building, you can feel the prayers and pride that people have placed in this station throughout the ages.

Kotohira. As a town in front of Kotohira Shrine, affectionately known as ``Konpira-san'' since ancient times, this station has received the enthusiasm of religious people from all over the country. The Western-style station building, built in 1930, has an elegance that befits the bustle of the temple town, and even the sound of footsteps echoing on the high ceiling heightens the anticipation of a visit. In the past, many special trains and group passengers disembarked on this platform, creating a lively sound of laughter, and that liveliness can still be seen in the lanterns in front of the station and in every corner of the old townscape. Transferring to the Kotoden also makes you feel the ``wonder of transfers'' in railway travelogues, and it has an atmosphere that is worthy of being the highlight of a trip to Sanuki. Watching people leave the station and walk up the long stone steps is also a great experience.

Add salt. As the train passes Kotohira and finally enters the heart of the Sanuki Mountains, this modest, unmanned station appears. Behind the station is Manno Pond, the largest reservoir in Japan, associated with Kobo Daishi, and it quietly tells us the history of this area, which has lived with water since ancient times. Although there are few people living in the surrounding area, once you get to the platform you can feel the pleasant wind blowing through the mountains, making you realize that the railway weaves through the rugged terrain. The memories of steam locomotives struggling to climb hills have now melted into the whispers of the lush green trees, but the strength with which railways have opened up the land can still be felt from this quiet station. It's the perfect place to listen to the sound of trains moving away while savoring the word "luxury."

Kurokawa. This station is located in a place that is like a prelude to the peaceful scenery of the Sanuki Plains that is about to change into a rugged mountainous region. Beyond the simple platform on one side, the mountains of Sanuki overlap like a folding screen, quietly watching over travelers. Surrounding us are endless views of peaceful countryside and orchards, but if you listen closely, you can hear the sound of the wind coming over the mountains from a distance, silently telling you that you are at the entrance to the steep mountain line known as the Dosan Line. The remnants of the days when large steam locomotives, accompanied by auxiliary machinery, ran powerfully across this land spewing out black smoke can still be felt in the grass beside the tracks and in the corners of old waiting rooms. Although it is an ordinary small station, it is a truly profound stop that reminds us of the memories of the struggle that the railway carved into the earth.

Sanuki Zaida. It is the last base on the Kagawa Prefecture side, and is a historic station that has seen off travelers along with the ``Saida no Tabunoki'' since ancient times. The splendid gambrel-style station building is an eloquent testimony to the importance this area once had as the center of the region and as a strategic point for the railway that was about to cross the mountains. When you stand on the platform, the deep shadow cast by the large, old trees will make your travel experience even more intense. Although the times have changed, the scenery that passengers would have seen from the windows of the limited express trains ``Nankaze'' and ``Shiokaze'' while waiting for oncoming trains at this station has not lost its serenity. Once you pass this point, you will finally pass through the dark corridor called Inohana Tunnel and enter the country of Awa, and it can be said that it is a place that forces you to be one of the major ``preparations'' on your train journey.

Tsubojiri. This is truly a gem of a structure that was left behind at the bottom of a deep mountain valley by the civilization known as railways. The only way to reach this station, which is not even accessible by road, is to take the railway or follow a narrow mountain road, and its isolated appearance is the true identity of the ``unexplored region'' that modern travelers crave most. It's like seeing a living witness to railway history, and I can't help but feel deeply moved by the fact that the switchback, a product of wisdom devised by the weak locomotives of the past to overcome steep gradients, is still functioning today. The silence that comes after the roar of the train is different from that of the city, and you can hear the breath of the forest and the murmur of water even more clearly. This small, unmanned station proves that the railway was not just a means of transportation, but a device for confronting the harshness of the land.

Chopstick store. This station, which appears the moment you cross a steep mountain and open the train window, boasts a view worthy of being called a ``station in the sky.'' Below you, the rushing Yoshino River and the cityscape of Miyoshi spread out like a miniature garden, and the magnificent panorama will take your breath away. Hashizo-ji Temple, from which the station's name originates, has long been worshiped as ``Konpira Okunoin,'' and many worshipers used to get off at this station and proceed to the ropeway. Even in the structure of the station building, you can feel the formality and dignified air that befits a station that is located at a sacred place. The sound of trains echoing through the mountains of Awa is like a tribute to the mountain gods, creating a rare space in which railways, faith, and nature are in perfect harmony.

Tsukuda. It is a crossroads for travel, where the Dosan Line and the Tokushima Line meet side by side, and time passes quietly on the banks of the Yoshino River. The sight of two lines merging and heading toward a single iron bridge gives us a sense of a strange connection, as if travelers from different walks of life were enjoying a fleeting companionship. Although the station itself has a simple structure, the variety of trains that pass through it is a testament to the richness of the railway network that once spanned all of Shikoku. Just before crossing the Yoshino River, hearing the unique sound of rail joints and looking out at the majesty of the mighty river spreading out from the train window, makes you feel strongly that you are at the throat of Awa Province. Because it is not a flashy tourist destination, it is a unique stop where you can take your time to appreciate the vastness of the roads connected by the railway.

text_en: Awa Ikeda. Located in the center of Shikoku, where the Dosan Line and Tokushima Line intersect, this station has long been known as the ``belly button of Shikoku'' and has a unique atmosphere. Memories of the area being once used as a distribution center for shredded tobacco and as a strategic point for crossing steep mountains, where many travelers and cargo came and went, are etched in every corner of the spacious premises. When you get off the train in front of the station, you'll feel a unique sense of confinement surrounded by mountains on all sides, combined with the quiet vibrancy that comes with it, creating a sense of travel that can only be experienced at a mountain railway hub. In this place, where the limited express ``Nankaze'' once proudly stopped and steam locomotives gasping for water, there is still a hint of the authority of the railway in the air. It is a stop that can be called a keystone of a trip to Shikoku, maintaining its dignity as a railroad crossing point, yet offering a sense of calm that is somehow unrelated to the hustle and bustle of the city.

Three ropes. Immediately after leaving Awa-Ikeda, this quiet station stands where the train begins to nestle into the rapids of the Yoshino River. In the past, there was a history of transporting materials for the construction of a dam on the opposite bank in this area, and evidence that the railway supported the modernization of the area behind the scenes can be seen in the stonework on the old platform. From the train window, you can see the mighty surface of the Yoshino River that weaves through the mountains, giving you a sense of the prologue of the journey across the gorge that is about to begin. The sight of the roofs of houses clinging to the mountainside is a landscape unique to the mountainous regions of Shikoku, and once again reminds us that railways are a thin ``lifeline'' that connects people's lives. Although it is not a glamorous tourist destination, the railway has a solid appearance that makes you feel at ease, as if it is integrated with the earth.

Iya mouth. As the station name suggests, it is known as the entrance to Iya Village, one of Japan's three most unexplored regions. The station itself is unmanned and has a quiet appearance, but the view of the confluence of the Yoshino and Iya rivers from here is as impressive as the condensed beauty of nature. In the past, many travelers disembarked from here on their way to the rugged Kazurabashi Bridge by bus or on foot, and I feel that the expectations and anxieties of those travelers are ingrained in the atmosphere of this narrow platform. The greatest appeal of this station lies in the contrast between the railway, a modern product, and the thin ``mouth'' that connects it to primitive nature. Listening to the sound of trains echoing through the deep green mountains while thinking about the legends of the Heike fugitives is one of the secret pleasures of traveling by train.

Awa River mouth. When you step onto the platform, the first thing that catches your eye are the adorable raccoon dog statues. This area has been known since ancient times as a place where the legend of the raccoon dog lives on, and it is very funny to see that even the railway station functions as a part of that story. However, contrary to this tranquil atmosphere, the mountains that loom in the background are becoming increasingly steep, and the flowing waters of the Yoshino River are also causing white waves that are chewing on the rocks. This station also has a history of being a base for exporting forest resources to the city, and you can feel the footsteps of the industry of the past overlapped with the silence of the raccoon dogs watching over you. This station, where stories, reality, and harsh nature coexist, provides travelers with a moment of peace, but also foreshadows the ruggedness of the journey deep into the mountains ahead.
