text_en: Koboke. When you get off at this station, which is one of the Dosan Line's most scenic spots along with Oboke, you will be simply overwhelmed by the beauty of the gorge, which looks like a piece of sculpture carved by nature over tens of millions of years. As the origin of the place's name, ``dangerous to walk,'' suggests, the steep rock walls come right next to the railroad tracks, and you can see for yourself how the railroads have overcome such harsh terrain. The unique blue-white color of the crystalline schist of the Yoshinogawa River below is deeply engraved in the hearts of travelers. The sound of the express train roaring through the valley is like a reenactment of the wisdom of humans and nature, and the sound of the river returning after a moment of silence further emphasizes the sacredness of this place. When we stand in this place, which is more like a grandstand surrounded by nature than a station building, we are forced to reaffirm the greatness of railways.

Oboke. This station is located in the midst of Shikoku's largest and most beautiful gorge, carved by the Yoshinogawa River over tens of millions of years. This station, which was once called ``Awa Akaishi,'' is now the Dosan Line's premier tourist hub, and a proud stopping point for limited express trains. Once you arrive at the platform, the sight of the white crystalline schist rock and the sparkling emerald green surface of the river below will captivate your eyes. While there is a bustle of tourists, the sheer cliffs surrounding the station and the roaring sound of the water silently remind us that this was once a difficult place that was said to be ``dangerous even if you took long strides.'' It gives us a strong sense of the tenacity with which the modern railroad was forced to cut through this steep natural crevice. It is a truly luxurious stop where you can enjoy the breeze that crosses the valley and think about the history of humanity carved out by railroads.

Tosa Iwahara. This is the first station where we bid farewell to Awa and finally set foot in Tosa. The moment you cross the prefectural border, the density of the air changes, and you get the illusion that the strength of the tropical island of Kochi is rising from the depths of the mountains. There is almost no flat land around the station, and the appearance of houses dotted around the mountainside is a landscape that can be said to be the true essence of the Dosan Line. It is likely that forestry resources were once shipped here as well, and the few traces of the side tracks that remain quietly convey the bustle of the past. The flow of the Yoshino River is still steep, but the shadows of the mountain are deepening little by little, giving us a quiet sense of the rigors of the journey ahead over even steeper peaks, and of the expectations for the Tosa Plain that will lie ahead.

Toyonaga. This station, located deep in the heart of the mountains of Tosa, once had a unique vitality as an important base in the mountainous region and a node with the forest railway. Although the village that spreads out in front of the station is surrounded by steep mountains, it gives a sense of a dignified lifestyle. If you think about the history of how the high-quality lumber transported from this station once supported Japan's modernization, you can't help but feel that even this quiet platform bears the weight of time. Today, it is a quiet, unmanned station where only limited express trains pass by, kicking up dust, but even so, the lively memories of when express trains once stopped seem to still be alive in the corner of the old waiting room. This is a stop where you will want to breathe in the cool mountain air and quietly reminisce about the lives of the people in the mountains that were connected by the railway.

Otaguchi. As the train winds its way from side to side along the flow of the Yoshino River, this station appears quietly and is like a ``punctuation point'' on the journey. Surrounded by deep greenery and with no sign of people around, this place gives the illusion that the only thing in the world is the sound of the creaking rails and the voices of wild birds chirping in the distance. Although there is no major industry worth mentioning, for the people living in this area, the railway continues to be the only and reliable link to the outside world. The old cherry blossom trees, which must have sucked in the soot emitted by the steam locomotives and saw off countless travelers, quietly testify to the long history of this station. It is a place that teaches you the essence of train travel, where you forget about rushing to your destination and just surrender to the depth of the greenery flowing through the train window.

Tosa Anai. This station, located close to the Anauchi River, a tributary of the Yoshino River, is one of the quietest places on Tosa's mountain lines. If you look around the station, the mountains are approaching and the sky seems to be narrowing down, as if it has been cut out slightly, but that sense of confinement is what makes you feel that the real thrill of the Dosan Line, which goes over mountains and cuts through valleys. There was a time when a lot of agricultural products were transported from this station, and the smell of life filled the platform, but now only the occasional roar of passing trains temporarily breaks the silence in the mountains. However, the contrast between that moment of movement and the deep silence that follows can be said to be the height of lyricism in railway travel. Like a roadside flower blooming without anyone knowing, the sight of the station quietly continuing to fulfill its duties as a station in the midst of harsh nature gives me a sense of preciousness that cannot be expressed in words.

Osugi. Home to Japan's largest cedar tree, this station is truly a gateway to a sacred area. The anecdote that Hibari Misora, a Showa diva, once nearly died in an accident, vowed to make a comeback here is very famous, and the appearance of the station building also gives off a mysterious sense of dignity, as if the god of entertainment resides somewhere. This area has flourished as a distribution center for high-quality timber since ancient times, and it is easy to imagine that the refreshing scent of cedar trees packed into freight cars would have filled the entire platform. Although it is a small town in the mountains, the wishes of the people brought here by the railway and the breath of the giant trees that mark eternity combine to leave a deep impression on the hearts of travelers. It is a quaint stop where the weight of history is carried away on the wind every time an express train stops.

Tosa Kitagawa. The station is well-known among dilettantes as it has a unique structure, unlike any other in the country, with the station located inside a railway bridge. This appearance was created by replacing the tracks from the old railway era, and the appearance of the platform floating directly above the roaring Anauchi River seems to symbolize the fate of railways, which conquer the terrain but are forced to become one with nature. Peeking out onto the river surface through the gaps between the steel frames, you'll feel a thrill that will make your legs tremble, and you'll be reminded once again of the steepness of the Dosan Line. The sound of trains passing through the inorganic truss bridge is like the deep bass of a giant musical instrument, giving us a sense of the power of modern civil engineering technology. Getting off at this station and looking out at the mountains and rivers from the iron cage-like platform is nothing short of an ``experience in another space'' in a railway travelogue.

Kadomo Valley. This small station, nestled deep in the mountains of Tosa, is a place dominated by the quiet sound of water, with faint memories of the forest railway. Surrounded by steep mountains, there are a few private houses and shops lined up in front of the station, but its modest appearance gives the impression that it is the original scenery of a mountain line. This land, once rich with forestry, now only quietly welcomes the occasional visitor, but as you sit on the bench on the platform and look out at the deep greenery on the opposite bank, you can feel the weight of the days when the railroad was the only hope for this isolated village. Although it does not have any flashy designs, it is a truly tasteful station that highlights the integrity of the railway. Every time the humid wind blows through the mountains, the sound of the old timber trains can be heard, almost like a hallucination.

Shigefuji. This station, located at the summit of the Dosan Line at an altitude of 347 meters, is filled with the solemnity of being the watershed that separates the Yoshino River system and the Monobe River system. A cenotaph stands next to the station that still remembers the painful memory of the massive landslide that occurred in 1963, which was etched in the history of railways, and it quietly tells visitors about the ferocious forces of nature and the history of the railways that overcame them. The cool mountain air stagnates on the platform, and the sight of an express train passing over a mountain pass with the sound of its engine echoing through it gives travelers a sense of sadness, as if they are headed to some far-off land. I feel that the pride of the railways, which faced the harsh nature and silently carried out their duties, is still alive in this high place. As the train rides over the mountain pass and descends into the Tosa plains, everyone may think about the turning point in their lives.

New reform. This is the essence of switchbacks, where a train stops once to cross a steep mountain pass and then changes direction as if to catch its breath.This is a masterpiece of railway engineering. There is not even a sign of people around the station, just a dense forest surrounding the platform, but even now in this silence you can still feel the passion with which the steam locomotives of the past breathed out smoke in the face of this steep slope. The series of rituals in which a train crosses a complex switch and slides backwards onto the platform may be the height of irrationality in today's efficiency-obsessed world, but that is the essence of the emotion of travel. In this ``place where time stands still,'' completely removed from the hustle and bustle of civilization, we will peer into the abyss of romance called railroads.

Tosa Yamada. This station is located on the border of the Tosa Plain, where the trains that have struggled to cross the steep Shikoku Mountains are finally released into the bright light of the Tosa Plain. It has a history of being crowded with many vacationers and mountain climbers, as it was once the starting point of a bus route heading to the mountainous area upstream of the Monobe River, and as the gateway to Ryugado Cave, a nationally designated natural monument. When you look at the station building with its heavy tiled roof, you can imagine a scene from the past, when travelers who had overcome difficult terrain breathed a sigh of relief as they were exposed to the soft tropical air. The sight of the express train proudly stopping and the lively people coming and going on the platform symbolizes that this area is an important node that connects the ``end of the mountains'' and ``the beginning of the village.'' Even though modern transportation systems have long since been introduced, the somewhat nostalgic atmosphere surrounding the station quietly conveys to us the pride that this place has long been an important transportation hub.

Yamada Nishimachi. This small station, which quietly appears in a residential area next to the railroad tracks, is a place where the daily life of the area is condensed, just as the lingering impressions of the large station called Tosa Yamada have faded. The simple platforms on one side are in contrast to the heavy equipment that the main trunk line had in the past, but when you hear the fresh voices of students commuting to nearby study halls in the morning and evening, it makes you realize that the railway is still alive and well as the bloodline of this area. Surrounding us is a calm townscape reminiscent of a subdivision in the Showa era, and the scenery we see from the train window during our journey reminds us of the preciousness of the name ``life'' on an extraordinary journey. Although there are no flashy tourist attractions, the smell of people's lives right next to the rails gives you the feeling that a warm blood flows through the inorganic existence of railways.

Tosa Nagaoka. This station is a platform floating like an island in the endlessly flat and rich rural landscape of the Tosa Plain that stretches out from the train window. As the name Nagaoka District suggests, this fertile land has supported Tosa's food for a long time.If you think about the history of this fertile land, even though it is just an unmanned station, you can feel a kind of sacredness in its appearance, which has been with the land. The vastness of the unobstructed sky and the rippling sea of ​​rice ears that change color with each season. The fact that a single railway runs through them, connecting it to a distant city, seems to accentuate the tranquility of this area. At dusk, with the distant silhouette of the Shikoku Mountains in the background, the sight of a diesel car approaching with its unreliable headlights is exactly the kind of ``original landscape of lyricism'' that resembles Michinoku and is often depicted by railway travelogue writers.

Gomen. As the name suggests, once you hear it, you will never forget it. It is a historical place that once prospered as a transportation hub in Tosa Province and as a historic post town. Currently, it serves as a connection point with the Tosa Kuroshio Railway Gomen-Nahari Line, and as the starting point for Tosaden streetcar transportation, giving travelers the pleasure of crossing a multi-layered railway network. When you stand in front of the station, you will be greeted by adorable characters created by Takashi Yanase, a manga artist who loved this area, but behind the scenes are the proud memories of the land that was once carried by the privileged place name ``Gomen''. Looking at the complex intertwining of elevated and overground lines, one cannot help but feel the strength of the railway, which has continued to fulfill its role of connecting people, even though its appearance has changed with the times.

Tosa Otsu. Located at the entrance to downtown Kochi, this station still retains the vestiges of the old Otsu village, and is a place with a unique tranquility, where residential areas and farmland gently blend together. Looking at the calm surface of the Funairi River that flows right next to the station brings to mind the tranquil landscape of logistics in the days when water transport and railways coexisted. As modernization progresses, the station has become more of an everyday station for people commuting to work or school in the city, but if you look into the distance from the edge of the platform, you can still feel the rich nature of Tosa still alive here and there. As the speed of the train rushing towards the city passes by the simple platform of this station, we are reminded once again of the exquisite balance between the ever-changing appearance of the city and the unchanging scenery of the local area.

Fushida. This station is located right in front of the city of Kochi, just before the train crosses the gentle flow of the Kokubun River. It used to be a quiet small station that ran above ground, but due to the Heisei Era construction, it was transformed into an elevated station, and the view from the train windows became even more expansive. The surface of the Kokubun River spreading out below and the flowers on the embankment that change color with the seasons provide a final sense of peace to the souls of travelers heading into the city. The surrounding area is a mix of old houses and recently built study halls, giving you a sense of a quiet but reliable lifestyle. As the train crosses the river and enters the city, the unique joint sound changes, but by the time it passes this station, it resonates even more lightly, quietly heightening expectations for its final destination in Kochi.

Tosa Ichinomiya. As the name of the station suggests, this station is close to Tosa Shrine, which is the main shrine in Tosa Province, and has long been known as the entrance to the sacred area. A look at the spacious grounds, which once welcomed many worshipers, shows how closely this place has been tied to people's faith. Nowadays, Kochi City has strengthened its character as a commuter town and is a lively neighborhood with densely populated residential areas, but as soon as you step off the station, you can feel the clear, crisp air of a shrine forest flowing out from somewhere. The daily life of this station, where limited express trains often pass or pass each other, is proof that the railway still functions as a key regional hub, and for those who know the bustle of the past, it has a somewhat proud atmosphere.

Akino. It used to be a solitary station with the sole purpose of allowing trains to pass each other, but it was upgraded to a station in 1951. With the construction of continuous grade-separated intersections around Kochi Station, this station has also been reborn as a modern elevated station, but the greenery of the mountains that loom behind the station remains as quiet as it was when locomotives took a break during the signal station era. The progress of land readjustment in the area and the appearance of suburban stores and new housing clearly shows the changes of the times, but the weight of the history carved by the railway is still deeply engraved in this area, like the shadow that spreads under the elevated railway. I feel that the functional beauty of the city and the atmosphere of the good old mountains are in perfect harmony with the sound of the train running.

Kochi. It is the majestic gateway to Tosaji, where travelers are welcomed by the magnificent Whale Dome roof that reflects the strong tropical sunlight. The memories of the old above-ground station era, the smell of machine oil that tickled your nose the moment you stepped off the long platform, and the sea breeze that evoked the feeling of traveling, have not lost their spirit even now that the station has been elevated. The sight of all the rails coming to a halt here, or connecting to new journeys, gives a sense of dignity befitting a tropical terminal. Standing in front of the station, the sound of the tram and the statues of Ryoma Sakamoto and other patriots seem to remind us of the enterprising spirit of this place. The passion of the Tosa people and the 100-year history of railways are harmoniously blended into modern facilities, making it a place worthy of being called the ``Railway Castle.''

Arrive at dawn. Away from the hustle and bustle of Kochi Station, it is a simple elevated station in the middle of the city that appears just as the train begins to accelerate westward. This place, located near Kochi Castle and on the outer edge of what was once a castle town, is now a quiet residential area and a row of academic buildings, creating a calm daily scene. When you look around from the elevated platform, you can see the tower of Kochi Castle peeking out over the waves, reminding you that you are in the midst of a historic city. In between the momentary roar of express trains passing without mercy, you can hear school chimes and children's voices, creating a silence that feels like an urban air pocket. Although it does not have flashy equipment, the way it silently continues to support the progress of the local people reminds us of the origin of the existence of railways.

Engyoji Exit. This is a simple stop that appears unexpectedly as you travel west through the city of Kochi on an elevated line. In the past, when it was an above-ground station, the noise of the railroad crossings and the hustle and bustle of the city were right next to you, but now you can look down on the rooftops of the castle town from a high place, giving you a somewhat out-of-this-world perspective. Engyoji Temple, from which the station's name is derived, still conveys the vestiges of the history that the patriots ran through at the end of the Edo period, and even though it is located within a modern concrete structure, it suddenly makes you feel the tranquility of good old Tosa. There are many educational facilities in the area, and I feel that the vibrancy of young people pouring in every time the train doors open is proof that the railway has evolved with the growth of the city, and even though its appearance has changed, it continues to carry people's hopes.

Asahi. This station, which plays a central role in the western part of Kochi City, still retains the warmth of the wooden station building, providing a sense of peace to visitors. The majestic appearance of the station building quietly preserves the memory of a time when this area once had its own commercial area and was bustling with people. Kochi's representative preparatory school is located nearby, and the sight of students filling the platform in the morning and evening symbolizes this station's face as an ``town of education.'' Watching the express train stop and passengers change places in a hurry makes me realize once again that railways are an important node for nurturing local culture and passing it on to the next generation. As you sit down on the old bench, you will feel a pleasant mixture of the vibrancy of the Showa era and the peaceful daily life of today.

In front of Kochi Commercial. As the name suggests, it is a small station with a clear purpose, built close to the gate of the school. This station, which was created in the 1980s in response to the wave of privatization and seeking convenience for the region, truly symbolizes the progress of the railway as a ``citizen's railway.'' The simple platform with only one side has no frills, but it is filled with the dedicated energy of young people who are working toward their goals every day. This is a part of the detailed service that was unimaginable in the days when long-distance express trains were at their peak. When I look out the train window at the sight of students running across the field, I can't help but feel a little moved by the fact that trains are more than just a means of transportation, they are deeply engraved in the background of someone's youth.

Asakura. It is truly a crossroads of culture in western Kochi, where the JR Dosan Line and the Tosaden Kotsu tram line are close together, and where young minds from Kochi University gather. The interplay of the somewhat academic calm of the station building and the light hanging sound of the streetcars running nearby creates an irresistible atmosphere for railway enthusiasts. This area once prospered as a post town and has been visited by people since ancient times, and the underlying strength of the land that existed before the railroad was built is still alive today. When you look out over the spacious premises, you can almost hear the remnants of the past freight transport and the quiet sighs of trains waiting to pass. It is a station with such depth, where a modern educational setting and a historic railway scene blend into one in the soft light of a southern country.

Edagawa. This quiet station is located on the border of leaving Kochi City and finally entering Ino-machi, the village of Tosa Washi. Of particular note is the Saden Kotsu railway that runs right alongside it, and the sight of JR's strong rails and the slender tram rails competing with each other is a valuable sight that shows the diversity of railways. A tranquil rural landscape begins to unfold in the surrounding area, and you can feel the cool air brought by the clear stream of the Niyodo River from the train window. Although there are no flashy designs, it makes us realize that the railway is both a tool for daily life and a part of the landscape. As the diesel train departs with the sound of a dry engine, it gives us a sense that the journey will finally change from a mountainous route to the atmosphere of a ``paper town'' interwoven with water and greenery.

Ino. It is the central station of Ino-cho, which has long been famous throughout the country as a production area for Tosa Washi paper. Looking at the majesty of the station building, you can feel the lingering scent of the golden age, when freight cars were loaded with high-quality paper and transported to the city, still wafting in the silence in front of the station. While the limited express train is stopping, the Tosaden Kotsu tram is approaching the end of the road right next to it, and the sight of the heavy railway of Japan National Railways intersecting with the track line that conveys the breath of the city creates a scene that railway enthusiasts will not be able to resist. Located close to the clear waters of the Niyodo River, this station has the calmness of a craftsman's town and the pride of a transportation hub, encouraging travelers to calmly prepare themselves to enter the interior of Tosa, deep in the mountains.

Namikawa. Just before the train leaves Ino and crosses the Niyodo River, a clear stream known as the ``Niyodo Blue,'' this station is a platform quietly set up next to an embankment. There is no station building, and the sight of only one platform exposed to the wind blowing across the river makes you realize that the railway is diving deep into the bosom of nature. The memory of steam locomotives once taking a breather in front of the massive iron bridge has now melted into the murmuring of the river, but the view from the viewpoint looking up at the bridge is still one of the most beautiful on the Dosan Line. In early summer, the voices of people playing on the riverbank can be heard all the way to the platforms, vividly conveying that the railway is inseparably connected to the area's recreational areas.

In front of Komura Shrine. Although it is a new station built in the Heisei era, as its name suggests, it retains the scent of old history as it is the entrance to Komura Shrine, which is revered as Tosa's Ninomiya Shrine. Although the station itself is modern and simple, the solemn atmosphere emitted by the forest of shrines in the background tells travelers that this is more than just a transit point. It can be said that old and new time are in a strange harmony, as the railway, a tool of civilization, is quietly nestled in this sacred place where the national treasure Kindosho Kanzudachi sword is passed down. The tranquil countryside that surrounds you and the occasional sound of train joints seem to accentuate the tranquility of this divine precinct, allowing you to once again appreciate the atmosphere of Tosaji, which deepens with each station.

Kusaka. The station once had a unique vitality as a transport hub for forest resources cut from the surrounding area and as a center where local supplies gathered. When you look at the spacious grounds and the remains of the former freight siding, you can almost hear the powerful pulsation of the days when heavy freight trains were frequently changing trains. Although it is now a quiet, unmanned station, the old townscape around the station and the buildings reminiscent of storehouses quietly tell of the prosperity of the past. Every time the humid wind blows through the mountains, I feel a rush of nostalgia for the days when railroads were the backbone of life in this area. Although it does not have a flashy design, it is a stop that lets you feel the ``thickness of time'' that the railway has carved in its purest form.

Okahana. As the train passes through Kusaka and makes a gentle curve through the countryside, this station is the platform that suddenly appears. Surrounded by the peaceful rural landscape of Tosa, the unobstructed expanse of the sky frees the hearts of travelers. The deafening silence that comes after an express train passes by, kicking up dust. That is the moment of bliss that only those who get off at a small station on a local line can experience. The ridged roads where people in the past would have rested their plows and gazed longingly at the trains spewing smoke are still there today. This quiet stop quietly tells us how grateful we are that the railway is completely integrated into the landscape and continues to mark the precious time we call everyday life.

Tosakamo. After passing Okahana, the train continues its gentle curve through Tosa's rich countryside until it arrives at this quiet station. The area around the station is a rural landscape of the past, with a tranquil atmosphere that makes it seem as if time has stopped, and the unobstructed expanse of the sky frees the hearts of travelers. There was a time when a lot of agricultural products were loaded onto freight cars and transported to the city from this station, but now only the wind pressure from the occasional passing train shakes the flowers on the side of the tracks. However, I feel that its unpretentious appearance is proof that the railway has blended into the local landscape and continues to be a part of daily life. It is a truly profound stop where you can enjoy a momentary ``peace of the plains'' before heading off to the full-scale mountain route, away from the hustle and bustle of Kochi city.

Nishisagawa. As the western gateway to the town of Sagawa, it is a station that somehow makes you feel the weight of its profound history. In the past, it had a unique vitality as a collection and distribution center for lumber and goods, and as a node for truck transportation that supported nearby industries. When you look at the structure of the station building and its spacious interior, you feel as if you can hear the powerful heartbeat of the days when heavy freight trains were frequently coming and going. It has now blended into a quiet residential area, but if you look out into the distance from the edge of the platform, your expectations for the old townscape of Sagawa that you are about to head into will quietly rise. There is still a sense of pride in the atmosphere at this station that the railway is not just a means of transportation, but has formed the backbone of the city and driven industry. It gives off a sense of honesty and solidity.

Sagawa. It is the gateway to this culturally rich town, famous as Tosa's ``sake brewery town'' and the hometown of botanist Dr. Tomitaro Makino. When you get off at the platform where the express train stops, the faint smell of koji and the atmosphere of the old town lined with white-walled storehouses tickle your nose. The station building itself exudes a sense of calm and dignity befitting a historic castle town, and we are once again reminded of the role that railways have played in connecting this region's rich culture to the rest of the country. When we remember the sight of freight cars loaded with Tsukasa Botan's sake leaving this station, we can realize that the railway was not just a road, but an ``artery'' that carried the tradition and pride of the land. This station, which has an intellectual yet somewhat glamorous atmosphere, leaves a particularly vivid impression on your Tosaji journey.

Erinono. This simple stop appears as the train passes through the gorgeous cityscape of Sagawa and returns to the silence of the mountains. As the name of the station is derived from, ``the fields spread out like a lapel,'' the sight of a single platform set amidst a delicate landscape of mountains and fields truly embodies the ``beauty of everyday life'' that is the real pleasure of railway travel. There are no large station buildings or bustling shopping streets, but because of this, you can hear the creaking of the rails and the voices of wild birds in the distance even more clearly. As I watch local students waiting for trains on this platform each morning and evening, I cannot help but feel a deep sense of how the railway continues to be the only window through which the dreams and hopes of the young people of this area are conveyed and connected to the outside world.

Togano. In the past, it was a vibrant industrial hub where freight trains carrying limestone produced from this area frequently departed and arrived, and the smell of white dust and machine oil mixed together. Nowadays, the freight trains have disappeared and the area around the station is quiet, but the vast remains of the station and the scars of the mining site that can be seen on the mountain surface eloquently tell us about the profound history of the past. After passing this station, the train would finally have to face the steep slope of Osaka Pass, the difficult passage to Susaki, and for the railway, this was also a ``place of rest before the battle.'' Even though its role has changed amid the waves of modernization, the desolate appearance of this home gives us a sense of pride in having once supported the construction of Japan. It is a truly significant station, where the strength of the railway and the sadness of changing times coexist.

Agokuwa. This is a station nestled in the mountains, where the train descends after passing over the steep mountain pass of Togano and finally descends to a place where you can feel the sound of the waves in Tosa Bay. In the past, steam locomotives would pass by with their long horns, breaking the silence in the mountains, but now only the occasional local train passes by and stops to listen to the breathing of the local people. Surrounded by mandarin orange and other orchards that cling to the slopes, you can feel the brightness of a tropical country coexisting with the rigors of a mountain route. If we remember the times when it served as a signal station, we can see from the quiet platform of today that it was not just a passing point, but an important ``junction'' to support safe operation. A calm atmosphere flows here, like a momentary respite when a train descends from the mountains and heads toward the sea.

Tanogo. We arrive at this lively station just as the city of Susaki approaches, and the roofs of factories and warehouses begin to stand out from the train window. Tanosato retains strong memories of its industrial past, when limestone and wood cut from the surrounding mountains were transported to ports using the convenience of civilization, the railway. Although the landscape has now changed to a modern one lined with concrete buildings, the strong atmosphere you feel every time the train door opens makes you think that this place is a reflection of the pride that has supported Tosa's heavy industry. The footsteps of commuters are also incredibly light, making us realize once again that the railway is in perfect sync with the heartbeat of the city. It's fun to quietly look for the remnants of the heavy freight trains that rocked this land in the days of the Great Trunk Line, in the calm appearance of the platform today.

Oma. Away from the hustle and bustle of Susaki, it is a ``small station'' located quietly in a residential area with the ocean behind it. A simple platform with only one side may not have been looked upon in the days of the great trunk lines, but for this reason, it has become a valuable ``window'' through which to peer into the simple daily life of modern railway travel. As you sit down on a chair in the wooden waiting room exposed to the sea breeze, the sound of waves crashing in the distance mixes with the sounds of everyday life coming from nearby houses, giving you a sense of peace that is different from the feeling of traveling. This quiet stop shows us the mysterious intimacy of how deeply the single thin thread of railways penetrates into the folds of people's lives. When we suddenly see the small light of this station from the window of an express train rushing to our destination, we all feel the warmth of home.

Susaki. It has prospered as a good natural port since ancient times, and has a reputation as the gateway to the sea in Tosa, making it a truly important station on the sea. When the railway from Kochi reached this area, the city was filled with the joy and excitement of modernization, but the grandeur of the past still lingers in the spacious grounds and massive station building. As you step off the station, the smell of the sea brings back memories of the lively port that was once a hub for shipping limestone and lumber, and the story of a time when railways and shipping worked hand in hand to support this country comes vividly before your eyes. Every time the express train stops, we are reminded once again that this is an important ``checkpoint'' on the journey to southern Tosa. It is a truly enjoyable stop, with a modern operating system, a sense of openness unique to a port town, and a rich history built on railways.

Tosa Shinso. This station, located near the mouth of the Shinjo River just before the train departs from Susaki and once again takes in the spectacular scenery along the coast, is now a place steeped in the legend of being the ``last habitat of the Japanese otter.'' The river that can be seen from the platform is crystal clear, and travelers can feel the breath of nature that has remained unchanged since time immemorial. There is a universal beauty here that makes you think that the impression people felt when they crossed this river and looked out at the sea in the past was no different from the scenery seen from the windows of cars today. The quiet village around the station and the expansive Tosa Bay just across the tracks gently embrace the civilization of railways. It is truly a rare stop that combines the desolation of the farthest north with the inclusiveness of a southern country. Once you cross this river, your journey will finally take you back to the memories of the rough waves of Tosakure.

Anwa. At the moment when the train window of the Dosan Line shines brightest, this small station stands quietly right next to the beach. When you step onto the platform, the unobstructed deep blue of Tosa Bay spreads out before your eyes, and the majestic breath of the Pacific Ocean turns into the sea breeze that touches your skin. There was once a time when steam locomotives would climb up the hill against this spectacular view, spewing white smoke and competing with the sound of waves. The station is now unmanned, and silence reigns supreme, but as I sit on the bench and gaze out at the horizon, I am once again deeply reminded that railways are not just a means of transportation, but a precious ``connection'' that connects people with the landscape. The creaking sound of the rails that can be heard among the sounds of the sea is like a monologue from the sea speaking to the railway, and as you approach the end of your journey, you feel a refreshing feeling that cleanses your soul.

Tosakure. It is the gateway to a traditional fishing town that embraces the rough ``Kure no Hachiman-sama'' sea. The handsome station building with its tiled roof conveys the vibrancy of the town, which once flourished with pole-and-line fishing for bonito, and seems to symbolize the good spirit of the Tosa people. The faint scent of the ocean floating around the station and the somewhat nostalgic appearance of the townscape evoke the proud memories of when the railway brought the wind of modernity to this area and shipped seafood across the country. Every time the limited express ``Ashizuri'' stops, the formality of a historic temple town and the sense of openness unique to a port town overflow throughout the platform. The strength of the fishermen who overcame the rough seas and the tenacity of the railroad that crossed the steep mountains are fused into one at this station. It is truly a stately stop where you can't help but feel the spirit of Tosa.

Shadow field. This quiet station awaits you after climbing the steep Ushi-no-Kubi Pass from Tosakure to the roar of a diesel engine. A complete change from the humid air of the seaside, this place is already on a hill over 200 meters above sea level, and we are once again reminded of the harshness of the Dosan Line as a mountain route. The area around the station is surrounded by a peaceful rural landscape, but it has a history of serving as a base for auxiliary locomotives traveling through difficult areas, and as a signal station, and the remains of its spacious grounds testify to the stately operation of the past. In this place, where the sense of relief of having crossed the mountain pass intersects with the expectations of the Kubokawa Plateau that we are about to head towards, the traces of the tenacity with which the railway overcame its fate due to its topography live quietly but with a certain weight.

Rokutanji. A lone home sits apologetically in the gentle undulations of the Konan Plateau. That's what this station is all about, but its lack of decoration actually makes the railway travelogue more lyrical. What surrounds us is the ever-honest rural landscape of Tosa, where the only sounds of time are the sound of rice ears swaying in the wind and the sound of railroad crossings in the distance. It seems that the longing wishes of the era when the pioneers of the past cultivated this ``Rokudan'' land and waited for the light of civilization that was the railway still blend into the atmosphere of this simple station. There is no large station building, nor is there a lively shopping street. However, there aren't many places where you can experience the luxury of just waiting for a train to pass. It makes us realize that the railway is closely connected to the breathing of the land, and that it continues to beat quietly but without ceasing.

Niida. As you approach this station, you can see the fertile rice fields outside the train window, and in season, the fragrant scent of Niida rice, a local specialty, is carried on the wind. This area, which symbolizes the rich blessings of the Kubokawa Plateau, has flourished as a base for agriculture since ancient times, and the railway was an important ``main artery'' that carried rice, the pride of this area, to the city. Sitting in a corner of the simple waiting room and looking out at the golden rice fields, it becomes painfully clear how deeply the railways have supported the lives of this region and how they have become inextricably linked to the lives of the people. Although it doesn't have a flashy design, the atmosphere that mixes the smell of earth and iron can be said to be the true richness of traveling on the Dosan Line. This small station is filled with the strength of the earth and the integrity of the railway that has continued to quietly watch over it.

Kubokawa. The journey on the Dosan Line that started from Tadotsu is finally coming to an end, and at the same time, the dream of ``traversing Shikoku'' in the direction of ``Nakamura/Sukumo'' and continuing on to the Yodo Line intersects, and it is truly the cornerstone of the Ougi of Southern Shikoku. As the center of the Konan Plateau and a transportation hub, the spacious grounds still exude the dignity of an important station. The deep memories of the days when steam locomotives used this as their final stop after completing their long journeys, letting off the soot and resting, can still be felt faintly in the wind that crosses the platform. Once you get off the train in front of the station, you'll be greeted by the quiet vibrancy of the temple town next to Iwamotoji Temple, the 37th temple of the Shikoku Sacred Site, giving you a sense of the end of one journey and the beginning of the next. All the rails are once bundled here, and then extend to their respective futures. The sight is worthy of the most spectacular finale of the history of railways.

Aoimori Railway. This 120-plus kilometer railway from Metoki to Aomori used to carry the glory of the Japanese National Railways' ``Tohoku Main Line,'' a major artery connecting the imperial capital and the northern reaches of the country. In response to the demands of the times to extend the Shinkansen line, its sash was transferred to the Third Sector as a parallel conventional line, but in the remains of the sturdy structure next to the tracks and the vast station premises, there is an indelible sense of pride that the limited express Hatsukari once ran at speed and the night train carried countless lives.

As the train crosses Metoki, the border with Iwate, and heads north through Sannohe and Hachinohe, the gentle hills of the southern region alternate with the powerful scenery of the harsh northern winter. Once you pass Noheji, the calm waters of Mutsu Bay will spread out on your left, and its significance as a branch point on the railway that leads to the Shimokita Peninsula, as well as the appearance of Japan's oldest railway windbreak, will make you feel the depth of your journey. Nowadays, the train moves effortlessly over the 1,000-hike slope that steam locomotives once tackled while spewing soot, but as the train approaches its final destination, Aomori Station, the unique sense of elation and desolation felt by the travelers as they hurried to the former Seikan Ferry can be felt through the joints of the rails.

Eye time. It is a station that has etched its name on the map as the boundary between the former Tohoku Main Line, now the Aoimori Railway, and the Galaxy Railway. This place, surrounded by tranquility in the mountains, is a meeting point for travellers, straddling the prefectural border between Aomori and Iwate. The memories of the long express "Hatsukari" and the sleeper express that cut through the silence of the night on the old main line are now buried in the quiet appearance of the platform, but it still gives us a sense of the pride it has as a border station. Although there are few people living around the station, the strong curves of the railway and the slopes of the cut-throughs quietly remind us that this area was once Japan's main artery. The atmosphere of this unmanned station still conveys that the railway was not just a means of transportation, but a ceremonial place to cross the ``boundary'' that separated one land from another.

Three doors. It is the gateway to a historic town that carries the long history of the Nanbu domain. The majestic appearance of the station building conveys the vibrancy of the post town that once welcomed many travelers. The station itself is located a little far from the main street of the town, but that sense of distance is reminiscent of the era when railroads came to this area as a wave of modernization. There are orchards surrounding the station, and when the season comes, the sweet scent is carried by the wind, which somehow seems to symbolize the richness of the northern country. This area is also known as the hometown of manga artist Noboru Baba, and when you get off at the station, you will be greeted by ``11 Piki no Neko'', so you won't forget the sense of fun. You can feel that the atmosphere of a historic castle town and the peacefulness of modern times are in perfect harmony with the sound of the railway.

Suwanohira. When you stand on the platform of this station, you can see orchards of famous apples and cherries that fill the window of the train, pleasing to the eye. In the past, a lot of agricultural products were loaded onto freight cars from here and transported to large consumption areas such as Tokyo and Osaka, but now it is a simple station that quietly tracks the changing seasons. However, its unpretentious appearance makes me think that it is the true luxury of traveling in Michinoku. Old fruit sorting buildings and other buildings lined up along the railroad tracks still bear faint traces of the energy of logistics in the past, reminding us of a time when railroads were the backbone of local life. There is a calm atmosphere here, where you can feel the accumulation of time in the simple daily life.

Kenkichi. This area, overlooking the graceful appearance of Mt. Nakui, has flourished as an agricultural base since ancient times. If you look at the structure of the station, you can see the remains of the former freight siding, which quietly tell us that it was a key logistics hub in the past. Even in today's streamlined timetables, the ``earth smell'' of this station never disappears, and the station retains a strong lingering scent from the days when railways were closely connected to local life. The appearance of small villages and old warehouses that spread out in front of the station gives the illusion that things have essentially remained the same since the days when steam locomotives parked there spewing smoke. It's nice to travel quickly to your destination, but the real pleasure of traveling by train is to take a breather at these stations and listen to the breathing of the land.

Tomabechi. This station, located along the clear waters of the Mabuchi River, is a place that is deeply etched in people's memories, along with its unique-sounding place name. It is no exaggeration to say that the idyllic countryside surrounding the station symbolizes the ``beauty of everyday life'' that is the real pleasure of railway travel. Today's trains run lightly over the slopes where steam locomotives of the past would have struggled to find water, but the scenery of their hometowns still remains alive in the landscape. The murmur of the river and the occasional sound of rail joints make this place feel even more serene. Although there aren't any flashy tourist spots, I'm sure I'm not the only one who feels a sense of freshness that cleanses my soul just by getting off at this station and seeing off the train.

Kita-Takaiwa. When you get off at this station, you are surrounded by the gentle flow of the Mabuchi River and the tranquil atmosphere of the northern country that surrounds it. Although it is located at the entrance to the industrial city of Hachinohe, the scenery is surprisingly peaceful, and this is what makes you feel the contrast between ``stillness and movement'', which is the real pleasure of traveling by train. From today's quiet platform, it may be difficult to imagine the memories of long freight trains that once passed through the slopes of this area panting. However, the old overhead wire poles next to the railroad tracks and the somewhat melancholy appearance of the waiting room still convey the profound history of the past. I feel that this station has a mysterious gravitational pull that makes me want to stop in front of my destination.

Hachinohe. It was once called ``Shiriuchi,'' and was a major hub where the Tohoku Main Line separated from the Ominato and Hachinohe lines. It has now been transformed into a modern elevated station where the Shinkansen departs and arrives, but when you look around the spacious grounds, you can feel that the steam locomotives of the past emitting soot and the pride that once served as a route to the Seikan Ferry continue to flow like an underground water vein. When you step off the station, you can feel the smell of the ocean and the powerful pulse of the industrial area that supports this city, making it the heart of northern logistics. It is the nature of old train enthusiasts like me to quietly look for the unique sadness and reverberations of train whistles that were once associated with ``journeys to the north'' behind the urban convenience.

Mutsu Ichikawa. When you stand on the platform of this station, you can't help but feel a sense of military strictness and the vastness of the land that follows. It goes without saying that the existence of the adjacent Self-Defense Forces base is deeply involved in the establishment of this station, but the large site where large freight trains and special vehicles were once frequently replaced still remains with a unique blank space. The inorganic concrete structure and the way the dry northern wind blows through give us a sense of the harshness of the journey to some far-off land. As times have changed, the role of the station has changed to a passenger-centered one, but the sense of ``protection'' that this place has is still firmly engraved in the memory of the railway.

Shimoda. You can feel the cool air carried by the clear waters of the Oirase River passing through the platform. This is a land where nature and human activity have been closely linked, as the sight of salmon swimming up the river was once an autumnal tradition. There is a quiet residential area surrounding the station, but in recent years, large-scale commercial facilities have expanded, creating a strange mixture of the good old railway scenery and the breath of modern life. The memory of long express trains running through this area still seems to be ingrained in the cracks in the ballast of the tracks, quietly conveying the pride that the railway has powerfully led in the modernization of this town. It is a station with a unique atmosphere, where the tranquility of the waterside and the heartbeat of the railway coexist.

Mukaiyama. This station, which stands quietly in the middle of a dense forest, has the atmosphere of a hidden village. There is a mysterious silence here, where you can hear the chirping of birds and the rustle of trees in between the roar of express trains passing relentlessly. Part of the station premises, which was once bustling with activities such as transporting lumber, has now been renovated by volunteers as the Mukoyama Station Museum, and it is heart-warming to see how the passion of people who love railways is keeping this small station alive. There is a saying called luxury without anything, and this station, where railways, nature, and people's thoughts intersect quietly, is the embodiment of that phrase. You don't just want to look out the window, you want to get off the train and breathe in the air.

Misawa. It once enjoyed a unique bustle as a connection point with the Towada Kanko Railway and as a gateway to a cosmopolitan town that was home to a U.S. military base. When you look at the vast grounds, you can feel the afterimages of the days when the limited express ``Hatsukari'' and sleeper express ``Michinoku'' proudly stopped at every corner of the platform. This station, which was once a sightseeing base for Lake Towada, now has a quiet appearance as the main station of the Aoimori Railway, but the sound of planes taking off from the base and the sounds of rail joints intersect, giving you a sense of tension and travel that is unique to this area. One of the secret pleasures of railway travel is imagining the soot from the steam locomotives that ran past your feet as you cross an old overpass.

Ogawara. As the station name suggests, it is a truly refreshing place where you can feel the presence of vast Lake Ogawara up close. There was once a time when it was crowded with vacationers coming to the lakeside, but now it is a quiet, unmanned station where you can only hear the sound of the windbreak pine trees rustling in the wind. However, if you stand on this simple platform and look out towards the lake, you will be reminded of the richness of the marine resources that once supported this area and the history of railways that have coexisted with nature. After the moment of silence as the express train passes by, stirring up dust, the peaceful atmosphere of the northern country once again gives us the feeling that it is the unpretentious truth of Tohoku that can be shown to us.

Kamikita town. This station, which was once affectionately known as ``Numazaki,'' still carries its pride as the eastern gateway to Lake Towada. When you get off the station, the faint smell of sulfur in the air tells you that you are in a high-quality hot spring area. The liveliness of travelers that filled the platform every time an express train stopped in the days of the Great Trunk Line has now been replaced by a calmer daily scene, but the appearance of the station building still gives a strong sense of its importance as the center of the region. I feel that this station, which has a history as a distribution center for agricultural products and the atmosphere of a hot spring town, plays a role like a ``punctuation point'' on a journey, something you can never experience just by rushing to your destination.

Otsu offering. The quaint and somewhat mysterious-sounding place names greatly stimulate the imagination of travelers passing by. The quiet village that spreads out around the station and the scenery of the mountains and fields of the northern country that envelops it testify to how deeply the modern device of railways has integrated into the life of this region. It doesn't have any flashy tourist attractions, but as you sit on the bench on the platform and listen to the sound of the wind passing by while waiting for the next train, you can feel the life-size weight of the peaceful but reliable history of this land. It is truly a stop that encourages thought, worthy of the name ``travel.''

Senbiki. The former Tohoku Main Line has a history of many hardships to overcome the steep terrain in this area. Although the station was relocated to its current location due to a large-scale relocation of the tracks, the presence of the deep forest surrounding the area still faintly evokes memories of crossing difficult points in the past. When you get off at this quiet station, where there is little sign of people, you can feel the tenacity with which the railway carved out the mountains and filled in the valleys to carve out a path, even through the concrete structure. The sense of solitude unique to this station, which stands on the border between civilization and nature, makes us feel that it is the height of lyricism in railway travel.

Noheji. This station, located at the deepest part of Mutsu Bay, was once connected to the Nanbu Jukan Railway and is still a branch of the Ominato Line, giving it the appearance of a transportation hub. Of particular note is Japan's oldest railway snow forest surrounding the station, where the indomitable spirit of our Meiji era predecessors to protect the railway from snow is still alive in the rows of lush coniferous trees. As soon as you step into the station building, you can quietly feel the history of the area as a port of call for Kitamaebune ships and the energy of the era when railways, a symbol of modernization, intersected. The memory of the limited express Hatsukari running alongside this snow-protected forest has now been transformed into the quiet daily life of local railways, but the pride of this important station is still engraved on every corner of its vast grounds.

Karibazawa. As the train passes Noheji and finally approaches the shores of Mutsu Bay, this modest station appears. From the station platform, you can see an unobstructed view of the peaceful ocean, and the shadow of the mountains of the Shimokita Peninsula on the opposite shore nestle in close to you, as if sharing the solitude of the traveler. There is evidence that many marine products were once transported from here, giving us a sense of how the railway was a thin thread connecting the sea and land. It is a harsh place with relentless snowstorms in winter, but it is in this harshness that I feel that the strength of the railways that run through the north resides. There is a sense of silence here, with only the sound of waves and the sound of railroad crossings in the distance.

Shimizu River. As the name suggests, this station is reminiscent of a clear stream of water, and is nestled in a quiet cove of Mutsu Bay. The surrounding area retains the atmosphere of an old fishing village, and the faint scent of the sea wafts all the way to the platform, which evokes the nostalgia that is unique to train travel. The expanse of the station premises, which was once a busy place for transporting lumber, still conveys memories of the industry of yesteryear. Amidst the tranquility of the area, which seems to have been left behind by today's high-speed transportation networks, I feel a certain sense of pride in the fact that the railway has supported the lives of the region. The contrast between the blue ocean flowing through the train window and the greenery next to the railroad tracks can be said to be a refreshing breath of fresh air on your journey through Michinoku.

Kominato. This station, located in the center of Hiranai Town, is known as the gateway to the Asado coast, which has long been famous as a visiting place for swans. In the winter, the fluttering wings of swans that cross the sea from faraway Siberia add a special atmosphere to the atmosphere here. In the structure of the station building and the streetscape, you can feel the pride of being a former base of local autonomy and the accumulation of history. The story that members of the imperial family once stopped by to admire the local swans also confirms the quality of this station. Even the sound of the trains running on the railway here has a mysterious elegance to it, making it a place worthy of being called an ``graceful stop'' on the journey north.

Inside Nishihira. After leaving Kominato, the train once again threads its way between the calm countryside and the sea, until it arrives at this simple station. What spreads out around the station is an unpretentious everyday scene that can be called the original scenery of Michinoku. Although there aren't any grandiose facilities reminiscent of the bustling days of yesteryear, it makes you feel that the railway is completely integrated into the local landscape. The benches and signboards on the platform, which have faded due to exposure to the sea breeze, are evidence of the people who have continued to watch over this area over the years, and they can suddenly soothe the hearts of travelers. There is nothing there, but there is a reliable way of life for the people and the integrity of the railway that continues to watch over it.

Asamushi hot spring. It was once simply called ``Asamushi'' and is the gateway to the hot spring town of the north, where the limited express trains ``Hatsukari'' and ``Michinoku'' on the Tohoku Main Line proudly stopped. When you arrive at the platform, the scent of the ocean and the faint smell of sulfur mix together, filling your soul. The bustling hot spring town that spreads out in front of the station retains the splendor that welcomed many groups of tourists during the high economic growth period of the Showa era, and it somehow evokes a nostalgic feeling. The luxury of being close to the calm waters of Mutsu Bay and soaking in the hot water while listening to the sound of the waves can be said to be the crystallization of a culture brought to Japan by the railroad. In the structure of the station building and the appearance of the surrounding inns, you can feel that the elegance of train travel in the past coexists with the calmness that has passed through the ages. Indeed, the pride from the days when it was called the Atami of the North is still alive in this station.

Nouchi. In the past, there was a vast oil storage base in this area, and countless tank cars were lined up, making it a station where you could feel the pulse of industry. However, due to the relocation of the entire Tohoku Shinkansen line, the location of the station has changed significantly, and it is now located in a quiet residential area and close to schools. Although the echoes of the heavy freight trains and the smell of oil from the old station are a thing of the past, the view of Aomori Bay from the new platform continues to soothe the eyes of travelers. Even as the role of railways changes, we can't help but feel the resilience and perseverance of railways in meeting the needs of the times as they continue to play a role in local life. Even within the new station building, the multi-layered history that the former name "Nouchi" carried has been quietly inherited.

In front of Yata. As the train approaches its final stop in the city of Aomori, the roofs of houses crowd in front of the train windows, and the appearance of the station begins to take on a sense of everyday life. This station reminds us that the old major trunk line was not only used to transport long-distance travelers, but also as the ``axis of life'' that supported the irreplaceable daily lives of local people commuting to work and school. Although the platform is simple, it is filled with layers of noise from the morning and evening noises and the laughter of young people, making you realize that the railway runs through the city like a bloodline. Although it may not be as flashy as a large-scale hub station, there is a life-sized version of Aomori life here, and the air that flows in every time the train door opens is laced with the scent of the solid life of the northern country.

Koyanagi. This station, located in the eastern part of Aomori City, is surrounded by a quiet residential area and is a place where you can feel the beginnings of the city and the end of your journey. It makes you think about how railroads guided people's footsteps and shaped the bones of cities during the history of what was once a vast wilderness that was gradually swallowed up by cities. If you stand on the platform and look out at the end of the track, you will see the glow of the rails leading to the final station, Aomori, as if quietly announcing the end of a long journey. Although there are no notable tourist attractions, there is a calm and quiet atmosphere that is typical of a station that is used casually in daily life. We are once again reminded that each of these small stations forms a large network called railways, and continues to transport people's small thoughts.

East Aomori. When you get off the train at this station, you will be reminded of the vast old railway yards, along with the clusters of rusted railroad tracks. Once a gigantic heart that supported Aomori's logistics, and where countless freight cars were replaced, its majesty has now quietly blended into the surrounding residential area. However, if you look at the site of the spacious grounds, you can almost hear the powerful heartbeat of the days when railways were the backbone of Japanese industry. Currently, it serves as a base for commuting to work and school, providing a peaceful landscape that is close to the local people, but beneath its feet lies a solid history of past heavy freight transportation. I feel that this is a stop with a mysterious margin, where the pride of being a major trunk line and the peace of mind of a lifestyle line coexist.

Tsutsui. This station, which was newly carved after becoming the Aoimori Railway, gives us a sense of the breath of a new era that was not present in the long history of the Tohoku Main Line. If you look around from the elevated modern platform, you can see at a glance the progress of development in the eastern part of Aomori City, where the former countryside has been transformed into educational buildings and housing. As a travel writer from the Showa era, I can't help but feel a little confused by these new stations, but when I see the fresh energy of students overflowing in the mornings and evenings, I feel relieved that the railway continues to weave new memories of the city. This simple but functional elevated station quietly teaches us about the strength of railways, which not only respect the past but also transform in response to the demands of the times and have deep roots in the city.

Aomori. At the northern end of Honshu, all the rail lines converge here and then disappear into the sea, making it the most fitting place in Japan to be called a "terminal station." As you walk along the long overpass that leads to the former Seikan Ferry, you can still feel the expectations for the north that travelers had in the past, as well as a hint of loneliness, still floating in the sea breeze. Although the limited express trains Hatsukari and sleeper express Hakutsuru have become silent, and the whistles of ferry boats are a thing of the distant past, the majesty of this station and the unique silence that marks the end of a journey still brims with an irreplaceable emotion. Even if the station building is reborn in a modern form, just by standing here we can feel deep in our souls the sure feeling that we have arrived at the ``northern terminal''. It is truly a sacred stop where the history of the railway is melted into the sound of the waves.

text_en: Awa Kainan. It is now the de facto terminus of the JR Mugi Line, and at the same time, it is also the starting point of the world's first ``DMV (Dual Mode Vehicle),'' which replaces the track and road. In the past, it was just a small station on the way to Kaifu further south, but as times changed, this place became to play an important role as a junction between railways and rubber tires.It is truly a strange fate. If you look in front of the station, you can see a vehicle that has transformed into a bus smoothly descending the slope, but behind this is the tenacity of those who once dreamed of a magnificent ``Shikoku Loop Railway'' that would circumnavigate Shikoku, and the earnest prayer of local transportation that resists harsh reality. As I stare at the boundary between the ruts carved on the asphalt and the railway under the strong tropical sunlight, I get a strange feeling that the definition of a railway is being quietly reconsidered here.

Kaifu. This place, which was once the border station between the JR Line and the Asa Kaigan Railway, is famous for its lonely platform on an elevated platform and the ``mountainless tunnel'' that opens at the end. When the town was carved out, the mountain was carved away, leaving only the tunnel structures behind. This strange landscape has a somewhat surreal atmosphere, but it is also proof that the hot wind of large-scale development once blew through here. The station is located in a high position, and the views of the Ama townscape and the shimmering blue of the Pacific Ocean in the distance are beautiful enough to open the eyes of travelers. The memories of high-power Kiha 65s and other cars rushing down this elevated track with the roar of their engines have now been replaced by the quiet sound of the DMV running, but the structure still retains its majesty. The word "remains of a dream" sounds too lonely, but the silence that swallowed up the ambitions of the past is certainly flowing here.

Shishikui. Straddling the prefectural border between Tokushima and Kochi prefectures, this station is well-known as the base of the Asa Kaigan Railway. When you step inside the station building, you can feel the memories of the former "Ise Ebi Station Master" and the warm touch of the local people who worked so hard to support this short railway. The construction of this line, with its continuous viaducts, is a truly splendid ``main line specification'' with the assumption that it will be extended in the future, and because of this, the contrast with the small size of the rolling stock gives train travelers a sense of loneliness and, therefore, a deep sense of affection. If you look down from the station window, you can see the rugged yet beautiful coastline washed by the Kuroshio Current beyond the intricate roofs of the fishing town, and this is what gives you the feeling that this is the unique atmosphere of this area, located on the border between Tosa and Awa. Railways as an industry may be in a difficult situation, but the people who work here seem to continue to cherish and protect the ``relationships'' that railways connect, and this lights a warm light in the hearts of travelers.

text_en: Kaura. I have finally set foot in the land of Tosa, and I can't help but sigh deeply when I think of the fact that this was once the final destination of the grand, unfinished plan to reach Kochi via Muroto. The platform built on top of a high viaduct had an abrupt ending, as if shouting ``From here, further ahead'', but now a DMV ramp has been installed, and vehicles rush down to the ground as if to avenge their regrets. Below the station, the old townscape that once flourished as a port town for Sankin-Kotai still remains, and it is truly interesting to see how the modern dream of railways intersects with history from the Edo period. Illuminated by the strong tropical light, the concrete structure exudes the tranquility of an ancient ruin, and is the most poignantly beautiful culmination of the railroad's fantasy of an ``aorta connecting north and south.''
